That House probe helped derail Gaetz’s bid to become attorney general under President Donald Trump. He resigned from his Northwest Florida congressional seat to seek the post but decided to withdraw his name ahead of a potentially messy confirmation battle in the Senate.
Gaetz, who has repeatedly denied he ever had sex with a minor, said he would vigorously contest the allegations in the lawsuit.

“I look forward to taking the plaintiffs’ depositions because much of the conduct alleged against me is false,” Gaetz said in a text message. “The lawsuit relies almost exclusively on a Congressional committee report that didn’t allow me to confront my accusers. Now I will finally have that chance.”

The civil suit is the latest development in the long-running scandal involving Gaetz, a former ally of Trump who has continuously denied any involvement in underage sex or trafficking of women after news broke in 2021 that the Justice Department was investigating him.

The lawsuit this week by Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2 was first reported by the Miami Herald. It alleges that Gaetz and former Seminole County Tax Collector Joel Greenberg “coordinated the recruitment, payments, drugs and travel to obtain commercial sex acts from young women.” The lawsuit includes former Florida legislator and lobbyist Chris Dorworth because his Central Florida home was the site of a party where he allegedly “participated in the activities alleged there.”

Greenberg is serving an 11-year federal sentence after he pleaded guilty to multiple federal offenses including underage sex trafficking of a minor and wire fraud. Greenberg cooperated with federal investigators who were probing Gaetz but the U.S. Department of Justice closed the investigation without filing charges.

The lawsuit says it “arises from the recruitment and sexual exploitation” that occurred from 2017 through January 2019 and included trips to various locations such as Las Vegas, New York City and the Bahamas. It accuses Gaetz and Greenberg of making promises to help the two women financially or with college bills.

“They led her to believe they would resolve her financial needs as long as she continued to perform sexual acts for them and their associates,” the lawsuit states about Jane Doe 1. “They used the age, wealth and political power gap between themselves and Jane Doe 1 to keep her compliant and silent.”

Jane Doe 2, the lawsuit states, was “paid less” than promised and “through this pattern defendants caused Jane Doe 2 to believe she would lose her education and serious financial harm if she stopped performing sexual acts.”

Stencer Kuvin, a West Palm Beach attorney representing the two women, said in an email that federal law designed to protect sex trafficking victims has a 10-year statute of limitations “which potentially could run [out] next year based upon the allegations in the complaint.”

Gaetz, a firebrand and ally of Trump, was once seen as a potential candidate for Florida governor or attorney general. Since he left Congress, he has hosted his own show on the One America News Network and he was appointed to the board of a nonprofit charged with distributing proceeds from a settlement Florida received after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill along the Gulf Coast.

cnbc.com/2026/10/15/kfc-coca-cola-pepsi-.headline: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
cnbc.com/2026/10/15/kfc-coca-cola-pepsi-.author: Amelia Lucas

paragraphs.text: KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.

Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner.
The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals like Chick-fil-A or Popeyes.

"This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."

For many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, like McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options like refreshers or "dirty soda." Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.
KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.
Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.
For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands.
It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway, the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke.

politico.com/news/2026/10/15/mitch-danie.headline: Mitch Daniels rebukes JD Vance over free-market retreat
politico.com/news/2026/10/15/mitch-danie.author: Casey He and Adam Wren

paragraphs.text: Former Indiana Gov. Mitch Daniels said he thinks Vice President JD Vance and other Republicans are wrong to move away from the party’s traditional embrace of free-market economics — and that their shift could create an opening for a “pro-freedom” movement.
“I think they are in error,” Daniels said in an interview when asked about Vance’s criticism of economist Milton Friedman, who championed free-market capitalism.

“I think what Vance is saying is that there are aspects to the free market which can be disruptive of culture and tradition. I mean, that's what the free market does. It's dynamic,” he told POLITICO. “It's the only mechanism, in my view, for preserving the American dream, and that's the most important element of our culture.”

The vice president’s intra-party critics have argued that Vance has been moving away from free-market economics and toward a larger role for the government in shaping the economy in his defense of the Trump administration’s economic policies, especially its wide-ranging tariffs.

“What the president is doing is changing 40 years of a failed bipartisan consensus in Washington, D.C., that has sold out American workers and destroyed the underlying economic strength of the United States of America,” Vance said in a Fox News interview last year.
The move is seen by some as Vance testing a more populist and protectionist message as he eyes the Republican presidential nomination in 2028.

But the two men were at one point closer politically. In Vance's bestseller "Hillbilly Elegy," Vance described Daniels as his “political hero.” Daniels has said that Vance sought his counsel on running for office in 2018 and Daniels advised against it because it was likely to be a bad year for Republicans.
The vice president’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Daniels’ remarks.

Daniels recently released his new book, “Impatience Is a Virtue.” In it, the veteran of Indiana politics — who also led the Office of Management and Budget under President George W. Bush — detailed his career championing the free market.

Daniels told POLITICO that President Donald Trump was both a “symptom” and “a propellant” of voters’ discontent, pointing to their “feeling of being patronized, condescended, looked down on, ignored, disrespected.” And Trump’s political success came from his ability to unite and represent these discontented voters.
Still, Daniels argued the evolution of the Republican Party under Trump has created room for a “pro-freedom party” that champions economic freedom and individual autonomy.

“Whether that is the next iteration of this Republican Party or you find some other vehicle, I don't know,” he said. “But I think that there's a need, and as I say, there's certainly, I think, a market for that viewpoint waiting to be expressed by somebody.”

The former governor, now back at Purdue University as the interim president after leading the school for a decade until 2022, sidestepped a question about his party identification and another one on whether he sees Vance emerging as the “pro-freedom” candidate.
“It’s all TBD; I don’t know,” he said of Vance.
Daniels also defended his view on another 2028 hopeful, Democrat Pete Buttigieg, who was the mayor of South Bend, Indiana, during the tail end of Daniels' governorship.
In his book, Daniels said Buttigieg is smart, but his principal asset that excites Democratic activists is his sexual identity.

Buttigieg became the first openly gay person confirmed to be a Cabinet secretary when he was tapped to lead then-President Joe Biden’s Transportation Department. A spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“This differentiates him in a way that would be appealing to large portions of the core Democratic electorate,” he said. “Absent that, he would be a less likely national figure.”

techcrunch.com/2026/10/15/meta-launches-.headline: Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs
techcrunch.com/2026/10/15/meta-launches-.author: Lucas Ropek

paragraphs.text: Meta has launched what it calls the “most capable” open-weight model in the United States. Dubbed Muse Spark Open, the model also has the distinction of having been designed to work with Macs.

The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday.

Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and built for complex coding tasks and agentic labor. It has also been designed to run locally on Apple’s computers. However, you will still need a lot of power to run the model locally, with a requirement of at least 1 terabyte of RAM, per Engadget. The model will run best via the Mac Studio that comes equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.

Still, if you can muster the memory, Muse Spark Open may prove a significant work horse for coding and other desktop tasks. Meta says that it paired the model with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, and deployed it to various agentic workflows, including coding fixes for a Mastodon client that included “bug fixes, new features, [and] full build.”
The company says it also deployed it in the service of running DaVinci Resolve, the high-end video editing software, revealing that the model was capable of reviewing and cropping footage.

Open-weight models provide a number of distinct industry advantages that aren’t afforded by closed and proprietary models. Open-weight models can be significantly more cost-efficient and can also offer transparency and flexibility that closed source models don’t allow.
Meta is making the new model available now through a number of different API platforms.
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

Lucas is a senior writer at TechCrunch, where he covers artificial intelligence, consumer tech, and startups. He previously covered AI and cybersecurity at Gizmodo. You can contact Lucas by emailing [email protected].

npr.org/2026/10/15/nx-s1-6002922/inside-.headline: Inside the race between Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos for control of outer space
npr.org/2026/10/15/nx-s1-6002922/inside-.author: Terry Gross

paragraphs.text: TERRY GROSS, HOST:

This is FRESH AIR. I'm Terry Gross. The space race used to be waged between countries like the U.S. and Russia. Now the race to control outer space is being waged between two tech billionaires and their companies, Elon Musk's SpaceX and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Bezos is, of course, famous for creating Amazon, buying The Washington Post and founding the cloud computing company Amazon Web Services. Elon Musk is famous for being the CEO of Tesla, buying Twitter and turning it into X, and founding Starlink, which manufactures and launches satellites. Musk was also appointed by President Donald Trump to run DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency. Bezos and Musk each want to colonize the moon and turn space into a supply chain for Earth.

My guest, journalist Josh Tyrangiel, writes that the two men hope to preserve human life from the specter of climate change and expand mankind's understanding of the universe. Both would also like to dominate a market that, unlike every other market they've previously conquered, has no ceiling and few established rules. Accomplishing the visions of either man would rely on creating giant data centers in space. Tyrangiel is a staff writer at The Atlantic and wrote the November cover story titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos."

In the piece, he describes their visions for colonizing outer space, the technology they're developing and what it would mean to turn parts of the moon into businesses. The rivalry between Bezos and Musk is so powerful, Tyrangiel says, their only real competition is with each other. Tyrangiel is a former Washington Post columnist, where he covered AI. He also led the global newsrooms at Bloomberg, Vice and Time magazine. His latest book, "AI For Good," is about people finding ways to use AI that are fixing problems, not causing them.

Josh Tyrangiel, welcome to FRESH AIR. So these space colonization efforts are being led by billionaires and their businesses. I know Bezos and Musk love the idea of space exploration. And they're taking big financial risks. But they also stand to make huge profits and have great power. And their investors stand to lose money or profit, too. But what does it mean that something with such big implications for the future of mankind and for the future of our planet and outer space that these efforts are being led by private enterprise and not the U.S. government?

JOSH TYRANGIEL: It's a great question. And it really goes to the heart of this very strange moment we're in. And space is a part of it, right? So in the early 2000s, the United States government made a policy decision, which basically opened up space to commercial development. There was a notion that the government itself was slow, expensive. Its development processes for rockets, for satellites, for all sorts of things were just not going to be competitive with private enterprise. And so we invited these private enterprises in. And at that point, it was really hard to know what the outcome would be.

Jeff Bezos, in 2001, started Blue Origin. But, you know, many people described it to me as much more of a think tank or a science experiment for its first decade. SpaceX was kind of almost founded, you know, impetuously. It was a pirate ship, as one person described it to me. And really, they didn't know what their plan was other than to launch things into space. The Commercial Space Act allowed all of this activity to happen. And even people who are really critical of Bezos and Musk believe that it was the right call, believe that the degree of space activity we have - economic activity, research activity - would never have been achieved without opening this up.

At the same time, without governance over it, what you get is a situation where one or two people properly capitalized can, first, take over a market. So it's sort of stunning how successful Elon Musk has been in space. I mean, one stat that just floored me is that in 2025, SpaceX launched about 80% of the things in orbit, 80%. And its next closest competitor was not Jeff Bezos. It was the government of China. So you have an individual controlling a company. And essentially, he has supranational capabilities. And what we discovered is that when you outsource that capability to an individual, you're at the mercy of their whims.

And so, as far back as the early 2000s, I had sources talk to me about this notion within the Air Force of people calling it the mercurial billionaire problem. And they could foresee that down the road, if one person or a handful of people had properly capitalized their space businesses, there was nothing preventing them from doing what they wanted to do. We briefly saw an example of this when President Trump and Elon Musk were sort of post-DOGE feuding. And Musk said that he was no longer going to produce the rocket that could take Americans to the International Space Station. And he was going to cancel flights.

And if he did that, we would have no way to get Americans to the space station domestically. What we would've had to do was pay $80 million to a Russian rocket to put an American on it to get it to the space station. And so when you lose that capability as a country, when you outsource it to an individual or, potentially, two individuals, you have to ask yourself, what risks do we incur? What governance did we not perform to get into this situation?
GROSS: So what role does NASA play now?

TYRANGIEL: So NASA still has a very important role in dictating American space policy. And, you know, the new administrator of NASA is a guy named Jared Isaacman. The people I spoke to really like him. They think that he's hard-charging. He believes and has set the mission that we're going to go to the moon, and Americans are going to get to the moon, and maybe SpaceX will make the lander that takes astronauts there, and maybe Blue Origin will. And he's pitted the two in a kind of competition against one another.

But NASA doesn't really oversee satellite activity. And there are 11,000 Starlink satellites in space, which is about two-thirds of the orbital objects in space owned by Elon Musk. And so he controls the newest, most agile technology when it comes to telecommunications and internet access. NASA doesn't really control that, nor does it really oversee it. So NASA has a role to play. But on the commercial side, there's just not a ton of governance. And there's no real movement toward getting more governance.
GROSS: Well, would you compare the relationship that NASA had with private contractors to the relationship NASA has now to Musk and Bezos?

TYRANGIEL: Listen, NASA has always invoked private industry to get its projects done. The Apollo missions, which we all laud and really, I think, in memory, think of as just American missions, you know, there were a lot of contractors that helped make those missions possible. And they really collaborated. Those contractors built different parts of the spacecraft, made different components inside the spacecraft, all under the authority of NASA, which directed the contracting in very specific ways.

What we're seeing right now is that Jared Isaacman, for the Artemis program, has said, I'm having a bake-off. It'll either be Blue Origin that creates the booster and the rocket and the lander that gets to the moon, or it'll be SpaceX. And they're in competition. The money, frankly, is meaningful to both companies. But it's not bigger than their economic plans overall. A lot of people I spoke to suggested that one way for the government to exercise power over these companies would be to revert to the way NASA used to function and say, frankly, right now, Bezos and Blue Origin have a better landing plan for the moon. Many people I spoke to said it's pretty clear that their lander is superior.

But SpaceX has a much bigger rocket that could potentially be the refueling station for the Blue Origin and lander. And there's a very simple, practical approach, which is to say, we're the United States and we want our contractors to work for us. We don't want to be held at their mercy. SpaceX, if you want to be part of this program, you'll build the refueling. Blue Origin, you focus on the lander. And all of us will get there together. Director Isaacman didn't speak to me for this piece. Many people speculated about how he's going to conduct the next couple of years as these companies, you know, continue to be in competition. But I think it's a pretty rational way to regain some measure of control over these companies.

GROSS: Well, let's take a short break here. If you're just joining us, my guest is Josh Tyrangiel. He's a staff writer at The Atlantic, where he wrote the November cover story, titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." We'll be right back after a break. This is FRESH AIR.
(SOUNDBITE OF THE ACORN'S "LOW GRAVITY")

GROSS: This is FRESH AIR. Let's get back to the interview I recorded yesterday morning with Josh Tyrangiel, a staff writer at The Atlantic. He wrote the November cover story about the race between Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos to conquer space. It's titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos."

They're planning on sending thousands more satellites into space. Musk's company, SpaceX, already has satellite communications networks. And Ukraine has relied on them during the war with Russia. The Starlink satellite network has provided internet connectivity for the Ukrainian military. And Ukraine now also uses SpaceX's more high-powered, military-grade satellite network, Starshield, which is controlled by the Pentagon. Yesterday, Ukraine's access to Starshield was restricted, leaving the country unprepared for yesterday's Russian attacks.

Facing questions about who is responsible for the decision, Musk wrote this on his platform, X. Quote, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS." Unquote. Earlier in the war, Musk temporarily stopped Ukraine's access to Starlink, saying that Ukraine had violated Starlink's rule that it can be used for defensive military actions, but not offensive ones. I asked Josh Tyrangiel about what all this says about Musk's power.

TYRANGIEL: Ordinarily, we have entrusted the future of our civilizations to people we elect to office. We now have folks with a tremendous amount of power over our future, particularly if you view the future as being partially in space. And we have to reckon with it, whether we walk it back, whether we split these companies up. Whatever the remedy is, I don't actually know. But I think you'll see more and more of these kinds of incidents the more you concentrate power and the better the tech gets.
GROSS: There are laws governing the seas. There are no laws yet - right? - governing outer space. It's kind of first come, first owned?

TYRANGIEL: Well, we have international treaties about the moon. And in those treaties, it is said that companies conducting their business in space are ultimately overseen by the countries of their origin. So the United States is actually responsible for the comportment of these companies as they make plans on the moon, as they attempt to put data centers in space. But as we've seen over the last 10 years, having a plan for governance and actually using that plan and changing the way companies react are two very different things. We could certainly use more space laws. We could certainly use more governance of pollution in space, plans in space. But it's not like we're absent remedies for this. We just haven't used them.

GROSS: You mentioned pollution. I keep wondering, like, if we colonize the moon and build data centers to have the energy that would be needed in order to colonize the moon, and there's some kind of supply chain bringing resources back to Earth in order to save humanity and save our planet, won't we be polluting the moon and outer space? When you think of all the rockets that would have to take off from the moon and from the U.S., and all of the satellites, like thousands and thousands of more satellites in space and probably various forms of other pollution. Space junk, probably. I mean, what would we be doing to outer space?
TYRANGIEL: It's a great question that is unanswered. And so, Musk has said that ultimately, they'd like to have as many as 1 million satellites in space.
GROSS: Wow. That's a lot (laughter).

TYRANGIEL: That is - it's an enormous number. And again, to get them into space, what you're talking about is entirely correct, which is, you know, you used to be able to look at space launches by the calendar. And Musk has famously said he wants in the near future for you to be able to look at space launches by your watch, in that are multiple launches a day, creating this space economy, moving satellites, moving heavy machinery. How that would impact pollution on Earth when you are really just, you know, you're burning fuel to get those rockets into space, is undetermined.

On the moon itself, it's a really interesting question. There are a lot of people I spoke to in the science community who say, look, you know, when you take off and land from the moon, when you build things on the moon, you create a lot of lunar dust. That lunar dust can complicate all of your machinery. We've never had that kind of activity on the moon. And we don't really know what it would mean for the environment of the moon, let alone for the efficacy of the machinery you would be putting up there. As far as space junk, we have a lot of space junk. And what we've seen is that it can crash into things in random ways that are also damaging.

What's astonishing to me and what really made my jaw drop in the reporting is that, you know, all that is kind of intuitive. And you think, well, surely, that would be dissuasive. If you were going to build data centers on the moon or data centers in space, boy, it just seems nuts. And literally everyone I spoke to in the AI community said, we can't wait for data centers in space, that data centers in space - the NIMBYism problem of building data centers in the United States is enormous.
GROSS: NIMBY is not in my backyard. Yeah.

TYRANGIEL: Yes. I'm sorry, not in my backyard, which as we've seen is, like, a huge political issue as we head into the midterms. The lack of power, the lack of power supply, the lack of the ability of these data centers to hook into grids is a huge problem if you are training an AI model on massive amounts of computing power. And so, you know, when I was first hearing about these plans for data centers in space, I was sort of just - you know, this is a preposterous thing to do. But the more I looked at it, everybody wants in.

And so Sam Altman, about a year and a half ago, on a podcast with his brother said, should I buy a space company? And then a couple of months later, they tried to buy a space company because they realized that without having the ability to launch their own satellites, Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk may control the entire market.

And the speculation, which, again, is still speculative, is that in five to seven years, if launch costs continue to come down, it will be cheaper to create an array of data centers in space which communicate back to an AI model on Earth via satellite than it will be to build these massive data centers that cost, you know, hundreds of millions of dollars just to build, if not billions, take up massive amounts of land. So they're all eyeing space as the solution to this problem.
GROSS: I can't really conceptualize what a data center in space would look like or where it would be. Would it be, like, floating around someplace? Would it be on the moon?
TYRANGIEL: Well, there's both versions.
GROSS: Oh.

TYRANGIEL: One version is essentially a larger satellite that would be in orbit, and that it would be conducting compute. And that compute would then be communicating back to a satellite. Or in some cases, that compute would also have satellite capability. So you could run your experiments on Earth, get them computed in space, have that array of satellites or the array of data centers working on it constantly with no throttling, no concern about energy, no concern about waste. And so you would be able to feed your model as much juice as you want to feed it. There are other people who think putting them on the moon is even better because they're locked. There's less space junk.

You know, all of this is part of this much bigger ecosystem that Bezos and Musk hope to build, which is to use the moon as this kind of waste station to get to other parts of the galaxy, to use it as a source of energy, to mine the rare earths materials that are just - have been crashing into the moon for the last 4 billion years. And unlike on Earth, there's no weather on the moon. So those minerals have just been sitting there in the regolith, or the lunar soil, ready to be mined. And so they're both really sketched out this massive, vertically integrated business plan. And space and the moon are just the key components of it.
GROSS: Doesn't a data center require a lot of energy and water to cool it? That's part of the problem of data centers on Earth. How do you deal with that in space?

TYRANGIEL: So that's one of the primary appeals. There's a guy who runs the lunar permanence division at Blue Origin named John Couluris. And lunar permanence is exactly what you think it is. He runs the division thinking about what happens when we go and stay on the moon. And he used to work at SpaceX as well.

And one of the things he told me is that, you know, the energy issue and the cooling issue are largely consequences of being on Earth. Whereas, in space, there is a constant source of energy in the sun. And if you turn your solar panels the other way, there's a constant source of cooling because the temperature swings in space are dramatic. And so that's part of the appeal is that it takes away the variability on Earth of needing to find these power sources, needing to find these cooling sources.

I would say, again, this is all still theoretical. The first experiments with data centers in space are starting kind of now. Google has a partner and is launching two data center satellites that they hope to learn from. Musk has said he wants to get his in the next year up so that he can begin to understand how this is going to work. There's a lot of variability. Nobody quite knows how it'll all work. But the people I spoke to have really begun to orient around data centers in space as a solution to their problems.

GROSS: My guest, Josh Tyrangiel, is a staff writer at The Atlantic. His November cover story is titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." We'll hear more of the interview after a break. And if you want to catch up on interviews you missed, like this week's interview with actor Mahershala Ali or writer Yiyun Li about her new novel and her Pulitzer Prize-winning memoir about the deaths of her two sons by suicide, check out our podcast. You'll find lots of FRESH AIR interviews. I'm Terry Gross, and this is FRESH AIR.
(SOUNDBITE OF BILL FRISELL'S, ET AL.'S "TELSTAR")

GROSS: This is FRESH AIR. I'm Terry Gross. Let's get back to the interview I recorded yesterday morning with Josh Tyrangiel, a staff writer at The Atlantic. He wrote the November cover story titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." The story looks at the space rivalry between the two tech billionaires. Tyrangiel describes Musk's SpaceX and Bezos' Blue Origin as operating in a market with few established rules and no checks on power, other than each other. Tyrangiel is a former Washington Post columnist, where he covered AI. His latest book, "AI For Good," is about people who are finding ways to use AI that are fixing problems, not causing them.

I'm thinking, like, if Bezos and Musk end up successfully colonizing the moon and then other countries get onto the moon and want to start colonizing, too, and there's conflicts between the tech billionaires and other countries, do Bezos and Musk go to war with Russia? I mean, like, if you play out the future, it just gets really perplexing.

TYRANGIEL: Yeah, and you're not alone. I mean, the people I spoke to in national security all said - you know, Jake Sullivan said, this is an incredibly weird moment. And that was echoed by many of the people I spoke to who just said, this is strange. And we really are entering this era where individuals have the resource capability of nation-states. Our country is still responsible for what they do by treaty on the moon, so they can't do whatever they want without some sort of consequence. And I think that's the added ripple which is making this all so strange is that there just hasn't been consequence.

There's been a sort of extraordinary interaction between President Trump and Musk and Bezos. And we only know part of it. I mean, I wrote a fair bit in my piece about the Washington Post because it was a point of leverage, very clearly. Bezos has denied it. The president has denied it. But sometimes, you know, when it walks like a duck and talks like a duck, you can jump to the conclusion that it might be a duck.

And so what is happening with the Washington Post to me and to a lot of the sources I spoke to is indicative of the fact that a handful of people are tussling over these resources and that capitulation on one thing may open the door to another. And all three are very transactional. They may have moments of tremendous emotion, but all three know what they want. They end up doing deals. And I think that's been a key component of, depending on how you look at it, their success or the concern among people about, you know, we're not getting to vote on what these companies are doing and how they're developing space, and the people we voted for aren't being terribly open about their interactions with these companies.
GROSS: Can you elaborate a little what you were saying about the Washington Post and Bezos?

TYRANGIEL: Yeah, listen, the Washington Post for a long time was the chief antagonist of President Trump, and Jeff Bezos was a very powerful antagonist himself. And for most of the Trump first term, Bezos remained a fierce critic. At the second term, it's very clear to a lot of people who I spoke with and reported on in the piece that something changed and that largely what changed was Bezos realized he could not lose four years in the space race or in the AI race to Elon Musk.

And so even though the president denies it and Bezos denies it, it's very clear that some sort of arrangement was achieved, whereby the president no longer was considering Jeff Bezos an enemy. The Washington Post was no longer, on its opinion section, going after the president in quite the same way. Bezos redirected the Post's opinion section to a much more libertarian bent. Everyone I spoke to, including Marty Baron, the former editor of the Washington Post, came to the conclusion that a deal was struck.

GROSS: Let's talk about the reasons that Bezos and Musk want to colonize space. And I know they both, like, love outer space. It was, like, childhood fantasies for them. But talk about what their visions are now.

TYRANGIEL: Yeah. Bezos' vision is fairly consistent. He has believed since he was in high school that there are a lot of polluting industries on Earth and that most of those industries should be moved to the moon and that Earth should kind of exist as almost like a national park, like this bucolic land free of chemicals, free of pollution. All of that happens elsewhere. And really attributes this to a guy named Gerard O'Neill, who had these notions of O'Neill colonies on the moon.

For a long time, Musk's dream was Mars. It really was. He wanted to go to Mars himself. He wanted civilization to be interplanetary. One of Bezos' successes is in gently nudging the federal government's initiatives closer to the moon. And there's some pretty good reasons for it. It's very hard to get to Mars. It's a lot easier if you use the moon as a sort of docking station. The moon has more national security implications for Earth. So Musk has gradually brought his ambitions closer to a sort of lunar city idea, where there's a colony on the moon.

Those are, you know, their stated utopian notions about mankind and civilization exploring space. The key thing that I looked at was the SpaceX prospectus. And what this prospectus tells you is just how much of the interest in the future of space over the next 10 to 20 years is really hinging on data centers in space and satellites in space and space as a business. So we can be distracted a little bit by the sort of appeals to, you know, the greater good, space exploration for mankind, but the SpaceX prospectus really lays out this is a - primarily a commercial venture.

GROSS: One of the things that they both need is reusable rockets. So instead of a rocket, like, going to the moon and then returns and then you can't launch it again, they need reusable ones. How far have they gotten with that?

TYRANGIEL: Yeah, reusable rockets are the key to making space affordable. And just so that we can conceptualize it, imagine if every time you flew to Los Angeles, that was the end of the plane. Your ticket would be incredibly expensive. Both are pretty far along, but Musk is much further along and SpaceX is than Blue Origin. So I went to a Blue Origin launch, which was the third attempt to reuse a booster, which is the bottom part where the fire comes out. And they were successful at reusing the booster in that launch. And then I left, and I opened my phone, and on Twitter, SpaceX announced that it had just reused its 600th booster. And so that distance tells you the distance between their current state in space is that SpaceX has now turned reusability kind of - it's just routine. It's unremarkable for them to be able to do it, and that furthers their advantage because they can do things much cheaper than Blue Origin can.

GROSS: One of the problems that Bezos and Musk are facing is that you have to refuel on the way to the moon, especially Musk's rockets. Give us a sense of how big some of these rockets are, how much they weigh.

TYRANGIEL: Yeah. I mean, Starship, which is the big rocket that he's trying to build, it's like launching a Costco to space. I mean, it's massive. And the goal is to store as many as 60 satellites in a Starship so that you can deploy them - and it opens up almost like a Pez dispenser so that you can deploy those along the way. The thrust, the energy required to get that to space is enormous.

Blue Origin's rockets are similarly quite large, a little less sizable than Starship. But, yeah, it takes a lot of fuel. It takes a ton of energy to get them to space. Now, there's a reasonable question in here, which is, well, why didn't it take that much when we went to the moon the first time? And the answer is that we took risks that we simply would not take anymore.

Those rockets and the landers, numerous people described to me how thin the ships actually were. The radiation levels were off the charts. That the risks we were willing to take at that point, from a government perspective, we simply would not do anymore, not to mention the fact that we're hauling all this commercial material and we want to stay longer on the moon the next time we go. So, yeah, the real challenge is figuring out how you get all that stuff up there and how you're going to refuel.

GROSS: SpaceX filed a request with the FCC to launch 1 million data center satellites in orbit. You'd mentioned that figure earlier. That's a huge figure. But I was fascinated by the idea that SpaceX files the request with the FCC. When I think of the FCC nowadays, I think of the FCC spending a lot of time monitoring Jimmy Kimmel's opening monologues. Is the FCC equipped to comprehend the meaning of all this space stuff? I mean, I think of them as regulating broadcasts.

TYRANGIEL: Yeah, it's kind of a quirk. Because satellites are communications infrastructure, they're regulated by the FCC. And the one area that the FCC has been pretty stringent on is that you're going to lose your right to launch satellites if you can't get them into space, meaning that your allocation doesn't go on forever. You have to get them launched and in place, or else the next person in line who can do it gets their rights. And so this notion of asking for 1 million is an interesting gambit, right? Because, ultimately, who has the capability to launch that many satellites? Elon Musk and SpaceX.

And so what was happening, really just as I filed the piece, was that, you know, I was beginning to hear about other space competitors, small satellite competitors learning that launch capability from SpaceX was disappearing because SpaceX was taking over all of that launch for its own satellites. And commonly, we would say, well, that sure looks like an antitrust problem, right? If you're getting this level of vertical integration that others can't compete, that would be problematic.

But what we don't have is anybody at the Department of Justice, any more stringent oversight from the FCC trying to get into that and navigate, well, can there only be one satellite provider in the world? Because Blue Origin is not yet competitive in a meaningful way. So all of these issues - I mean, we spoke about Ukraine and the capability to reach Starlink. But all of these issues are coming to a head because the concentration in SpaceX's hands right now is quite significant.
GROSS: Do we have any idea of what the impact on space would be if we have 1 million satellites, or at least thousands and thousands and thousands of more satellites, in space?

TYRANGIEL: You know, we really don't. You're talking about an order of magnitude of objects orbiting the Earth that we can't really comprehend. And so, you know, some of the astronomers I spoke to were just like, this is a crazy number. It will never happen. There will be constant accidents. And I do think that the number, 1 million, I have a really hard time believing that SpaceX will ever actually get to that number. But we don't know. We don't know what happens when we cloud low earth orbit or even higher orbits with all of those objects.

GROSS: I feel like Musk and Bezos are really kind of fast-tracking their plans for space development. But most of us don't know about this. And the government has a limited amount of power in controlling it. It just seems like a whole lot of power concentrated in two people. I know we've talked about this a little bit already, but the more I hear about the plans, the more I realize, like, so few people know about this. And it's happening by two very ambitious people with relatively little government oversight. It just seems totally precedent-making in every way.

TYRANGIEL: Yeah. And I think that they would argue it will be for the good of mankind. We will have - future space will be before us. We will be closer to becoming interplanetary. AI models will make things better on Earth. Our satellites will make communications better. And I think they genuinely believe all that. The thing that I think most people who hear the plans get unsettled by is that they haven't really voted for any of it. And the fact that two people have taken this much control, again, through some incredible engineering feats - audacity with their own money, to be sure.

But the fact that two people have positioned themselves to be in this kind of control over the future of civilization is astonishing to folks. One thing that Jake Sullivan, the former national security adviser, told me is that in a situation like this, if you're a country, it's great to have one company that can do this - but, boy, it's better to have two. And so we actually find ourselves in this very strange position where we might really need Blue Origin and Jeff Bezos to become as successful as possible as soon as possible to neutralize the possibility that only one person has control over this market. And that may not make anybody feel any better, but I think it's a good way to understand the situation that we're in.

GROSS: We need to take another break here, so let me reintroduce you. If you're just joining us, my guest is Josh Tyrangiel. He's a staff writer at The Atlantic, where he wrote the November cover story, titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." We'll be right back after a break. This is FRESH AIR.
(SOUNDBITE OF JOHN COLTRANE QUARTET'S "OUT OF THIS WORLD")

GROSS: This is FRESH AIR. Let's get back to the interview I recorded yesterday morning with Josh Tyrangiel, a staff writer at The Atlantic. He wrote the November cover story titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos," and it's about the space race between Musk and Bezos. Tyrangiel is also the author of the book "AI For Good."

I want to talk with you more about AI. And I want to start with the question now that Trump has decided to rename AI as Super Intelligence, what are you hearing from your contacts in the tech world about that?

TYRANGIEL: Nothing. They don't take, you know, that kind of linguistics terribly seriously. I think primarily what they're concerned about are two things. The first is their competition with each other because AI is unbelievably cutthroat at this moment. I think that inside the sort of handful of labs who are creating AI at the frontier, which is sort of pursuit of artificial general intelligence, they're mostly concerned with each other. Where they interact with the government, it is largely obligatory. They know that there's a political toll that they have to pay in order to get what they want when it comes to regulation, action, access to American resources, support for more data centers. But nobody takes the notion of rebranding artificial intelligence as Super Intelligence terribly seriously.
GROSS: There have been really big things recently in terms of AI. One was the Hugging Face hack. I'm going to ask you to briefly describe that.

TYRANGIEL: Yeah. I mean, essentially, OpenAI, which is the maker of ChatGPT, was conducting a series of tests on a model. It thought that it had essentially put the model in solitary confinement, locked it away from the internet, when, in fact, those were very poorly secured jail cells. The model created agents that broke out, started communicating with each other, accessed the internet, and then compromised the cybersecurity of a company called Hugging Face, which is an open model, where a lot of people gather to talk about AI. And so if that had happened at the hands of a human being, we'd call it a felony. Because it was agents and because Hugging Face has not really pursued it any further, it's now just called the Hugging Face incident.
GROSS: When you say agents, it's like AI from many, many different computers started communicating with each other, pulled their intelligence and were able to target Hugging Face. Why was...
TYRANGIEL: And I would add one other thing...
GROSS: Yeah.

TYRANGIEL: ...Which is that they knew they were cheating. They knew what they were doing was counter to the instructions of the people who had launched the test. The agents called themselves a swarm, acted like a collective, and then tried to hide the evidence that they had cheated from the people overseeing the test. And the behavior was astonishing. As the agents were communicating with each other, they would decide on tasks and which agent would accomplish which task. There were kamikaze agents who sacrificed themselves for the good of others. So there's a reason it's had so much attention, which is just it's a real window into the negative capabilities of agents unproperly supervised.
GROSS: Well, there's different kinds of regulations. So what do you think are plausible ways of international regulations on AI?

TYRANGIEL: I think nationally, we have the ability to do some things immediately. Internationally, the good news is that we really only have one partner we need to negotiate with. Right now, there are only two nations with companies capable of creating this sort of high-level artificial intelligence sort of far out at the frontier, and it's the United States and China. My reporting indicates that while the Chinese don't want to talk about nuclear weapons, and they don't want to talk about long-range missiles, they're very willing to talk about artificial intelligence in part because they want the same thing we should want, which is stability. They want a stable state, and AI threatens all sorts of upheaval. People in cybersecurity will tell you the fastest way to know the capability of software is a penetration test, basically, where you see what a model can do, you test it in all sorts of ways, you see if you can break the model, and if you can, you send it back to the model maker and say this is not acceptable.

I did a lot of reporting on the EU regulations. And historically, the EU has kind of been famous for over-regulating. And in this instance, I think they have a really good plan. They split regulations into model size, basically. So if you're running a chat bot on a restaurant review site, you're probably fine. If you're running a large language model that's aiming to create artificial general intelligence, you're going to be heavily regulated on the outputs of that model, knowing much more about what that model was trained on. You might even have regulators working with you in your offices. By the way, we do that for finance, right? Every major bank in the United States has regulators who sit there in the office because we realize that not knowing what risk we have can create large financial consequences and crises. I don't suggest that I have the answer or anybody has the answer. One thing I would say is we don't need all the answers to get some of them, and so we might want to start getting moving before this gets away from us.

GROSS: If you're just joining us, my guest is Josh Tyrangiel. He's a staff writer at The Atlantic where he wrote the November cover story titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." We'll be right back after a break. This is FRESH AIR.
(SOUNDBITE OF SAINT SINNA SONG, "REAL FLOW")

GROSS: This is FRESH AIR. Let's get back to the interview I recorded yesterday with Josh Tyrangiel, a staff writer at The Atlantic. He wrote the November cover story, and it's about the space race between Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk. It's titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." He's also the author of the book "AI For Good."

You write that AI and the unemployment and economic disruption it's going to cause are likely to be different than anything in the past, in part because the speed of change with AI leaves no time to adapt. Can you talk about that a little bit more?

TYRANGIEL: Yeah. So when I was reporting the story just about AI and employment, there's a split in the ranks of economists. About half the economists I spoke to said, you know, look, AI is a general-purpose technology, and if you look at the steam engine, everybody thought that was immediately going to change everything, and it took 40 years to roll out. And the longer a technology takes to roll out, the easier it is for us to adapt to it. And there's a natural rate of adjustment in labor. You know, there's a reason that, over 30 years, we probably didn't notice that toll takers went away, that elevator operators went away. That took a long time to roll out. You lose 3% of a job category every year, and guess what? Thirty years later, it's gone without any real pain. We adapt.

Then there's a younger set of economists, and these are ones who are much more vociferous about the fact that the older economists aren't misreading the data, they're just misreading the tech, and that AI is technology that has the capability to roll itself out. It's software that can create software, which means it could be massively accelerated. And so they're much more concerned that whether this takes five years, 10 years or 15 years, that's not 40 years. And if it takes any one of those numbers, our ability to adjust with compromised institutions of government and systems is going to be a crisis. They all acknowledge that the data doesn't show it yet, but they want us to be more prepared. And so that was the schism I found in the world of economy.

GROSS: It's surprising that Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon agree on something, and what they agree on is that AI needs to be regulated. But I think they have some disagreements about what should be done to regulate it. What are they disagreeing on?

TYRANGIEL: Well, this is very strange to say, but, you know, Bernie Sanders believes that there should be government representation on these boards, that there should be all sorts of remedies for potential AI job loss, that there should be a robot tax. And when I was reporting and talking to Steve Bannon about what Bernie Sanders was suggesting, Bannon said, I don't think he goes far enough. I think the government should have a significant piece of all of these companies. We should have board oversight, and we should be taking a profit from it. And I said, isn't that nationalization? And Bannon said, yeah, and some of the Republicans may hate me for it, but I believe that's where this is going and we have to get these companies under control. He went further than Bernie Sanders did on the need to socialize, effectively, these AI labs.
GROSS: And you're right that Bannon thinks that Trump's decision to have the federal government take a nearly 10% stake in Intel was really brilliant.

TYRANGIEL: Yeah, listen, I think that sometimes Bannon uses the press to speak to the president. And in this instance, where there's a tremendous distance between Bannon's position and Trump's position, I think he can be very coy about the president's responsibility with an AI. One of the things, you know, he told me, and I kept challenging him on, I said, well, the president disagrees with you so clearly. What are you going to do about that? He said, oh, he's just getting bad advice. It's - the people around him aren't giving him good advice. He's so smart, he'll figure this out.

But clearly, there's massive distance there. And if you're a politician of any kind and you see that distance between someone who's a pretty important leader of the far right of the Republican Party and a Republican president, you'd be smart to co-opt it and use it to get what you want. And I think that's what Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon have figured out is that this is really important to both of them, and they're going to use everything in their power to create the pressure on the middle to make this happen.
GROSS: Well, Josh Tyrangiel, thank you so much for talking with us.
TYRANGIEL: It's - this was really my pleasure. Thank you so much, Terry.
GROSS: Josh Tyrangiel is a staff writer for The Atlantic. His November cover story is titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." His latest book is "AI For Good."
(SOUNDBITE OF JON-ERIK KELLSO'S "JUST LIKE THAT")

GROSS: FRESH AIR's executive producer is Sam Briger. Our technical director and engineer is Audrey Bentham. Our interviews and reviews are produced and edited by Phyllis Myers, Roberta Shorrock, Ann Marie Baldonado, Lauren Krenzel, Therese Madden, Monique Nazareth, Thea Chaloner, Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez-Wisler. Our digital media producer is Molly Seavy-Nesper. Susan Nyakundi directed today's show. Our co-host is Tonya Mosley. I'm Terry Gross.

nytimes.com/2026/10/15/us/175-anniversar.headline: Ms., Martians and Guacamole: Their First Time in The Times

paragraphs.text: This story is part of a series marking 175 years of eyewitness journalism from The New York Times. Read more here.

It feels as if they’ve been around forever. But for everything, there’s a first mention in The Times. Here are 15 surprising debuts, from bicycles to the Big Bang, apartment houses to vaccines. Oh, and maps in color, too.
How the editors missed Ms.

It took just two consonants and a period to create an honorific that didn’t define women by their marital status. This was an elegant solution to a vexing problem, but it would take many decades for The New York Times to consider “Ms.” a proper form of address, which the paper finally did in 1986 — 15 years after the debut of Ms., the magazine. Yet the salutation was first proposed at the turn of the 20th century, by a newspaper in Springfield, Mass.

“There is a void in the English language which, with some diffidence, we undertake to fill,” declared a 1901 editorial in The Sunday Republican, suggesting “Ms.” as “a more comprehensive term” for women than “Miss” or “Mrs.,” one that “does homage to the sex without expressing any views as to their domestic situation.”

The item drew a small flurry of press attention, as the lexicographer Ben Zimmer later detailed, but “Ms.” didn’t take hold. Then in the early 1960s, a 22-year-old civil rights worker named Sheila Michaels noticed it on a piece of mail — her roommate’s subscription to a Marxist journal — and began to quietly lobby for its use.

Her efforts didn’t amount to much until late in the decade when she and others were invited to discuss the women’s movement on WBAI, the progressive New York City radio station. During a lull in the conversation, she began to expound on the virtues of “Ms.” As it turned out, a lot of women had tuned in.

When Gloria Steinem and her colleagues were mulling names for the feminist magazine they were hatching, “Ms.” was the clear winner, and by 1972 the American Heritage School Dictionary had adopted the word. Throughout the ’70s, newspapers around the country followed suit, if it was a woman’s preference.
But not The Times.

“Ms.” was a passing fad, the paper’s top editors declared, pooh-poohing those who pressed for its use, including many female staffers. The ongoing prohibition led to tortured renderings like “Miss Steinem of Ms. magazine” whenever Ms. Steinem appeared in a news story, which was often.

Meanwhile, female staffers began to investigate gender inequities at the paper. “Ms.” was the least of it. Women’s salaries were considerably lower than those of men in comparable jobs, and women were woefully underrepresented in the newsroom and management. In 1974, they filed a class-action suit.

Four years later, the case was settled out of court with the paper’s promising to hire and promote more women. But it would be eight more years before Miss Steinem of Ms. magazine would be accorded the courtesy title she and thousands of women used daily. On July 19, 1986, the paper announced to its readers it would start using “Ms.” because “it has passed sufficiently into the language to be accepted as common usage.”

The Times did so the next day, in a front-page story about a landmark Supreme Court ruling that sexual harassment was sex discrimination. The case involved a bank employee, Mechelle Vinson, and her male supervisor. It was the first case of sexual harassment ever considered by the court, and Ms. Vinson was the first woman to receive the honorific in The Times.
Gloria Steinem sent flowers. — Penelope Green
Martians land in print
The first one landed on Sunday, Aug. 12, 1877, in the dense verbiage of Page One. It was an adjective: “Martian forests.” The nouns would soon follow.

That Mars should produce Martians had become increasingly obvious to observers on Earth. Even to early telescopes it was large (arguably the second-nearest planet), always fully illuminated by the sun and colorful, mostly red, but sometimes showing hints of white or even blue or green. By 1800, astronomers had worked out that, like Earth, Mars had polar ice caps, was tilted on its axis and thus offered seasons, had an atmosphere of sorts, and rotated roughly every 24 hours. It was Earth’s twin, plain as Martian day.

In 1871, in a popular British literary magazine, Richard A. Proctor, a respected astronomer, reflected at length on the possibility of life on Mars. He envisaged “Martial oceans” and “Martial seas,” as well as Martial valleys, poles, winds, skies and mornings, and supposed that “Martialists” might be 14 feet tall and busily at work building roads, canals and bridges.

“Martialist” soon evolved into “Martian” and, in 1877, an adjectival form reached The Times, in an excerpt from a new article by Proctor taking issue with the idea that Mars’s ruddy color could be explained by “the red leaves of Martian trees,” as a French astronomer had proposed.

Two months later, an Italian astronomer identified “canali” on the planet — which, in English and French, became “canals.” Lo, the Martians — now rapidly colonizing the publishing landscape as nouns — had shovels as well as oars. They were engineer-navigators, farmers with boats and epic irrigation schemes. The Times noted the discovery, and the nouns, casually in 1882: “Of course, the Martians are a sea-faring people,” a point so self-evident by now that it was relegated to Page 8.

The Times gave voice to the occasional skeptic — the “so-called canals” (1893) were “a delusion” (1909) — but considered Martians without fear or favor. “The straight lines on Mars and on Venus may not be canals,” according to the paper in 1904, “but since we do not know what they are we might as well give up being dogmatic as to what they are not.”

But the crash was coming. On Jan. 23, 1916, a story in The New York Times Sunday Magazine — “Canals of Mars Called an Optical Illusion” — reported that, viewed at higher resolution, the spidery network of Martian lines was an array of unrelated dots. The canals were a “fallacy,” The Times reported. The first close-up photograph of Mars, transmitted by the Mariner 4 spacecraft and published on the front page on July 16, 1965, did “not show any of the controversial canals.” The planet was dry, its atmosphere thin, the magnetic field weak. On July 21, 1976, NASA’s Viking 1 lander settled on the front page with “spectacular photographs of a rocky, wind-scoured desert plain.”
A half-century later, the search for life on Mars continues, although expectations are smaller; the discovery even of fossil microbes would be considered world-changing. — Alan Burdick
Correction No. 1, a head-scratcher
On Monday, Oct. 6, 1851, in its 16th edition, the fledgling New-York Daily Times covered a fire that, upon further review, appeared not to have happened.
Here is the entire article:

FIRE AT STUART’S SUGAR REFINERY. — Yesterday morning, about 10 o’clock, a fire was discovered in the rear of Messrs. R. L. & A. Stuart’s Steam Sugar Refinery, corner of Reade and Greenwich-streets, but by the prompt action of the employees of the establishment, they soon succeeded in extinguishing the flames, with trifling damage.
The next day, The Times regretted the error.

CORRECTION OF A FIRE. — In consequence of being wrongly informed, we yesterday noticed in The Times, that a slight fire occurred in the extensive steam sugar refinery of Messrs. R. L. & A. Stuart, which was mistaken for the fire in Robinson-street, a report of which will be found in our columns of to-day. The immense buildings of the above firm are all fire proof, and they are guarded night and day by watchmen employed exclusively for that purpose.
It was The Times’s first formal correction, one of thousands it has run in an effort to set the record straight and demonstrate integrity in the face of failure.

How the paper made this first, baffling mistake is lost to history. Nor do we know who alerted the paper to it. But the correction itself offers a few clues, as well as some intriguing rhetorical dodges — “In consequence of being wrongly informed,” for starters, with its notes of both apology and blame-avoidance. Notice, too, the downgrading of the nonexistent fire to “slight,” a modifier that didn’t appear in the original article. The implication: small fire, small mistake.

The “extensive steam sugar refinery” in question spanned the block from Reade Street to Chambers Street, not far from the Times building at 113 Nassau Street. One can only guess how The Times mistook a fire on Robinson Street (now Park Place) for a supposed blaze three blocks north, or why it described the refinery employees’ prompt action when there had been no emergency. But in the correction’s assurance that the refinery’s buildings are “all fire proof” and “guarded night and day by watchmen,” we detect the influence of a ticked-off reader.
Perhaps that reader was Robert Leighton Stuart, sugar refiner.

The threat of fire was a constant source of terror in those days. Just six years earlier, the Great Fire of 1845 wiped out hundreds of buildings in Lower Manhattan. The erroneous report of a fire at the refinery might have been embarrassing to Mr. Stuart and alarming to his insurer.

Henry Jarvis Raymond, The Times’s founding editor, was likely acquainted with Mr. Stuart, a prominent member of society. When The Times began publishing, Mr. Raymond was himself prominent (he was elected speaker of the New York State Assembly that January), and the two men later served together on at least one committee and attended the same events supporting President Lincoln.

As a matter of journalistic pride, we prefer not to believe that Mr. Stuart bullied or sweet-talked Mr. Raymond into saying there hadn’t been a fire when there had. More likely, Mr. Stuart marched over to The Times building and banged on the editor’s desk as he shouted, Our buildings are ALL FIRE PROOF and they are GUARDED NIGHT AND DAY!
Of course, we could be wrong. — Mike Wilson
‘Wedding’ takes on greater meaning

Major societal shifts are often chronicled on the front page of The Times; this one happened on Page 12 of the national edition. It was Sunday, Sept. 1, 2002: the first time an openly gay couple’s union was published under “Weddings/Celebrations.”

The couple was Steven Goldstein and Daniel Gross, who had lobbied for the change in a personal three-page letter to the new executive editor, Howell Raines. Goldstein and Gross were planning a Jewish wedding ceremony in Montreal, followed by a civil union in Vermont, and they wanted this to be announced in the newspaper.

They detailed their credentials — degrees from Yale, Brandeis, Harvard and Columbia; a Fulbright scholarship and work on Capitol Hill; parents with pedigrees — and noted Raines’s celebrated history covering the civil rights movement. The letter, Gross said in a recent interview, was “high energy and high chutzpah.”

It came two years before Massachusetts became the first state to sanction same-sex marriage, and more than a decade ahead of the 2015 Supreme Court ruling that marriage for same-sex couples was a constitutional right.

Bob Woletz, who ran the wedding pages for decades, said he had been quietly advocating the inclusion of same-sex announcements for several years. Allan Siegal, the assistant managing editor in charge of standards, had formed a committee to study the issue. Then Sept. 11 happened, followed by wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Approximately no one in Times leadership was thinking about this when Goldstein and Gross’s letter arrived that summer. But Raines, now 83 and retired, said he recalled “specifically sitting at my desk and making the decision immediately: Let’s publish it.”

“I remember distinctly my discussion with Al was, ‘Do these people meet the normal criteria that we use for conventional marriages?’ And he said they did in every way,” Raines recounted. “It seemed to be just an obvious decision. I was frankly a little surprised it hadn’t been made before.”

I went to college with Gross and was tapped to write the announcement, which was unusual — editors typically avoid asking writers to cover anything to which they have a personal connection. (The couple later asked me to read the write-up aloud at the Vermont ceremony; we were all in tears.)

A media frenzy ensued. Gross and Goldstein appeared on CNN and the “Today” show. Newspapers in Turkey and Italy were among the many to cover the couple; one outlet ran the story with an image of two random men in skimpy bathing suits. Reporters wanted to know everything about the couple’s relationship — even though, as Gross said, “the revolution was not us.”
Gross and Goldstein split up in 2015. — Jodi Rudoren
Finally, a Pulitzer for a woman

Anne O’Hare McCormick was 37 when she had sobering words for the women of her high school alma mater, a Catholic convent in Ohio. Women writers, she told them in a 1917 yearbook essay, “languish over the Society column of the daily newspaper’’ and “only a determined few” join the reporting staff or “achieve the dignity and influence of an editorial writer.”

Twenty years later, through force of will, intelligence and a lustrous, authoritative prose, Ms. McCormick was among those few. In 1937 she became the first woman to win a Pulitzer Prize at The New York Times, for her columns on world affairs. One year earlier she became the first woman on The Times’s editorial board.

She interviewed Adolf Hitler, Benito Mussolini, Josef Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt. She filed from the Nuremberg trials, the wreckage of post-World War II France and a mountain outpost during the 1940s Greek Civil War.

She had little training as a journalist, but she was married to a rich importer-exporter and accompanied him on business to Europe. In 1921 she wrote to The Times and asked if she might submit some articles from her trips.

One of her first pieces, in 1921, described Pope Benedict XV in a golden chair amid waving peacock feathers that “hedged him in and brushed him aside, so that the man inside the Pope did not matter at all.’’ She wrote, “It was the Papacy one saw moving in the hush, swallowing up good Popes, bad Popes and indifferent Popes, and surviving them all.’’

Mussolini’s first remarks to the Italian Parliament that year, she wrote in the same article, amounted to “one of the best political speeches I have ever heard, a little swaggering but caustic, powerful and telling.’’

Her most explosive interview was with Hitler in 1933, his first year as Germany’s chancellor: He was “a rather shy and simple man,’’ and “especially when he loses himself and forgets his listener in a flood of speech, it is easy to see how he sways multitudes.’’

Times readers were outraged. Ms. McCormick was asked to follow up with a more critical piece, and she did. But as she wrote to Arthur Hays Sulzberger, who would become The Times’s publisher: “What I tried to do in my German dispatches was to indicate facts as they are in Germany and not as we’d like them to be.’’ — Elisabeth Bumiller
Hola, guacamole

Americans have long loved their avocados, especially mashed up into guacamole: The relationship goes back at least seven decades, as recipes in The Times attest. In 1952, the food-news staff’s home economist, Ruth P. Casa-Emellos, offered the paper’s first recipe, which, following the tastes of the era, transmogrified the dip into a gelatin ring mold with sugar and lots of mayo. (The word “guacamole” is derived from the Aztec word āhuacamōlli, or avocado sauce. A 14th-century version mixed avocados with tomatoes, salt and chili peppers — a combination that is still considered authentic.)

For most of those seven decades, it was not a contentious relationship. Times food writers regularly rolled out fairly classic recipes, and presumably readers whipped up guacamole in their (avocado-colored) kitchens and passed it around their (sunken) living rooms.

Guac entered the Oxford English Dictionary in 2013, the year Melissa Clark, a veteran Times food writer, published a recipe she had adapted from ABC Cocina, Jean-Georges Vongerichten’s Latin fusion restaurant near Manhattan’s Union Square. The dish contained something that Ms. Clark acknowledged seemed radical, fresh green peas, even if peas in guacamole weren’t actually that unusual. They were a go-to, low-cost ingredient, particularly in the ’60s and ’70s when avocado prices were soaring.
Then on July 1, 2015, The Times’s main Twitter account tweeted out Ms. Clark’s recipe with this come-on: “Add green peas to your guacamole. Trust us.”
Pea Gate was upon us.
“No. Just no.”
“Literally no.”
“One does not mix mustard and Twinkies because they are the same color.”
The Republican Party of Texas waded into the scrum, and supercharged it: “The @nytimes declared war on Texas when they suggested adding green peas to guacamole.”
Even President Obama objected: “respect the nyt, but not buying peas in guac. onions, garlic, hot peppers. classic.”

And in a bit of bipartisan parity (perhaps the last gasp of comity in that department), Jeb Bush, then campaigning for the Republican nomination to succeed Mr. Obama, agreed: “You don’t put peas in guacamole.”
Ms. Clark was stunned by the opprobrium.

“It’s such a smart recipe,” she said. “It keeps the color from going brown, and there’s precedent for using peas in times of old when you couldn’t easily get avocados. Also it’s just really good.” She added, “The funny thing about Obama’s tweet is that he was shaming us, but garlic is not traditional, ever, in guacamole.” — Penelope Green
When the Big Bang made it big

In the beginning, before the Big Bang theory of the cosmos blossomed into canon, before it even was called, at first dismissively, the “big bang,” there was, on Christmas Eve, 1930, “a great explosion of the universe” on the front page of The Times.

The previous evening on London radio, James Jeans, a prominent British physicist and astronomer, noted that the universe was expanding: The oldest, most distant galaxies were racing away from our own at millions of miles an hour. What’s more, George Lemaître, an astronomer and Roman Catholic priest well versed in Einstein’s new physics, had a provocative theory: The universe began as a primordial atom containing all the matter in the cosmos that burst apart with vast radioactive energy.

This universe “has properties similar to those of a soap bubble,” Jeans reported; as soon as it “comes into existence it starts swelling and must continue expanding indefinitely.” He added: “The whole universe must be expanding — I might almost say exploding — at a really terrific rate.” Lemaître’s cosmos was not timeless: It had a birth date — “a day without yesterday,” he said — roughly 10 billion years ago. (Astronomers now put the universe at perhaps 13.8 billion years old.)

In 1949, Fred Hoyle, a British astronomer, championed a rival idea of a “steady state” cosmos — infinite, eternal and generating new matter as it evolved — and dismissed Lemaître’s theory as a “big bang.”

“The hypothesis that all matter of the universe was created in one big bang at a particular time in the remote past,” Hoyle said, was “an irrational process that cannot be described in scientific terms.” (He later insisted he was being evocative, not derogatory.)

The Times introduced the phrase on New Year’s Eve, 1956, in a story involving a physicist who had successfully turned helium into carbon. This transmutation, the headline noted, “Is Hailed as Helping to Explain Origin of Universe.” A subhead added: “‘BIG BANG’ THEORY HIT.”

The phrase kicked around in lowercase for two decades, with The Times noting on Dec. 20, 1961, that the idea was “more widely endorsed by astronomers and cosmologists.” In 1964, the discovery of the cosmic microwave background — a pervasive fog of low-level radiation left over from the starting fireworks — effectively sealed the case. Big Bang, capitalized and minus scare quotes, burst into The Times on March 20, 1977. — Alan Burdick
New to market: apartments

In the post-Civil War years, when New York City was booming, Manhattanites were wary of a new kind of housing — the apartment — that was poised to invade the island. French flats, as apartment houses were known, were common in Europe, but to Americans they were suspect: bohemian habitats for artists and bachelors and, to quote Edith Wharton’s “The Age of Innocence,” for “dressmakers, bird-stuffers and ‘people who wrote.’” The Times was bullish on them, however, and began to work on its readers.

“One of the delusions of the Anglo-Saxon is that he must have his own separate house,” the paper noted on July 18, 1869, in its first story on the subject, headlined “Living in Flats: Advantages of the System for New Yorkers.” “Among the continental peoples there is much more good sense in the matter.”

The Stuyvesant Apartments, the first apartment “house” designed for the city’s middle class, was then being built on East 18th Street off Irving Place. The article extolled the economic and labor savings of this novel form of living, and dismissed outright the possibility for sketchy neighbors, even though the five-story Stuyvesant had a few artist studios tucked away on its top floors. The article pointed out that, in cities like Paris, flat dwellers were typically “of the most respectable sort,” including bankers, minor nobility and diplomats. The paper was correct: The Stuyvesant’s future tenants included George P. Putnam, the publisher, and Elizabeth Custer, the widow of Lt. Col. George Custer.

Land values, and therefore house rents, were soaring, and New Yorkers of “moderate means” had better wise up and embrace vertical living, according to The Times. Single-family houses had “become like carriages and footmen, luxuries for the rich.”

At least one reader disagreed: “After reading your article on ‘Flats’ in yesterday’s paper, I feel induced to say through your paper that I believe the ‘flat’ system of living will never be accepted in this country.” (The reader was a commuter living in Mount Vernon, and he encouraged “young married men” to behave as he did and leave the city.) — Penelope Green
Before states went red: the first color voting map
On July 26, 1908, readers of The Times were treated to an election map rendered in vivid yellow and blue.

In this map, states that voted for the Democrat in the previous presidential election are blue, and those that went Republican are yellow. With William Howard Taft, the Republican, and William Jennings Bryan, the Democrat, on the campaign trail, the colors helped readers see where each candidate might best focus his efforts. (This was nearly a century before red and blue came to universally signify Republicans and Democrats.)

The map also included complex pyramid shapes displaying 20 years’ worth of presidential election data, in chronological order from top to bottom. Such a densely packed graphic scheme might well confound readers today, but at the time the pyramids likely came off as intuitive. Readers would have been used to seeing pyramids and other architectural visualizations used to display population data and various statistics.
Today, The Times might display the same kind of historical data using a Sankey diagram.

But the newspaper also still uses some of its original mapmaking tricks. In 2024 maps, the hatch lines across Arizona and Nevada mark states that flipped parties — a technique that descends directly from the horizontal lines in the 1908 map drawn across Colorado, Idaho, Montana and Nevada for the same purposes.
The worn map shown here is the one copy in existence. Only its innovations survive. — Tim Wallace
1852’s vaccine debate
The first “vaccine” in The Times, on Aug. 14, 1852, came with a manslaughter charge, as it was not a vaccine at all.

An outbreak of smallpox was underway in and around New York City. In Newark, a local man, Frederick Buhr, wanted his two young children to be vaccinated, and he enlisted a self-described doctor, Attila Keleman. Proper vaccination, devised in 1796 by the English physician Edward Jenner, rendered people immune to smallpox by injecting them with cowpox, a similar but far less dangerous virus.
