But Keleman merely “pretended” to vaccinate, The Times reported, and used an older, riskier method called variolation: He injected Buhr’s children with live smallpox, taken from a child who subsequently died of the infection. The Buhr children, a 13-month-old girl and an older boy, soon died of smallpox, too. Keleman was charged with manslaughter.

Variolation was known to work sometimes — but when it didn’t, even those patients who survived could spread the disease and exacerbate an outbreak. Indeed, weeks earlier, Newark passed an ordinance, evidently prompted by Keleman’s work, requiring people who opted for the method to leave Newark until they recovered from smallpox. “It is said that he has extended this dreadful contagion not only through the city to some extent, but also in the neighboring villages,” The Monmouth Democrat wrote of Keleman on Aug. 19, 1852, adding: “Dr. Keleman was a tailor two years ago in Newark.”

The ordinance was among the first to embrace vaccination as a public health measure. The following year, Britain passed the Vaccination Act, which made smallpox vaccination mandatory for infants born in England and Wales. Opponents of such strictures formed anti-vaccination leagues in the U.K. and, in 1879, the Anti-Vaccination Society of America. But by 1895 in the United States, several state courts had ruled that school boards and local governments could bar unvaccinated children from enrolling.

On Nov. 22, 1892, The Times ran an obituary of Keleman, “one of the oldest physicians in the city.” He emigrated from Hungary in 1840 with a medical degree, “started a large sanitarium on upper Broadway” — probably one of the many hydropathic centers catering to wealthy clients — and in 1879 received an honorary degree from Eclectic Medical College of the City of New York, an institute for alternative medicine. Until his last days, The Times reported, “he had always enjoyed the most perfect health.”— Alan Burdick
An untimely obituary

When a weeping blonde arrived at The Times’s headquarters on New Year’s Day in 1980 and in tremulous tones announced the death of her husband, Alan Abel, possibly the editors should have been a bit less credulous. Mr. Abel, then age 50, was a notorious prankster, having snookered the press for more than two decades.

His first major masquerade, which began in 1959, was an organization known as the Society for Indecency to Naked Animals, or SINA, whose mission was to “clothe all naked animals that appear in public, namely horses, cows, dogs and cats.” SINA famously picketed the White House to persuade Jacqueline Kennedy, the first lady, to put underpants on her horses. According to the many, many press reports it garnered, the group boasted some 50,000 members who rallied to a marching song, “Wings of Decency,” and deployed an emergency “clothes mobile” to patrol the streets of New York, dispensing decorous garments to critters in the buff.

The Times, among other outlets, covered SINA’s adventures with a surprising lack of irony. “Pickets Ask First Lady to Clothe Her Horses,” read a headline on March 6, 1963. (Mr. Abel was outed by Time magazine later that year.)

Mr. Abel went on to produce ever more elaborate shenanigans, aided by his wife, Jeanne, and a gang of actors and accomplices. Pranks included a presidential campaign for a Jewish grandmother from the Bronx named Mrs. Yetta Bronstein, whose platform included a promise to put truth serum in the Senate water cooler and whose campaign slogan was: “Vote Yetta, Watch Things Get Betta.” Other highlights of his long career: a school for beggars led by a character named Omar, who appeared on the “Today” show; and a green card marriage for Idi Amin, the murderous Ugandan dictator, in a ceremony at the Plaza Hotel before a roomful of aghast reporters along with officials from the C.I.A., the F.B.I. and the State Department.

Yet The Times listened to the weeping blonde, confirmed the death with several of Mr. Abel's accomplices and took the bait, publishing his obit on Jan. 2, 1980 (“Alan Abel, Satirist Created Campaign to Clothe Animals”). It reported his death of a heart attack in Utah, where he was purportedly scouting a location for a movie (“Who’s Going to Bite Your Neck, Dear, When All of My Teeth Are Gone?”). The next day, Mr. Abel revealed his hoax at a news conference at the Biltmore Hotel in Manhattan. The duped obituarist, Walter Waggoner, attended, rather grumpy, and was reported to have said, “As far as I’m concerned, Abel’s dead, who are you?” The correction ran on Jan. 4.

Waggoner’s editor, Sydney Schanberg, the Pulitzer Prize-winning reporter who covered Cambodia’s fall to the Khmer Rouge in 1975, was more sanguine. “Everybody’s asking, ‘Is this the first time this has ever happened to us?’ I don’t know. I kind of doubt it. It’s never the first time for anything.”
Mr. Abel finally died, for real, on Sept. 14, 2018. The headline: “Alan Abel, Hoaxer Extraordinaire, Is (On Good Authority) Dead at 94.” — Penelope Green
A peloton in petticoats

Throughout the last quarter of the 19th century, The Times was positively giddy about the bicycle, a contraption that replaced the awkward velocipedes, a generic term for all manner of human-powered vehicles, some of which were made of wood and known as bone-shakers. The bicycle was something else altogether: “a mustang of steel who knows his rider and never needs a lasso,” as one writer enthused in 1878.

The paper’s first mention of the gizmos was in 1869 and involved a patent infringement. But much of the paper’s coverage focused on “wheelwomen,” or female bicyclists: their clothes, their clubs, their races. Wheelwomen raced horses, men and each other. Competitions lasted hours — and often days — during which contestants sometimes fainted, as one favored rider did during a six-day event at Madison-Square Garden in 1889. (An advertorial a few months later proposed “pure whiskey” as a remedy.)

An ad for “lady cyclist detectives” in “The Lady Cyclist, an English wheelwoman’s paper,” delighted one reporter, who noted that such a job would “be free from the humdrum routine of the office.” And there was the curious case of the woman who had a compulsion to leap off her bike for no reason, and wrote in to inquire what she might do about it. “I resist this impulse as strenuously as possible,” she said, “but the result is always the same — willy-nilly, I spring to the ground.” The reporter suggested she see a doctor.

But what really confounded and divided the public was what was proper for a woman to wear astride her bike. Many column inches were devoted to the topic. Bloomers and knickerbockers caused much hand-wringing, despite their benefits. (One noted tailor made bloomers with ample pockets, to hold combs and revolvers, and fasteners at the edges, to “keep the mice out.”)

In 1895, in Little Rock, Ark., a woman was arrested for riding her bike in bloomers. A testy judge dismissed the case, declaring, “Women have a constitutional and God-given right to ride a bicycle, and they are bound to have some comfortable and appropriate dress therefor.”
The headline read, “Mrs. Noe’s Bloomers Vindicated.” — Penelope Green
The iceman leaveth: the first electric refrigerator

In 1905, none but the most affluent American families had electricity at home, and those who did used it only for lighting. But it was already possible to envision the convenience of a wired kitchen — at least for anyone who attended the gleaming Electrical Show that year at Madison Square Garden (the old MSG, the Beaux Arts palace that once stood northeast of Madison Square Park). There on display were electric stoves and ovens, coffee urns, kettles, “laundry irons” and more.

A short article in The Times on Dec. 16, 1905, describing a meal prepared with these ultramodern appliances, noted that “dishes which should be served cold” were chilled in an “electric refrigerator.” The phrase was new to The Times and to the times: Until then, “refrigerator” was just another word for an old-fashioned icebox, insulated but not electric, and it would be nine more years before any electric fridge was available for purchase (the first was the DOMELRE).

But when the show was over, Times editors seemed to lose interest in the electric refrigerators, leaving it to advertisers to herald the arrival, in the 1920s, of the Frigidaires, Kelvinators and GE Monitor-Tops that would soon stand in American kitchens.— Mary Duenwald

techcrunch.com/2026/10/15/amazon-devices.headline: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay on the importance of failure and bouncing back from it
techcrunch.com/2026/10/15/amazon-devices.author: Aisha Malik

paragraphs.text: Amazon executive Panos Panay has a message for startup founders: Failure is an inevitable, required part of building a successful product.

Panay, Amazon SVP of Devices, Alexa, and Leo, shared that advice onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco, drawing on his own experience at Microsoft, where he spent more than 19 years and weathered one particularly expensive failure.

“You have to be willing to fail, and actually, not just willing, you actually have to go fail,” Panay said. “If you haven’t failed, you probably haven’t pushed the boundary. It’s literally about harvesting the lessons learned when you fail. You have to be willing to face it, and as you face it, learn from it.”

Panay said it’s possible to recover from all sorts of failures, even catastrophic ones, noting that he experienced one himself at Microsoft. He described the launch of the Surface RT, Microsoft’s first tablet computer, as a significant failure during his tenure at the company, one that ultimately led to a nearly $1 billion write-down.

“I remember being on the front cover of a newspaper, and it just said failure,” Panay said. “But, here’s the thing, it was easy to admit failure. The trick was, and always is, did you harvest the learnings and understand what happened? All right. What did you learn? Because the failure wasn’t that moment. It was decisions that led up to it two years before that, whether the software wasn’t complete or the inventory was wrong or how we balanced into retail. There were all these steps along the way.”
He said founders need to be willing to understand what went wrong, and avoid making excuses, and ultimately accept the failure.

“Here’s the other side of it,” he said. “You want to succeed, yeah? You take that failure, but you don’t let go of your vision. That’s it. Surface has done pretty well. You don’t let go of your vision. You don’t break it.”

Panay emphasized the importance of staying committed to a vision, learning from experience, and moving quickly. He believes that by embracing failure and learning from setbacks, founders can adapt and make progress faster, even as they encounter new obstacles.

“It goes back to the same fundamental, like, have you learned?” he said. “Were you learning along the way? Because if you were learning, then you just change your vector. Usually, it’s not 180 degrees. Usually, it’s just 30 degrees. Take your lessons learned, change a little bit, adapt your vision where it needs to be, and then go. I believe there’s people that hang on too long, but it’s because they haven’t accepted the moment of failure at all.”

finance.yahoo.com/markets/currencies/art.headline: Dollar Wraps Its Worst Day in Over a Month on AI Risk Concerns
finance.yahoo.com/markets/currencies/art.author: Melos Ambaye and Anya Andrianova

paragraphs.text: Melos Ambaye and Anya Andrianova
Thu, October 15, 2026 at 1:14 PM PDT 3 min read
(Bloomberg) -- The dollar fell the most in more than a month, erasing gains fueled by hotter-than-expected inflation data.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index declined 0.3% Thursday, its biggest drop since Sept. 3, as artificial intelligence-related concerns fueled a bond rally that pushed yields lower and weighed on the currency. The greenback fell against nearly all of its major peers, falling about 1% against the Swiss franc.

"As AI debt has sold off, there has been a flight to safer assets like Treasuries, which is pushing down yields, which is pressuring the dollar," said Andrew Hazlett, a foreign-exchange trader at Monex Inc.

The slide came despite new economic data pointing to ongoing inflation pressures. US producer prices advanced 1.3% in September, the most in more than four years, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Thursday. Meanwhile, retail sales also beat forecasts, boosted by gasoline spending.

That followed a better than expected consumer inflation report which revived expectations for Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes just a day earlier, briefly boosting the dollar to its highest level since May 2025.

Traders will turn their attention to Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's remarks at the International Monetary Fund-World Bank Group annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, late Thursday New York time for more clues on the central bank's policy path. It will be his last chance to send any signal on rates since the Fed enters a so-called blackout period on Saturday before its October policy meeting.

Ahead of raising rates in September, Warsh had sent a hawkish message to markets, prompting traders to adjust their rate-hike predictions. While Warsh has vowed not to steer markets with his own near-term outlook for monetary policy, the inflation surprise will likely heighten scrutiny of his remarks.

"Markets are in a bit of a weird place right now," said Alex Cohen, a strategist at Bank of America, noting that while AI concerns have investors flocking to safe havens, the dollar's close tie to AI spending means any trouble in the sector could ultimately weigh on the currency.

"If the market is pricing rising odds of peak AI capex, the USD is a sell," Brent Donnelly, president of Spectra Markets, said in a note. "The entire US economy is a one-legged stool balanced on the AI trade."

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Anthropic Stands Alone as Rest of US IPO Market Slows to a Crawl
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Anthony Hughes and Bailey Lipschultz

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- A cocktail of risks is threatening to stall the US IPO pipeline, leaving Anthropic PBC's potential blockbuster debut as one of the few offerings that investors can count on.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Several deals have already come unglued, with smart-ring maker Oura Inc. and Bamboo Insurance Services Inc. postponing their plans as interest rates climbed higher and the Iran war dragged on. High-profile candidates SB Energy Inc. and Nscale Ltd. have filed publicly but haven't yet started formal marketing, further muddying the fourth quarter outlook.

Even with some deals falling by the wayside, equity capital markets bankers will be celebrating one of their best years ever for fees. Anthropic is seeking to match or exceed SpaceX's record-setting debut as soon as next month, in a listing that would dwarf all of the other potential deals combined.
Bankers concede that marketing IPOs has become much harder due to factors including the upcoming midterm elections, and investors are more choosy.

"This is the first time this year that there has been a bit of a pause in the IPO market where folks are saying, 'There's got to be a little bit of differentiation in terms of how we evaluate what we buy and at what price'," said Aloke Gupte, Citigroup Inc.'s co-head of global equity capital markets.
It doesn't help that the end-of-year calendar is trickier than normal due to the Nov. 3 midterm US elections, where AI safety and data centers have become part of policy debates.

"When you look at the US political landscape and geopolitics overall, the number of unknowns has gone up over the past six weeks alone," said David Bauer, JPMorgan Chase & Co.'s head of equity capital markets for North America. "That increase in uncertainty inevitably has an impact on how the market is going to behave."

A warning for the market sounded in September, with IPO activity slowing as US 10-year bond yields jumped more than 50 basis points. Only five sizable companies went public, raising $1.9 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg, making it the slowest month since March.
That's in stark contrast with the picture for the year to date, bolstered by SpaceX and South Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix Inc.'s listings.

Companies have raised $163 billion in US IPOs this year, or more than three times last year's haul, according to data compiled by Bloomberg that excludes listings by blank-check firms and other investment vehicles.
The action in the final quarter of the year may be concentrated in one deal.

"In the midst of the best year for IPOs in a long time, it'll likely be a very quiet two months for the broader IPO market, even with the possibility of a marquee deal coming to market," said J.D. Moriarty, vice chairman and global head of technology ECM at Bank of America Corp.
"At the moment, investors are more focused on what they own than what bankers want to show them."
Most bankers remain optimistic that investors and companies can find a middle ground on valuation, despite expectations being challenged by the AI selloff in recent days.

Even as 7 of the year's 10 largest US deals trade below their IPO prices, SpaceX's resilient performance isn't lost on portfolio managers, not to mention the implications if a big deal like Anthropic's delivers similar gains.
"There is as much interest overall in IPOs as there has been. Anything we see going on is a bit temporal and mark-to market," said John Kolz, Barclays Plc's global head of ECM.
"The same people saying that IPO performance has not been great are still asking what do you have coming," Kolz added.
Companies with live IPO filings are keeping their options open, after several outbreaks of volatility this year that faded almost as rapidly as they arrived.

"Even if a company decides to move their timeline into early 2027, they won't go pens down for the rest of the year," said JPMorgan's Bauer. "They're still engaging with investors, still talking about ways to refine the equity story. They're staying ready. People will move quickly when the opportunity opens back up."
To some, all the IPO market needs to regain momentum is a win or two, and that could yet come from sectors not as exposed to the AI theme.

"It would help to have some degree of diversity, but we just need a few regular-way IPOs to price and trade well," said Rob Stowe, Barclays' head of Americas ECM. "That will get things moving in the right direction."
--With assistance from Tonya Garcia.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Democrats Target Epstein Ties to Banks for Action After Midterms
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Erik Wasson

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Key Democrats on Thursday unveiled legislation that would force federal regulators to disclose financial records related Jeffrey Epstein and his associates.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The measure also would require regulators to investigate banks and their executives for potential related legal violations.
The disgraced financier conducted substantial business during his career with JP Morgan Chase & Co., Deutsche Bank AG and Bank of America Corp.
Republicans currently control the congressional agenda but Democrats have previously succeeded in enacting legislation related to Epstein even with GOP lawmakers in the majority.

Last year President Donald Trump signed a bill requiring the Justice Department to release files after Republicans joined Democrats in demanding transparency related to Epstein, who died in prison awaiting trial related to sex trafficking of minors.
If Democrats win control after November midterms — an increasingly likely outcome — elections which would give them more power over what legislation moves forward.

In that case, bill author Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts would likely be the next chairman of the Banking Committee and co-author Robert Garcia is in line to head the House Oversight panel which has broad subpoena powers. Other sponsors include Democrats Ron Wyden of Oregon, who would likely head the Senate Finance Committee, and Connecticut's Richard Blumenthal who may head up the Senate's investigative subcommittee.

The Epstein Wall Street Record Act would force federal regulators including the Securities and Exchange Commission, Federal Reserve, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to make public within 120 days any supervisory records, including internal communications, related to Epstein or his former girlfriend Ghislaine Maxwell, who was convicted of sex trafficking offenses.

The law would require regulators to investigate any violations of banking, securities or anti-money laundering laws revealed in the files. Senior executives found in violation of the law could be barred from the banking industry, hit with fines or referred to the Justice department for possible criminal prosecution.

"I have spent the last year calling on Donald Trump's financial regulators to launch investigations into the big banks and executives who may have enabled Jeffrey Epstein's horrific crimes. Since they have failed to act, Congress must," Warren said in a statement.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: CoreWeave Founders Shield Fortunes With $3.3 Billion Stock Sales
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Dylan Sloan

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Three CoreWeave Inc. co-founders have sold $3.3 billion in company shares since last year's initial public offering, taking money off the table as rising credit risks and investor wariness around AI spending spark volatility in the stock.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Michael Intrator, Brian Venturo and Brannin McBee joined the Bloomberg Billionaires Index of the world's 500 richest people last year after CoreWeave's shares soared following its March 2025 IPO. The stock gained 359% from the offering price to a peak three months later, vaulting Intrator's net worth to $11.8 billion.

As the company's shares have fallen more than 60% from that high-water mark, the trio have cashed out billions, including $2.4 billion this year alone. At today's closing price, the stock they've unloaded since the IPO would be worth nearly a third less than their pretax proceeds from the share sales.

"Our co-founders remain three of the top six shareholders in CoreWeave, together owning approximately 20% of the company," a company spokesperson said in an emailed statement. "They're making personal financial planning decisions that any responsible founder with concentrated holdings would make. All sales are pre-scheduled, fully disclosed, and entirely standard."

CoreWeave shares slumped 15% Wednesday before rebounding slightly on Thursday. The drop came as a measure of the company's credit risk climbed to an all-time high after McBee talked of tapping "unlimited" capital from insurers in an interview with the Financial Times.

After cashing out less than $70 million in shares last year, Intrator has ramped up the pace of his sales in 2026, offloading more than $907 million in company stock since Jan. 1, according to data compiled by Bloomberg from filings.
That's made him one of the five largest insider sellers at any US firm for each of the past two quarters. He's sold the equivalent of 16.5% of his undiluted equity holding as of the IPO date.

On a percentage basis, McBee has sold even more — his $1.06 billion in sales since the IPO, including $577 million this year alone, represent a 40.4% drawdown from his undiluted holding as of the firm's public debut. Nearly 40% of McBee's wealth is now held in cash and equivalents, according to Bloomberg's wealth index.

Venturo's $734 million in share sales in the second quarter made him the second-largest insider seller at any US firm during the period, and helped push his total sales to more than $1.2 billion since CoreWeave's IPO. He's sold off more than 35% of his IPO stake.

Despite the sales protecting some of their net worth, CoreWeave's slide has handed each of the three billionaires significant losses. Collectively, they've lost $15 billion in paper wealth since CoreWeave's high-water mark in June 2025.

Even before the firm went public, the three co-founders had already cashed out millions through pre-IPO sales. Intrator, Venturo and McBee together sold $488 million in shares via separate tender offers in 2023 and 2024, according to a prospectus filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

politico.com/news/2026/10/15/trump-lashe.headline: Trump lashes out at Republicans as Ken Paxton struggles in Texas
politico.com/news/2026/10/15/trump-lashe.author: Cheyanne M. Daniels

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump is blaming fellow Republicans as his endorsed candidate, Ken Paxton, appears to be in a fierce struggle for a Senate seat in Texas with Democratic challenger James Talarico in a state the GOP has long taken for granted.

Trump, in a lengthy post to Truth Social Thursday, singled out longtime Republican strategist Karl Rove and Sen. John Cornyn, the incumbent who failed to secure the president's endorsement in a heated primary.

Rove and Cornyn, Trump said, are doing “everything possible” to make it harder for Paxton to defeat Talarico, a state lawmaker and Presbyterian seminarian who is making a suprisingly strong run for Senate in deep red Texas.

“They are hurting Texas and, more importantly, hurting the United States of America!” Trump wrote. “If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career.”

Cornyn, a longtime fixture in Texas politics, lost his bid for reelection in a contentious Republican primary in which he and his supporters portrayed Paxton as a deeply flawed candidate. As Election Day approaches, public polling over the past two months has shown Talarico with a narrow edge against Paxton, the state's attorney general.
Trump urged his supporters to back Paxton.

“Your favorite President (ME!) is asking all of those who supported Senator John Cornyn to UNITE, and immediately switch your support to Ken Paxton,” Trump said. “He will be a Great Senator, just like he is a Great Attorney General. "

The race has also become one of the most expensive non-presidential battles. Talarico raised $64 million this summer — the largest third-quarter haul of any Senate candidate in history. He has raised more than $134 million since launching his campaign last year.

Paxton raised $18 million in the third quarter of 2026 and last month announced a new $20 million ad buy. Earlier this month, though, a Trump operative told POLITICO that MAGA Inc. and its affiliates are could spend nearly $45 million on direct mail, TV and digital advertising in Texas through Oct. 12.
Already, $235 million has been spent by outside conservative groups and party committees against Talarico as national Republicans scramble to boost Paxton.

Some Republicans have grown concerned that the cost of the Texas race is diverting money needed in other states and have expressed frustrations with Paxton after leaked audio showed him blaming Trump for his woes.
Trump easily won Texas in 2024, winning just over 56% of the vote. But concerns about Republicans’ chances this November have surged as the president’s approval rating plummets.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Europe Reckons With a World Where Trump Is Now Helping Putin
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Andrea Palasciano, Alberto Nardelli and Ott Tammik

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- European leaders know they can't stop courting Donald Trump. But as the US president menaces Ukraine and offers Russian an economic lifeline, they are preparing for a world where he effectively sides with Moscow.
Most Read from Bloomberg

In the span of a week, Trump has trashed years of energy sanctions on the Kremlin, pressured Kyiv to quit bombing Russian oil refineries and suggested Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy was an illegitimate leader — echoing Moscow's propaganda. At one point, Ukraine also lost full access to the Elon Musk-owned Starlink system, leaving it hobbled on the battlefield.
In response, Zelenskyy let rip. He felt betrayed, he said. He called out Trump in public.
It was a dismaying moment for the Europeans, according to people familiar with the conversations at a leaders' summit in Brussels this week.

For many, it exposed a painful reality they've been avoiding for months: Trump's instinct is to bash Kyiv and boost Russia. And that's unlikely to change, several European Union leaders, including those of France and Germany, said during their private conversations.
Zelenskyy himself will address the meeting on Friday.

"The western alliance is in a weaker position now than it was a few days ago," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told reporters as she arrived for talks in the Belgian capital Thursday. "If you do not support Ukraine, then you put Europe as a whole, and in my view therefore also NATO as a whole, in a much, much more dangerous situation."

Trump and Zelenskyy have been here before, of course, and always found a way to patch things up. Their first meeting in the Oval Office last year descended into a shouting match and prompted the US to briefly curb intelligence sharing. Later, the US tried to convince Kyiv to accept a 28-point peace plan that overwhelmingly favored Russia, prompting Zelenskyy to warn his country risked losing its key partner.

By this summer, European leaders had managed to persuade Trump to show a degree of sympathy for Ukraine's long fight against the Russian invasion. At the Group of Seven summit in France, President Emmanuel Macron engineered a brief meeting between with Trump at which Zelenskyy showed him pictures of cathedral in Kyiv decimated by Russian missiles.
Their latest falling-out is happening at a particularly inopportune moment.

Winter is setting in and Ukraine has a shortage of the US-made Patriot interceptors needed to shoot down Russian missiles. Kyiv's military costs are also blowing a hole in its budget that Europe is struggling to fill. Meanwhile, Russian is striking more civilian targets, leaving Kyiv experiencing intermittent power and water supply cuts.
Next month, Russian leader Vladimir Putin will have a chance to meet with Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China — where neither Zelenskyy nor the Europeans will be present.

Trump, for his part, is weeks away from a midterm election where his Republican party is expected to suffer heavy losses — sending him searching for quick ways to lower gas prices. That fixation is informing Trump's push to buy Russian diesel despite sanctions, and his calls for Ukraine to halt attacks on oil refineries, even if experts say the US war on Iran is the largest culprit behind high fuel costs.

For now, most Europeans are recommending that Zelenskyy temper his criticism of Trump, given there is no alternative to working with the US, the people said. The country continues to sell Ukraine weapons and share intelligence vital to Kyiv's defense.
If that intelligence disappeared, Europe would not have a good solution, one official said.

That's likely why EU leaders were careful not to be too publicly critical of Trump as they arrived Thursday for their summit in Brussels. Behind closed doors, however, several still expressed shock at the US president's recent behavior, the people said.
An Elysee official said France's priority is for Europe to continue supporting Ukraine. A German chancellery spokesperson didn't immediately reply to a request for comment.

Europe is sticking to its guns by upholding sanctions and insisting that Ukraine shouldn't cede territory in a peace settlement, especially after Kyiv's forces regained some lost ground in the eastern region of Donbas Putin wants to control.

US leverage over Ukraine has also diminished over the last few months. While intelligence remains an important factor, the money to support Kyiv and buy US weapons comes primarily from Europe. Ukraine is also finally receiving ammunition for F-16 fighter jets to shoot down Russia's menacing jet-powered drones.

Meanwhile, Washington's efforts to deliver peace, which Trump promised to bring shortly after taking office last hear, haven't made much headway. The latest meetings in Florida over the weekend, which the Ukrainian delegation cut short following Trump's Russia diesel deal, largely focused on going over the same set of points that the president's envoys — Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner — drew up months ago, according to people familiar with the matter.

During a meeting on Monday, EU foreign ministers privately agreed that Europe's policy on Ukraine must remain constant, regardless of the gyrations in Washington, according to people briefed on the discussions. They resolved to engage the US when it's possible, and maintain their support for Kyiv when it's not.

"We definitely have a different approach to this war," EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas told reporters in Brussels on Thursday. "We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender. Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach."

techcrunch.com/2026/10/15/when-it-came-t.headline: When it came to Cal AI’s viral success, a small army of influencers paid off
techcrunch.com/2026/10/15/when-it-came-t.author: Lucas Ropek

paragraphs.text: Zach Yadegari has enjoyed an immense amount of success for someone who only recently graduated from high school. Founder of the AI-fueled calorie tracking app Cal AI, Yadegari is only 19, but his company has rocketed to viral fame over the past two years. At TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday, Yadegari shared details of that surprising rise to prominence.

Cal AI, which was founded in 2024, exploded its presence on the internet thanks largely to Yadegari’s strategy of deploying a small army of influencers to promote the brand. The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitness for an undisclosed amount of money in March.
Discussing his social strategy onstage, Yadegari noted that an early sign of success came when an influencer’s post about them led to approximately a thousand new users over the course of two days.

“From there, we figured out, okay, this can actually work for us, and so we started recruiting influencers as fast as we could — paying as many people as possible to start posting for us,” he said. “What we saw was that it was a clear formula. It was pretty linear, but it was extremely fast. I guess linear in the sense that every post they did would get a certain number of viewers that would convert.”

The Forbes 30 Under 30 alumnus told the audience that part of his company’s strategy was to negotiate rates with influencers, promising them certain payouts for a certain scale of reach. A lot of influencers are “broke college kids” who are “just want cash,” Yadegari added. “You just ask them, okay, we’ll pay you this, but we need to get us at least this amount of use and keep posting until you get there.”

Another important component of success was finding the right influencers whose reach can be quantified. “The biggest thing for us was finding influencers that had very tight communities,” the founder said.
Yadegari, whose father was in the audience, also credited his family with giving him the freedom to go after his ambitions. Does he also credit higher education for his success? Not so much.
“I think the only real reason to go to college is if you want to have a fun social time as a kid and be with other people,” he said, to audience laughter.
Earlier this month, Yadegari also launched Persona, a new AI agent startup that has already raised $10 million.

Yadegari said the “overarching mission” with Persona is to “make computing seamless with human life.” The company’s personal AI assistant will “live anyplace with internet connection,” he said, including “iMessage, app, email, phone call.” He added that part of what distinguishes the company’s plans for this AI assistant is to build a “hardware ecosystem around” the app.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/15/and-the-winner.author: Sean O'Kane

paragraphs.text: For three days this week in San Francisco, 20 eager startups participated in the Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. The top 20 were chosen to represent the best of the Startup Battlefield 200, and they competed for a chance to take home the Startup Battlefield Cup and $100,000. With that intense pitching now complete, we have a winner.
These startups were handpicked to compete in Startup Battlefield, and all of them presented a live demo in front of the VCs and tech leaders who judged the competition.
After hours of deliberations, TechCrunch editors pored over the judges’ notes and narrowed the list down to five finalists: Apate, Flox Intelligence, Intero Biosystems, Industrial Next, and Satlyt.

The final five made their way to the finale to demo in front of our final panel of judges: Alexa von Tobel of Inspired Capital, Chi-Hua Chien of Goodwater Capital, Dayna Grayson of Construct Capital, Karl Alomar of M13, and Stacy Brown-Philpot of Cherryrock Capital.
We’re now ready to announce that the winner of TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 2026 is:
Winner: Intero Biosystems

Intero Biosystems is a Denver-based startup founded by Charlie Childs and Madeline Eiken that spun out of the University of Michigan. It’s developing 1mm human intestinal “organoids,” lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut, offering another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. The startup sells its flagship product, GastroScreen, to pharmaceutical, biotech, food, and chemical companies for testing drugs and other compounds.
Read more about Intero Biosystems in our separate post here.
Runner-up: Apate

Apate is an Australian startup founded by Dali Kaafar, who came up with the idea while doing research at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia. It deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims, answering scam calls, responding to shady messages and emails, following phishing links, and joining social media groups to bait fraudsters. In addition to access to Apate’s fleet of agents, customers get an insights portal that offers intelligence and analytics on scams targeting their end users or employees, brands, products, and more.
Read more about Apate in our separate post here.

These two companies now join the ranks of Startup Battlefield winners and finalists like Trello, Discord, Cloudflare, and Mint on the Disrupt Stage. With more than 1,700 alumni having participated in the program, Startup Battlefield Alumni have collectively raised over $30 billion in funding with more than 200 successful exits.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/15/tesla-reveals-.headline: Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style
techcrunch.com/2026/10/15/tesla-reveals-.author: Sean O'Kane

paragraphs.text: Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle he has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.”

Tesla CEO Elon Musk showed off the car at an event outside Waco, Texas, with a demonstration that saw the car use a mixture of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and ease itself to a landing on the pavement below. The car also used the thrusters to lift itself up over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while in motion.
Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price.

“This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed going 0-60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.”

Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 nozzles connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in mid-air. That air tank can be re-charged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, calling out the vessels that have been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels.
Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — a famous gap that Evel Knievel tried to jump in a steam-powered rocket.

Musk has positioned it as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said the that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.

“If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year. Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.

“This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”

Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.” An earlier version of the reveal event had reportedly was going to include the car being driven upside down on a magnetized ramp before hovering, which Musk had allegedly scrapped.

The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini, or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the Bond character in The Spy Who Loved Me — a car Musk owns, which was on display at the event.
In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 and F-35 fighter planes.
“Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote.

Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-gen Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Included as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the company promised the revamped Roadster would be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions.

Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …”

But the Roadster project took a back seat. Later that year, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan. The company then moved onto other projects like the Model Y SUV, which became the best-selling vehicle in the world, and the Cybertruck, which was a commercial flop by Tesla’s own standards. Along the way, Musk delayed the new Roadster in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024.

As Tesla got more distance from the launch of those new vehicles, Musk started talking about the second-gen Roadster again. Late last year, he said on Joe Rogan’s podcast that he wanted to reveal it by the end of 2025. One week later, at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026. Musk an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again.
“Like, I could say I was just kidding,” he said at the time. Tesla wound up pushing the reveal again. It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay.
These repeated delays caused a number of high-profile customers to speak out over the years, like YouTuber Marques Brownlee and OpenAI head Sam Altman.

“They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028,” Brownlee posted Thursday. “This is a prank, right?”

finance.yahoo.com/markets/options/articl.headline: JPMorgan, Goldman Boost Yield on Volta AI Loan to Lure Investors
finance.yahoo.com/markets/options/articl.author: Laura Benitez and Jeannine Amodeo

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. hiked the yield and sweetened terms on a $5 billion leveraged loan sale for Volta Infrastructure Holdings Ltd. as investors demand greater compensation to buy risky debt tied to the artificial intelligence boom.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The banks have been marketing the offering for Volta, an AI cloud startup, since last week and sold it on Thursday at 6.5 percentage points above the benchmark rate and a discounted price of 95 cents on the dollar, according to people with knowledge of the matter.
That price point pushed yields up past the 11% that banks had earlier floated, rivaling the highest rates paid so far to finance the AI buildout.
Click here for Bloomberg News' AI Debt Tracker

The deal also offered greater investor protections, and included structural changes that would require the borrower to pay a penalty if the debt is repaid early, one of the people said, asking not to be identified because they're not authorized to speak publicly.
A representative for JPMorgan declined to comment, while those for Goldman Sachs and Volta didn't respond to requests for comment.

Volta is among a group of AI companies known as neoclouds, which rent access to chips and other AI infrastructure. The company's deal will be used to finance a data center complex in Norway that will be managed by Volta Infrastructure in partnership with Bitdeer Technologies Group, a Bitcoin miner that operates data centers.
Anthropic PBC has already signed a six-year agreement for compute capacity at the site, Bloomberg previously reported, citing people familiar with the agreement.

The loan sale immediately rankled managers of collateralized loan obligations — the biggest buyers of leveraged loans — for a number of reasons. For one, it's unrated, which makes it harder for CLOs to buy the debt. But on top of that, it's a large transaction from a debut borrower tapping the market at a volatile time.
Among other changes, the interest rate on the debt will change if Volta gets certain ratings, the person added.

The debt is split into two parts: a $1.3 billion term loan and a $3.7 billion chip loan. The transaction was initially pitched at spreads in the range of 6.25 to 6.5 percentage points above the benchmark rate, and a discounted price of 97 to 98 cents on the dollar.

The $1.3 billion term loan will be used to make lease payments to Bitdeer to use the data center, Bloomberg previously reported. The $3.7 billion chip loan will be used to purchase about 36,000 graphics processing units, or GPUs, made by Nvidia Corp.

The deal has faced increased scrutiny amid a tech selloff that sent AI cloud-computing provider CoreWeave Inc.'s junk bonds plunging into distressed territory. Yields on CoreWeave's debt topped 15% this week, with a measure of credit risk climbing to an all-time high.

Volta was founded earlier this year by Ricard Boada and Sofia Gumuzio, two former executives from Brookfield Asset Management Ltd.'s infrastructure business. The company's goal is to make it easier for top AI labs and smaller startups to pay for Nvidia's cutting-edge chips.
