politico.com/news/2026/10/16/senate-repu.headline: Senate Republicans are getting smoked in fundraising
politico.com/news/2026/10/16/senate-repu.author: Lisa Kashinsky and Andrew Howard

paragraphs.text: Republican Senate candidates are hurting for cash.
Nearly every Democratic candidate in battleground Senate races outraised their GOP opponent from July through September. And in some cases, the disparities were stark.
• In Texas, Democrat James Talarico trounced Republican Ken Paxton $60.2 million to $10.2 million in their main campaign accounts.
• In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff raised $33.1 million to Rep. Mike Collins’ nearly $2.8 million.
• In North Carolina, Democrat Roy Cooper raised $12.2 million to Michael Whatley’s $2.1 million.
• In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed hauled in roughly $33 million to former Rep. Mike Rogers’ nearly $10 million.
• In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson raised $20.5 million to GOP Sen. Susan Collins’ $5.2 million.
• In Ohio, Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown hauled in $23.1 million to GOP Sen. Jon Husted’s $4.8 million.
• In Iowa, Josh Turek raised $13.9 million to Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson’s nearly $3.3 million.
• In Alaska, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola raked in $17 million to GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan’s nearly $2.7 million.
• In New Hampshire, Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas brought in $8.1 million to Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu’s $1.5 million.
• And in Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton raised nearly $9.9 million to GOP Sen. Roger Marshall’s just $866,000.

Across those 10 Senate races, the Democratic campaigns raised more than five times as much as the Republican ones. Put another way: Talarico alone raised more than all those Republicans combined. Marshall and Whatley each started October with less than $1 million left in the bank. Mike Collins wasn’t much better-positioned, entering the final weeks of the election with just over $1 million cash on hand.
These numbers do not include joint fundraising committees, which allow candidates to raise money and may have some more cash that has not yet been transferred to the campaigns.

Democrats have consistently outraised Republicans on the candidate level this cycle. But the yawning gaps heading into the midterm’s home stretch stand as the latest example of the deteriorating environment for the GOP.

And while GOP outside groups have significantly more money than Democrats, this candidate cash advantage matters because candidates get TV ads for much cheaper rates, letting their dollars stretch much farther.
To underscore how lopsided some of these figures are: At least half a dozen House Democratic challengers raised over $3 million in the third quarter — a sum higher than several GOP Senate incumbents.
There are some silver linings for the GOP.
In Minnesota, Republican Michele Tafoya raised $4.9 million to Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan’s $4.3 million. Tafoya started the month with $2.1 million to Flanagan’s $1.5 million.
Sullivan, Husted, Hinson, Rogers and Susan Collins all entered October with millions more in cash on hand than their Democratic opponents.

And Republicans are getting air cover from GOP super PACs bankrolled by billionaire Elon Musk and President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. that have pumped hundreds of millions of dollars into the midterms in recent weeks.

Musk was revealed on Thursday as the primary funder of Texas PAC, which has spent $131 million so far boosting Paxton and attacking Talarico. Musk gave $158 million to Senate Republicans’ super PAC arm last quarter, the filings showed, with the group in turn transferring the funds to the pro-Paxton PAC.

Republicans are also benefitting from a recent Supreme Court ruling that allows party committees to spend unlimited sums in coordination with candidates, allowing the National Republican Senatorial Committee to offset at least some of the differences.
Since the tranche of reports filed Thursday only cover until Sept. 30, the full scope of each candidates’ coffers is unknown.

But there are other signs that some are strapped for cash in the final sprint: Whatley has gone dark on television, a clear indication of him running low on funds even as his campaign insists it’s a temporary pause.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/15/even-benchmark.headline: Even Benchmark thinks AI is eroding the venture pact against backing rivals
techcrunch.com/2026/10/15/even-benchmark.author: Connie Loizos

paragraphs.text: For decades, the unwritten rule of venture capital was that a firm doesn’t back two companies that compete head-on. But speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this week, the partners of Benchmark readily acknowledged that the AI boom is straining that rule.

It’s been on the verge of snapping for some time. The towering AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic share dozens of the same investors at this point. Then, at the end of September, Factory, a startup that builds an AI agent to write software, said it was firing board observer and adviser Chris Degnan for “unethical conduct involving Cognition,” its direct rival and the maker of the Devin coding agent. Factory’s CEO alleged Degnan had discussed a job at Cognition while privy to Factory’s board-level discussions. Degnan said he had already resigned and denied sharing anything confidential. Soon after, he announced he was joining Cognition as chief revenue officer. Powerhouse investor Vinod Khosla sided with Degnan on X, blasting Factory’s CEO and calling the company “a struggling second tier competitor.” Khosla Ventures backs both companies.

Even Benchmark, a firm whose reputation rests on 10-to-15-year partnerships with founders at the earliest stage, said the old rule can no longer be counted on. Asked at Disrupt whether the pact against backing rivals still holds as portfolio companies expand into each other’s territory, its partners described the conflicts as a matter of necessity, not preference.

“The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly,” said Eric Vishria. Companies pivot and change, he said, and “you are going to get conflicts, and that’s just the reality of the current dynamic.”

Vishria said Benchmark stays committed to each founder and keeps what it learns confidential, and he downplayed how much a VC could pass along anyway: “We are not product or technology experts.” Seemingly referring to the Factory-Cognition dispute, he said Benchmark has been fortunate not to land in “that type of insane direct conflict.” Exclusivity, he said, remains “really important” at the very early stage Benchmark favors. “But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.”

Chetan Puttagunta said AI is accelerating the problem. As the cost of building software “effectively goes to zero,” he said, founders are “incredibly ambitious.” Because they now see a “surface area” and want to claim all of it, he continued, “[i]t’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other.”
He drew a line between a direct competitor at the outset, which he called “an easy answer,” and a portfolio company that expands into another’s turf over time. “That happens,” he said.

Peter Fenton called the issue “kryptonite” and the firm’s toughest problem. He described a spectrum of how investors relate to their companies. At one end is the co-founder, who would never work on a competing company. At the other is the public-market stock picker, who can own several rivals because he is merely allocating capital, not shaping any of them. Benchmark sits nearer the co-founder end, Fenton said, and treats transparency as a golden rule. “There shouldn’t be the surprise after the fact.” If a conflict does emerge, a founder should never feel shortchanged, he added.
Benchmark isn’t declaring the pact dead. At the same time, when a firm that built its name on loyalty says conflicts are coming, founders might rightly wonder who else will be this candid.
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

Loizos has been reporting on Silicon Valley since the late ’90s, when she joined the original Red Herring magazine. Previously the Silicon Valley Editor of TechCrunch, she was named Editor in Chief and General Manager of TechCrunch in September 2023. She’s also the founder of StrictlyVC, a daily e-newsletter and lecture series acquired by Yahoo in August 2023 and now operated as a sub brand of TechCrunch.
You can contact or verify outreach from Connie by emailing [email protected] or [email protected], or via encrypted message at ConnieLoizos.53 on Signal.

theguardian.com/global-development/2026/.headline: Saudi Arabia to execute man for being at protests and funerals when he was 15
theguardian.com/global-development/2026/.author: Tom Levitt

paragraphs.text: A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.

Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.
The charity Reprieve says Manasif was tortured and coerced into signing a false confession and only met his state-appointed lawyer for the first time in 2022 – five years after his arrest.
Manasif’s death sentence has now reportedly been upheld by the Saudi supreme court, which was likely to be his last hope of avoiding execution.

His family have not spoken in public about the case and could face harassment or arrest if they do so. “There is nothing they can do now but wait,” said Duaa Dhainy, a consultant for Reprieve and the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights.

Saudi Arabia has seen what activists describe as a “horrifying” surge in executions under the rule of the crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. Last year saw a record 356 people put to death in the country. Most of those executed are foreigners convicted of minor and non-violent drug crimes.
At least 17 people, who were children at the time of their alleged offences, have been executed in Saudi Arabia since 2015, according to Reprieve.
Saudi Arabia issued a royal decree abolishing the death penalty for children in 2020, stating that individuals would not be sentenced to death for crimes committed when they were minors.

However, it has since upheld the death penalty in a number of cases involving child defendants. In April, it executed Ali al-Subaiti, along with his uncle, Mustafa al-Subaiti, for non-lethal “terrorist” offences committed when he was 12 years old.

The UN’s independent human rights experts have previously expressed concerns about Manasif’s case. It said Saudi Arabia should immediately halt planned executions of people convicted of offences allegedly committed when they were under 18. “They are using execution as a tool to show how powerful they are and how they can threaten anyone who does not follow their rules,” Dhainy said of the Saudi regime. “We think he should be treated as a minor and not sentenced to death as his charges relate to when he was under 18.”
Human Rights Watch said executing Manasif for a non-violent crime committed as a minor would be “an unconscionable new low”.

wsj.com/finance/investing/indonesian-sto.headline: Indonesian Stocks Dive as MSCI Weighs Downgrade to Standalone Market

paragraphs.text: Indonesian stocks suffered their biggest drop since the 2008 global financial crisis after index provider MSCI said the country risked being removed from its indexes, reigniting fears about the investability of the Southeast Asian economy.
The Jakarta Composite Index plunged more than 10% on Friday, on track for its biggest daily percentage drop in 18 years. The benchmark index had opened 8% lower, triggering a temporary halt.
The selloff pushed the JCI's losses this year to nearly 40%, making it the worst-performing Asian stock market. The rupiah weakened to around 18,045 against the dollar.

MSCI on Thursday launched a consultation on a potential reclassification of Indonesia from emerging-market to standalone status, which would remove the country's equities from its main indexes. Indonesia would be the first Asia-Pacific market to have a standalone status if the proposed downgrade takes place.
The latest move marks an escalation from January, when MSCI warned it could downgrade the country to frontier-market status, citing investability and transparency concerns.

Under scrutiny by global index providers and credit rating agencies, Indonesian authorities have announced reforms and sought to address market concerns. MSCI in its statement said investors' feedback suggests a frontier-market reclassification won't properly recognize the depth of the market problems.

"Market participants have indicated to MSCI that, to date, sufficient progress has not been observed consistently across the Indonesian equity market," MSCI said. "Significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behavior and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement."
The index provider is taking feedback through April 2027 and will announce its decision by the end of June.

npr.org/2026/10/16/g-s1-148366/owl-famil.headline: A rare family of barn owls moved into Manhattan's Upper West Side. New Yorkers are captivated
npr.org/2026/10/16/g-s1-148366/owl-famil.author: The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: NEW YORK — Manhattan's Upper West Side has been reveling in the company of its latest celebrities: A family of barn owls nested in a water tower atop a building near Central Park.

This is the first documented instance of barn owls nesting in Manhattan in modern history, according to one expert, and the owls have attracted nightly crowds of people in the street eager to get a glimpse of the elusive birds.

"It was, like, totally shocking," Andrew Farnsworth, a migration ecologist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, said of the barn owls. "To the best of our knowledge, like the collective birding knowledge, there hasn't been a nest in, you know, in Manhattan, at least in recorded history."

Word of the barn owl family didn't get around until last week, when Elisabeth Williams, an Upper West Side resident, notified a local news outlet on Oct. 6 that she and her husband saw multiple owls at the water tower atop a building on West 75th Street close to Central Park West.
The couple had previously seen a single owl on an apartment windowsill a few days earlier and were shocked even then, Williams recalled.
"In a place like Manhattan, you normally really have to go out of your way to encounter nature," she said. "And here it was, just sort of right outside our window."
Barn owl sightings are rare in New York City

It's not the first time that birds have captivated New Yorkers. Residents have fallen in love with American woodcocks, who are known to stop in Midtown Manhattan's Bryant Park every year as they migrate north in early spring.

After Flaco the Eurasian eagle-owl died in 2024, dozens of mournful fans gathered to say goodbye to the beloved creature who flew around Manhattan and became a joy to many after someone let him out of his zoo enclosure the previous year. Then there was Pale Male, a red-tailed hawk who nested above Fifth Avenue for three decades before dying in 2023.

But barn owl sightings in New York City parks are very rare, according to the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation. New York is at the northern fringe of the barn owl's range and the barn owl population has declined "at an alarming rate" over time, according to the state Department of Environmental Conservation.

"There's lots of excitement among New Yorkers, both birders and non-birders alike, about these owls because owls really capture the attention," said Jessica Wilson, executive director of NYC Bird Alliance. "They're magical, they're nocturnal, they are secretive, they're not commonly seen, especially on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. And to have this chance to see these birds is really thrilling."
Photographers and casual onlookers have gathered on the street on a nightly basis to spot the owls.

"I've only seen one barn owl ever, and that was in California," said Val Coleman, a retired New York City resident who was on the Upper West Side earlier this week trying to spot the owls. "At dusk, we hope they will come out to hunt. We hope they don't eat poisoned rats with rodenticide in 'em."

David Barrett, a Manhattan-based birder who runs the popular social media account, Manhattan Bird Alert, said he's observed at least one adult barn owl and five fledglings at the water tower. He's also seen an adult owl carrying rodents back to the water tower. There are believed to be two adult owls, and some photographers have claimed to have seen six fledglings, Barrett added.
"Having one barn owl is a rarity, but it's not national news. Having a family, for the first time ever, breeding in Manhattan in recorded history, that's special news," Barrett said.
Screeching was heard by residents

Before the recent barn owl sightings, Williams and her husband heard periodic screeching noises outside going back to early September. They initially assumed it was a bird of some kind but were skeptical when a phone app indicated the noise was from a barn owl.
Thomas Obersteiner said that he first heard bizarre screeching and wailing noises from outside one evening in mid-September. It sounded like someone was "being murdered outside," he said.
"That lasted for two or three weeks, every night, sometimes more, sometimes less, coming from different directions," Obersteiner added. "But I had no idea what that was."

On multiple occasions, Obersteiner or his wife ran into their children's bedroom after mistaking the owls' screech for a child in pain, he said. It wasn't until he saw a news report that he realized that owls were making the sounds.
Farnsworth said the screech is typical of barn owls, who use it to communicate with one another. The screech is like a "horror movie kind of experience," he said.

Obersteiner, who said his roof deck is "probably the best location in town right now" to watch the owls, has been letting nature photographers access that perch to observe the owls "almost every night" since news of the barn owls spread. On one night last week, 20 people had gathered.
"We can't say no because it's so much fun and these people are so serious," Obersteiner added. "It's beautiful."
Williams and her husband were not bird watchers before the barn owl family moved in to the water tower. But that may change soon after their "delightful" experience.
"I think we're about to become birders," Williams said.

wsj.com/pro/central-banking/bank-of-engl.headline: Bank of England Governor Says Too Early to Make Call on Second-Round Inflation

paragraphs.text: The U.K. has felt the first round of inflationary impact from war in the Middle East in higher energy prices. The question for the Bank of England is whether that is passing through into broader price growth, Gov. Andrew Bailey said Friday.
Inflation in the U.K. is above the central bank's target but it is too early to tell if that is spilling over into indirect and second-round effects, Bailey said.
"To the extent we have seen evidence, it's quite subdued," he said at the Institute of International Finance's annual membership meeting in Bangkok.
Before the war broke out in late February, inflation was on track to reach the BOE's target late spring, Bailey said. "It's enormously frustrating."
Preconflict, markets had been pricing in a couple of rate cuts by the BOE, which Bailey said seemed "pretty reasonable."
That came off the table in March.
"So we have effectively tightened policy. We haven't raised the official rate, but we've effectively tightened policy relative to where it was expected to be," the governor said.
That has been reflected in U.K. mortgage rates, which are among the top end of Group of Seven economies in terms of increases, he said.
Though he cautioned against prematurely forming strong views on second-round inflation, Bailey said he isn't taking the impact for granted.

Discussions with companies around the country showed a "very big focus on cost-cutting," he said. "That's the inflation story at the moment. That's the judgment we have to keep making at every meeting: what are we going to see in terms of...the pass-through."
On the positive side, the economy has turned out to be more resilient than expected, Bailey said.
"But it's not as strong a growth as we need and as we've had in the past," he added.
The remarks came ahead of the central bank's next meeting in early November, shedding some light into what Bailey described as the building blocks of its thinking on rates.
To anyone thinking they have worked out what the BOE is going to do from those comments, however, Bailey had a clear message: "You haven't."

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.headline: Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case not ‘prioritised’ due to high workload, inquest hears
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.author: Andrew Messenger

paragraphs.text: Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case was not “prioritised” or worked intensively because the staff member assigned to her case was “very busy”, a coroner has heard.

The Queensland coroners court also heard the case worker may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of Struhs’ “upper class home”, putting cases that believed to involve a more immediate risk ahead of Elizabeth’s.

The eight-year-old died on 7 January 2022 of diabetic ketoacidosis, after her father, Jason Struhs, stopped providing insulin to treat her type 1 diabetes at their home in Toowoomba, Queensland. A long-term sceptic of his wife’s beliefs, he had converted to them and joined her religious sect – which subscribed to an extreme form of Christianity and denied the use of medicine – in 2021.

Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard is holding an inquest into Elizabeth’s death. She has previously heard the eight-year-old came to the attention of child safety after a 2019 incident where she presented to hospital in a coma.
Child safety ended its involvement with the family after just 17 weeks of what was supposed to be an intensive intervention, assessing her as “safe”.

But the single child safety officer assigned to Elizabeth’s case told the court on Friday her approach wasn’t intensive and she didn’t make weekly check-ins during that period, despite departmental guidelines.

The department chose to release her back into Jason’s sole care over the objections of specialist doctors who treated Elizabeth in Brisbane, subject to a voluntary intervention with parental agreement (IPA).
The coroner heard just a single child safety officer was assigned to the case, and would often conduct home visits alone.
The officer gave evidence on Friday.

“Ideally I wanted to visit with the family at least once a week, in accordance with our IPAT (intervention with parental agreement team) guidelines,” according to her statement, presented to the court.

“During my management of the IPA for the Struhs family, I recall that I was not always available to conduct home visits with the family. I recall this being a very busy time for the CSSC (child safety service centre) and I also recall being regularly out of the office travelling to visit other families.
“I note that one of the home visits to the Struhs family was conducted by a student who was working in the team at the time.”
She said Elizabeth’s case wasn’t treated as a complex case, which it should have been due to the intervention.

But at the time, she had a “big caseload” – approximately 25-28 children in 15 families on the same intervention– she said. The coroner has previously heard that the Toowoomba region was among the busiest in the state for child safety.

Counsel assisting Simon Hamlyn-Harris said most of them were experiencing significant domestic violence, drug use, sexual abuse and it was not often that she was required to work with “upper class families” like the Struhs.
The case worker agreed that she may and may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of the Struhs home.
“I believe that we may have prioritised other cases at the time for children who were presenting at more immediate risk,” she told the court.
She also told the court that she may have had a bias because her own child had nearly died of type 1 diabetes at age 6. She had asked not to be assigned to the case, she said.

Several witnesses have previously told the coroner they expected the intervention to last months or a year, but the case worker said they were supposed to not last longer than three months, because they were an intensive approach.
On Friday, Kirkegaard asked another child safety witness whether they felt “organisational pressure to get a matter like this finalised quickly”.
“Absolutely,” the witness said, adding an IPA could be intrusive and potentially harmful to a child if dragged out.
“I don’t believe it impacted our decision making,” she said.
On 13 November 2019, a more senior child safety officer assessed Elizabeth as “safe” and the intervention was ended.
The case worker told the coroner on Friday that she hadn’t appreciated the danger of Elizabeth’s mother’s church group, which was considered a source of support for the family.
All 14 adult members of the sect – known as the Saints – were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including Elizabeth’s parents, Kerrie and Jason, and the group leader, Brendan Stevens.
In her statement she said Jason had agreed to continue to treat his daughter against his wife’s beliefs and that she had “faith” that should Kerrie stand in the way he’d leave her.
None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.
The inquest continues.

theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/16/.headline: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/16/.author: Stefano Valentino, Ajit Niranjan

paragraphs.text: Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.

Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.

Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland.
Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people.

“We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.”

Electric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined.

Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes.

In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam.

Public filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL.

The investigation, published in partnership with Voxeurop and other European media partners, traced shipments from mines and refineries in Sulawesi to China, and then again from Huayou cathode and CATL battery factories to the assembly lines of carmakers in the US and Europe. Volkswagen’s facility in Braunschweig, for instance, received a shipment in October 2024 of 24 tonnes of cell modules worth about $390,000, according to data from Volza, a trade platform.

The shift to a carbon-free economy is pushing up demand for critical minerals in countries with weak environmental safeguards, though experts have argued the mining boom can be tempered without slowing the shift away from dirty fuels. In 2023, a report found lithium demand in the US transport sector could be reduced by 18% to 66% compared with a business-as-usual scenario, by improving public transport, walking and cycling more, and buying smaller cars. Better recycling could bring demand reductions as high as 92%, the report found.

Global demand for nickel is set to double to 5.5m tonnes by 2040, according to the International Energy Agency, much of it mined in Indonesia and then refined in China. The loss of trees in mining concessions means the carbon footprint of nickel from the worst mines may be up to 500 times greater than previously reported, a study in Nature Communications found last year.

The Cahaya and Hengjaya mines are located in woodlands designated as “production forest”, which are intended for forestry rather than industrial activities. However, successive Indonesian governments have weakened safeguards and carved out exemptions for miners as demand for nickel has soared.

Nickel mining may be responsible for two-thirds of the forest loss recorded since 2001 within the area encompassed by the Cahaya concession, and over half of the loss in the Hengjaya concession, spatial analysis conducted by geospatial firm TreeMap suggests.

Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral (SCM), the company that operates the Cahaya mine, contributed to clearing an additional 330 hectares of forest in 2024, according to an analysis by Auriga, an Indonesian nonprofit. The same year, it delivered 11m tonnes of limonite ore – almost all of its production – to Huayou’s smelter. Deliveries increased to nearly 12.5m tonnes throughout 2025. The plant also continued to receive ore from the Hengjaya mine by road, local lorry drivers said.

SCM received two administrative sanctions last year for illegally clearing more than 450 hectares of forest beyond the boundaries of its permitted clearing area. The company is a subsidiary of Merdeka Battery Materials, part of a group whose shareholders include Huayou and CATL.

The carmakers identified as end-users of Huayou cathodes or recipients of shipments from CATL include Volkswagen, Volvo, Ford, General Motors, Tesla, BMW, Stellantis and Hyundai. Mercedes-Benz was separately linked to Huayou.

Many of the companies said they did not source nickel directly, they assessed and mitigated adverse impacts, and they required suppliers to comply with responsible sourcing standards. They declined to share the results of on-site audits.
Volkswagen, Europe’s leading manufacturer, which powered one-quarter of its vehicles with CATL systems in 2024, said it could not rule out that the companies may fall within its supply chain.

Volkswagen said: “We take potential risks in our supply chain very seriously. However, due to contractual obligations with our business partners, we cannot disclose specific details on our supplier relationships or their supply chain.”
Ford said: “We are committed to protecting human rights and the environment. We are reviewing the allegations and will determine any appropriate next steps based on that review.”

Mercedes-Benz said: “We take reports of environmental and social harm in raw material supply chains – including nickel from Indonesia – seriously and assess them as part of our risk-based due diligence.”

Renault Group said: “We have identified a nickel mining site in Sulawesi, Indonesia, as being a tier-n supplier (eg. indirect) in our battery supply chain. We have engaged with the relevant business partners to verify some ESG information concerning Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral.”

Volvo Cars said: “During 2025, we conducted […] onsite audits […] on suppliers [who are] part of our battery supply chains, two of them located in Indonesia […] with further battery supply chain partners during 2026 and onward.”
General Motors said: “We are aware that nickel mining in Indonesia presents significant environmental, human-rights and community-related risks.”

Stellantis said: “We are aware of the environmental and social challenges associated with nickel production in Indonesia, including risks related to deforestation, biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation.”

Hyundai said: “We recognise the importance of protecting forests, biodiversity and local communities. We regularly monitor and assess our suppliers, including mineral suppliers, to ensure compliance.”
CATL, Huayou, SCM and Tesla did not respond to requests for comment. Tsingshan, the main shareholder of Nickel Industries, which operates Hengjaya mine, did not respond to a request for comment.
This investigation was supported by Journalismfund Europe and The Pulitzer Center. Lorenzo Di Stasi and James Jackson contributed reporting.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.headline: Greens leader denies knowledge of ‘secret dossier’ on how to handle Jordon Steele-John misconduct allegations
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.author: Sarah Basford Canales

paragraphs.text: Greens leader David Shoebridge has denied knowledge of the existence of an alleged crisis management document on how to deal with allegations against Jordon Steele-John being made public.

The Nine newspapers reported on Friday afternoon the existence of a “secret dossier”, first drafted in 2016, which contained misconduct allegations against the Western Australian Greens senator and how to suppress their media coverage.
Guardian Australia has not independently confirmed the document’s contents.
In a statement responding to claims that the federal leader’s office had access to the 47-page document, Shoebridge said it was not “made by, used by, or seen by the leader’s office”.
“The office is committed to having the matters comprehensively investigated with a fair, independent and timely process,” he said.
“Everyone deserves a safe workplace, and all complaints should be considered in a fair and robust process.”

Steele-John confirmed he would leave the party room on Thursday after some details of historical complaints about inappropriate comments made to women ranging between 2017 and 2025 were publicly aired in the media.

The 32-year-old senator rejected the claims and said he had referred them to the Western Australian Greens for a “fair, independent process” that “upholds the principles of natural justice and ensures procedural fairness for everyone involved”.
“I utterly reject this characterisation of me, which tries to assert I am someone I am not,” Steele-John said in a statement.

Shoebridge told ABC on Friday morning he referred the complaints outlined in a letter to the parliamentary workplace support service, which he said was “unable to deal with it because of the circumstances and nature of the allegation”.

The PWSS’s chief executive, Leonie McGregor, said the office had not been given the letter but had provided Shoebridge’s office with options, including referring the complaints to the independent parliamentary standards commission.
Guardian Australia understands Shoebridge has now referred the matter to the IPSC.
The WA Greens confirmed on Thursday they would “seek legal advice on how best to establish an independent inquiry” into the matters raised.

A statement from the co-conveners, Giz Watson and Simone Collins, and state director, Dean Smith, said: “Our party is built on the contributions of members, volunteers, staff and supporters, and every one of them deserves to feel safe and respected when they take part in our work. Maintaining that safety is a responsibility we hold seriously.”
Shoebridge confirmed Steele-John would not return to parliament until the independent investigations had been completed.
“It’s my understanding that leave means leave,” he told ABC.

“I have responsibility for the party room and the Greens’ functions, and I have some capacity to direct in relation to the party room. But Senator Steele-John has indicated to me that he’s on leave, and that leave means leave.”

technologyreview.com/2026/10/16/1145840/.headline: This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration
technologyreview.com/2026/10/16/1145840/.author: Linda Marsa

paragraphs.text: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) affects more than 5 million people around the world. And until now, no treatment could restore their vision. The Prima system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones.

Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off. Prima’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and medical director for Prima.
CAPTURE

Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing camera capture what someone is seeing in real time. The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV. The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a fiber-optic cable.
CONVERT

A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses. The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom.
DISPLAY

A laser projector on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of near-infrared light directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength. This signal passes through the pupil and on to the retinal implant in the back of the eye.
SEE

The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an electrode and two photovoltaic cells, which do double duty. They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain. They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery.
Linda Marsa is a former Los Angeles Times reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Taiwan to Curb AI Chip Exports to China as Part of US Trade Deal
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Tom Giles, Miaojung Lin and Debby Wu

paragraphs.text: Tom Giles, Miaojung Lin and Debby Wu
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 12:49 AM CDT 3 min read

(Bloomberg) -- Taiwan is preparing to tighten export controls on AI chips to further align with US restrictions, according to a senior official in Taipei, joining a Trump administration clampdown on the smuggling of cutting-edge semiconductors to China.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Taipei plans to add artificial intelligence servers and cutting-edge semiconductors to a list of controlled items, Taiwan's Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin told Bloomberg News. After the measures take effect, he said, shipping restricted AI hardware to China will become a criminal offense under the Foreign Trade Act.

"Going forward, some of our measures on controlled items will correspond to American ones because we have made quite some commitments in the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade," Kung said in an interview on Oct. 12, referring to the trade deal that the US and Taiwan signed this year, though he declined to elaborate on when the government will implement the new measures.

The US has long restricted Chinese purchases of AI chips from Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc., but companies in China have still managed to get their hands on the coveted accelerators through a sophisticated black market. US officials have alleged that billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia hardware has made its way to China over the past few years.

Taiwan currently doesn't treat unauthorized AI chip exports to China as a crime. While Taiwanese officials warn potential sellers that they may be violating US rules if they ship to China, the only legal recourse through the island's courts is to charge suspected smugglers with violations of other, existing local laws.

Once the new measures are in place, the controls would be among the strictest measures from President Lai Ching-te's administration to safeguard Taiwan's technological and national security interests, as Taipei tests its comfort levels with more assertive policies — and manages pressure from American officials on multiple fronts.
Lai has previously said Taiwan will address unspecified US concerns over export controls, without offering details.

Local authorities were exploring more legal tools to address diversion of advanced hardware to enable Taiwan to prosecute AI chip smuggling to China as a criminal violation for the first time, Bloomberg News reported earlier this year.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Warsh Boosts Market Expectations of Fed Hold in October
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Catarina Saraiva

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh did nothing to dispel market expectations that the US central bank will hold interest rates steady when it meets at the end of the month.
Most Read from Bloomberg

In a moderated discussion Friday morning in Bangkok at the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings, Warsh made no remarks on monetary policy or his outlook for the US economy, save for reiterating that the Fed will deliver price stability.

"We made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago," Warsh said. "I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year."
Investors pared their bets for a rate hike at the central bank's Oct. 27-28 policy gathering. The odds, which were hovering around 27% before Warsh spoke, dropped below 15% following his remarks.
"It was clear that he wasn't going to deliver anything that the market could latch on to as hawkish," Derek Tang, an economist at Monetary Policy Analytics, wrote in a note to clients.

The Fed raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point in September, the first hike since 2023. It was backed by all 19 policymakers, and a majority also saw another increase as likely this year.
A few key officials in recent weeks reiterated that additional rate hikes may be needed, but emphasized they have time to gather economic data before acting again.

Warsh repeated his bullish views on artificial intelligence, calling it the most important innovation in the global economy during his lifetime. But he also warned that it may be driving demand in the near term.
The Fed chief said that as a central banker, he's taking the new technology seriously but also "soberly, responsibly."

"It's obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it's going to hit the supply side of the economy," Warsh said. "If you're a central banker, you're in the business of trying to ensure stable prices and full employment, you've got to recognize this as a shock."
While it's a positive supply shock in the medium term, Warsh argued, it's driving increases in aggregate demand now.
Some of Warsh's colleagues have expressed similar concerns, even questioning whether the surge in investment that's buoying the AI build-out could lead to an overheating of the economy.

Warsh also announced that his task force on productivity and jobs – which is grappling with the implications of AI — will hold a field hearing in the San Francisco Bay Area on Nov. 16. It's one of five task forces Warsh convened that will present recommendations to the Federal Open Market Committee late this year or early in 2027.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Trump’s AI Task Force to Commission Report on Technology’s Risks
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: John Harney

paragraphs.text: Thu, October 15, 2026 at 11:22 PM CDT 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump's artificial intelligence task force in its first meeting agreed on Thursday to address risks related to cybersecurity, biosecurity and "model control and accountability" as fears rise over the potential dangers posed by the technology.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The panel known as the Super Intelligence Force — using the president's preferred term for artificial intelligence — will commission a report from the President's Council of Advisers on Science and Technology to evaluate those and other concerns, according to a White House account of the meeting.

The task force will also "develop protocols and mechanisms for labs to provide early warnings and systemized notifications to the government of breaches, hacks, jailbreaks, and other issues," it said.

In addition, the group, led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, plans to "establish a law enforcement and consumer protection coordination committee including the Department of Justice, Federal Trade Commission, and various agencies," the White House said.

AI has emerged as a volatile issue in the midterm elections that will decide control of both houses of Congress. Lawmakers of both parties have particularly taken notice of the widespread opposition around the country to data centers, which have been associated with surging electricity costs.
Alarm over the possibility of widespread job losses and the potential for disaster if humans lose control of AI have largely drowned out promises of its benefits.
Even so, Trump has rejected pleas for more government regulation of AI, insisting that would hinder the US in its AI competition with China.

He instead forged a voluntary agreement with industry executives that uses outside auditors to assess AI system safety. Under the accord, which Trump brokered with top technology leaders at the White House last month, AI executives pledged to regularly meet to set best industry practices.

The task force, according to the White House account, did not discuss any new laws or rules, but "will engage with frontier model developers and other SI companies, consumer protection groups and civil liberties advocates, industry stakeholders, and federal and state law enforcement agencies to inform and implement its efforts."

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Taiwan to Fund $4 Billion Texas Complex for AI, Nvidia Partners
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Tom Giles, Miaojung Lin and Debby Wu

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Taiwan plans to raise billions of dollars to develop industrial parks in the US that would build a base for a comprehensive supply chain for Nvidia Corp. and other AI hardware makers in the country.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The initiative is starting with a complex in Texas that would cost as much as $4 billion to build, according to Taiwan's Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin. The facilities would help smaller suppliers that are essential to the operations of Nvidia's main production partner Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and AI server assemblers including Foxconn Technology Group to set up shop in the US, Kung said.

Each complex would run between $2 billion and $4 billion to build, and the government is planning "more than one" site on US soil, Kung said in an Oct. 12 interview with Bloomberg News. The Taiwanese government is partnering with the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers' Association, which will be responsible for raising required funding to develop the complexes, he said.
"We are going to establish a long-term, sustainable supply chain there that can also be joined by American firms and local workers, and not just Taiwanese companies," Kung said.

Companies like TSMC, Foxconn and Wistron Corp. provide essential hardware for data centers and are critical to the success of US AI chipmakers including Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices Inc., and cloud service providers such as Meta Platforms Inc. and Microsoft Corp. These Taiwanese manufacturing titans depend in turn on lesser-known partners that make a wide range of parts from chip packaging substrates to cooling modules — everything that's required in an AI data center.

But while TSMC and Foxconn are capable of funding and managing their own US expansion, that's not always the case for smaller firms. That's how Taiwan is hoping the new industrial complexes in the US could help.

Many of these suppliers got a boost from Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang when he cited the names of a few dozen parts makers during a keynote presentation in Taipei earlier this year, a gesture that signaled how indispensable the firms are to the global AI ecosystem.

Taiwanese officials will back suppliers that seek to operate in these parks, including by offering loan guarantees and helping communicate with local and federal officials in the US on needs ranging from visas to land, Kung said. Earlier this year, Taiwan pledged to help support $250 billion in credit guarantees for further investment in the American semiconductor supply chain as part of its trade deal with the US.

Taiwan has already secured a plot of land for an industrial park in Texas, according to a person familiar with the matter. In response, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said it will elaborate on the plan at a suitable time.

Developing a robust supply-chain on US soil has taken on new urgency for Taiwan, which is under pressure to deliver on its investment commitments under the trade deal forged with the Trump administration earlier this year. The self-governing island is also seeking to mitigate the geopolitical risks to its biggest tech manufacturers from long-standing tensions with China.

TSMC alone has pledged to spend $265 billion to build advanced chipmaking plants in Arizona, the largest-ever foreign investment in America. Meanwhile, Nvidia's major server assembly partners including Foxconn and Wistron have been expanding their US production capacity to capture growth opportunities from the domestic AI infrastructure buildout.

AI demand is so massive that it's offering a great opportunity for manufacturers to reshore production to the US, the minister said. Lucrative margins from such business can help cover the high costs initially incurred when building factories in the US, he added, and costs will gradually fall as companies scale up their operations.

At the same time, Taiwanese suppliers are under huge time pressure to fulfill AI orders and are ramping up production both at home and overseas, Kung added. He said that while TSMC is making a major commitment in the US, it's going to build "many, many more" plants at home. The Taiwanese government isn't worried about TSMC's global expansion, which is a move to turn its customers into strategic partners, Kung said.
Read: TSMC Open to Working With Terafab But Must Control Plants
Texas has become a popular destination for Taiwanese companies after both Foxconn and Wistron recently expanded their presence there.

TSMC said on Thursday it's also exploring Texas as a new site in the US, although when asked whether the company has decided on the Lone Star state, Kung said the chipmaker is looking at "many locations" for additional investments without elaborating. TSMC declined to comment.

Kung quipped that Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk, who has vowed to take on TSMC in chipmaking, is welcome to use the new supply chain created by Taiwanese companies in the US, "though we will not completely transfer our technology to him."

politico.com/news/2026/10/16/haley-steve.headline: Haley Stevens is everywhere — except on the trail for El-Sayed
politico.com/news/2026/10/16/haley-steve.author: Adam Wren and Lisa Kashinsky

paragraphs.text: Haley Stevens is highly visible in the wake of her Senate primary loss: Meeting with the Dalai Lama, crashing “TMZ Live” with her new fiancee, getting spoofed on The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon.
One place she hasn’t been spotted: alongside her former rival Abdul El-Sayed.

Even though the representative quickly endorsed El-Sayed after their bruising Aug. 4 primary, she’s done little to help him since. That absence is becoming more conspicuous in the closing weeks of a crucial Senate contest, as some of her old supporters continue to vocally resist backing him.

In an interview, Stevens said El-Sayed is building a “new coalition” in the race against GOP former Rep. Mike Rogers — and suggested it’s not her place to push some of her more skeptical supporters into joining it.

When asked if she was encouraging her former donors to help El-Sayed, she said she believes her role this election is to “be part of the coordinated campaign, support where I can,” mentioning Michigan House races. When asked again if she would push donors to back him, she responded: “That’s Elissa’s thing,” referring to Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who has been fundraising for El-Sayed. “I didn't win a Senate primary,” she continued. “It's not like a salty grapes deal or anything.”
Stevens said she’d checked in with El-Sayed’s team, but hadn’t met with the candidate himself recently because she’d been traveling.

“There's changing dynamics, and there's a new coalition that Abdul has built, and some people are a die-hard part of it, and some people are not. We’re seeing some constituent community pain coming out,” Stevens said, referencing resistance to El-Sayed among some Black and Jewish voters who backed her in the primary.
“Rogers is working the Black community harder and more successfully than we have ever seen a Republican do or at least that I can remember — ever," Stevens said.
“But we’re also seeing Abdul go up to the UP [Upper Peninsula] and we’re seeing him fill venues in rural Michigan and it’s very real in terms of this coalition he’s built,” she added.

El-Sayed ran particularly strongly during the primary with young voters and in the state’s large Arab-American community, as well as in some rural, more populist parts of the state, and is working hard to expand that coalition in the general election.

Stevens’ remarks come as some of her former backers and financial boosters continue to publicly withhold support from El-Sayed and in some cases openly embrace his Republican rival. The ruptures are most visible among the Jewish and Black communities that largely broke for Stevens, and point to enduring friction within Michigan Democrats’ traditional coalition after a bitter primary that she could be in a unique position to mend.

Debbie Rosenman, the chair of Birmingham-Bloomfield Area Democratic Party Club in Stevens’ backyard and an El-Sayed supporter, said Stevens has been “absent” on the trail and said she was “very concerned” her coalition is not coalescing around El-Sayed.
“I feel that that could change with more of her public support,” Rosenman said.
El-Sayed’s campaign said the former rivals’ teams keep in close touch and noted several Stevens staffers joined the nominee’s team after the primary.
“The Abdul campaign is grateful for Congresswoman Stevens’ immediate and sustained support,” El-Sayed campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner said in a statement.

El-Sayed has worked to repair relationships with Black and Jewish leaders. He has endorsements from several of them and is campaigning with prominent Democrats from both communities, including former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris and Slotkin, who is Jewish. He has made more than two dozen visits to Black churches and participated in more than 100 events and meetings with Black leaders, according to his campaign. He has hired a liaison to the Jewish community, keeps in regular contact with Jewish leaders and has apologized for his controversial remark after a synagogue attack in West Bloomfield in the spring that “hurt people hurt people.”

“I take very seriously that I'm going to represent a large community of Jewish Michiganders, and I want them to know that I'm committed to their safety and their well being, even if there are points in foreign policy on which we might disagree,” El-Sayed said in an interview.
Not everyone has come around.

David Kramer, Stevens’ primary campaign chair and a vice chair of the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus who introduced Stevens to her fiance, is now working with Nonnegotiable Michigan, a group of Jewish leaders who have pledged to withhold their support from El-Sayed unless he adjusts his approach to Israel.

Kramer, a prominent Democratic fundraiser in the state who has also previously worked with Slotkin and Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, told POLITICO he’s not tapping his donor network for the general election and estimated he’s left upward of seven figures on the table that he could have raised to boost El-Sayed.

Brian Hermelin, a normally Democratic donor who backed Stevens in the primary and leads the Jewish Federation of Detroit, co-hosted a fundraiser for Republican nominee Mike Rogers shortly after the primary that raised roughly $200,000.

Rogers’ campaign has attempted to capitalize on those cracks by launching a “Democrats for Mike Rogers” group and making overtures to Jewish and Black voters. Bobby Schostak, a former Michigan GOP chair who is serving as Rogers’ finance chair, estimated the Republican’s campaign has brought in roughly $3 million to $4 million since the primary from “nontraditional Republican donors” across the country, including Democrats.

“The Democratic Party is still divided,” said Democrat Mary Waters, a Black Detroit city councilor who’s met with both El-Sayed and Rogers but remains undecided. “People are still so torn about what it is that they want to do.”

Joe Tate, a Black state representative from Detroit who supported Stevens, acknowledged there has been some lingering apprehension around El-Sayed. But he said Stevens’ endorsement of El-Sayed helped convince him to back the candidate and predicted Democratic voters would largely stand by their party, too.

El-Sayed’s donor network may look different from Stevens’, but he’s still posted big numbers. He raised nearly $33 million from July through September, which included some raised before the Aug. 4 primary, compared to Rogers’ nearly $10 million, and has been outspending Rogers on the airwaves.

Some of El-Sayed’s prominent surrogates have also taken steps to court apprehensive Democrats. Jewish leaders like former Rep. Andy Levin, a former synagogue president who Stevens defeated in a 2022 primary, are holding house parties with voters coordinated by the grassroots group Michigan Jews for Democracy. Slotkin has privately pressed senators and donors to boost El-Sayed’s bid.
That includes hosting a fundraiser for El-Sayed in Washington, D.C., in late September with donors who she described as initially “skeptical” of the nominee.

“I talked to them about why I thought it was important and how I don't agree with Abdul on everything … but we agree on the really important things, and that's putting a check and balance on this president,” Slotkin told POLITICO in a brief hallway interview on Capitol Hill the next day. “And they donated.”

finance.yahoo.com/real-estate/articles/c.headline: Canada’s Housing Market Slips Further as Mortgage Rates Climb
finance.yahoo.com/real-estate/articles/c.author: Ari Altstedter

paragraphs.text: Fri, October 16, 2026 at 5:00 AM EDT 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- The Canadian housing market dipped in September as a surge in borrowing costs added to the broader economic uncertainty holding back buyers.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The number of homes that traded hands across the country fell 2.3% in September from the previous month, according to data Friday from the Canadian Real Estate Association. The benchmark price of a home edged down 0.4% to C$652,800 ($459,900) in the same period, the data show.

The accelerating decline in Canada's housing market came as rising borrowing costs compounded the fallout from the country's ongoing trade war with the US. Credit conditions have been tightening around the world as bond investors spooked by government debt loads demand higher rates. Because many mortgage rates in Canada are priced off the government's bonds, that's meant higher borrowing costs for prospective home buyers too.

Higher fuel prices from the war in Iran have also added pressure to inflation, increasing the odds the Bank of Canada will raise interest rates. At the same time, the US and Canada have slapped new tariffs on each other's goods.

"Many of Canada's housing markets took a step back in September," Shaun Cathcart, the real estate board's senior economist, said in a news release. "This was hardly surprising given the latest jump in fixed mortgage rates, and with the Bank of Canada now widely expected to follow with a rate hike before the end of the year."
The number of properties put up for sale also fell in September from the previous month, with a 1.8% drop, the data show. Benchmark prices are now down 3.5% from the same time last year.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: CoreWeave Stock Wipeout Exposes Divide Between AI Fear and Greed
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Jeran Wittenstein and Ryan Vlastelica

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- CoreWeave Inc. has become ground zero in a tug of war between investors who see rising bond yields as a potential rally killer for the AI trade and those who think demand for computing power will make those concerns seem passe before long.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The cloud-computing services provider's shares plunged 20% in the first three sessions of the week, including more than 15% on Wednesday, as its debt tumbled to levels that typically indicate distress. On Thursday morning, the cost of protecting CoreWeave bonds against default rose to the highest intraday level on record, while swaps priced in a more than 60% chance of a default within the next five years.

But by Thursday afternoon, the sense of panic appeared to be alleviating as the stock bounced into the green with Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia Corp., which is a CoreWeave shareholder and supplier, expressing confidence in the company. In addition, Deutsche Bank called the selloff a "buying opportunity." The shares ended the day up 5.9%, their best performance in over a month, though they gave up some of that recovery in Friday's premarket trading.

"The macro backdrop has created a sell-first, ask-questions-later market," said Thomas DiFazio, exchange-traded fund strategist at Roundhill Financial. "In the short run, it is hard to say with a straight face that the all-clear is here."

As a so-called neocloud provider, Coreweave is at the heart of the infrastructure buildout needed to develop artificial intelligence technology. The safety of its debt is a key issue for investors because its spending on building data centers is being funded by issuing bonds. With Treasury yields climbing and inflation remaining stubbornly high, the cost of that financing is rising fast.

All of which has led to a bumpy ride for CoreWeave shares. The stock is up 74% since its troubled initial public offering in March 2025 that had to be backstopped by Nvidia. But it's down 2.7% this year and 62% since hitting a peak in June 2025, and it's less than $30 from its debut price.

However, the upside for CoreWeave is pretty obvious, as demand for AI computing services continues to outstrip supply. And there are few signs that dynamic is going to change any time soon, DiFazio said.
That was the view taken by Deutsche Bank analyst Brad Zelnick, who has a buy rating on the stock and is urging investors to snap up the shares before they fully rebound.

CoreWeave has "a strong customer base, established record of execution, backlog conversion and leading infrastructure performance," Zelnick wrote in a research note on Thursday. "While more capital will be needed, this can happen at a steady pace and is backed by robust customer backlog."

Of course, CoreWeave wasn't alone in this week's selloff. The Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index, known by its ticker SOX, has dropped 7.9%, leaving it down 21% from a June peak. Server makers Dell Technologies Inc. and Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. have fallen about 20%.

But CoreWeave is considered one of the riskiest stocks in the AI trade because of its heavy reliance on high-yield debt to finance its data centers. The company's goal is to keep winning high-grade ratings, co-founder Brannin McBee told the Financial Times on Wednesday, which just underscores how much more CoreWeave plans to borrow.

The company's close relationship with Nvidia could provide a source of capital if its market access tightens, according to Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Robert Schiffman. But Huang pushed back against that idea on Thursday, saying there's no need for a bailout.
"CoreWeave's strength is improving every day," Huang told Bloomberg at an event in Stockholm. "I'm optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing."

Still, even with all the risks posed by higher interest rates and the stratospheric level of AI spending, the fundamental backdrop remains encouraging for CoreWeave, according to Matt Bartolini, global head of research strategists for State Street Investment Management.

"We're still very early on in the AI capex cycle, so I don't think rates will be the barrier that's hard to jump over, but it does change the calculus behind the continued issuance of debt, and ensuring whether the financing of that debt can be met with credible growth in the future," Bartolini said. "The secular demand story is what's funding the capex cycle, and I think demand is likely to continue irrespective of what's happening with rates."
Tech Chart of the Day

• Taiwan is preparing to tighten export controls on AI chips to further align with US restrictions, according to a senior official in Taipei, joining a Trump administration clampdown on the smuggling of cutting-edge semiconductors to China.
• Tesla Inc. unveiled its long-delayed new Roadster sports car Thursday in Texas, reviving and refreshing a model that it stopped producing more than a decade ago.

• Netflix Inc. is replacing its chief creative officer with a veteran TV and film executive, Peter Rice, accelerating efforts to reinvigorate growth and reverse a slowdown in viewers and revenue at the streaming giant.

• Meta Platforms Inc. made one of its new artificial intelligence models available for developers to download and modify, while keeping its most advanced technology closed in an effort to convert its AI investments into revenue.
• No major earnings expected
