theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/16/amel.headline: Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed
theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/16/amel.author: Oliver Holmes

paragraphs.text: A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.

The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.

While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website.
The negatives were found more than a decade ago by the archivist Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch.

Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.

What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, and filled with false leads.

A leading theory is that the aviator who broke several records, including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.

The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream.

This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll had been visited dozens of times.

In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said “severe weather” had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours.

“Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said.

“We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience,” said Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute. “This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.”
The New Zealand military images are some of the earliest photographic evidence of the island. There is no immediate sign of an object in the Taraia area.

slowboring.com/p/the-lost-wisdom-of-the-.headline: The lost wisdom of the Old Moderates
slowboring.com/p/the-lost-wisdom-of-the-.author: Matthew Yglesias

paragraphs.text: This is not worth a whole article, but one of the craziest takes I’ve read in a long time was a Jacobin piece arguing that the decline of reading isn’t about streaming video but rather the nefarious influence of “the consolidated corporate publishing industry that made books pricier, more generic, and harder to find.”

I promise you, though, that it has never been cheaper to read classic works of literature. On your smartphone you can download the complete works of Jane Austen for $0.49 or get all of Shakespeare for $0.99. Public libraries still exist. In inflation-adjusted terms, hardcover books are much cheaper than they used to be. It’s true that the specific publishing genre of cheaply produced mass-market paperbacks has gone into decline, but that’s because (a) ebooks have displaced them as the lowest cost option and (b) as reading has declined there is less of a low-end market to serve.

The problem is that the exact same technology that has made it cheaper and easier than ever to access the classic works of literature has also made it easier to access a bottomless pit of content and there’s only so much time in the day.

As a reminder, some questions in this week’s Mailbag don’t have links because they come from readers who contributed to last November’s GiveDirectly fundraiser and are entitled to ask a must-answer question. Slow Boring will be doing the fundraiser again next month, so look out for that if you’d like to get in on the action.

David E: A few weeks ago you tweeted that you thought the public defender community had “lost the plot sometimes,” and quoted a case in which a public defender was arguing that the Second Amendment protected their client’s right to possess a gun. You have written before about the differing obligations of politicians (who must, by and large, cater to the public will) and activists (who must, when their cause is unpopular, seek to persuade the public that it is right). I understand you’re not an ethics lawyer, but how do you view the political role of public defenders or other actors who have obligations to particular individuals but may also have broader political goals?

My basic read of the public-defender situation is this. One of the core ideas of our criminal justice system is that providing zealous legal representation to each defendant, including the guilty ones, serves to protect the interests of the innocent. This principle extends to the indigent. In some ways it is particularly important for them.

So it is honorable and appropriate that there are people kicking the tires in every criminal prosecution, seeking to expose improperly obtained evidence or to impeach the credibility of law enforcement officials or to reveal the shortcomings of witness testimony or expert analysis. The existence of public defenders doing this work is an annoyance to the law enforcement apparatus and causes some problems, but it also prevents serious abuses.

My sense from looking at the Public Defender Service for the District of Columbia, and many other major public-defender operations in America, though, is that the ideological basis of the work has shifted.

theguardian.com/news/2026/oct/16/jamaica.headline: ‘Opening the lid of a horrible secret’: Jamaicans confront enslavement with taboo-busting stories on screen
theguardian.com/news/2026/oct/16/jamaica.author: Natricia Duncan

paragraphs.text: A woman opens a 300‑year‑old box, unleashing a violent spirit – it is the spirit of colonialism and oppression roaring back to life. It is a pivotal scene in Sky’s supernatural series Possession and symbolises a wider shift in Jamaica’s film industry, where directors are increasingly using the landscape to tell Jamaican stories – including those that confront enslavement, trauma and historical memory.

The series is about a biracial British lawyer who travels to Jamaica to investigate a multimillion-pound inheritance dispute, only to uncover a dark, vengeful spirit tied to the plantation’s brutal colonial past.

For the Jamaican director, Storm Saulter, ensuring that the trauma and enduring legacy of enslavement and colonisation were powerfully represented was critical. Caribbean countries are increasingly arguing that centuries of enslavement have left the region at a lasting disadvantage – fuelling renewed calls for reparations.

Dr Lisa Tomlinson, a lecturer in film studies at the University of the West Indies, says the themes in Jamaican films are changing. “They’re now very much connected and reflective of Jamaican stories – stories that were previously taboo or avoided.”

While Jamaican films are not always explicitly about reparations, she argues that many are engaging with the legacies of enslavement through cultural memory. “Reparation is not just a political act,” she says. “It’s also culture. These African‑derived spiritualities, the historical knowledge – when they come through creative expression, what they do is give us authority to tell our own stories.”

This, she says, is a form of “cultural reparation”, a reclaiming of narratives devalued or suppressed under colonialism, and a way of educating audiences about the past in ways that academics or politicians struggle to do. “The arts play a critical role in how we are educated in public awareness around reparation,” she says.

Jacqueline Jackson, Jamaica’s film commissioner, sees the shift too. She says productions such as Possession and Delroy Lindo’s Jabari’s People – shot entirely in Jamaica – reflect growing confidence and ambition among Jamaican creatives. “We are well established as a destination for international productions,” she says. “But what we want to see more of is local production and international collaboration that enables us to tell our own stories.”

Both productions, she notes, worked closely with Jamaican talent to ensure authenticity and demonstrate what is possible when international financing and distribution unite with Jamaican creativity. “They show the growing interest in Jamaican stories and their potential for global audiences,” she says.

Tomlinson believes diaspora film-makers are playing a particularly important role in this shift. Unlike foreign productions that often use Jamaica as an exotic backdrop, diaspora directors are “moving away from the tourist‑gaze depictions” and are “capturing Jamaican everyday life”.

Saulter sees his series as part of a broader political awakening. “The mask has slipped … We’ve been told it’s one thing, and that thing is proven to be false. So there’s a seeking of what is true,” he says.

He says the box‑opening scene is not simply a plot device, but a metaphor for something larger: the resurfacing of long‑suppressed histories and the growing willingness among Caribbean creatives to confront the legacies of enslavement, inherited trauma and colonial violence through film.
“Literally, we’re going to open up the lid of a 300‑year‑old horrible secret,” Saulter said. “It’s the spirit of colonial enslavement and oppression coming roaring back.”

That “spirit”, he explains, is embodied in a character who has lived through centuries of brutality – “a witness to history” – whose presence forces the protagonists to reckon with the past they have inherited.
Saulter’s interest in the subject is rooted in his upbringing. “I grew up in the countryside,” he says. “The Obia man, the church … nine nights … I’ve lived through all of those things.”

His experiences inspired him to tell stories that educate and have “real societal political impact”, while remaining thrilling, intriguing and entertaining. That approach, he argues, allows film-makers to tackle difficult histories. “As opposed to doing something that was like talking heads … we’re bringing you on a journey,” he says.
For Dr L’Antoinette Stines, a Yoruba priestess and cultural expert who advised on Possession, the series’ engagement with Afro‑spiritualist traditions is part of a longer history of resistance.

“Black people have been fighting and using the arts for a very long time. It’s just that there is greater attention on it today,” she says. For decades she has choreographed similar work, she says, and stresses the importance of honouring the academics, poets and creatives who paved the way for today’s boom in authentic Jamaican storytelling.

She praises Saulter’s insistence on authenticity and creating a series that feels both contemporary and deeply rooted, exploring inherited trauma, ancestral memory and the unfinished business of colonialism.

cnbc.com/2026/10/16/nike-india-campus-ch.headline: Nike's India campus is a long-term growth bet amid turnaround
cnbc.com/2026/10/16/nike-india-campus-ch.author: Laya Neelakandan

paragraphs.text: Nike is making a big bet on India.
The retailer, which has been struggling to revive its business and regain momentum under CEO Elliott Hill, is hoping the world's most populous country can help it turn the page on its performance.

As it reported its fiscal first-quarter earnings on Oct. 1, the company announced it will create a new global campus in Bengaluru, India, as part of its growth strategy. Hill wrote in a letter to employees that the new facility would be a "long-term investment" to help position Nike for success.
"India is already an important growth market and manufacturing hub for Nike, with strong capabilities and access to talent," Hill wrote.

The new campus is expected to open in the next few years and span corporate roles across the organization, including the namesake Nike brand, Jordan Brand and Converse. Nike plans to discuss its India campus in detail at its investor day next month.
In a statement to CNBC, a Nike spokesperson said expanding into India is a "natural" next step for the company as it looks to grow its global presence.

"As participation in running, basketball, football, fitness and other sports continues to grow across India, we see an opportunity to better serve athletes through stronger local capabilities, consumer insights, and innovation," the spokesperson said.

India will be the world's third-largest retail market by 2030, according to Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries. Its e-commerce market was valued at $159.25 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach $332.94 billion by 2031, according to IBEF, a business advocacy organization created by the Indian government.

Nike has endured a yearslong slump and is trying to right its business under Hill's turnaround plan. Nike also announced this month that it would lay off workers across the company as part of what it has dubbed its Pace strategy, which includes supply chain changes and reorganization of the company's geographic segments. Nike expects the effort to deliver approximately $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031.

Nike's decision to invest further in India as part of its comeback comes as the sportswear company sheds revenue in another critical international market: China. Though its fiscal first-quarter North America revenue came in just above Wall Street expectations, Hill said that performance wasn't enough to offset pressures abroad.

Nike has been particularly struggling in the Greater China market, where its revenue dropped by 26% in its fiscal first quarter. It's part of what experts have said is a broader trend of American companies losing relevance and traction to domestic brands as the once-lucrative market matures.

On a call with analysts earlier this month, Hill said the company was taking "deliberate actions" to strengthen its China business, though he said those effects will take time to materialize. Hill said the company plans to refresh its physical retail, spearhead a digital cleanup and create higher quality experiences for consumers.
The Nike spokesperson told CNBC the company is "deeply committed" to China and sees the region as one of its "most important long-term growth markets," even as Nike expands its presence in India.
"China remains a long-term priority for Nike, while India represents another important opportunity to invest in the future of sport and the next generation of athletes," the spokesperson said.
Investing in a long-term vision

The company's expansion in India may be coming at both an opportune and inopportune time, according to experts. Investing in a growing international market does not guarantee higher sales — it also requires persuading Indian consumers they want the Nike brand, a challenge the company has struggled to overcome in China.
"What Nike, I think, is doing right now is going region by region and working to reestablish what the brand stands for," Simeon Siegel, a senior managing director at Guggenheim Securities, told CNBC.

Siegel said part of the dissonance for Nike is that each region and segment of the business is at a different stage of its turnaround. He said investing in India may set the company up for a more sustainable future if the China business continues to lag, but Nike needs to have a compelling product, solid storytelling and extensive distribution in the region to be successful there.

"I think the company needs to look inward and figure out what is the right way to reestablish profitability," he said. "And that involves, in certain instances, shrinking and saving and cutting, and, in certain instances, investing and looking toward the future, because the goal here is not to shrink to oblivion; it's to shrink to stability, and then ultimately growth."

The global strategy may also focus too much on a long-term vision rather than more immediate fixes, according to Jessica Ramirez, co-founder and managing director at advisory firm The Consumer Collective, who specializes in retail and apparel. Ramirez said she already thought Nike and Hill's vision were "out of touch" and the plan for the India campus didn't necessarily help its case.

"I don't know that this plan of India is an immediate solution to their problems right now," she said. "They have to plan long term, right? But they also need to plan short term, which is continuously falling apart."
She said Nike has not shared plans that are concrete enough to win back momentum in China and has to develop both regions hand in hand.

While Nike under Hill has improved its wholesale and performance categories, Ramirez said it has yet to master its direct-to-consumer and sportswear segments, which would allow the company to flourish in all of its markets.
The Nike spokesperson told CNBC the retailer is committed to investing in both countries as it tries to expand its global presence.

"Importantly, this is not an either/or decision between India and China," the spokesperson said. "We always invest market by market based on long-term opportunities to serve athletes and grow sport around the world."
A growing market opportunity
Still, India presents an attractive opportunity for many companies looking to unlock growth abroad.

Ramirez said Nike is just the latest to join a cohort of American companies looking to establish their presence in the market. While many brands began investing in China years ago, she said that trend is now pointing toward India instead, as U.S. companies see more spending pressures in the Chinese market and navigate geopolitical tensions between the two countries.

"It's to get in there for the long term and to make sure that they are there for when they can reap the positive effects," she said. "I want to say this conversation started getting a bit more engaging in the last two to three years, when companies started investing more in India."

India is one of the world's strongest market performers, driven primarily by domestic demand, investment and supply-chain diversification, according to an analysis from Accenture. With a population of over 1 billion, the country presents a growth opportunity similar to the one China offered in the early 2000s.

"It's going to be a fast-growing consumer base where we assume their income levels will continue to go up and they'll have much more purchasing power, and so maybe could we be tapping in on that market from a consumer lens," Chris Tomsovic, who leads Accenture's macro foresight team, told CNBC.

Still, one of the biggest focus points for the Indian consumer is price sensitivity, which will pose a challenge for American companies trying to break into the market, he added. Even so, many domestic brands on the market are younger, meaning there could be more opportunities right now for Western companies to take market share.

Another challenge is that the Chinese consumer has historically been receptive to American brands, whereas it will still take more data to understand how Indian shoppers feel about those businesses, he said. For sportswear retailers, the focus of the sports most popular in each region will also factor into that equation.

"Can they really localize the product, make the price point work? Can they adapt to the local social media technology ecosystem? Can they adapt to the local cultural values and norms that the consumer wants?" Tomsovic said.

"If you're able to nail that, then I think you're right. Whether you're a footwear brand, whether you're an athleisure brand, I think there's a huge opportunity there with a billion consumers," he said.

npr.org/sections/planet-money/2026/10/16.headline: What this bankruptcy says about AI startups
npr.org/sections/planet-money/2026/10/16.author: Cooper Katz McKim

paragraphs.text: After you win the economics Nobel, what would your first act be? Buy a Corvette? Gloat to your childhood bully? For co-winner Michael Woodford, his first act was … proctor an exam. The DAY that Columbia professor Michael Woodford found out that he and Robert Hall won the economics Nobel, he returned to his class with the pithy title "Cognitive Mechanisms and Economic Behavior" to administer an exam. He was welcomed to the classroom with cheers and applause. He held up his arms in triumph.
Coming up:
• Character.ai is going through bankruptcy. What can we learn from the AI startup's decline?
• Why President Trump wants to import diesel fuel from Russia
• Why stagflation was John Maynard Keynes' Achilles' heel
News We're Watching
When AI startups get vacuumed up, what's left behind?

What to know: Character.ai is a company that allows you to speak with a "companion" — an AI-powered fictional character, historical figure, or whatever you decide to build. It came out just before ChatGPT and quickly went viral in part thanks to its adoption on TikTok. It hit 28 million monthly active users at its peak.

Character.ai had a lot of engagement, a big customer base, lots of talent … and Google promptly picked 'em up for $2.7 billion back in 2024. But Google didn't buy the company and absorb it! No, that traditional "acquihire" model would require all sorts of legal and regulatory approvals. Instead, they hired away the founders (and other big hitters on the team) and bought the nonexclusive license to the technology, leaving the company itself behind. That's called a "reverse acquihire," and it's happened at least six times in the past two years with AI startups. Now this week, Character.ai is filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.

Why it matters: A "reverse acquihire" doesn't leave a company in the greatest position. After the Google deal, Character.ai had to change its business model away from the quite costly LLM training and toward developing AI characters. Its founders were gone. Sure, the shrunken company had $2.7 billion in the bank, but leadership was still looking to raise money as they struggled to monetize their user base.

So is the "reverse acquihire" what caused the pain? Or was it a symptom of a larger issue? Character.ai faced a mountain of litigation over alleged harm to minors plus copyright concerns from Disney. So what's left behind? A once very promising company, which Disney is very excited to pick over for parts of it for $20 million.
Will this Russian diesel deal affect price?

What's going on: President Trump signed a deal last week to get diesel from Russia in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterms. Two weeks ago, we talked in the newsletter about the potential of a diesel export ban to lower prices. It didn't happen. One week ago, we talked again about Trump issuing an executive order to defer a tax from diesel. Now, this!

It's safe to say people were surprised by the move, given Trump signed a Russian sanctions law just last month that looked to tamp down on their energy revenues. Beyond surprise, a bipartisan group of senators is openly calling for the president to rescind the deal. They said it gives Putin the funds to power his war machine and "enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians."

Will this do anything? The same bipartisan group of senators said this deal will mean "limited to no relief to Americans." Goldman Sachs estimated the release of Russian oil would affect wholesale prices by $1 to $2 per barrel. The price of a barrel of diesel is around $200. So a $1 to $2 impact? Neil Atkinson, an independent energy analyst, says, "Frankly, [it's] a rounding error. It makes no fundamental difference to the global diesel market."

What's weirder to Atkinson, though … Russia hasn't really been exporting diesel. Its refineries have been damaged, and it's literally been importing diesel to make up for shortfalls. " So where these barrels of Russian diesel are going to come from to go either to the United States or elsewhere in the global market is a bit of a mystery," said Atkinson.
Today's Indicator
The Nobel Prize that wasn't

If you HAVEN'T listened: Reporter Greg Rosalsky opens the piece describing WHAT exactly Michael Woodford and Robert Hall won the economics Nobel for. They helped shape what's known as NEW Keynesian economics by bringing microeconomic principles to the traditional models of John Maynard Keynes. BUT THEN, Greg goes on to explain that the Nobel Prize did not initially include an economics award. No, that changed when the Swedish Central Bank, the oldest central bank in the world, wanted to celebrate its 300th anniversary with a bang. They would fund a new award for economics. It's a fascinating story which you can listen to below.
Listen to the full episode

If you HAVE listened: A leading philosophy of John Maynard Keynes is that governments could fight recessions by boosting spending, and deal with inflation by holding spending back. In the initial draft that didn't make it into the final episode, Greg touched on how STAGFLATION was a central thorn in the side of this concept. Specifically, back in the 1970s, during the Arab oil embargo, the U.S. dealt with the one-two punch of high unemployment and high inflation, bringing about stagflation. It challenged the Keynesian idea that when lots of people are out of work and spending less, inflation comes down. Because at that point, unemployment and inflation rose together. Isn't that nice? Greg Rosalsky writes Planet Money's newsletter … you can catch that here.
Rest of the week
In Our Spare Time
Producer Cooper Katz McKim is reading The AGI Chronicles

Man oh man, this is the page-turniest nonfiction book I've read in a while. Kevin Roose, co-host of the upcoming NPR podcast Machine Gods, formerly The New York Times' Hard Fork, tracks the handful of characters racing to make AI a commercial reality. It is far from a clear-cut story. There's no one character who came up with the idea and executed it … the existence of AI today comes down to many papers, many individual discoveries, and a whole lot of obsession. I didn't realize how much progress had been made in AI prior to 2020 and how concerned many industry leaders were about even creating AI (looking at you, Amodei) for fear of creating a super-intelligence that moves outside of human control. It's gossip-y, it's matter of fact … I would recommend.

Paul Rankin’s account of a father-son camping trip and an exchange with an inscrutable stranger reads like it was plucked from an anthology of Southern gothic tales. It’s a tense, slightly spooky meditation on how private faith can grow wild and unruly, how isolation breeds suspicion, and how readily we project our fears.

The more I affirmed my faith, the more suspicious the man became, as if he hadn’t come to share the good news but to catch us in a damnable lie. As the interrogation persisted, I couldn’t help thinking of how Flannery O’Connor once described the South as a Christ-haunted place. I love Jesus, but, good Lord, his ostensible followers can be irksome and even sinister at times. Clearly unconvinced by my profession of faith but out of ideas—or maybe just weary with the effort—the stranger finally walked the three steps back to his camp site. For lack of a better idea, I relit the stove and was adjusting the flame when the man returned, holding one hand behind his back. With a flourish he brought out a cross fashioned of two sticks and thin binding wire. This he presented to Fish, then added that he’d have a big surprise waiting in the morning. With that, he turned and walked away, into the woods and out of sight.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/st.headline: Nathan Fielder's new Elizabeth Holmes doc: 10 biggest reveals
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/st.author: Josh Rottenberg

paragraphs.text: Nathan Fielder would rather you not read this article. At least not until you’ve seen his new movie.
He has a point.

Now in theaters, “You Can See Everything,” the nearly three-hour documentary Fielder co-directed with filmmaker Lance Oppenheim about convicted Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, is full of head-spinning twists and turns best left unspoiled, and the filmmakers have gone to extreme lengths to keep them that way. At its secret premiere at the Telluride Film Festival last month, audience members were required to lock their phones in pouches and warned that security guards with night-vision goggles would be watching for anyone trying to record the screening. Afterward, Fielder pleaded with the crowd to keep the film’s biggest surprises to themselves.

Holmes was convicted in 2022 of defrauding investors in her failed blood-testing company and sentenced to more than 11 years in federal prison. Fielder and Oppenheim began filming her and longtime partner Billy Evans, an MIT graduate and heir to a family-owned San Diego hotel business, shortly before she reported to prison in 2023, gaining extraordinary access to the couple and their two young children.

Holmes and Evans welcomed the cameras, hoping they would help vindicate her. But the closer Fielder and Oppenheim got to the couple, the harder it became to distinguish candor from calculated performance. Fielder, whose series “Nathan for You” and “The Rehearsal” put real people through elaborate, often uncomfortable experiments, began to wonder whether the tables had been turned.

“I really am struggling to this day to understand exactly what I experienced in this,” Fielder admitted during a post-screening Q&A at Telluride. “I don’t quite know what I went through.” He said he hoped audiences might help him make sense of the “glitchy feeling” it left in his head.
Having seen the film twice, we’re not entirely sure we can help him.

In deference to Fielder’s wishes, this is your last chance to turn back: Major spoilers follow. For those still with us, here are 10 of the film’s strangest moments — by no means the only ones — along with a few clues from Fielder himself about how they came to be.
Evans takes ’radical transparency’ too far

Evans has a theory about why the world sees his partner as a monster: Nobody really knows her. “In the absence of knowing somebody, it’s really easy to make them feel other and scary,” he tells the filmmakers. His proposed solution is “radical transparency” — a familiar Silicon Valley mantra with an ironic resonance given Theranos’ notorious culture of secrecy. The filmmakers are allowed virtually unlimited access to the family’s life, with Fielder even invited to move into their rented house in Del Mar, near San Diego. In one scene, Evans stands completely naked in the shower, brushing his teeth with the bathroom door wide open and the cameras rolling, as Fielder stands awkwardly nearby. At Telluride, Fielder, who had initially planned to stay behind the scenes, admitted he was still perplexed by the couple’s openness. “I’m a weird guy — why do they want me there?” he said. “That messed with my head a little bit.”
Theranos, the sequel

A federal fraud conviction apparently hasn’t ended Holmes’ ambitions to revolutionize medical testing. Before heading to prison, she and Evans begin laying plans for a new venture involving lasers and artificial intelligence that Evans describes as “2.0” — a chance, he says, “to put the band back together and do it all again.” Holmes declares, “From wherever I am, I’m going to continue to work inventing, even if it’s inventing from a cage.”
Holmes claims she’s never told a lie

For someone convicted of defrauding investors, Holmes has a remarkably uncomplicated view of her own honesty. Asked by Fielder whether she’s ever told a lie in her life, she replies, “I don’t think so.” Pressed — surely she’s pretended to be sick to get out of a party? — she concedes she has, explaining that she thought he meant the criminal case against her. In a scene that became the centerpiece of the film’s teaser trailer, Holmes fixes Fielder with an unwavering stare. “Why would I deceive you?” she asks. “There’s no reason for me to do that.” When Fielder asks whether she’s being real with him, she doesn’t miss a beat: “I’m always being real.”
The Theranos device gets a second look

Holmes hauls out of storage the infamous Theranos device, the machine that helped bring down her company. “So this is the famous scam device,” Fielder says. “It is not a scam device,” Holmes replies. When she insists the machine can perform any medical test, Fielder finds himself drawn into an absurd debate over the meaning of the word “can.” Did she mean it could actually perform those tests, or that it theoretically would once the necessary chemistry had been developed? The man who has made a career out of baffling other people seems genuinely baffled himself, reduced to explaining the word “can” to the founder of Theranos.
Elizabeth Holmes meets Abbott and Costello

Still trying to make his point, Fielder turns to Abbott and Costello. He plays Holmes the classic “Who’s on First?” comedy routine — two people hopelessly talking past each other. Holmes watches politely and says she finds it funny. But she seems to have missed the central joke: The first baseman’s name is actually Who. “I didn’t pick it up,” she admits. Fielder’s attempts to explain the joke and why he showed it to her get him nowhere. Evans, watching the exchange, regards his wife’s difficulty following the joke as further evidence that her mind simply works differently from everyone else’s.
Fielder gives Holmes an escape kit

On the morning Holmes is due to report to prison, Fielder arrives with a parting gag gift: hair dye and glasses, in case she’d prefer to disguise herself and flee the country. Fielder is famous for excruciatingly awkward deadpan comedy, but Holmes’ parents are there, the family is preparing for an emotional goodbye and he seems to realize almost immediately that he has misjudged the situation. “I didn’t know your parents would be here,” he says, assuring everyone that it’s “just kind of like a joke.” The more he tries to explain himself, the more uncomfortable things become. “Maybe not appropriate for the moment,” he concedes.
Amanda Seyfried becomes a surprise co-star

Seyfried won an Emmy for playing Holmes in Hulu’s “The Dropout,” which Holmes had avoided watching for fear it would be too emotionally disturbing. Fielder persuades Holmes to watch it for the first time, on a laptop in the couple’s bed. She soon breaks down in tears and asks him to turn it off. Later, Fielder visits Seyfried at her apartment and shows her footage of Holmes watching her performance. So we watch Seyfried watch Holmes watch Seyfried playing Holmes as Fielder watches her. And things only get weirder from there.

At Telluride, Fielder said the filmmakers initially doubted Seyfried would want to participate. But after a brief phone call, she invited them over and agreed to be filmed. Neither side knew where things would lead. “It just actually evolved in that organic way, which was really exciting,” Fielder said.
Seyfried plays detective

Seyfried soon finds herself reenacting Holmes’ conversations with Fielder as he tries to make sense of their encounters. She becomes so invested that she joins Fielder on a visit to Evans’ home, hoping she might get him to open up in ways Fielder can’t. “I feel like an undercover cop right now,” she says, clearly getting a rush. There, after meeting the couple’s children, she unexpectedly winds up on a prison phone call with Holmes herself. With only two minutes for the family to talk, Seyfried suddenly seems mortified to be intruding. “I’m so sorry — I don’t want to ruin your two minutes with your beautiful family,” she says. Fielder, naturally, has a camera running.
Evans takes control of the narrative

With Holmes behind bars, Evans seems determined to manage her public image himself. Armed with power of attorney, he takes over her verified X account, posting messages in her name, some of which sound nothing like the carefully controlled Holmes, including one telling another user to “f— off.” “There’s just so much trust that most things I don’t really consult her on,” Evans says at one point. “I know what she’d want.”

Evans’ attempts to steer the documentary itself begin even before Holmes reports to prison. In a meeting later reenacted in the film, after Holmes leaves the room, he raises the subject of money with Fielder, Oppenheim and executives from A24, the studio behind the film, demanding a share of the profits. Fielder says A24 reluctantly agreed, leaving him worried that the integrity of the project may have been compromised. When Holmes later insists she has no financial interest in the film, Fielder is taken aback. Either she’s “fully sincere,” he tells Seyfried, or “she honestly might be the most manipulative person that’s ever lived.” (The film notes at the end that Evans later changed his mind and decided not to accept payment.)

On Oct. 5, Holmes’ X account promoted the documentary with a tantalizing warning: “I really don’t think you are ready for this doc.” Whether that was Holmes speaking or Evans speaking for her is anyone’s guess.
Seyfried confronts Evans

Things turn ugly during that same visit to Evans’ home. A conversation about conjugal visits and Evans’ sex life gives way to a heated argument over his use of Holmes’ X account. Evans brings up the social media backlash Seyfried faced for criticizing Charlie Kirk after his shooting death, then attacks her portrayal of his partner in “The Dropout.” Soon he’s threatening vengeance against people he believes have wronged Holmes. “I’m going to ruin their lives,” he declares. Asked whose lives he means, Evans replies, “F—ing everyone. I’ve got vengeance in my heart.”
Later, away from Evans, Seyfried offers her own assessment: “He is bat— crazy.”

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Palantir, Apple and Microsoft Brace for Democrats to Go on Offensive
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Ted Mann and Joshua Green

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- For two years, congressional Democrats furious over corporate America's cooperation with the Trump administration have been limited to the sternly worded letter.
Most Read from Bloomberg
After the midterm elections, some of them will likely have subpoena power. Companies in their sights are armoring up accordingly.

Tech and defense leaders like Palantir Technologies Inc., Apple Inc., and Microsoft Corp. are hiring Democratic Party insiders including former Senator Mark Begich and mega-lobbyist Steve Elmendorf. Other companies that scored contracts helping to facilitate mass immigration raids or sought favor by bankrolling presidential pet projects are scouring internal documents in advance of a push of subpoenas. CEOs are bracing for an uncomfortable inevitability: public testimony before hostile questioners about how they cooperated with a domineering president's demands, and why.

Insiders across K Street describe the flurry of preparations as unprecedented, driven by an acknowledgment of the unusually transactional nature of President Donald Trump's second term — and outrage from Democrats toward those they see as complicit.

While changing political winds always prompt new hires and strategic shifts, prospective Democratic committee chairs are signaling an unsparing blitz that will look to channel voters' anger over alleged corruption and the direction of the economy. With polls indicating Democrats are clear favorites to take back at least one chamber of Congress, corporations are treating the looming confrontation as a crisis — and spending like it's an emergency.

New lobbying registrations have exploded this fall as companies sign up representatives with ties to the Democrats likely to investigate their dealings with Trump, and with experience preparing corporations and CEOs for congressional oversight hearings.
Take some of the companies that donated to the White House ballroom project.

Apple, which hired the Trump-connected lobbyist Jeff Miller during the presidential campaign in 2024, last month tapped Arshi Siddiqui, a onetime aide to former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, to join its roster of lobbyists, advising on "tax, trade and technology-related issues." The company has also hired Liz Allen, a former senior official in President Joe Biden's State Department who served as Tim Walz's chief of staff during his 2024 vice presidential bid.
Microsoft, another ballroom donor, in August reported contracting with Rivendell Group, adding a pair of former Democratic aides to its stable of outside representatives.

And Palantir, which has seen a major expansion in federal contracts over the past two years, has added bipartisan firms to its slate of outside lobbyists. In late spring, the defense contractor hired a team led by Elmendorf, a longtime senior adviser to House Democrats who worked on John Kerry's presidential campaign, and Begich, a former Democratic senator from Alaska.

The Washington Post reported this week on a spreadsheet that tracked $333 million in donations for the ballroom from private donors, including some companies whose contributions hadn't previously been disclosed. Donors included Salesforce Inc., which made a pair of $1 million donations, the Post reported, as well as Marc Benioff, the company's chief executive. Benioff has cultivated a close relationship with Trump as the company has increased its business with the US government.

The software company has also bolstered its lobbying, records show, this summer signing up longtime Democratic lobbyist Mary Beth Stanton, as well as Checkmate Government Relations, a firm with close ties to Trump's inner circle.

Anxiety isn't limited to firms that donated to the ballroom project. One Republican lobbyist said that companies that helped fund Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's "Great American Road Trip" this summer — a group that included many with interests before the department — have expressed concern that they could be called before Congress to explain their interactions with the administration.

Companies that contributed to Trump's inaugural fund, his MAGA Inc. political action committee and various events tied to the country's 250th anniversary, which Trump largely molded into a celebration of himself and his administration, are also worried, this person said.
'Reputational harm'
Potential targets of Democratic scrutiny are generally reluctant to talk publicly, but are bracing for lawmakers to probe anything that smacks of graft.
A prominent financial executive described months of repositioning, including rebalancing political contributions in an attempt to curry favor with the party expected to take power.

A corporate consultant said clients are frantic to avoid being called to explain their cooperation with politically unpopular policies. A K Street lawyer said firms are advising executives to get honest answers ready about their interactions with Trump and his administration's officials — and to comb through internal emails to see what insiders really said about how they were reconciling the president's demands.

The lobbying giant Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck warned in a client alert this month that companies should be preparing now for aggressive oversight, including hearings at which chief executives will be questioned in order to score "political points."

"The practical consequences can be substantial, including reputational harm, stock market impact, executive testimony, extensive document production obligations, parallel regulatory inquiries and legislative initiatives targeting a company's business practices," the memo said.

Democratic strategists say lawmakers can expect heavy pressure from supporters to investigate companies and CEOs with financial ties to Trump and his administration. Lindsay Owens, president of the progressive economic think tank Groundwork Collaborative, says voters across party lines increasingly believe America's political and economic systems are rigged in favor of powerful interests.
"That's now the diagnosis that the American people share — broadly, firmly and coherently," Owens said.

In recent weeks, Owens and her team have been meeting with congressional staff to share a dossier of potential targets for investigation. It includes Tesla Inc. and SpaceX, the behemoths run by Trump ally Elon Musk, as well as Palantir, OpenAI, Amazon.com Inc. and Apple. There's particular interest in companies in the technology industry that benefited from a permissive regulatory posture or tariff carve-outs after contributing sizable donations to the president's inaugural committee or White House projects.

The Groundwork list also names companies outside the tech realm, including McDonald's Corp., Walmart Inc. and Intuit, the parent company of TurboTax. Live Nation Entertainment Inc., which saw an antitrust case with the Justice Department settled after Trump's personal intervention, according to the Wall Street Journal, was also singled out.
'A lot of tension'
Corporate concern has been growing all year, in lockstep with Democrats' increasingly rosy outlook for taking the House, and possibly the Senate, too.

"What may happen if the House does flip is that there will be a lot of hearings, there will be a lot of subpoenas, a lot of tension between the legislative branch and the executive branch over executive privilege and so on," said Peter Orszag, the chief executive of the investment bank Lazard Inc. and the former budget director in the Obama administration, on an earnings call in January.

"It starts with staff asking questions, then a letter, then a request for documents," said Syd Terry, a lobbyist at BGR Group. Terry previously worked for Congresswoman Jan Schakowsky of Illinois when she chaired a consumer protection subcommittee. "By the time anything reaches the hearing room, the story is mostly set. That's what we're telling clients through BGR's oversight working group: The time to prepare is now, not after the first letter arrives."

Veterans of Capitol Hill see plenty of investigative opportunity for Democrats: "There's a lot of red meat there," said the retired Congressman Henry Waxman of California, a crusading liberal Democrat who led investigations and chaired the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform during George W. Bush's administration.

With polls showing rising concern about government corruption, Congress has a duty to investigate, he says. A September Gallup poll found that 89% of US adults say government corruption is "widespread," including large majorities of both Republicans and Democrats.
"It's been eye-opening for the public to see what's been going on under the Trump administration," says Waxman.

Firms that have benefited from the Trump administration's light touch on antitrust enforcement could also be in for particular scrutiny, said Seth Bloom, a lawyer who has represented leading companies and was the longtime general counsel of the Senate's antitrust subcommittee.
Representative Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat, is poised to take over the Judiciary Committee that oversees antitrust issues in the House and recently spoke on the issue at a conference.

"Congressional Republicans have acted like toadies and sycophants, mindlessly rubber-stamping the president's bad deals instead of engaging in meaningful oversight," Raskin said. "They say nothing while shady deals cause prices to go up, wages to go down, and economic disparities to widen."

The recent merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery to create Skydance — and particularly whether the administration's approval hinged on promises about favorable media coverage from impacted networks like CBS News and CNN — could earn particular scrutiny.
"I would expect a lot more oversight," Bloom said. "What happened with these mergers?"
'Hostile administration'

Waxman says Democrats will also "absolutely" want to examine the expansive role Musk has played in the Trump administration as head of the Department of Government Efficiency, calling the tech CEO "an easy oversight target."

But getting answers may be harder than posing the questions. Waxman believes conducting effective oversight will be more difficult than it was during his heyday in the 1990s and 2000s. Congressional staff has been cut in recent years, he notes, leaving committees with fewer investigators to conduct complex inquiries. He also expects the Trump White House to resist investigations.

"It's a hostile administration," says Waxman. "It's much worse today than when I was chairman. I think the executive branch will just shut down any cooperation in giving Congress information. But that only makes the task more vital."
--With assistance from Max Chafkin.

(Bloomberg) -- Risk aversion is set to dominate markets in coming weeks as investors seek shelter from higher interest rates and volatility around US midterm elections and the AI trade, according to Bank of America Corp.'s Michael Hartnett.

A summer of "extreme bull sentiment" has come to an end, while the broad selloff in global bonds has driven yields adjusted for inflation to 3%, the strategist said in a note. Higher energy prices and sticky inflation are also adding to investors' list of worries.

"We continue to lean risk-off next 3-4 weeks given 3% real yields," Hartnett wrote. The BofA strategist's call for a rate hike, published in a note on Oct. 15, is more hawkish than broad market pricing. Swaps traders pared bets on an increase on Friday after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh did nothing to dispel market expectations that the central bank will hold interest rates steady when it meets at the end of the month.

Investors have become increasingly concerned about whether the massive investment in AI infrastructure, and the borrowing to fund it, will be justified. Bets on the AI trade have powered the rally in US stocks, with technology funds attracting record annualized inflows of $196 billion in 2026, the BofA team said, citing figures from EPFR Global.
Hartnett said his team favored adding exposure to "peak yield" beneficiaries in small caps, real estate investment trusts and the consumer discretionary sector. "We don't add tech."

techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/replits-ceo-sa.headline: Replit’s CEO says the future of work is the ‘self-driving company’
techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/replits-ceo-sa.author: Sarah Perez

paragraphs.text: Replit CEO and co-founder, Amjad Masad, has seen how AI is impacting the workplace first-hand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software. At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them.

He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgement and taste.

“The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said.
He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year.

“Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.”

Illustrating the shift, the Masad said that when support tickets come in at Replit, they’re first examined by an agent, which performs the initial triaging by looking at GitHub issues, the codebase, and Linear tickets. By the time the support request reaches a person, they have all the additional information that helps them decide how best to proceed.
And when that support person decides to submit a patch to apply a fix, it’s just a click to deploy another agent.

“You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon. You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained.
The end result is that instead of taking jobs from people, agents are changing what people work on.

“We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding. We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things. And so I think the future of work — the self-driving company idea — is really trying to discover what AI transformation means.”

He also noted that when Replit talks with other businesses, the conversations are more about how AI can help people become more productive and happier at work. (The latter because the AI agents make work less boring and more creative, he said).
“There’s a positive vision of the world that Silicon Valley is not really putting out, and we’re hoping to do that,” Masad added.

paragraphs.text: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
—Michal Luria, Aliya Bhatia, and Danah Boyd

Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds.
The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15.
But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented.
Here’s what we ought to do instead to keep kids safe.
Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.
—Jessica Hamzelou

I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated.

Almost 30 years later, pet owners have an expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing?
Read the full story on the promises and pitfalls of pet life extension.
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Form Energy and its iron batteries
Form Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.
As wind and solar power grow, utilities need cheaper ways to store electricity for longer periods. Form Energy aims to meet that need with batteries that can store energy for 100 hours.

The company has developed a new type of battery using iron, a far more abundant and cheaper metal than those used in many existing batteries. It uses a process that Form calls “reversible rusting,” in which iron turns to rust as the battery discharges and back to iron when it charges.

Inside the experimental world of animal infrastructure

In the mid-2000s, toads were meeting a gruesome end near Ede, a leafy old town in the Netherlands. Residents responded by building wildlife tunnels beneath the road to help them reach their breeding ponds safely.
The crossings became popular. But a few years later, researchers found the local toad population had crashed from more than 10,000 to fewer than 1,000.
The case reflects a wider global push to build wildlife crossings and other forms of “animal infrastructure.” But do they actually help animal populations recover? Read the full story to find out.

wsj.com/economy/central-banking/bank-of-.headline: BOJ Must Ensure Underlying Inflation Doesn't Go Above 2%, Ueda Says

paragraphs.text: BANGKOK--Bank of Japan Gov. Kazuo Ueda continued to strike a hawkish tone at a news conference Friday, saying Japan's underlying inflation rate shouldn't be allowed to exceed 2%.
Ueda, speaking at a news conference in Bangkok after attending the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings, reiterated that the Japanese central bank is in tightening mode.
He cited the Middle East situation, artificial-intelligence demand and foreign-exchange rates as factors that would affect the timing of the decision, without giving further specifics.

Japan's consumer-price inflation has been running above 2% for several years but the Bank of Japan has yet to determine that underlying inflation has risen to 2%, excluding short-term factors such as the pandemic or the recent wars in the Middle East.
Ueda said underlying inflation was quite close to 2% and reiterated that the BOJ wants to anchor the rate at the central bank's target of 2%. "We cannot allow it to rise above that," he said.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/veritas-is-bui.headline: Veritas expands its anti-counterfeit chip to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles
techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/veritas-is-bui.author: Ivan Mehta

paragraphs.text: Counterfeits of luxury goods are a major problem for fashion houses. Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands’ marks and passing off dupes, known as “superfakes,” as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods.

Veritas was founded by Luci Holland, a former Tesla technical product manager who also has a background in design and art. Its chip is built to be easily inserted into products without damaging them. Brands can use it to verify whether a product is the real deal, and customers can show a certificate of ownership through the company’s app.
Holland said other approaches are easier to defeat, because a digital record can be reproduced through a copied QR code or static NFC link.

“Our approach combines secure, authenticated chip responses with integration into the product itself. Our chip generates a secure response with each tap and includes a tamper-detection wire. We make the connection between the object and its digital identity part of the proof,” Holland said.
The Veritas founder told TechCrunch over email that the company has just introduced the second version of its chip, which works on metal surfaces and can be scanned through glass.

“The next-generation chip is ready for production and supports a broader range of applications, including jewelry, trophies, hard-surface products, and glass objects such as fragrance bottles,” Holland said. “Alongside our garment integrations, this gives brands more ways to incorporate authentication directly into their products.”

This week, the startup announced a partnership with ATHLOS, a women’s track-and-field competition founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, who is also an investor in Veritas. As part of the partnership, all 18 championship crowns will include Veritas’ chips so they can be verified.
The company also embedded a chip into a pair of LeBron James’ first Nike shoes, reimagined by artist Adam Port. Tapping a phone to the shoe brings up its history and story.

The company has so far raised $1.75 million in pre-seed funding led by Ohanian’s venture firm Seven Seven Six, with participation from DoorDash co-founder Stanley Tang; Gloria Zhu, co-founder of skincare brand Reys; and former TechCrunch editor Josh Constine.

Since its February fundraise, the company has shipped an iOS app for consumers and a brand portal that lets companies manage product records and build owner experiences. Through the app and the portal, brands can offer experiences such as clubs, event check-ins, and segmented early access to product drops.
Veritas competed in this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield, which ran Tuesday through Thursday. A winner was announced Thursday afternoon.

cnbc.com/2026/10/16/ai-espionage-openai-.headline: AI 'espionage' is a reality that companies need to be 'wary of,' DNI Jay Clayton says
cnbc.com/2026/10/16/ai-espionage-openai-.author: Kevin Breuninger

paragraphs.text: U.S. companies and the Trump administration both "need to be wary" of foreign espionage attempts as the race for artificial intelligence dominance continues, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC on Friday.

AI "amplifies" existing cybersecurity risks toward U.S. digital infrastructure, which is interconnected with critical systems related to everything from public goods to the national defense and global communications, Clayton said on "Squawk Box."
It's "why we're focused on hardening those systems" and using "our commitment to continue to lead to stay ahead of those nefarious actors," said Clayton, who leads a new White House AI task force.

Clayton was asked how concerned Americans should be with the threat of foreign spying in light of the recently revealed case charging Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan with allegedly installing a recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room. Alfozan has not been charged with espionage; the federal charge involves alleged interception of oral communications.
Alfozan, who was an OpenAI employee, had booked a one-way plane ticket to Saudi Arabia with his wife and another family member prior to his arrest, according to federal prosecutors.
"The short answer to your question is espionage, both commercial espionage, and I would say state-sponsored espionage, are realities," Clayton said.
"It's something that our private sector companies need to be wary of. We, as a government, need to be wary of," he said.
The OpenAI incident "shows the lengths that people will go to try and supplant our leadership in this, or at least stay close to us in this emerging technology," Clayton said.
An ex-CIA official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss non-public information, told CNBC this week that the case is "probably the tip of the iceberg."

Clayton, who was appointed AI czar earlier this month, said that the task force's "very good" inaugural meeting at the White House on Thursday built on the accord signed by President Donald Trump and a number of AI leaders at the White House last month. Trump had described the agreement, which includes industry pledges to police AI risks itself, as "morally binding."

The task force also established three subcommittees that are focused on different AI-related issues. One is tasked with reporting and response, another with assessing critical infrastructure and working with the private sector, and a third with law enforcement and responsibility, Clayton said.
The DNI reiterated to CNBC that the Trump administration is intent on staying ahead in the AI race.

"We're not the only ones developing it. There are vectors in this technology that are coming from some of our known adversaries and competitors," he said. "The Chinese, the Russians, the Iranians, the North Koreans all have significant technical capability. We need to stay ahead of them."

cnbc.com/2026/10/16/coreweave-openai-ant.headline: Here's how the CoreWeave sell-off is affecting OpenAI vs. Anthropic valuations
cnbc.com/2026/10/16/coreweave-openai-ant.author: Oliver Renick

paragraphs.text: OpenAI's valuation is down more than 4% the past 24 hours after briefly slipping under $1.5 trillion, according to perpetual futures pricing on decentralized exchange Hyperliquid. Meanwhile, Anthropic perps are up 2.4% over the same time period, recovering an overnight dip and indicating a valuation of just over $2 trillion.

Perpetuals are bets that never expire. They maintained by "deployers" on Hyperliquid's blockchain infrastructure that determine a funding rate for going long or short the futures based on a spot "oracle" price that uses third-party data like private funding rounds and secondary market transactions to estimate private-market prices.

Open interest, defined by Hyperliquid as the sum of long and short positions on a contract, is more than five times bigger in Anthropic than OpenAI — more than $41 million, compared to less than $7 million in OpenAI.

Right now the deployer behind these pre-IPO contracts – the developer building the exchange – is Entropy IO. TradeXYZ, the most prominent developer on the platform, typically does not list pre-IPO perps until S-1s are public, according to David Schamis, CEO of Hyperliquid Strategies, the publicly traded treasury company that invests in the HYPE token that powers the exchange.

"Liquidity will probably be deeper once TradeXYZ lists these companies," Schamis said in a call. "Generally these will trade at a premium to the IPO price but they do a good job predicting where it will be post-IPO."

The bigger price drop in OpenAI perps reflects the company's closer ties to GPU rent-a-center CoreWeave, whose shares touched a new one-year low Thursday, extending a decline over that period to 54%, as concerns mount over the company's debt-financing strategy.

In April, CoreWeave announced a deal with Anthropic to power the company's Claude products, but did not disclose the value of the deal. The company's relationship with OpenAI stretches back further, and as of September 2025 was worth at least $22 billion including a 5-year agreement to provide datacenters and technology.
While OpenAI perps are falling more than Anthropic the past 24 hours, the two are both down about 15% from highs last month, according to Hyperliquid pricing.

kanebridgenews.com/amazon-in-talks-to-bu.headline: Amazon in Talks to Buy AI Startup Decart for Around $7 Billion
kanebridgenews.com/amazon-in-talks-to-bu.author: Kanebridge

paragraphs.text: 29%increase; is in talks to acquire artificial-intelligence startup Decart in a deal that could be valued at around $7 billion, according to people familiar with the matter. San Francisco-based Decart’s software makes it easier for developers to switch between different AI chips, a capability that is becoming increasingly important as companies race to secure more computing power. A deal could come together soon, the people said, assuming talks don’t fall apart or another suitor doesn’t emerge.

Decart has raised more than $400 million in venture capital funding from investors including Sequoia Capital, Benchmark and Radical Ventures, according to PitchBook. It was valued at nearly $4 billion in May. The company was founded in 2023 by three Israeli engineers, brothers Dean and Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev.

Decart is also developing world models called Lucy and Oasis. World models can generate and simulate real-world 3-D environments. Amazon has developed its own custom AI chip, Trainium3, in competition with Nvidia, which continues to dominate the market for graphics processing units, the specialized chips powering the AI boom.

Amazon Web Services gave Decart early access to the chip in 2025 after meeting with the company and being impressed by its founders, The Wall Street Journal has reported. 5 billion deal for the MGM movie and television studio in 2022 and a roughly $11 billion deal for Starlink rival Globalstar announced earlier this year.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/mark-wahlberg-.headline: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/mark-wahlberg-.author: Aisha Malik

paragraphs.text: Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way.

Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy.
The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role.

“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. But if you can use it to enhance what you’re doing, I’m all for that.”
That said, Wahlberg made special mention of his belief that storytelling should remain at the heart of filmmaking.

“I’ve done big, effects-driven movies,” Wahlberg said. “I think I was in that kind of sweet spot when the first Jurassic Park was made, or when Perfect Storm came out, and you had that wave, the 100-foot wave that was in the trailer. Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.”

When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault, a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.

“I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.”
He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.

“I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life […] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. I think people are going to have massive opportunities to watch whatever it is they want, and if there’s a real audience for that, they should be entitled to have what they want to see.”
