theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/16/israel.headline: Israeli settlers attack olive farmers and Washington Post journalist in West Bank
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/16/israel.author: William Christou

paragraphs.text: Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank in a coordinated movement to disrupt the annual olive harvest, burning cars and trees and injuring Palestinians and a Washington Post photographer.

Masked settlers wielding clubs and other weapons attacked people attempting to harvest their olives in towns across the West Bank on Friday. At least six people were injured in the town of Abu Falah near Ramallah, the Palestinian Red Crescent Society said.

At least 80 settlers, some of whom were carrying firearms or clubs, gathered to stop Palestinians from harvesting their olives in Abu Falah, using slingshots to hurl rocks at the farmers in view of Israeli military vehicles. When some of the Palestinians then picked up rocks to defend themselves, the Israeli military fired teargas in their direction.

The Israeli Foreign Press Association said in a statement: “This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities.”

Among those injured was the Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was beaten by settlers in an attack that lasted more than 10 minutes, according to witnesses. Settlers stole her passport, phone, wallet and equipment.

“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me,” Levine said from a hospital bed in Ramallah. She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.
In a statement, the Washington Post said Levine had been wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist.

There has been a surge of settler violence against Palestinians over the past month. Settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks since 27 September, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group.
Every year, settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest their olives, but this year’s harvest has seen an uptick in violence as Israel’s elections approach at the end of October.
At least four Palestinians have been killed and more than 100 others have been injured over the past month, Palestinian authorities said. Thousands of trees have been damaged.

Israel imposed new rules on the olive harvest this year, barring Palestinians from harvesting their trees located in Area C – an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.

The new orders prohibit Palestinians from entering about 8,800 hectares (21,800 acres) of agricultural land – a 30% increase from the year prior – without approval of the Israeli military. By contrast, the military gave Israeli citizens access to more land this year.

The rights group Peace Now says the military decreased the amount of land Israeli citizens were prohibited from entering from about 1,070 hectares in 2025 to 680 hectares in 2026, for the purpose of preventing settler violence.

The olive harvest is an economic lifeline for Palestinians and has grown in importance since Israel revoked work permits for many Palestinians in the West Bank after the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023.
Photos and videos showed large swathes of agricultural land with uprooted olive trees in Kufur Malek, outside Ramallah, where Israeli bulldozers had razed trees.

Settlers rarely face accountability for their violence, even when well documented. Rights groups say settlers enjoy the protection of the Israeli military, which intervenes only if Palestinians try to defend themselves.
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has on occasion condemned the violence, which he says is due to just about 100 settlers, but he has taken few steps to stop settler violence.

Settlements have rapidly expanded across the West Bank under his rightwing government, leading to international condemnation. The UN and most countries judge settlements to be in violation of international law.
Friday’s attack in Abu Falah followed a similar attack hours earlier near the West Bank village of Turmus Ayya, where settlers burned three cars after attacking Palestinians harvesting olives.
Videos shared by the Israeli rights group B’tselem showed hundreds of bags of olives “violently” stolen by Israeli settlers from Palestinians and taken to Israeli olive presses.
Sarit Michaeli, an independent activist, said settlers were stealing Palestinians’ olive crop on a scale “never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue”.
A spokesperson for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack and declined to comment further due to privacy laws.

finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/german.headline: Germany, France Push to Scrap Climate Neutrality Goal for Cars
finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/german.author: John Ainger, James Regan and Kamil Kowalcze

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Germany and France will push to scrap a landmark European Union goal to reach climate neutrality for cars by 2035, after agreeing a deal to protect their domestic industries against intensifying global competition.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The two sides struck an accord Friday that reflects both the German push for looser CO2 standards for the auto sector and the French desire for a strict "made in Europe" definition. The end result is that the two will lobby for a significant watering down of a key pillar of the EU's green deal to reach net-zero by 2050.

Paris and Berlin will seek to lower overall emissions cuts for autos to 90% by 2035, without having to compensate the remaining 10% through offsets via green steel, which underpinned a reform by the European Commission earlier this year. Instead such offsets will be counted as part of the 90% target.

It marks a significant shift in approach. At the beginning of the year, EU automakers were facing obligations for new car sales to be 100% electric by 2035. The Franco-German deal would mean the goal of reaching climate neutrality in cars no longer exists.

Germany had been pushing for looser goals to safeguard jobs throughout the supply chain, and French carmaker Renault SA Chief Executive Officer Francois Provost warned this week that output would have to be curtailed significantly if changes weren't made.

"We have a clear ambition: to successfully transform our automotive industry, whilst maintaining our climate targets and our production in Europe," French President Emmanuel Macron said in a post on X following the deal which was negotiated during a summit in Brussels.

Still, there will be concern that the deal struck between Europe's two biggest countries could leave the region's carmakers even further behind in the electrification race against China. It also comes at a time when electric vehicle sales are picking up, as the Iran war boosts gasoline and diesel prices.

"Germany and France are making a historic mistake," said Anna Krajinska, senior director for vehicles and industrial transformation at T&E, which campaigns for clean energy and transport. "German and French political leaders claim they are acting to save jobs, but this may well be the deal that buries Europe's auto industry."

The two sides opened the door for the UK to qualify for European subsidies under "Made in Europe" rules set out by the Industrial Accelerator Act, something that has been long sought by London. To benefit, however, the country will have to align on the EU's rules on foreign direct investment and trade defense, a thinly-veiled reference to measures the bloc has taken against China.

Agreement on the deal was delayed after the Social Democratic Party, the left-leaning junior coalition partner in Germany's government, demanded assurances on protections for German jobs and manufacturing.

The Franco-German accord provides political momentum but is not yet a done deal: changes to EU car-emissions rules and the Industrial Accelerator Act still require agreement among member states and the European Parliament. The Irish presidency of the EU is seeking a deal among nations on cars by the end of the year.
Christophe Perillat, CEO of French auto parts supplier Valeo SA, welcomed the Franco-German deal.
"We are all fully engaged and working in a coordinated manner to defend the European industry," he wrote in emailed response to a Bloomberg query.

The development comes days after the EU and China reached an understanding that would cap China-made hybrid imports into the bloc at 350,000 vehicles in 2027, compared with about 800,000 expected this year. Hybrids had not been covered by the EU's 2024 tariffs on Chinese battery-electric cars, helping shipments surge.
EU leaders discussed how best to boost industrial competitiveness at a meeting in Brussels Thursday.

"We have made the right decisions for the hundreds of thousands of employees and the locations of the German auto industry," said Lars Klingbeil, Germany's foreign minister. "Automakers have a responsibility to invest in the future of German manufacturing sites and to secure jobs."
--With assistance from Michael Nienaber and Albertina Torsoli.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65ynk7212vqo.headline: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65ynk7212vqo.author: Lucy Williamson

paragraphs.text: Middle East correspondentReporting fromAbu Falah
Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank.

A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt.

Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence: a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby.
The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car.
"We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys … started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck – look, I am bleeding!"

Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured.
Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars – including one of his own.
"As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him.
Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports.
"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible," the spokesperson said.

Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me.
The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year.
Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack.

In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could – one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below.

Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts.
All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts – small encampments on hilltops – are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support.

"This is a hotspot – there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today."
But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees.
There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave.

But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return.

As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back.
American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene.

"I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes."
In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined.
As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing.
Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation – a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts.
The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank.
Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves.
What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase.

The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers, and fuelling Jewish claims to the land.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/elorians-first.headline: Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them
techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/elorians-first.author: Aditya Mehta

paragraphs.text: Elorian, the Palo Alto AI startup that raised a $55 million seed round at a $300 million valuation before it launched a product, released its first model on Friday, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.

The model, Glimpse, is launching as a research preview with API access and a chat interface is waitlist-only, so for now it’s a results table and a thesis. The thesis? Today’s AI models, for all their skill with language and code, still can’t really see.

Most multimodal models look at an image once, convert it to tokens, and then reason about it in text — like describing a photo from memory. Glimpse keeps going back to the source. Mid-reasoning, it can crop into a region, pull specific frames from a video, or run code to measure or compare what it’s looking at, a mechanism Elorian calls a “visual scratch space.” Think of someone pinching to zoom on a phone photo to double-check what they thought they saw.
For former Google DeepMind researcher and Elorian CEO Andrew Dai, one of the clearest signs that AI still couldn’t really see came on game night.

Last year he photographed a board game he’d just finished with friends and asked a frontier model who was winning. It couldn’t say. Board games “each have their own visual language, each have their own iconography, symbols,” he told TechCrunch. “To an adult, it’s quite easy to understand what’s going on with minimal text, but these models aren’t able to intuit what the symbols mean.”
“Humans can look at IKEA diagrams, with no text, and assemble IKEA furniture, right? Why can’t AI models?” he said.

The approach isn’t completely new — OpenAI added crop-and-zoom during reasoning to its o-series models in 2025 — but Elorian’s pitch is that it built the whole model around it, cheaply. The company says a small team trained Glimpse on a few hundred GPUs and that the model is substantially smaller than the frontier systems it’s benchmarked against.
Glimpse costs $0.60 per million tokens in and $3 per million tokens out — cheaper than mid-level models like Sonnet and Sol but more expensive than lightweight models like Haiku and Luna.
But according to Elorian’s evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks.
Elorian came out of stealth six months ago with a round co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Altimeter Capital, with participation from Nvidia and Google chief scientist Jeff Dean.

The initial targets are companies sitting on lots of video: robotics firms, scientific labs, media and creative companies. Longer term, Elorian wants to move from seeing to doing. That means building a model of a scene using that to choose an action, including directly controlling robots. Next year, Dai said, the company aims to build “the world’s best visual reasoning model,” one that leads on every visual reasoning test.

theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/16/tough-t.headline: ‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: what the reviewers say about NAZA documentary
theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/16/tough-t.author: Sammy Gecsoyler

paragraphs.text: Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary NAZA as a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”.

NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, was released in UK cinemas this week and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.
The investigative documentary, which contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders speaking anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, has received widespread praise.

In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus”.

British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”. The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”.

Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region. As a work of cinema, it is exemplary. As a work of journalism, it is inarguable. As a document, it is an indictment.”

The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”. The Los Angeles Times says NAZA is a “stone-cold frightening” film that “burns the conscience”. And in New York magazine, it is described as “one of the most important films of our time”.

The Hollywood Reporter praises NAZA as a “sober and thoroughly documented bombshell of an expose” that “leaves one with a deadening feeling, as if humanity may have lost all hope”. The Toronto Star says “NAZA is heartbreaking but essential viewing, questioning the systems that cause and quantify civilian death in modern warfare”.

The Spanish outlet El Mundo hailed NAZA as “the film of our time, a superb, electrifying, and devastating documentary about the systematic model of annihilation of the Palestinian people” that ultimately “points the finger at us. At night, in silence.”

The French newspaper Le Monde says the film “has the effect of an uppercut that leaves the viewer stunned”, while the Danish culture magazine Soundvenue calls NAZA a “soul-crushing testimony to the genocide in Gaza” that is an “example of how the world increasingly seems like a dystopia”.

The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”.

When the film opened in Italy last month, it topped the charts. The Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera says NAZA lasts “only 80 minutes, but no more is needed: the ‘scientific’ coldness with which the interviewees reconstruct how they are destroying Gaza is something unforgettable”.

The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.

Various bodies, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/tressfecta-wan.headline: Tressfecta wants to make hair braiding a less arduous task for hairstylists
techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/tressfecta-wan.author: Dominic-Madori Davis

paragraphs.text: Aisata Diallo, 24, calls herself a lifelong braider. “I’ve always braided my hair growing up and, at some point in my college career, started braiding other people’s hair,” she said. At Northeastern University in Boston, she found limited access to braiders and textured-hair specialists, so she decided to fill that gap by starting a small business of her own.

“Throughout that experience, I was very close to some of the pain points in the styling process and complained about it constantly,” she said. Braiding is a manual task, and a single style can take eight hours to complete. Many professionals deal with issues like cramping and carpal tunnel syndrome after spending long days standing behind a chair weaving hair into patterns.

At first, Diallo said she didn’t know what to do about it. “I stopped braiding, and one of the reasons that I stopped braiding was due to the physical toll it has on your body.” She wanted to find a way to make braiding less painful andwondered whether new AI technology could automate some part of the process. Building hardware for braiding is expensive, difficult, and complex, which is one reason there have been few innovations in this space. The textured hair market has also long been overlooked by the mainstream.

Then, last year, she had an idea: Tressfecta, a company building products for textured hair. Its first project is a tool called Plait Pilot that helps braiders with the initial process of separating hair from packs before braiding begins. That process alone can take hours, especially when a client wants small braids. Diallo said the device is designed to work like this: A stylist places the braiding hair on top of it and sets the size they want the hair separated into, and the device separates the pieces and dispenses them back to the stylist so they can grab them while braiding.

“It’s very challenging to build this kind of tool in this space,” she said, citing the nuance and complexity of the braiding style process. Different types of textured hair also need to be accounted for, especially when length and density are considered. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all solution.”

Tressfecta is still technically pre-launch, and it is working on the prototype of Plait Pilot. Diallo has been bootstrapping the company, while also drawing on funding from grant and accelerator programs. “I am preparing to fundraise,” she said, noting how hard it can be to raise money for hardware, especially beauty hardware. For now, Diallo said she’s connecting with stylists and braiders who can test the technology. She also spent this week in San Francisco as one of TechCrunch’s Battlefield 200 companies.

She doesn’t remember exactly where she first heard about Disrupt, possibly on LinkedIn or in a founder resource group, but when we talked ahead of the show, which wrapped up on Thursday, she was looking forward to connecting with people and showing off her product. She was especially excited to connect with people and for others to see her product. “It feels like a great opportunity,” she said.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/in-you-can-see.headline: In ‘You Can See Everything,’ Elizabeth Holmes meets her equal in comedian Nathan Fielder
techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/in-you-can-see.author: Amanda Silberling

paragraphs.text: “Isn’t it weird that I like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like… a business scam?” comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes.

One month before the notorious Theranos CEO surrendered to begin her eleven-year criminal fraud sentence in 2023, Holmes and her husband contacted A24 as a last-ditch effort to exonerate her in the public eye, suggesting they send a film crew to document her final days of freedom. Alongside director Lance Oppenheim, Fielder — a cringe-comedy mastermind whose work often walks the line between fact and fiction — embraced the impossible project of figuring out who the infamous Stanford dropout really is.
“I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.”

No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche. His satirical docu-reality show “Nathan for You” catapulted him to cult stardom as he assumed the role of an exaggerated, deadpan version of himself who tries to help struggling small business by executing asinine interventions. In one early episode that went viral, Fielder convinces a coffee shop to change its name to “Dumb Starbucks” as a marketing stunt, but consults a lawyer to help him toe the flimsy line of parody law and escape legal trouble.
“If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot free,” Fielder says to Holmes.
“It was real.”
“I was just kind of making a little joke. Maybe it was in bad taste.”

We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent. What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes it when she says she did nothing wrong. Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered.

Across Fielder’s body of metatextual comedy, even his most reverent fans can’t quite figure out when he’s acting, when he’s being himself, and if Fielder himself even knows where to draw that line anymore.
In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: after over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas.
“The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” she tells Fielder. “I know I didn’t commit any crime.”
[The rest of this review contains spoilers.]

Early on in filming, The New York Times has just published a profile of Holmes, which was widely criticized at the time for allowing Holmes to portray herself as an innocent mom deprived of the chance to watch her kids grow up.
And yet, Holmes and her husband, hotel heir Billy Evans, were livid about the article.

At one point in an interview, Holmes tells the Times reporter that she wasn’t offended by actress Amanda Seyfried’s portrayal of her in Hulu’s miniseries “The Dropout” because, “They’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.”

She and her husband insist that the quote was taken out of context. They claim that they have evidence that Holmes actually said, “They’re playing a character they created,” relieving her from any implication that she admitted to concocting an inauthentic persona as CEO of Theranos.
Fielder asks Evans multiple times to share this evidence so he can prove that Holmes was misquoted. He never does.

Once Holmes reports to prison, Fielder is agonized as he tries to make something out of his month of footage. He calls in the perfect sidekick to help him dissect her confounding behavior: the very actress who portrays her in “The Dropout.”

Fielder plays Seyfried a brutal clip from his time with Holmes, when he tries watching “The Dropout” with the subject of the series itself. When they get to a tense scene involving Holmes’ manipulative ex-boyfriend and former Theranos partner-in-crime Sunny Balwani — who is also now in prison — Holmes can no longer bear to watch this fictional version of herself. She turns away and cries.

In other words, Seyfried is watching Holmes react to Seyfried’s portrayal of Holmes, who was probably also playing a character herself. But Seyfried is not the only one creating a crude approximation of the real Elizabeth. Evans has constructed a life-like AI avatar of his wife, trapped inside of a large vertical screen that he wheels over to the dinner table to sit with him and his kids as though she’s actually there.

The remainder of the film is a constellation of colliding personas. Though it’s a non-fiction documentary, it’s clear that everyone involved is, to some extent, also performing for the cameras. How could they not? Seyfried’s determination to understand Holmes’ story seems pure, but it’s not lost on the audience that she just scored a leading role in one of the most talked-about films of the year.
Meanwhile, Evans behaves in such an unfathomably egregious manner that he may even be intentionally playing the villain to drum up sympathy for his reviled wife.

Evans knows that Fielder and Oppenheim are not convinced of Holmes’ innocence. This documentary will not sway anyone to believe that his wife is being wrongly held in federal custody. But Evans makes himself appear so appallingly unlikable that some viewers may leave the theater feeling bad for Holmes, seeing her as a victim, and allowing her to double-down on another persona she adopted while on trial: a harmless, docile woman who was manipulated by her ex-partner to obliviously tell a cascade of increasingly harmful lies.

Once Holmes is in jail, Fielder is not allowed to bring recording devices when he visits her, so he tries to write a script of their conversations from memory, struggling to accurately recreate the nuances of a conversation where every last word carries immense meaning. With Seyfried reprising her role from “The Dropout,” we see the pair practice reading the script, editing the language as Fielder tries to recall Holmes’ exact phrasing and delivery.
In character as Holmes, Seyfried says, “People think Amanda’s show is a documentary. I get treated worse [in prison] because of how she portrayed me.”
As she reads the lines, Seyfried breaks character.
“I didn’t do that,” the actress says. “She did that to herself.”

techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/jev-is-vercels.headline: Jev is Vercel’s fastest-adopted AI model ever
techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/jev-is-vercels.author: Russell Brandom

paragraphs.text: Jev has become the fastest adopted AI model ever — at least by some measures.

Vercel data published on Thursday shows that, within two weeks of its launch, the buzzy decision model was being used by 35% of paid teams, with nearly double the reach of the second most popular model, Sonnet 5.5. It’s the fastest adoption a model has ever seen in its first two weeks, according to Vercel’s data, and a major accomplishment for the model’s creators, TypeSafe AI.

Published in limited release on September 15, Jev is designed as a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs. Limiting the outputs lets the model run cheaper and faster than alternatives like Sonnet, making it ideal for classifying large quantities of data quickly. That new approach has attracted significant buzz in the weeks since Jev’s release — inspiring competing offerings from OpenAI and Amazon, among others — but until now there has been little hard data to back up the good vibes.

The data comes from Vercel’s AI gateway, a unified API service similar to OpenRouter. It’s a necessarily limited view — particularly at risk of undercounting major labs like OpenAI and Anthropic that offer their own APIs — but it shows the buzz around Jev really did translate into actual usage. In fact, Vercel was an early adopter of Jev, using it to replace GPT-6 Luna for classifying harmful commands.
The report also shows continuing momentum for open source models, which now account for more than 70% of the tokens processed through Vercel’s gateway and nearly 25% of the total spend.

While open source models are capturing a larger share of the market, the market is also growing fast. Spending on frontier labs has grown tenfold, even as it accounts for a smaller share of overall spend, giving credence to the idea that frontier models and open source alternatives may turn out to be complementary rather than competitive.

cnbc.com/2026/10/16/republicans-midterms.headline: Why Trump and the GOP's billion-dollar midterm blitz isn’t working
cnbc.com/2026/10/16/republicans-midterms.author: Luke Fountain

paragraphs.text: A billion-dollar war chest was meant to be Republicans' great equalizer heading into a bleak midterm election environment defined by economic frustration, President Donald Trump's unpopularity and fallout from the war in Iran.
So far it hasn't worked.

From Labor Day through Oct 14., GOP groups injected more than $740 million into congressional races that will determine control of Congress, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. That includes at least $220 million in spending from Trump-linked groups. Elon Musk has separately given another $276 million to Republican groups since July and helped boost the GOP's Senate Leadership Fund super PAC to a record quarter.

Yet with less than three weeks until the Nov. 3 Election Day, the spending blitz has barely moved the map. Democrats lead in FiftyPlusOne's polling averages across nine of the Senate's most competitive races – Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas – little changed from before the Republican spending spree. Minnesota was expected to be solidly blue, making its tight race a concern for Democrats.
And Republican political operatives and independent election observers CNBC spoke with say the money hasn't had the effects its magnitude would be expected to in voter sentiment.

Meanwhile, the broader battlefield continues to deteriorate for Republicans. Democrats are favored to flip the House and remain competitive in the Senate, according to the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, forcing the GOP to burn millions protecting once-safe seats while abandoning former pickup targets.

"Money is an amplifier, not a magic wand," said Neil Newhouse, partner at Republican polling firm Public Opinion Strategies. "You can buy all the airtime in the world, but if the political climate is blowing 30 miles an hour in your face, ad volume alone isn't going to turn the weather around."
Musk flooding the zone
Republicans entered the final stretch of the midterm election with unusually deep pockets.

MAGA Inc. had nearly $416 million on hand at the end of August, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Across the broader ecosystem, major Republican organizations had roughly $1 billion available, eclipsing the $579 million available for comparable Democratic groups, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission filings.

Then came Musk — after saying he'd be less involved in this year's election. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has given more than $276 million to Republican groups since July, including $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund Republican-boosting super PAC and more than $76 million to his own America PAC, according to figures confirmed to CNBC by an America PAC spokesperson. Musk's known federal political giving this election cycle now totals roughly $366 million, making him the largest known donor of the midterms.

And Musk is far from alone. Nine of the 10 largest individual and family donor groups this cycle are Republican-aligned, accounting for 86 cents of every dollar contributed by the top 10, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC records.

"We are watching an unprecedented concentration and scale of political influence and wealth this election cycle," said Hilary Braseth, executive director of OpenSecrets, a nonprofit, nonpartisan group that tracks campaign spending.
AdImpact projects $11.6 billion in political advertising this 2025-2026 cycle, surpassing both the 2022 midterms and the 2024 presidential election.
Paying more for less
However, the size of Republicans’ financial advantage may overstate how much advertising that money can actually buy.

That's because much of the GOP's money, particularly spending by Trump-aligned groups, has arrived late and via super PACs, which can pay far more for airtime than candidates. Federal law entitles candidates to broadcasters' lowest unit rate during the final 60 days before a general election; outside groups get no such protection.
It's an edge for Democrats whose candidates have generally outraised their Republican counterparts.

In Dallas, for example, Democrat James Talarico's campaign spent about $2.4 million on local broadcast ads from Oct. 1 through Oct. 14, enough for the average viewer to see his ads about 48 times, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. The pro-Ken Paxton Texas PAC spent about $7.8 million for roughly 81 views per viewer – more than three times as much money for only about 70% more exposure, according to the analysis.

Airtime has become so expensive that Paxton's allies have begun buying ads during national sporting events, calculating that reaching enough Texans through a national broadcast can cost less than buying across the state's local television markets, according to the Associated Press.
"R money advantage not what it appears to be on [the] surface," Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who lost to Paxton in the primary, posted on X on Oct. 5.

Across the nine key Senate battlegrounds identified by the Cook Political Report as of Oct. 1, Republicans led broadcast TV spending in seven and outspent Democrats by 26% overall through Sept. 30, yet generated only 7% more airings.

To be sure, super PACs don't face the same pricing disadvantage on digital ads, where campaigns and outside groups compete on more equal footing. But broadcast TV still dominates political spending, with AdImpact projecting it will account for 48% of the 2026 cycle total.
Little movement in political polls
But the payoff from all that spending has been harder to see in political polls.

Despite more than $113 million spent on negative advertising targeting Talarico since the Texas primary, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, a Siena College poll released Tuesday showed Talarico leading Paxton 48% to 44%, down only slightly from his six-point lead in September.

In Michigan, after more than $87 million in attacks targeting Democrat Abdul El-Sayed this year, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, Fox News polling from late September found El-Sayed's favorable rating among registered voters up five points from its early August survey, while Republican Mike Rogers' fell four points.

Part of the challenge is diminishing returns on ads as Election Day nears. Political advertising experts tell CNBC that as campaigns repeatedly target the same small pool of persuadable voters, each additional dollar is less likely to reach someone who has not already heard the message.

"When an undecided voter has already seen 20 negative ads today, the 21st ad doesn't persuade them. It just gets tuned out," said Michael Beckel, money in politics reform director at Issue One. "Their eyes glaze over." Issue One works to reduce the influence of money in politics and has a board that includes former Democratic and Republican elected officials.

Still, some Republicans counter that topline poll movement is the wrong barometer. They say the September cash influx helped keep vulnerable candidates competitive as the political environment deteriorated.

In Texas, Republicans spent $121.5 million on the Senate race in September, up from just $5.5 million over the previous three months, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, while Musk's America PAC added direct mail and canvassing. Republicans involved in the race said the picture could have been far worse without that support.

"The spending hasn't put Paxton ahead, but it kept a messy race and flawed candidate from becoming an unwinnable one," said a Republican operative involved in the Texas Senate race, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the state of the contest.

Maine offers another test. Republicans have poured more than $50 million into the state to support incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, nearly twice Democratic spending, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. Since early September, FiftyPlusOne's polling average has tightened modestly, from about a three-point advantage for Democrat Troy Jackson in early September to roughly two points now.
From offense to defense
The clearest sign that the GOP's cash advantage has stalled, however, is where the money is migrating.

In April, the Senate Leadership Fund announced a record $342 million advertising program across eight states designed to protect the GOP majority and expand the map. Texas, Kansas and Nebraska were not among the states.

Since Sept. 1, the SLF and affiliated groups — according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data — have spent or committed roughly $180 million across those three states, all of which Trump carried by double digits in 2024.
"Outside groups are diverting millions into deep-red territory to build defensive moats, leaving pickup opportunities starved for cash in the final stretch," Beckel told CNBC.
But those emergency defenses have come at a cost, diverting money from races Republicans once hoped to win and forcing national groups to narrow the map elsewhere.

In North Carolina, the Senate Leadership Fund initially pledged $71 million to back Republican Michael Whatley. On Oct. 2, however, the group pulled most of its remaining ad reservations after spending about $32.8 million, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, as Democrat Roy Cooper continued to hold a double-digit lead in FiftyPlusOne's polling average.
It's a striking retreat in a perennial battleground where Republicans have won every presidential and Senate election since 2008.
The same triage is unfolding in the House.

The Congressional Leadership Fund cut off spending this week for vulnerable GOP Reps. Thomas Kean Jr. of New Jersey and Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa following grim internal polling. The group also shelved efforts to flip Democratic-held seats represented by Reps. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan and Greg Landsman of Ohio. The spending shifts were first reported by the New York Times.

Those four races had already absorbed about $13.7 million in Congressional Leadership Fund spending through Oct. 14, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. CLF is redirecting roughly $10 million from those races across 16 other districts, according to the Times.
The new spending includes the South Texas seat held by Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, a district Trump carried by 18 points in 2024. De La Cruz herself won reelection by about 14 points in 2024.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/waymos-robotax.headline: Waymo’s robotaxis are headed to Canada
techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/waymos-robotax.author: Kirsten Korosec

paragraphs.text: Alphabet’s self-driving car unit, Waymo, is expanding into Canada after receiving approval to participate in Ontario’s automated vehicle pilot program.

The company isn’t launching a robotaxi service just yet, though. Waymo tends to follow the same playbook for every new city, gradually proceeding from manual mapping to testing, and eventually operating a commercial service.

Waymo said in a blog post on Friday that its self-driving vehicles will be manually driven in Toronto to create high-definition maps of local street networks. The company will then test its autonomous vehicles on public roads with a human safety operator on board. These operators will eventually be pulled from the driver’s seat, and afterwards the company will invite the public to take rides in its robotaxis.

Waymo’s move into Canada is part of an aggressive push into new markets that’s picking up speed. Two years ago, the company was operating in only three commercial markets, and its robotaxis were not yet driving on freeways. Its expansion plans kicked off in March 2025 with a deployment in Austin, and later in Atlanta. Today, the company has robotaxi services in 15 U.S. cities, and is testing them in London and Tokyo as well.

The company’s co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana said the expansion into Canada marks an important milestone in its global journey. This is also the northernmost and possibly most wintry city that Waymo has so far tried to operate in, so these conditions will test its AV technology and operational savviness.

As part of its accelerated expansion strategy, Waymo has started partnering with third-party companies to manage its fleet in each respective city. Toronto is no different: Waymo said it has partnered with Toronto-based Element Fleet Management, and expects to support hundreds of jobs in spaces such as fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service and operations.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvx284w16z1po.headline: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back on front line where Starlink plays a key role
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvx284w16z1po.author: Dan Johnson

paragraphs.text: Ukraine correspondent Reporting fromnear Lyman, eastern Ukraine
A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.

Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.
This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.

The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.

While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September – and suffered few casualties in return.

The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".
Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.

He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.

This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.
Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.
Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability.

Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.
Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.
Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.
The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.
An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."
He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.
Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous".
"The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."

Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.

In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation.
"As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed."
"I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".

That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present.
"The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained.

"This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."
All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.

This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin.
Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.
But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.
The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.
I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."
Additional reporting by Kostas Kallergis and Anastasiia Levchenko

cnbc.com/2026/10/16/us-china-mastercard-.headline: U.S. raises Mastercard, Citigroup China market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says
cnbc.com/2026/10/16/us-china-mastercard-.author: Anniek Bao

paragraphs.text: BANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market access issues for Mastercard Inc and Citigroup Inc during at least two bilateral meetings with Chinese counterparts in Bangkok this week, according to a U.S. Treasury official.

The Treasury delegation, led by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke, held bilateral meetings with officials from the People's Bank of China and the finance ministry on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance meetings and the IMF-World Bank annual gathering this week, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door meetings.

The talks included market access for U.S. companies, including Mastercard, Visa and Citigroup, the official said, adding that regulatory approval was part of the agreement reached during the meeting between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping during the latter's state visit in Washington last month.
The sideline meetings in Bangkok continued discussions on implementing these deals, the official said.

The PBOC, China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, China Securities Regulatory Commission, Chinese embassies in Singapore and Thailand, the U.S. Treasury Department press office and Visa did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Citigroup and Mastercard declined to comment.

The progress follows China's Oct. 13 approval for Visa Inc. to begin preparing a wholly owned domestic card-clearing business. Visa has up to a year to prepare before it applies for an operating license, the PBOC has said.

China has opened much of its financial sector to foreign firms since 2018, gradually lifting foreign ownership caps on services such as securities, futures and fund management. It still limits cross-border capital flows and has kept state-backed domestic players dominant in payments.

Mastercard currently operates yuan card payments in China through a local joint venture with NetsUnion Clearing Corp., which began operating in 2024. The pending approval would allow it to operate as an independent entity, the person said.

Citigroup — which has hired several dozen employees for its China unit — is seeking a wholly owned securities license to conduct A-share brokerage, underwriting, research and principal trading businesses in the onshore market, two people familiar with the industry said, requesting anonymity for discussing private matters.
One of the two people close to Citigroup said the bank planned to increase its China securities staff to about 100.
The bank applied in late 2021, and Reuters reported last month that approval could come soon.
Trump and Xi are expected to meet in person for the third time this year in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November.
"The move suggests the US-China trade environment remains benign, and Beijing is keen to keep up the momentum," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group.

Licensing U.S. financial firms is a "limited concession" on market access, she said, though it signals China is continuing to open up, and "this should marginally bolster investor confidence in Chinese assets."

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/16/brazil.headline: Brazil’s Lula says he now backs lowering age of criminal responsibility to 16
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/16/brazil.author: Tiago Rogero

paragraphs.text: Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced that he now supports lowering the age of criminal responsibility for “heinous” crimes from 18 to 16, reversing a longstanding policy in what is widely seen as a desperate electoral gambit.

The U-turn, which Lula announced during a Thursday night interview with TV Globo, comes with the presidential runoff in just over a week. The incumbent faces an uphill battle to overturn the first-round victory of his opponent, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who remains slightly ahead at the polls.

Both the senator and his father, the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, have long supported lowering the age of criminal responsibility – they want it reduced to 14 rather than 16 – but Lula and his party have always opposed the change.

After repeated opinion polls, the latest of them this week, showed that 80% of the population supports lowering the age, Lula said: “My view, as a Brazilian citizen, is that for any and every heinous crime, I am in favour of lowering the age.”
He answered “yes” when the reporter asked whether he meant lowering it to 16.

The list of crimes classified as “heinous” under Brazilian law is extensive, ranging from murder and rape to the falsification of medicines and drug trafficking – the offence for which about a quarter of the 816,000 people serving prison sentences in Brazil were incarcerated.

Human rights organisations and security experts have long criticised proposals to lower the age of criminal responsibility, arguing that they do little to tackle violence while increasing recruitment into organised crime in Brazil’s overcrowded prisons.

On Thursday, before Lula’s interview, the proposal had been discussed in the senate. The Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation, had criticised it for “not addressing the causes of violence”, adding that placing young people “prematurely in the prison system tends to deepen cycles of violence and exclusion, undermining their rehabilitation”.

The columnist Josias de Souza wrote in his UOL column that, by reversing his longstanding position, Lula “decided to change himself. It was no ordinary transformation. On public security, Lula turned himself inside out. He began defending what he had always rejected.”

The incumbent has doubled down in recent days in an effort to overturn Bolsonaro’s 2.2 million-vote first-round lead by appealing to independents and undecided voters. He has secured congressional approval for a shorter working week – a proposal on which Bolsonaro himself U-turned and decided to support at the last minute, when it appeared ready to pass – and debt relief for microentrepreneurs, as well as promising free public transport on weekends.

cnbc.com/2026/10/16/netflix-peter-rice-c.headline: Here's who Netflix just brought in to run content — and what it means for the streamer
cnbc.com/2026/10/16/netflix-peter-rice-c.author: Sarah Whitten

paragraphs.text: Netflix is shaking up its C-suite in an effort to fix its engagement woes.

On Thursday, the streaming giant announced that former Disney executive Peter Rice will take over as the company's chief content officer, overseeing global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events.

Rice is replacing 10-year Netflix veteran Bela Bajaria, who most recently led the company's global content team with a focus on its live sports strategy. Bajaria was initially hired in 2016 to help the streamer launch an unscripted division as well as licensing and studio co-productions. She later transitioned to the top creative role, spearheading Netflix's $20 billion content budget.

She oversaw popular TV series like "Stranger Things," "Wednesday," "Bridgerton," "Squid Game," "Adolescence" and "Beef," as well as Netflix films like "Frankenstein" and "KPop Demon Hunters." Bajaria also helped push Netflix into live sports and events, including deals with the WWE and the NFL as well as programs like "The Roast of Tom Brady."

Prior to his stint at Disney, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group as well as Fox's lead executive on the Hulu board. He was also the president of Fox Searchlight Pictures and helped release "Slumdog Millionaire," "Juno," "Little Miss Sunshine" and "Sideways."

The executive change follows a tumultuous period for Netflix as it faces stagnating viewership and explores avenues for growth. It comes just days after the streaming giant laid off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce.
The last time Netflix made cuts of this size was in 2022 when it reported its first quarterly subscriber loss in more than 10 years.

"We believe this round of layoffs reflects more structural changes to the cost base than a reaction to near-term subscriber dynamics," wrote Brian Pitz, managing director and head of internet and interactive entertainment equity research at BMO Capital Markets, in a research note published Friday.
Flagging engagement
In July, Netflix reported viewership increased just 2% in the first half of the year as the streamer suffers from a lack of shows with water-cooler-level hype.
Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted last month during the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company is "not growing as fast as I want us to."
Those warnings, and now Bajaria's exit, have Wall Street bracing for more turbulence ahead.
"The sudden departure of Bajaria likely signals to us that user engagement may have remained soft throughout [the third quarter]," Pitz wrote.
Netflix is set to release fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday.
In July, Nielsen reported that Netflix had generated 7.8% of TV viewership, while YouTube accounted for nearly double that, at 14.2%.

YouTube has been Netflix's biggest threat in the battle for viewers' time. In response, the streaming giant has sought to diversify its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention.

"If the opportunity is to recast [Netflix] into a broader content hub, the risk is missing the watercooler originals," Steven Cahall, equity analyst at Wells Fargo, wrote in a research note last month. "We see breakout hits as a must for the stock to work again."
What Rice brings to Netflix

Rice has a wealth of experience in television and film, most recently serving as the chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the company. He managed a wide swath of channels across broadcast and streaming, including ABC, Disney Channel, Hulu and FX Networks. During his tenure, he oversaw the production of more than 300 shows, including "American Idol," "Modern Family," "Abbott Elementary," "The Bear," "Only Murders in the Building" and "Shogun."
He also headed up major sporting events such as coverage of the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup.
Under Rice's leadership, Disney earned roughly 300 Primetime Emmy nominations between 2021 and 2022. Of those nods, it won nearly 60 awards across its television networks and streaming platforms.
Meanwhile, Netflix's Emmy wins have slowed.
In 2021, it tied the record for most trophies won by an outlet in a single year with 44. This year, however, it only took home 16 prizes, its lowest Emmy haul in a decade.

With Rice, Netflix is also getting an executive with theatrical experience. After he was ousted by then-Disney CEO Bob Chapek in mid-2022, he transitioned into an independent producer role. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later." He's currently developing a movie adaptation of the video game "Elden Ring."

Late last year, Netflix struck a deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery's film studio and streaming assets, only to be outbid months later by Paramount Skydance, which completed its acquisition of WBD in early October.
Some on Wall Street have speculated that the streamer may be interested in further M&A, including acquiring assets from NBCUniversal after it splits from parent company Comcast.

"[Rice's] long tenure at Fox, and then Disney after its acquisition of Fox, gives him unique insight into the consolidation of two major studios, relevant if Netflix chooses to go after another studio," Alicia Reese, senior vice president of equity research at Wedbush, wrote in a research note Thursday. "Even if it doesn't, Rice's experience fits well as Netflix pushes deeper into theatrical and builds a broader platform with varied content across the entertainment ecosystem."

persuasion.community/p/not-to-be-a-pessi.headline: Not To Be A Pessimist, But These Midterms Won’t Change Much
persuasion.community/p/not-to-be-a-pessi.author: Damon Linker

paragraphs.text: Remember: We’re hiring! Click here to learn about our Junior Editor and Social Media Coordinator roles. We’re looking for driven people to build our social media presence and help us commission and edit the articles you love to read.

The midterm elections are now less than three weeks away—and I think we’ve seen more than enough to conclude that, short of a systemic polling error on a scale surpassing anything we have seen before, Republicans are going to get their asses kicked.

Here’s what that means in practical terms: Democrats are almost certainly going to take control of the House of Representatives. They would have accomplished that this year in almost any scenario, but with Donald Trump’s approval in a slow-motion downward spiral, the generic ballot leaning more and more heavily in the direction of the Dems, and external indicators all looking bad for the incumbent party, such an outcome now looks like a lock.

The only question is how big of a blowout it will be. With the current GOP margin of control in the House already so narrow and so many districts uncompetitive, it likely won’t be as large as the swings we saw to the right in 1994 (54 seats) or 2010 (63 seats), or the swing we saw to the left in 2018 (41 seats). But the Dems only need three wins to take the majority, and they will easily get there and quite a bit more. Nate Silver’s “deluxe” prediction model gives a 93.4 percent chance of Democratic control of the House, with the most likely seat split being 239 to 196.

In the Senate, things are more challenging—but not nearly as challenging as they seemed just a couple of months ago. It turns out that public opinion changes when the president initiates a war he can’t win and never made a compelling case for starting; gas and diesel prices surge; inflation rises; and interest rates shoot skyward. According to Silver’s aggregate tracking poll, Trump now sits at 37.5 percent, with his net approval languishing at an astonishing -22.3. (At this point in 2018, he was at -11.6, while Biden at the same point came in with -9.6.) The deluxe model now has the Democrats with just over a 74 percent chance of taking control of the Senate, with the most likely outcome a Dem majority of 52 to 48. Those are good odds, though nowhere near as good as the House. But as recently as last month, Silver’s Senate model had the odds exactly even, so there’s been a big swing in the direction of the Dems.
In other words, the election is the Democrats’ to lose.
Assuming that’s how things play out and the Democrats take control of both houses of Congress, what will that mean for the short- and medium-term future of the country?
The short answer, I’m afraid, is not much.
The political fact of our time is that ours is a populist era. In this era, electoral cycles work like this:
• A right-populist figure or party runs against the liberal-centrist “establishment” or “the system”;
• This right-populist figure or party wins power;
• This right-populist figure or party becomes the new establishment, overreaches, and makes mistakes;
• Representatives of the old liberal-centrist establishment run against this new establishment and defeat it;

• The old establishment returns to power and misreads its mandate as an endorsement of a return to the old liberal-centrist ways rather than a narrower repudiation of the governing mistakes of the right-wing populists;
• This sets up the right-populists to run and win another campaign against the liberal-centrist establishment;
• Rinse and repeat.

In sum: Voters are unhappy. They reflexively recoil from whoever is currently running the show—whether the old establishment or the newish counter-establishment. This makes for unstable politics, and anyone who wins has a very narrow time horizon in which to do things before they get booted out of office.

Where that leaves us, I’m afraid, is pretty much where we’ve been for the past decade: Republicans elated and Dems demoralized in November 2016; Republicans shell-shocked and Dems ecstatic in November 2018 and 2020; Republicans thrilled and Dems reeling in 2024. If I were a betting man (I am not), I would put a decent amount of money on Democrats winning back the White House in 2028—and on Republicans winning it back again in 2032.
Some will call it crazy that I’m willing to say anything at all about a presidential election that won’t take place for six years. We don’t even know who will be president after November 2028!

Good point. But here’s the thing: I think there might be something about our world (whispered: it’s the digital networking effects of social media) that is giving our politics its populist shape. That might change. But we don’t know if it will, let alone when, so the responsible thing to do when thinking about the near-term future is to extrapolate from the present that began roughly a decade ago.

I don’t like this. I don’t think it’s good. In fact, I think it’s bad, even dangerous. But I don’t know how to stop it. Neither do I think it can be traced to institutional quirks of the American electoral system that can be fixed by reforms. The patterns I’ve noted here are happening around the democratic world, in both presidential and parliamentary systems. That’s why, however illuminating it can be to examine the continuities and discontinuities between Trump and America’s political past, such work will not give us a roadmap for getting us out of our populist cul-de-sac. Something bigger has placed us here. If we didn’t have Trump, we would have someone else—just as we will eventually have Trump’s successor joining the show.

Lurking behind my prognostication is a wild card that I feel needs mentioning: How Trump responds to a midterm drubbing. Does he accept it like a normal politician, pick himself up off the floor, and promise to keep fighting for the American people? We have no reason to expect that he will.

But that just raises another question: What does Trump do to express his rage and frustration at being a political loser? Does he just rant and rave on Truth Social, vaguely accusing the “Dumbocrats” of cheating? Or does he try to get results reversed and even push Republicans to refuse to seat the new Congress?
In other words, does he precipitate a constitutional crisis that threatens to drive American democracy itself off the road and into a ditch?

The only thing preventing the above scenario from unfolding in the worst possible way is precisely how the election shakes out. If the Dems underperform expectations and end up winning only narrow control of either chamber of Congress, and there is a path to “victory” by cheating, Trump is almost certain to try it, just as he did after his loss in 2020.

The most dramatic scenarios involve Trump listening to the advisors and allies urging him to declare a national-security emergency surrounding the elections, with the pretext that foreign powers have been interfering in the process or have access to voting machines. Versions of this involve Trump invoking the Insurrection Act to quell protests, impose martial law outside polling stations, seize voting machines, or send ICE onto the streets for the purposes of intimidation. Trump has repeatedly refused to rule out the national-security scenario, most recently on October 1. (It should be noted that none of the experts recently interviewed by The New York Times thought such scenarios were “very likely,” and only a few thought they were “moderately likely.”)

There are also plenty of ways in which Trump could pressure state election officials or Congress itself to refuse to certify results, or bog down close races in procedural battles such that several members are unable to sit on January 3. (Again, these scenarios are generally considered unlikely by experts, though the fact that they are under discussion at all shows how bad things have gotten.)

What’s more likely than any of this is that the Democrats’ win is so substantial that cheating won’t work. Trump will probably grudgingly accept the result while “merely” lying about it day and night for the rest of his life—just like he has done with 2020 ever since. Which is yet another reason to think that these midterm elections won’t change much about the fundamental realities of American political life right now.

Damon Linker, a contributing writer at Persuasion, writes the Substack newsletter “Notes from the Middleground.” He is a senior lecturer in the Department of Political Science at the University of Pennsylvania and a senior fellow in the Open Society Project at the Niskanen Center.

cnbc.com/2026/10/16/tesla-spacex-merger-.headline: Prediction market odds on Tesla-SpaceX merger are above 50% for early 2027
cnbc.com/2026/10/16/tesla-spacex-merger-.author: Ananya Chetia

paragraphs.text: Following a Barclays note Wednesday that outlined what a merger between Tesla and SpaceX could look like, prediction market traders increased the odds of an integration above 50% for early 2027.
Odds of a merger happening before March jumped to 56% by Friday morning, up from 29%. Odds for an integration before April and May climbed to similar levels.
The contract asks, "When will Tesla and SpaceX merge?" and will be verified by news outlets and the Securities and Exchange Commission's EDGAR database.
Tesla, known for its electric vehicles, and SpaceX, a rocket and satellite company, have collaborated before. Both are controlled by Elon Musk.

On Thursday, Tesla showed off its long-delayed Roadster, which relies on SpaceX technology to make the vehicle hover. A video showcasing the Roadster's capabilities was also recorded from SpaceX's test site in Texas.
Beyond collaboration, the growing speculation of a merger comes after Musk spoke of "more and more overlap" between Tesla and SpaceX on the EV maker's latest earnings call.

Barclays now expects a merger could be announced before Tesla's annual general meeting, which must take place no later than Dec. 6, 2026. Analyst Dan Levy expects the merger may be proposed as an AI vertical integration, involving Tesla's Robotaxi and Optimus with SpaceX's Grok and Macrohard.
Terafab, the semiconductor project relying on Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, could also be a "key driver" for the merger, Levy added.
"Notably, while we suspect there would be some financial synergies, the true value would be in vertical integration," Levy said.
Earlier Friday, Evercore ISI recommended buying SpaceX shares ahead of its next scheduled earnings release, set for early November, and boosted its 12-month price target on the stock by 20% to $275.

cnbc.com/2026/10/16/trump-katie-zacharia.headline: Trump says new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia should 'reconsider' job
cnbc.com/2026/10/16/trump-katie-zacharia.author: Kevin Breuninger

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump on Friday opened the door for new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia to step down just days after getting the job.
Trump said he had just told Zacharia, "If I were you, I'd reconsider."
Zacharia has faced criticism in the days since she led a shaky first press briefing. She also has come under scrutiny about her legal background.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Trump's remarks.
Trump spoke outside the White House before heading to Georgia for a political rally as he hopes to boost Republicans' electoral chances with just 18 days until the midterms.

But Trump's efforts to sell his agenda have been muddled in part by Zacharia, who ended her first, and so far only, press briefing on Tuesday after delivering halting remarks and taking questions from just three reporters.
