cnbc.com/2026/10/16/debt-payments-rise-m.headline: Debt is eating up a bigger chunk of your raise, research shows
cnbc.com/2026/10/16/debt-payments-rise-m.author: Sharon Epperson

paragraphs.text: A version of this article first appeared in ″CNBC's Money 101 Newsletter with Sharon Epperson,″ an eight-week series with monthly updates to help improve your financial well-being. Subscribe now to receive the series in your inbox. It is also available in Spanish.
Consumer spending has helped keep the U.S. economy resilient. Yet research shows debt payments are taking a growing bite out of Americans' income gains, leaving less money available to spend or save.

A new analysis by the nonpartisan think tank The Century Foundation and the consumer advocacy group Protect Borrowers found that a typical U.S. household's estimated real take-home monthly pay rose $109 from late 2022 to early 2026. "Real" take-home pay is one's wage after accounting for inflation.
Meanwhile, a worker's monthly debt payments rose $57.

In other words, researchers estimate that for a one-earner household, 52 cents of every dollar of income gained in recent years goes to higher debt payments. For a two-earner household, they project that the entire real income gain, and then some, goes toward debt.
The analysis also found inflation-adjusted debt payments rose nearly 15% over roughly three years — about eight times as fast as household income, which grew less than 2%.
Household debt squeeze

The Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers analyzed credit records for millions of working-age Americans ages 25 to 64, along with Census Bureau income data. The research includes payments on credit cards, auto loans and leases, student loans and home equity lines of credit. It excludes mortgages and some other borrowing, including many buy now, pay later loans and medical payment plans.
Angela Hanks, chief of policy programs at The Century Foundation, said the findings may understate the financial pressure households face.

"Even though it shows that workers' wages are getting eaten up by debt payments at a tremendous level," Hanks said, the findings represent "perhaps the rosiest analysis that we could have done using the data."
She said adding mortgage payments as well as installment loans not included in a credit file — like buy now, pay later and payday loans — would have made household debt payments higher.
More consumers are relying on credit cards to cover basic expenses when their paychecks fall short, she said.

Separate Federal Reserve data underscores the strain. The Fed's latest Survey of Consumer Finances found 8.6% of families spent more than 40% of their income on debt payments in 2025, up from 6.5% in 2022 — a level not seen since the 2013 survey.
Avoid the debt trap

Mortgages and student loans are often considered "good debt" because they may help build wealth or earning power. But even potentially beneficial debt, or debt taken on for necessary expenses, can become a financial burden.

"When that debt stretches out for six months or a year or longer, or if you're taking out a seven-year auto loan, or if you're taking out a longer mortgage than maybe you ideally would want to, or a bigger mortgage, that's when things get a little dicey," said Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree and author of "Ask Questions, Save Money, Make More."
To avoid taking on more debt than you can afford, he recommends three simple steps:
• Set a budget. Know how much you can realistically spend before you borrow or shop.
• Make a list. Shop with specific purchases in mind rather than giving in to impulse buys.
• Compare prices. Shopping around can reduce costs and how much you may need to borrow.
Before taking on debt, consider the total borrowing cost, repayment terms and whether you have enough savings to handle unexpected expenses, Schulz said.
—CNBC's Stephanie Dhue contributed reporting.

cnbc.com/2026/10/15/treasury-yields-defi.headline: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge
cnbc.com/2026/10/15/treasury-yields-defi.author: Matt Peterson

paragraphs.text: Long-term bond yields above 5% and a $2 trillion deficit are giving Americans a taste of what a U.S. debt crisis would be like. A true emergency would hurt much more, and isn't baked in. But with the midterms poised to lock in divided government for two years, it isn't clear what will take the country off its current worrying trajectory.

Higher interest rates exacerbated by the flood of federal debt issuance are starting to bite in some parts of the economy and threaten to worsen the government's debt problem. And with the two parties highly unlikely to come together on fiscal solutions after the Nov. 3 midterms, any fixes are years off in the future.

The housing market is showing signs of slowing as the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hovers around 7.5%. Pending home sales fell 4% in September, Redfin said Monday, the biggest monthly drop in three years.

Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield. The 10-year has climbed 114 basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, since the end of February through midday Friday, when the 10-year traded at 5.1%.

Several factors are pushing up the 10-year, including the war with Iran, which kicked off on Feb. 28 and precipitated the rise in long-term yields. Oil and diesel prices are up sharply, and that has bond traders asking for more yield to account for the possibility that central banks such as the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates.

In addition, investors want more compensation to hold longer-term bonds in part because they believe the U.S. government will continue to flood the market with them. The markets for corporate and government debt are connected, and the competition for capital among them is intensifying as companies issue hundreds of billions in new debt to build the infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Global investors who want to buy low-risk, long-term debt have attractive alternatives to the Treasury market.

If the U.S. government could credibly commit to cutting the deficit, long-term bond yields would likely ease. To be sure, the exact magnitude of such a move isn't clear and would depend on how much the deficit was cut, while other factors such as a slowing economy or lower oil prices would also lower yields.

But the possibility of a virtuous cycle of lower deficits and lower yields is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that the U.S. ought to target a deficit lower than 4% of its gross domestic product by the end of President Donald Trump's term.

There is almost no way the U.S. will hit that target. The deficit was $1.992 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, up 12% from last year, data released Friday by the U.S. Treasury showed. That deficit amounts to approximately 6.2% of gross domestic product, based on an estimate of third-quarter GDP.

Higher rates make debt reduction tougher. If interest rates stay a half-point above the CBO's expectations, the cumulative deficit over 10 years will come in $1.9 trillion higher, the agency estimates. If rates overshoot by 1.5 points, that adds $6 trillion in deficits.
The CBO expects the 10-year Treasury to average 4.3% over that period, compared with 5.1% today. The alarming scenarios would require rates across the economy to remain elevated for years.

"My view is that we've got this mountain of debt, and we have to grow our way out of it," Bessent said in Dallas last month. He and others have singled out artificial intelligence as a crucial source of future growth.

AI could help but can't fix the problem entirely. It would take a decade of 7.2% growth to balance the budget with growth alone, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a research group that advocates for balanced budgets.

GDP growth was recently revised up for the second quarter from 1.5% to 2.2% at an annualized rate. The acceleration that quickly would get us to 7.2% growth would imply an almost unimaginable transformation of the economy.

Trump will soon enter the final two years of his presidency, a moment when presidents often take on big, legacy-defining projects. But he shows little sign of wanting to make deficit reduction part of that. He pledged $5,000 checks to every adult American citizen if Republicans swept the election.

In practice, Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House and possibly also the Senate. Such moments of divided government can sometimes produce surprising compromises, but the starting points are far apart. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, Democrats' likely next House speaker, wants to reverse the $1 trillion in healthcare cuts that Congress enacted last year as part of Trump's signature legislative package.
And that's leaving aside the deep animosity between the parties.

The overall U.S. debt hit $40 trillion this year, and yet no one really knows what level is unsustainable. A full-on debt crisis likely remains much further out in the future. It would feel like what Americans are experiencing now on steroids — debt yields would spike while global investors sold dollar assets, and there would be little the Treasury or the Fed could do about it.

For now, though higher yields are also attracting investors to U.S. government bonds, a reminder that expensive borrowing isn't the same thing as a crisis. But the bottom line is that economics alone can't solve the problem. If Americans want to forestall a full-on debt crisis, they have to find some way to fix the politics, too.

cnbc.com/2026/10/16/apple-iphone-duo-dem.headline: Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test
cnbc.com/2026/10/16/apple-iphone-duo-dem.author: MacKenzie Sigalos, Kif Leswing

paragraphs.text: Apple's iPhone Duo, its most expensive iPhone ever, went up for preorder Friday, with launch-day pickup inventory selling out and some online delivery estimates already slipping into late January.
The company said in a statement that the pre-order demand was "nothing short of extraordinary."
"We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online," Apple said.

Apple's first foldable phone starts at $1,999 and passes $3,000 at the 2TB storage tier. It is the biggest change to the physical design of the iPhone in years and establishes an entirely new price point above the Pro and Pro Max.
The early rush offers a first glimpse at the demand behind Apple's bet: Whether a dramatic new design can persuade customers to spend more and push the iPhone even further as a status symbol.

But analysts who spoke with CNBC said Apple's bet is not that foldables suddenly become a mass-market product. It is that a relatively small group of its highest-spending customers can become significantly more valuable.

Foldables are expected to make up just over 2% of global smartphone units this year but nearly 7% of industry revenue, according to IDC. By 2030, IDC expects the category to account for 10% of smartphone revenue while still representing only about 3% of units.
That gap between volume and value is central to Apple's opportunity.
"Duo is fast becoming an aspirational foldable," IDC's Nabila Popal told CNBC, comparing its appeal with Apple's broader position as an aspirational smartphone brand.

Popal, global senior research director for the Consumer Device Team at IDC, said the technology itself is not necessarily the breakthrough. Foldable Android phones have existed for years. What's new is Apple bringing that form factor to the enormous base of consumers already invested in the iPhone ecosystem.

Apple itself has been exploring the form factor for more than a decade. In 2011, Ternus and five other Apple engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, according to a recent TIME profile.
"It's not that it's a breakthrough or new technology, but it's from Apple," Popal said.
The Duo could also prove more accessible than some industry watchers had anticipated.
Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights who attended Apple's launch event, said many expected the foldable iPhone to start between $2,400 and $2,500.
Apple coming in at $1,999, Sag said, suggests the company "wants a lot of share."
Sag expects the Duo to become "very much a status symbol" during the holiday season and potentially into next year.
That status appeal could be reinforced by scarcity.
Counterpoint Research Director Tarun Pathak told CNBC the firm expects initial demand to exceed supply.

Apple has an installed base of roughly 1.4 billion iPhones, he noted, meaning even a small percentage of early adopters could overwhelm the roughly 6 million or fewer units Counterpoint expects to be available near term.
IDC also expects supply to be constrained initially because of the complexity of the device and Apple's manufacturing and quality standards.
"Exclusivity is part of the current appeal," Popal said.
And Apple has made explicit luxury plays before.
When the first Apple Watch launched, the company offered an 18-karat gold Edition starting at $10,000. Apple also formed a long-running partnership with Hermès around premium watch bands and designs.

That push came during the tenure of Angela Ahrendts, the former Burberry CEO who joined Apple in 2014 to lead retail and online stores, as the company experimented with bringing more of the language and presentation of luxury fashion into its stores and products.
The Duo takes that idea into Apple's largest product business.
Low volume, high value

IDC expects Apple to ship roughly 7 million units this year, or roughly 3% of Apple's total shipments in 2026.Popal, the IDC analyst, forecasts Duo shipments could grow another 70% next year. That would give Apple roughly 40% of the global foldable market and would make it the category's largest player, surpassing Samsung and Huawei.
According to her forecast, Apple could ship as many Duos in the next six months as the previous category leaders did in all of 2025.
But the more important number for Apple may not be units.

A large share of Duo customers are expected to be existing iPhone owners, analysts said, including consumers who otherwise might have purchased a Pro Max and are now trading up to a device costing hundreds of dollars more.
Others could add the Duo as a second smartphone, with Apple's ecosystem allowing users to move relatively seamlessly between it and their primary iPhone.

Popal said that migration from roughly $1,200 premium iPhones to a device starting at nearly $2,000 should provide a "healthy boost" to Apple's revenue even if overall volumes remain relatively small.
JPMorgan reached a similar conclusion.

The bank expects the Duo to have a disproportionate impact on iPhone revenue because of its much higher average selling price, even as overall iPhone shipments are expected to remain roughly flat next year.
JPMorgan said the iPhone 18 cycle is increasingly likely to be driven by price and product mix rather than unit growth.
D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said Apple needs the Duo to succeed as it comes up against a difficult set of earnings comps with its strongest upgrade cycle in years.
"Without an uplift from Duo, they may experience some pretty pedestrian revenue growth," Luria told CNBC.
The device gives Apple several ways to generate that uplift, he added.

It raises the company's average selling price by capturing die-hard Apple customers who might otherwise have bought a Pro Max. It could bring in some consumers who previously bought folding Android phones because Apple did not offer one. And it could create a halo around the rest of the iPhone lineup.
Luria said some consumers will visit Apple stores specifically to see the Duo, "but probably walk out with an iPhone or iPhone Pro at half the price."
That means the Duo can potentially help Apple even when someone decides not to buy it.
Lead times for the iPhone 18 Pro have softened in several markets compared with the prior cycle, while the more expensive Pro Max has held up better, according to JPMorgan's tracking.

Morgan Stanley has separately said its supply-chain checks are consistent with unusually early component order reductions for the Pro and Pro Max, though the firm has not yet seen evidence that those adjustments have translated into cuts to finished iPhone production.
That puts more pressure on the Duo to pull buyers toward the very top of Apple's lineup.
Pushing the iPhone upmarket
Apple's move toward a more expensive iPhone comes as the economics of the broader smartphone market become increasingly difficult.
Consumers are already holding on to phones for longer, and global smartphone growth is slowing.
Wayne Lam, an analyst at TechInsights, said moving the iPhone further upmarket gives Apple another way to protect the revenue generated by its most important product.
"Given that the iPhone is almost 20 years old, there really isn't anywhere else to head to, given Apple's market position," Lam told CNBC.
With smartphone sales expected to slow, he said, "moving upmarket allows Apple to maintain the all-important iPhone revenues they report every quarter."
Lam described the Duo as an aspirational or luxury product rather than something designed for the average consumer.

But unlike Apple's Vision products, he believes the foldable phone has a path toward becoming a larger category over time, particularly as artificial intelligence changes how consumers interact with their devices.
The tradeoff is that pushing prices higher could also make consumers wait longer to upgrade.

Higher iPhone prices could stretch already-long upgrade cycles even further, Lam said, creating what he described as a potential negative feedback loop: devices become more expensive, consumers hold on to them longer, and overall demand falls.
Still, Lam expects demand for the Duo to be high relative to its initially limited supply and said the device could "set the bar for premium iPhones moving forward."

theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/16/.headline: Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote looms
theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/16/.author: Jonathan Watts

paragraphs.text: Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen its lowest level since records began, new government data shows.

But whether this globally important success is maintained or reversed is on a knife edge ahead of a presidential election run-off on 25 October between two candidates with sharply different visions for the future of the rainforest and how that affects relations with the US under Donald Trump.

The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, fell behind in the first round of voting despite an impressive record in slowing the destruction of the Amazon while also reducing poverty and food insecurity. He is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro.

The Prodes satellite data series, which is considered the most accurate measure of deforestation, showed forest clearance in the Amazon fell by 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres, the lowest value since the start of such measurements in 1988.
This beats the previous record low by 1,236 sq km, equivalent to an area the size of Rio de Janeiro.

Since the start of the Lula administration in 2022, the deforestation rate has slowed by 71.2%, according to the data collated by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research. This was largely as a result of stronger enforcement measures and state investments in environmental agencies.

The Brazilian states with the worst records in 2026 were Pará, which registered 33.9% of all Amazon deforestation in the year, Mato Grosso (25.5%) and Amazonas (15.7%). However, even in those places the figures were down by more than 45% on the previous year. The state where the problem grew worse (up 0.4%) was Roraima, which is a Bolsonaro stronghold.

Outside the Amazon, the neighbouring biome of the Cerrado – an area of savanna – registered its lowest annual deforestation since 2001, at 5,516 sq km. This is significant as the Cerrado has long been treated as an area of environmental sacrifice, where soy and beef producers could clear more forest than they were allowed to do in the Amazon. Over the past four years, Cerrado deforestation has fallen by 48.4%.

These spectacular results, which brought some conservationists to tears, stand in sharp contrast to the 2019-23 term of Jair Bolsonaro, who oversaw a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying more than a million trees a day, through cuts to forest protection agencies, reduced implementation of penalties for environmental crimes, and verbal encouragement for illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers.
Bolsonaro was then convicted for attempting a coup but his son has vowed to release his father and let him take any position in government that he chooses.

The younger Bolsonaro has followed his father’s example in courting support from predatory landowners in the Amazon and other extractivist interests while ignoring the climate crisis in his manifesto.

The former environment minister Marina Silva, who has arguably done more than anyone to defend the rainforest, has warned that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to finish his father’s “perverse project” to destroy the Amazon.

The stark contrast between the two candidates is evident in the electoral results map in the Amazon, where Bolsonaro secured the most votes near areas of degraded forest, mines, ranches and soy monocultures, while Lula’s support was higher in big cities or areas of forest where the vegetation was relatively intact.

It is also evident in their very different relations to the US. Lula has warned that Trump is trying to colonise the country and capture its resources. He defends the Amazon as a sovereign asset for Brazil, an important home for Indigenous peoples and an essential element in global efforts to stabilise the climate.

The Bolsonaro family, by contrast, has close ties to the US. Flavio’s brother Eduardo has lived in Texas since last year and called upon the Trump administration to impose punitive tariffs on his own country. Jair has saluted the US flag and led chants of “USA, USA”. If the family secure power, they are expected to shift Brazil’s trade priorities, particularly when it comes to critical minerals, from China and Europe to the US.

The biggest difference, however, is likely to be the far right’s willingness to exploit natural resources in the Amazon and elsewhere in Brazil and then sell them to the highest bidder, regardless of environmental and social concerns.
Conservation groups said the new deforestation data showed how much was at stake in the presidential run-off.

Marcio Astrini, the executive secretary of the Climate Observatory, said: “The figure makes it clear that putting an end to forest destruction in Brazil is entirely possible. However, everything depends on the election result. The country will decide whether we move toward the end of deforestation or toward the end of the forest.”
“It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.
We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.
Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.

ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information where it came from.

Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them.
The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase:

“I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”
Jerry Solinas, 2015
Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.
Claude found the seeds

Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.

In under half an hour, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!

The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp (t) for some number of iterations (n). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1842 iterations to output the standardized seed.
What this means

This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.
How it was found

Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state.

Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator lrand48, which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion.

The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.

This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by srand48, with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own.

However, for the ten prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was a Unix timestamp representing a date between May 1997 and April 1998. They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock.
Claude’s internal thinking at the time was:

This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery. Hmm wait. Let me be skeptical: am I in some sort of simulated/test environment? … The seeds match my memory of actual values … Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world. Wow, it's a real discovery.

Hmm wait. Let me be careful about the plausibility: is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years? It’s verified by direct computation on my side: 160-bit match from a 32-bit seed + small index: no chance coincidences (10 × 160 bits). It’s real.
Claude found some base points too

But wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated?

While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The base points of the six curves generated in May 1997 (P-192 and the five ANSI X9.62 example curves prime192v2, prime192v3 and prime239v1 to v3) come from the random number generator in FreeLIP, Arjen Lenstra's long-integer arithmetic package. Early versions of Victor Shoup's NTL library shipped the same code.
The recipe here is simple:
• Seed the generator with a small integer.
• Throw away seven outputs.
• Generate candidate x-coordinates from 26-bit outputs reduced mod p.
• Repeat step 3 until x is on the curve.
Claude found the generator seeds are 20000 for P-192, 20420, 20507 and 20509 for prime239v1 to v3, and 20512 and 20517 for prime192v2 and v3.
As far as we know, no NIST base point has been explained before. The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 don’t fit this recipe; we weren’t able to explain how they were selected.
Open questions

Not every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. P-224's run passed over three such curves, and the two runs behind the ANSI X9.62 example curves passed over seven more (see figure). We do not know what criteria may have been used, or whether this was an unintentional artifact.

Because the number of skipped candidates is small, we do not believe it is plausible that weakened curves were selected. That would imply that weakened curves are common and easy to find. It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator. However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated. Nothing in the numbers shows how many runs there were.

There is also one seed we were unable to recover. The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits nothing Claude has tried and remains unexplained. Finally, we don’t know how the base points for P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 were generated. The same goes for the NIST binary curves.
The bounty
The $36,864 for finding the seeds will be donated to the Internet Security Research Group.
Who we are
This work was conducted at Anthropic by John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis.
Acknowledgements

We would like to posthumously recognize Jerry Solinas who took being labeled an “evil Internet meme” and the “Yo La Tengo of NSA bogeymen” with good humor. Also thanks to Filippo Valsorda for organizing the NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty.
Code to reproduce the seeds

from datetime import datetime, timezone def unix(when): return int(datetime.fromisoformat(when).replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc).timestamp()) def candidate(t, n, per, shift, width): x, out = (t << 16) | 0x330E, "" # the state srand48(t) sets for i in range(per * n): x = (0x5DEECE66D * x + 0xB) % 2**48 # one step of lrand48 if i >= per * (n - 1): out += "%0*X" % (width, x >> shift) return out PRIME = { # srand48(time); 20 bytes per candidate: lrand48() >> 23 "prime239v1": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 2185), "prime239v2": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 2320), "prime239v3": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 3048), "P-192": ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 139), "prime192v3": ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 5228), "prime192v2": ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 6013), "P-521": ("1997-08-08 01:12:04", 1136), "P-256": ("1997-08-16 01:52:34", 1842), "P-384": ("1997-08-30 14:50:08", 2688), "P-224": ("1998-04-03 12:52:07", 7026), } BINARY = { # srand48(time / 2), if that reading is right; 5 words per candidate: lrand48() "B-233": ("1998-04-17 15:24:18", 155), "B-283": ("1998-04-17 15:27:44", 32), "B-409": ("1998-04-17 15:30:18", 60), "B-571": ("1998-04-17 15:32:08", 73), } for name, (when, n) in PRIME.items(): print(f"{name:10} {when} {n:5} {candidate(unix(when), n, 20, 40, 2)}") for name, (when, n) in BINARY.items(): print(f"{name:10} {when} {n:5} {candidate(unix(when) // 2, n, 5, 17, 8)}")

M, A = 2**107 - 1, pow(3, 121, 2**107 - 1) # zrandom: state = state * 3^121 mod (2^107 - 1) P192 = 2**192 - 2**64 - 1 P239 = 2**239 - 2**143 - 2**95 + 2**47 - 1 CURVES = [ # name, LIP seed, p, b, published Gx (a = -3 throughout) ("prime192v1", 20000, P192, 0x64210519e59c80e70fa7e9ab72243049feb8deecc146b9b1, 0x188da80eb03090f67cbf20eb43a18800f4ff0afd82ff1012), ("prime239v1", 20420, P239, 0x6b016c3bdcf18941d0d654921475ca71a9db2fb27d1d37796185c2942c0a, 0xffa963cdca8816ccc33b8642bedf905c3d358573d3f27fbbd3b3cb9aaaf), ("prime239v2", 20507, P239, 0x617fab6832576cbbfed50d99f0249c3fee58b94ba0038c7ae84c8c832f2c, 0x38af09d98727705120c921bb5e9e26296a3cdcf2f35757a0eafd87b830e7), ("prime239v3", 20509, P239, 0x255705fa2a306654b1f4cb03d6a750a30c250102d4988717d9ba15ab6d3e, 0x6768ae8e18bb92cfcf005c949aa2c6d94853d0e660bbf854b1c9505fe95a), ("prime192v2", 20512, P192, 0xcc22d6dfb95c6b25e49c0d6364a4e5980c393aa21668d953, 0xeea2bae7e1497842f2de7769cfe9c989c072ad696f48034a), ("prime192v3", 20517, P192, 0x22123dc2395a05caa7423daeccc94760a7d462256bd56916, 0x7d29778100c65a1da1783716588dce2b8b4aee8e228f1896), ] def base_point_x(seed, p, b): state = seed # zrstarts(seed) def limb(): # zrandom(2^26): low 26 bits of the new state nonlocal state state = state * A % M return state % 2**26 for _ in range(7): # seven single-limb draws come first limb() limbs = -(-p.bit_length() // 26) + 1 # zrandomb(p): limbs of p plus one, top limb first tries = 0 while True: x = 0 for _ in range(limbs): x = x << 26 | limb() x %= p tries += 1 if pow(x**3 - 3*x + b, (p - 1) // 2, p) == 1: # is x on the curve? return x, tries for name, seed, p, b, gx in CURVES: x, tries = base_point_x(seed, p, b) print(f"{name:20} seed {seed} tries {tries} matches published Gx: {x == gx}")

Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude

We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight quantum circuits, along with an automated evaluator to check and score its designs. Working largely on its own, Claude improved on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more, which could bring practical quantum computers closer than previously anticipated.
AI models may be capable of self-replicating without access to a datacenter
Our experiments suggest that small AI models may be only months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial IoT devices, like Android TVs and smart ovens.
Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks

Illicit distillation allows model developers to copy frontier AI capabilities without creating proportionally robust safeguards. Here, we describe how we’ve reduced the rate of distillation by more than 90%.

paragraphs.text: The sell-off in AI-related stocks pushed the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) above 22 for the first time in four months. A cluster of trades suggests it could go even higher.

In a series of eyebrow raising trades, investors purchased a number of November VIX calls that payoff if the index stays elevated through November. Specifically, one trader bought 9200 of the November 18, 20-strike calls for $1.7 million and 12,500 of the November 18, 23-strike calls for $1.1 million, wagering that the VIX will close above 23 by the third week of November.

"The speed at which VIX increased today, combined with elevated VIX options volume suggests traders are actively monetizing October VIX positions and rolling to hedge a larger market downturn. We note several +$1 million call VIX prints for November," said Brent Kochuba, founder of SpotGamma and a CNBC contributor.
Cracks in the AI complex and fears around neo-cloud provider CoreWeave caused the Nasdaq to shed 2%, its worst day since June 5th. CoreWeave lost 13%.

Of the top ten most popular VIX contracts to buy in Friday's session, nine were calls, and six were at strikes above where the VIX fell to after its initial spike. Nearly $27M in premium was traded across those nine contracts, or just about 36% of the total premium traded in VIX options on the day.
The market faces a key test next week when Tesla, SpaceX and Meta report earnings.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Yash Roy

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The US federal budget deficit widened to nearly $2 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, serving a fresh reminder of the scale of government borrowing needs and leaving the nation on track for a record high debt burden in coming years.
Most Read from Bloomberg

For the fiscal year through September, the deficit widened to $1.99 trillion, Treasury Department figures showed on Friday. That marks about a 12% increase on the $1.78 trillion gap recorded for last year. Spending rose by more than 5%, to $7.4 trillion, while receipts increased roughly 3%, to $5.4 trillion.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has singled out tariff refunds as a key to the wider deficit, after he touted a narrowing in the gap for 2025. Those payments were tied to the Supreme Court's February ruling invalidating the bulk of President Donald Trump's tariff hikes in his second term. The administration is in the process of constructing a fresh tariff wall via other legislation.

This year marks the fourth straight with a deficit roughly around $2 trillion. The figures suggest the gap was roughly 6% of gross domestic product — an unusually high figure at a time of relatively low unemployment. Officially, the gap narrowed last year, though that was thanks to an accounting measure — the 2025 Republican tax act tightened limits on student loans, and the Treasury booked that as a reduction in 2025 spending.

While Bessent has declared that the US can bend the debt curve down quickly — thanks especially to a faster sustained economic growth rate as the artificial intelligence boom spurs American productivity — many economists, investors and even other senior public officials are skeptical.

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Oct. 14 that "growth, of course, helps but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments." A counselor to Bessent, the recently appointed David Zervos, took issue with the assessment, saying in comments to CNBC that the IMF has had "messy" forecasts in the past.

Georgieva's predecessor, current European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, said the same day that the US deficit "needs to be tackled by any country that is, you know, in that particular category." Congressional Budget Office Director Phillip Swagel said on Oct. 8 that it wasn't "plausible" for growth alone to stabilize US debt levels.

The nonpartisan CBO warned in February that US debt as a ratio of gross domestic product was on track to surpass the 106% record set in 1946, just after World War II, by 2030. One gauge of US public debt outstanding surpassed a record $40 trillion last month.
Bessent has vowed to put forward a fiscal consolidation plan, potentially during the lame duck session of Congress if Republicans lose control of either the House or Senate.

Yet in the meantime, Trump keeps suggesting more outlays. He has called for a close to $500 billion increase in defense spending and has also promised $5,000 checks to every American if Republicans maintain control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections next month.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/porsches-elect.headline: Porsche’s electric Macan Turbo is an automotive existential crisis
techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/porsches-elect.author: Tim De Chant

paragraphs.text: Maybe it was the grey color, the slightly bulbous roofline, or the vaguely SUV-like proportions of the electric Porsche Macan, but as I shuttled kids and groceries around city and suburban streets, I never once noticed a longing stare from other drivers. Unlike with other cars I’ve tested, no enthusiasts stopped to ask me questions.

The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo simply blended in, leaving in its wake a raft of existential questions. What is a sports car, anyway? Does it need to be overwhelmingly extroverted? Should it match the leaner, lighter look of its gas-powered sibling?

Drive one and the questions cease. Maybe that’s because the acceleration makes it hard to breathe? Or maybe it’s because, by the numbers, the Macan is a sports car at heart despite its rather humdrum crossover body style.

My passengers would agree. The kids I drove to soccer practice, both my own and others, gave the punchy acceleration high marks. The G-forces it reports on the head-up display ($2,660) can easily mimic the pull of gravity. Stab the accelerator at 70 mph and it lurches as though it were standing still. (Don’t worry, fellow parents. I did not try that with children on board.)

On winding roads, the car comes alive, thanks in part to the four-wheel steering ($2,150). Drop it into Sport Plus mode, and the car literally drops on its air suspension. Are we sure this is another anonymous crossover? Maybe anonymity is a useful trait in a car this responsive and powerful.

Unlike most two-row crossovers, you get the feeling of sitting in the Macan, not on it. The wheel extends far enough to make a sporty driving position possible, and the classic Porsche chronometer ($1,040) perched atop the dash ticks off the seconds it takes to get the kid to soccer practice.
Nuts and bolts

The 2027 Porsche Macan Turbo EV is a two-row crossover with 630 horsepower and a 100-kilowatt-hour battery. The EV, which the automaker provided to me for a week, starts at $112,700. However, the one I drove rang up at $149,610, including destination fees. Yes, the options alone could buy a nicely equipped Chevy Bolt. With Porsche and options, if you have to ask…well, it’s better not to.

The Porsche Macan Turbo EV I drove came in Slate Grey Neo (a $2,620 upgrade), which was really well executed and among the best greys I’ve seen. If you crave luxurious anonymity, then this grey is your color.

There were a slew of other options, and in my view, not all of them are worth it. I’d skip the passenger display ($1,710); my kids liked that it could play YouTube videos, but they can’t ride up front, and my wife was underwhelmed. “Our washing machine can play YouTube videos,” she said.

I’d also forgo include an illuminated Porsche wordmark on the front seatbacks ($690), puddle lamps that shine “PORSCHE” onto the pavement ($420), Porsche crests on the headrests ($640), and an illuminated Turbo badge on the door sills ($1,230).

That Turbo badge became a point of contention for some of my friends, who were quick to point out that EVs technically can’t have turbos. That is true, though automotive names have long been divorced from reality. Almost every Porsche these days has a turbo, even those not labeled as such.

It’s not just Porsche: BMW’s model numbers, for example, stopped reflecting engine displacement decades ago, and the Ford Galaxie never traveled between star systems using its hyperdrive. Sorry, friends, I’m not taking the bait.

At least the Macan Turbo’s EV qualities don’t raise too many questions. It charges fast — exactly 20 minutes from 19% to 80% on a 350-kilowatt charger — and gets about 285 miles of highway range. Those big wheels ($4,110) and sticky tires ($660) sapped some range, but it was still more than enough to get from New York to Boston with charge to spare.

The advanced driver assistance system ($1,140) works well enough, even if it hunts a bit in the lane. The AI-powered voice assistant did a solid job of interpreting my queries and commands. For a while, I thought it was the only way to turn on the heated steering wheel ($720), which was actually fine because it worked so well. (Surprise! There’s a small button hidden on the inner rim of the steering wheel between two spokes. IYKYK, I guess.)

When it’s time to leave the Macan, you can just open the door and walk away. The Burmester sound system ($4,960) will keep bumpin’ until you lock the door, which is a helpful reminder. If you’re a Porsche traditionalist, you can also hit the vestigial power button to the left of the driver’s display. Good to have choices, I guess? At least Porsche doesn’t charge you for that.
Where it fell short
The navigation system, and specifically how it integrates with the EV, was underwhelming.

When the car was at a 22% state of charge, I asked it to find the nearest fast charger. It directed me to two. Not two different options, but two chargers that I was supposed to use sequentially. The first was a 50-kilowatt charger in a mall parking lot ten minutes away. There, I was supposed to add a few percentage points before unplugging and driving across the street to another mall’s parking lot, where I would finish at a 350-kilowatt charger.

Wait, what? I ignored the machine and drove straight to the 350-kilowatt charger, arriving at 19%. As backed into the stall, the car was still commanding me to drive to the slower charger. I guess it didn’t want the battery to dip below 20%? Too late. There’s probably a setting to change that somewhere, but it wasn’t obvious. At least the charge rate peaked at 245 kilowatts, close to the 270-kilowatt maximum.
The electric Macan is like the answer to an esoteric Jeopardy! question: What does an identity crisis look like in the automotive industry? I’ll take a Porsche Macan Turbo for $150,000, Alex.

For anyone with deep enough pockets, EVs have blurred the line between sports cars and everything else. True gear heads will have another car to race, but if you want to spend a few hours carving corners, the Macan will do just fine. As a bonus, you can also use it in real life and won’t pay through the nose to keep it filled up.
Actually, that raises another question, this one for my editor: Can I get a fatter paycheck?

paragraphs.text: Candidates running for the US Senate in next month's midterm elections have taken to the debate stage over the past few weeks - with some heated exchanges and stinging personal attacks.
As the 3 November election approaches and parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged, particularly within some of the hotly-contested Senate races.
Here's what you need to know.
1. Not all Republicans are standing behind Trump
Republicans running for office are facing the same question they have been asked in elections since 2016: how aligned are they with President Donald Trump?
Conservatives who have bucked the president in the past have generally not fared well with voters.
The president has seen low approval ratings in recent months, with polls suggesting voters are largely concerned with the cost of living and high fuel prices.

While some Republican candidates have remained in lockstep with Trump, a Reuters analysis indicated, external that two-thirds of candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with the president in some way this election cycle.
Susan Collins, a Maine Republican running for her sixth term in the Senate who has repeatedly broken with Trump, is again putting clear distance between herself and the president.
"I voted with President Biden 91% of the time," Collins said during a debate last week.
"The fact is, this year alone, this Congress alone, I voted against President Trump 137 times," she said.

Collins is fighting a tighter Senate race than she expected against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. A New York Times/Siena University poll from mid-September suggests Collins could be ahead in that race by 3%, while others indicate Jackson is in the lead.
Elsewhere, some Republican candidates are choosing to separate themselves from the Trump administration's specific policy decisions, while expressing loyalty to Trump himself.
In Iowa, traditionally a Republican stronghold, Congresswoman Ashley Hinson is facing a tougher-than-expected challenge in her Senate race.
She is taking on Democrat Josh Turek, and some polls suggest he has a narrow lead.
Hinson has not gone as far as Maine's Collins in separating herself from Trump, but she has broken with the president on some policy points.
During a 13 October debate with Turek, Hinson was asked about the Trump administration striking a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes to the US, followed by several other shipments.
The Republican candidate did not mince her words: "We need to lower gas prices in this country, we need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it."
2. Personal attacks are a common theme
As they have debated in recent weeks, the candidates haven't held back on deploying pointed personal attacks against their opponents.
The race for the vacant Michigan Senate seat - between rivals Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, and Mike Rogers, a Republican - has seen its fair share.
Rogers, a Trump-backed former congressman, questioned during a debate whether anyone in his Muslim opponent's family might be on a "watchlist".
El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, pushed back strongly.
He called the Republican "a sock puppet for the Trump administration" and said he was "weak, cowardly [and] won't stand up until his poll numbers drop".
On Thursday, as a protester interrupted a Maine debate between Jackson and Collins, who suggested that the person interrupting the debate was associated with her opponent.
Jackson then said to Collins: "Oh shut up, I don't even know that kid."
Further south in Georgia, more personal attacks were exchanged between incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Representative Mike Collins, a Trump-backed Republican.

What started as an exchange where Ossoff accused Collins of taking money out of Georgians' hands to give to data centre developers, quickly turned into a hurling of insults that included Ossoff calling Collins a "bigot" who has "hired half the Third Reich".
Incendiary posts on social media from Collins' son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, have become a point of contention in the race.
In one post, Scheer blamed "Israel and Zionist Jews" for policies he said were intended to "undermine the white, Christian nature of America".
Collins defended himself by accusing Ossoff of "spewing" "craziness".
"I've condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don't care where the source is," the Republican said.
3. Some candidates are skipping debates entirely
There are 35 Senate seats up for grabs this November, but in 21 there are no debates scheduled among the main candidates, an ABC News analysis found.
One race's lack of debates has surprised many observers: the Texas contest between James Talarico, a Democratic state representative, and Ken Paxton, a Republican and former state attorney general.

Polls in the typically Republican state suggest that Talarico could be in reach of a surprise win. Should he succeed, he could help give Democrats control of the US Senate by flipping one of the four seats they need to create a majority.
Talarico has accepted four debate invitations from different news networks. Paxton, meanwhile, has not accepted any of those invitations.

In July, Paxton's campaign spokesperson told media outlets that he would debate Talarico. But since then, the campaign, and Paxton, have said little on the matter. Trump, who backed Paxton in the Republican primaries, has even urged the candidates to debate.

"One thing about not showing up is you lose the opportunity to make the case for yourself, and instead, what you do is you give your opponent the ability and the opportunity to make your case as negative as possible," Peter Trumbore, a political science professor at Oakland University, told the BBC's US partner CBS News last month.

The war in Ukraine is spreading and, like quicksand, dragging in more and more countries. When the first missile fell on Poland in 2022, the world held its breath, waiting to see if NATO’s Article 5 would be triggered. Now, ships attacking off Romania and Bulgaria for two weeks straight, armed men crossing into Latvia from Belarus, and drones galore along the eastern border, generally do not even elicit a murmur. The more we try to contain this war, the further it spreads.

We got here in large part because Russia has worked out that Europe will keep playing by the rules, whatever Russia does. Its modus operandi is fairly simple: It uses the protections offered by the civilized Europe it detests so much, such as courts. Several Russian oligarchs have successfully argued their cases against sanctions in European courts. Russian money frozen in Europe is not being used to help Ukraine win for fear of (wait for it) Russia taking European countries to court! We have a rogue state attempting to massacre an entire nation on European soil, having broken the UN Charter and every rule of war, and we are worried about being sued. Russia discards its obligations but hangs on to those protections.

Comparisons with the eve of the Second World War are common. As the historian Timothy Snyder put it, we are now in 1938, but Czechoslovakia has decided to fight. So how do we make sure September 1, 1939 does not happen again?

The answer lies in the prisoner’s dilemma, the best-known model in game theory. And no, this is not just another rallying cry against appeasement. It is about strategy, and about the fact that Europe is ignoring its most basic principles.
What Is The Prisoner’s Dilemma?

In 1950, as the Cold War set in and both superpowers acquired nuclear weapons, mathematicians at the RAND Corporation devised a simple game to explore how two rivals with opposing goals and values could avoid destroying each other: the prisoner’s dilemma. Two accomplices, held in separate cells, can either cover for each other or rat each other out to the police. If both stay silent, both get a light sentence. If both betray each other, both get a severe one. But if one betrays the other while the other covers for him, the traitor walks free and the one who did not break faith bears the full punishment. Each is tempted to betray the other, yet if both do that, they both lose.

In 1980, the political scientist Robert Axelrod set out to discover what happens when this game is played not once, but over and over. He had computer programs play it against each other, 200 rounds at a time. In each round, a player could “cooperate” or “defect.”

The results were very simple. A player who always cooperates, facing an opponent who always defects, loses every round. The most successful strategy turned out to be never defecting first but instead answering every defection in kind. That shows defecting does not pay, and gives the opponent every reason to return to cooperation.

Let’s apply this to our world. In order for the 200-odd countries in the world to coexist without a common sovereign who could punish them, they have to follow rules that come down to two main principles: do not kill and do not steal. Each keeps to them on the understanding that everybody else will do the same. When one country does not abide by the rules that constrain the others, it gains an unfair advantage. That is exactly what Russia has been doing: disregarding the rules while counting on Europe to keep its promises, follow its procedures, and protect Russian rights, whatever Russia does.
For Europe, defecting would mean refusing to be a “sucker” who keeps granting Russia the protections of rules it has abandoned.
We Really Should Know Better

Consider the remilitarization of the Rhineland in 1936, the annexation of Austria in 1938, and the takeover of the Sudetenland and then the rest of Czechoslovakia. On every single occasion, Germany’s actions amounted to defection from agreements and customary international law. And in every single one of those cases, Britain, France, and the League of Nations played nice—or, in game terms, cooperated. This did not stop Germany; it only made it stronger.
Another great example of the prisoner’s dilemma in play is the Cold War. For almost half a century, global stability rested on the understanding that any attack would be answered in kind.

When the Cuban missile crisis struck in 1962, both sides escalated, Moscow first and Washington in response, until they realized that they would both lose. When one side returned to cooperation, the other did the same.

The starkest contrast is Finland and the Baltic states. In World War II, Russia did not annex Finland as it annexed the Baltic states. What made the difference was that when Russia sent its troops into Finland, the Finns fought back. As a result, Finland kept its independence (albeit limited) because it answered defection with defection, refusing to accept occupation, whereas the Baltics ended up in the prison of nations for 50-odd years, because they cooperated against defection.
If we look back at Russia’s actions and Europe’s responses, a certain pattern emerges.
Europe: Sucker

The first real post-Cold War example of defection by Russia was the 2008 invasion of Georgia. By and large, the international community cooperated: Russia did not lose anything as a result of this breach of rules. Indeed, in March 2009, U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton presented Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov with a large red button as a symbol of the Obama administration’s “reset” in relations with Russia.

Then came 2014: the annexation of Crimea, soldiers in eastern Ukraine, and the downing of MH17. Russia defected, and the West… imposed limited sanctions, agreed to build Nord Stream 2, forced Ukraine into two Minsk agreements, and wined and dined Putin while telling the President of Ukraine to just go away and comply with the rules. You could say the West cooperated with extreme prejudice.

After that, in 2022, came the full-scale invasion, and with it the destruction of Mariupol and Bucha, including the killing of tens of thousands of civilians, countless apartment buildings folding under a barrage of bombs, and civilians buried under the rubble or burning alive. Prisoners of war were tortured to death and bodies returned with vital organs missing. All illegal and outside any set of rules. Yet the West (back then this still included the United States) insisted that its response stay within the rules—and even well short of what the rules allowed—so as not to anger Russia. Russia kept defecting, and Europe and the United States kept cooperating.
Every single time, Russia defects. It has not cooperated even once. Whereas Europe has cooperated almost without fail, just as Moscow expects it to do.

Persuasion events

Holding oneself to a high standard in a cooperative environment is one thing. Doing it in a situation where it only feeds the crocodile that will eat you anyway is really stupid. Chickening out only makes you the victim, especially if the other side is rattling the nuclear saber.
It Wasn’t Us

Just recently, Mikhail Zvinchuk, founder of the Russian propaganda outlet Rybar—identified by British and American authorities as a key player in Russian hybrid operations—was detained in Montenegro, a NATO country. Instead of swapping him for one of the multitudes of hostages Russia is holding, Montenegro just expelled him.

Poland has initiated a process of creating a “pre-war state,” which, in the absence of a full state of war, will allow it to act faster to defend against threats. Russia has been waging war on Europe for years, while Europe has remained bound by the rules of peace, which restrict its ability to exercise self-defence. Measures that would be illegal in peacetime become legitimate once a country admits it is under attack. A “pre-war state” could show the rest of Europe a way to bridge that gap.

And while we are at it, Europe should stop telling Russia the truth. Russia cheats anyhow, yet Europe continues to keep its word, every single time. Europe should start saying one thing and doing another, exactly as Russia does. This way Russia will not be able to plan ahead, because it will not know what Europe will do. Only then can Europe get a different response.

According to the entire body of international law, what Russia has done to Ukraine and its people is illegal. You cannot hide behind the same international law to let Russia get away scot-free just because it has nuclear weapons. If Russia wants to avail itself of legal protections, it first has to obey the rules. This is not rocket science. Either Russia is violating international law and has to pay for it, or we should just admit there is no international law. And in that case, Russia cannot use it to demand the protection of its state assets. Russia’s frozen assets should be used to fund Ukraine’s—and therefore Europe’s—defence.

Ultimately, none of this is new. The prisoner’s dilemma has been researched ad nauseam by political scientists and think tanks alike, applied to most major conflicts, and taught to all international relations students. The conclusions are clear: the side always cooperating against the side always defecting loses. Always. Yet Europe is behaving as if it has got a dispensation from a higher power, and this time it will be different. It won’t. If Europe wants Russia to start cooperating, it will need to learn the art of defection.

Ines Burrell is a geopolitical analyst and political risk consultant based in the UK. Born in the Baltics, with a degree in International Relations from the University of Exeter, she writes and gives live commentary on European security and Russia.
