latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/st.headline: Steven Soderbergh to help Matt Reeves finish 'The Batman 2'
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/st.author: Tracy Brown

paragraphs.text: Steven Soderbergh is stepping in to help finish shooting “The Batman Part II” while director Matt Reeves continues to deal with a personal matter.

“As Matt Reeves continues to attend to an ongoing family matter, Steven Soderbergh, as an admirer of Matt’s work, approached Matt and will step in, with the full support of DC Studios, to help the writer-director complete the final weeks of principal photography on ‘The Batman Part 2,’” the studio said Thursday in a statement first reported by Deadline. “Matt and Steven will work closely together with the actors and crew to fulfill Matt’s vision of the film.”
DC Studios chief James Gunn confirmed the news on social media Thursday while reiterating that Reeves remains the director of “The Batman Part II.”
“Matt is still the director of The Batman 2 and always will be,” he wrote on Threads. “I can’t express how profoundly grateful and moved we are by Steven’s offer to help him complete his vision.”
The announcement follows news earlier this month that production on the film had been temporarily paused so Reeves could focus on dealing with the family matter.
“Matt has the full support of DC Studios and we look forward to continuing the journey soon,” the studio said in a statement at the time.
The writer-director also took to social media Thursday to express his gratitude and to confirm he would be continuing his work on “The Batman 2.”

“Just to be clear, I am not leaving The Batman Part II,” Reeves wrote in a post on X. “I am profoundly grateful to Steven for coming to my aid during this challenging time to help me finish principal photography. Thank you to all for your concern and well wishes.”
Soderbergh expressed his appreciation for Reeves’ work while addressing his new role Thursday in a widely reported statement.

“I thought Matt Reeves’ work on ‘The Batman’ was stunning; it was intentional, specific, and rigorously coherent,” he said in his statement, first reported by Deadline. “The goal here is to work with Matt and his team to generate footage that will integrate seamlessly with what’s already been shot so Matt can properly finish his film.”

A follow-up to Reeves’ 2022 reboot, “The Batman,” the upcoming film will once again star Robert Pattinson as Gotham’s iconic Caped Crusader. “The Batman Part II” began filming in London in June after a number of previous delays while Reeves and Mattson Tomlin wrote the script. The movie is slated to hit theaters on Feb. 18, 2028.

alexwang.ai/posts/associative-memory.headline: You could have invented transformers from memory
alexwang.ai/posts/associative-memory.author: Alex Wang

paragraphs.text: Large language models today can recall obscure facts from every corner of the world. Most recently, I was running late for a friend’s board game night, so I asked Astra to remind me the rules to Dune: Imperium. It gladly narrated them to me as I drove over and helped me remember the rules well enough for me to play again. We’re so used to asking models about anything that we take their vast knowledge for granted.
How do models remember so much information? And how much can they store?

In this post, I’ll go through an intuitive way to look at linear maps, MLPs, and self-attention as different kinds of memory stores. From this intuition we can derive some heuristics for how much memory each layer can store.

The key property that characterizes a “good” memory store is its ability to recall what it stored. After all, even if we could store infinitely many facts, it’s not very helpful if we can’t recall them when we need to. The more memories we store, the more they interfere with each other when we try to recall one. So throughout the post we’ll focus on one quantity, the interference-to-signal ratio, which measures how much the other memories get in the way during recall. The number of memories a store can hold before the interference grows as large as the signal is its capacity.

We’ll develop this perspective and show how you can go from a linear layer to something better, an MLP, which improves both capacity and recall, and then all the way to self-attention, which has very good recall and can store a potentially unbounded number of memories. With 64-dimensional keys, that’s a jump from about 64 memories, to about 2,700, to over a million.

Here are the terms we’ll use throughout. A memory store is a function $f$ that holds $M$ memories, for $i = 1, \ldots, M$. A memory is one key-value pair: a key $k_i \in \reals^{d_k}$, used for lookup based on similarity, and a value $v_i \in \reals^{d_v}$, which is what we want to retrieve. To use $f$, we query it with an input $x$, and it recalls an output $f(x)$. A good memory store recalls $v_i$ when we query it with $k_i$, or with another vector similar to $k_i$. In the literature, a memory store that recalls by similarity is called an associative memory.
An outer product memory store#
The most basic memory store is linear: it simply accumulates memories via outer products,
$$W = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i k_i\transpose = V\transpose K$$
where the rows of $K \in \reals^{M\times d_k}$ and $V \in \reals^{M\times d_v}$ are the keys $k_i\transpose$ and the values $v_i\transpose$.1
To store a new memory $(k, v)$, we simply add $vk\transpose$ to the existing weights.2

Take a linear layer $y = Wx$ inside a network with a scalar loss $L$, and let $\bar y = \grad L(y)$ be the gradient of the loss with respect to the layer’s output. The gradient with respect to $W$ is $\bar y x\transpose$, so a step with learning rate $\eta$ is

This recurrence is a memory update: it updates the weights with a new memory with key $x$ and value $-\eta\bar y$. For more on this view, see Irie, Csordás & Schmidhuber, who express a linear layer trained by gradient descent as attention over all of its training inputs.
To query the memory store with an input $x$, we multiply the input by the matrix:
$$f(x) = V\transpose K x = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i\,(k_i\transpose x).$$
So recall is a lookup by similarity to the stored keys: we compare the query with every key, and return the sum of the values weighted by those similarities.
Recall picks up interference#
So storing memories is easy: just keep adding outer products to the weights. But what happens when we try to recall one?
Let’s assume for simplicity that every key is normalized to have length 1, i.e. $k_j\transpose k_j = 1$. Then
$$f(k_j) = \underbrace{v_j}_{\text{signal}} + \underbrace{\sum_{i\neq j} v_i\,(k_i\transpose k_j)}_{\text{interference}},$$
meaning we get back the value of the target memory, the one whose key we queried with, plus interference from every other memory whose key is similar to the query.

If the keys were all orthonormal, the interference would be zero and recall would be exact. But $\reals^{d_k}$ only has $d_k$ orthogonal directions, so we cannot get perfect recall once we store more memories than the key dimension: $M > d_k$.

What is the outer-product store’s capacity? Here’s an intuitive argument. There are $M-1$ interference terms. If the keys are random unit vectors, each similarity $k_i\transpose k_j$ is about $\pm 1/\sqrt{d_k}$. If the values are random too, with similar lengths, the $M-1$ interference terms add up like a random walk, so the interference’s squared length is about $(M-1)/d_k$ times the signal’s, and
$$\frac{\norm{\text{interference}}}{\norm{\text{signal}}} \sim \sqrt{\frac{M}{d_k}}.$$
Setting this ratio to 1 gives a capacity of
$$M \approx d_k,$$
once we store as many memories as the key dimension, the interference is as large as the signal, drowning it out.

Each bar below is one stored memory’s weight in a single recall, relative to the target memory’s weight (in red). Every bar adds a bit of its value to the recall. Drag $M$ past $d_k = 64$ to watch the small bars pile up until recall fails. The other buttons switch to memory stores we’ll build later in the post.
How do we reduce interference?#

Even below its capacity of about $d_k$ memories, the outer-product store produces significant interference during recall.3 To raise the capacity, or recall more cleanly below it, we need to reduce interference.
The brute-force way is to make the key dimension $d_k$ larger, since a linear store’s capacity grows with $d_k$. How large $d_k$ can be is governed by hardware constraints.

Alternatively, we can make algorithmic improvements. We can store memories more carefully: the outer-product store adds each memory without looking at the others, so it does nothing to cancel their interference. Or we can recall more selectively: every memory in a linear store contributes interference, even when its key has low similarity to the query, so we can improve recall by suppressing the less similar keys.

In the rest of the post, we’ll see that storing outer product memories more carefully gives us the optimal linear memory store, which has about twice the capacity. Recalling selectively via nonlinearities gives us MLPs and self-attention.
The optimal linear memory store#

The outer-product store writes each memory without regard to the others. Instead, we can choose the weights $W$ so that recall fits all of the stored memories at once. This is a linear regression problem:4
$$\operatorname*{minimize}_W \sum_{i=1}^M \norm{W k_i - v_i}_2^2.$$
When we store more memories than the key dimension, $M > d_k$, the least-squares solution is
$$W = \parens*{\sum_i v_i k_i\transpose}\parens*{\sum_i k_i k_i\transpose}\inverse = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse.$$

This is the outer-product store $V\transpose K$ with one change: before we compare the query with the keys, we multiply it by $(K\transpose K)\inverse$, which undoes the keys’ covariance $K\transpose K$. This whitens the keys, so the store no longer overweights directions that many keys share.

When $M \leq d_k$, the regression can fit every memory exactly, as long as the keys are linearly independent. So the optimal store recalls with no interference at all, even when the keys aren’t orthogonal.
When $M > d_k$, we start to get interference, since there are only $d_k$ directions for the memory store to work with. For random keys and values, our interference-to-signal ratio becomes
$$\frac{\norm{\text{interference}}}{\norm{\text{signal}}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{M}{d_k} - 1}.$$
This ratio equals 1 at
so the optimal store’s capacity is twice as large as before!
When $M \leq d_k$. If the keys are linearly independent, the $M\times M$ matrix of inner products between keys, $KK\transpose$, is invertible, and

fits every memory exactly. When $M < d_k$, the problem is underconstrained and has infinitely many solutions, and this one is the min-norm solution. The rows $\tilde k_i\transpose$ of $(KK\transpose)\inverse K$ are known as the dual basis for the rows of $K$: by construction, $(KK\transpose)\inverse KK\transpose = I$, so $\tilde k_i\transpose k_j = \delta_{ij}$. Then $f(k_j) = \sum_i v_i\, \tilde k_i\transpose k_j = v_j$, so there is no interference and we have perfect recall.

When $M > d_k$. Setting the gradient of the objective to zero gives $W K\transpose K = V\transpose K$, so $W = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse$. Both solutions are $W = V\transpose (K\transpose)\pinv$, where $A\pinv$ denotes the pseudoinverse of $A$: $(K\transpose)\pinv = (KK\transpose)\inverse K$ when the keys are linearly independent, and $(K\transpose)\pinv = K(K\transpose K)\inverse$ when they span $\reals^{d_k}$.

Now we can analyze the interference of $f(k_j) = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$. For a stored key $k_j$, the weight on each value $v_i$ is $k_i\transpose (K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$, which is exactly entry $(i, j)$ of the $M\times M$ matrix $P = K(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose$:
$P$ is the projection onto the column space of $K$, a $d_k$-dimensional subspace of $\reals^M$. Two facts about projections help us analyze the interference-to-signal ratio:

• The signal term: By the cyclic property of the trace, $$\sum_{j=1}^M P_{jj} = \trace{K(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose} = \trace{(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose K} = \trace{I_{d_k}} = d_k,$$ so the $M$ signal weights add up to $d_k$. If the keys are random, no key is special, so $P_{jj} \approx d_k/M$.

• The interference term: $P$ is a symmetric projection matrix, so $P\transpose P = P^2 = P$. Then $$\sum_{i\neq j} P_{ij}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^M P_{ij}^2 - P_{jj}^2 = (P\transpose P)_{jj} - P_{jj}^2 = P_{jj} - P_{jj}^2 \approx \frac{d_k}{M} - \parens*{\frac{d_k}{M}}^2.$$
If the values are random with similar lengths,
Compared to the outer-product store’s $\sqrt{M/d_k}$, the $-1$ is the $d_k$ memories’ worth of interference that the optimal store cancels.

We can check our predictions numerically. We randomly sample $M$ memories with unit-length keys in $d_k = 64$ dimensions, query the memory store with one of the stored keys, and measure the interference-to-signal ratio:

The outer-product store reaches its capacity at $M \approx d_k = 64$. The optimal store recalls exactly up to $M = d_k$. Past that, its interference rises from zero like $\sqrt{M/d_k - 1}$, and the store reaches its capacity near $M = 2d_k = 128$, as predicted. Since it cancels a fixed number of memories’ worth of interference, the gap between the two stores shrinks as $M$ grows.
This optimal memory store is still linear in the similarities though. It must scale small and large similarities by the same factor. To do better, we need to change how the store recalls.
MLP as a nonlinear memory store#
A linear memory store recalls
$$f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^M v_i (k_i\transpose x).$$
If we had a way to suppress the weight when $k_i\transpose x$ is small, then we can reduce the amount of interference from low similarity keys.
Let’s pass each similarity through a nonlinear function $\sigma$ before computing the weighted sum of values:
$$f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i\,\sigma(k_i\transpose x) = V\transpose \sigma(Kx).$$

We just rediscovered a two-layer MLP from first principles! The rows of the first weight matrix are the keys, the columns of the second weight matrix are the values. Sukhbaatar et al. pointed out this resemblance between feedforward layers and memory stores, and Geva et al. found that the feedforward layers in trained transformers often work this way, with keys firing on recognizable patterns in the input.

Ideally, the gating function $\sigma$ is chosen such that when the similarity is low ($k_i\transpose x \sim 0$ or even when $k_i\transpose x < 0$), its corresponding term in the sum gets suppressed to reduce interference. A ReLU activation zeros out keys with negative similarities, and adding a bias allows shifting that threshold5. A squared ReLU activation further suppresses the keys with similarities close to zero. A similarity of 0.1 becomes 0.01, while a similarity of 1 stays 1. In fact, squared ReLUs are one of the lesser known but established-at-scale improvements to MLP activations (So et al.).

A squared ReLU MLP is a GLU MLP whose gate and input projection share weights, since $\operatorname{ReLU}(Kx)^2 = \operatorname{ReLU}(Kx) \odot Kx$. The SwiGLU MLPs in today’s language models give the gate its own weights and use a Swish activation in place of the ReLU.

In practice, MLPs store facts in superposition: many facts share the same weights, and the output is a blend of many memories. Garcia et al. build one explicitly: the hidden units of a GLU MLP compute random features $\phi(x)$ of the input, the second weight matrix is an outer-product store $\sum_i v_i \phi(k_i)\transpose$ over those features, and the MLP stores far more facts than it has hidden units. Still, trained transformers’ ReLU MLPs can activate as few as 1% of their hidden units for a given input, so each recall draws on a small fraction of the memories (Li et al.).

The original transformer paper made this connection too, but only in v2 and v3 on arXiv. There, Vaswani et al. describe the feedforward layer as “a kind of attention,” with the rows of its two weight matrices as the keys and values, and ReLU in place of softmax. They even tried replacing the feedforward layers with attention over learned key-value parameters, and got about the same translation quality: one version did slightly worse, another slightly better, though the first one trained about 30% slower. The passage is gone from every later version of the paper. We’ll get to how self-attention relates to all this below.
Reducing interference with higher powers#

Squaring the similarities works because it shrinks low similarity weights much more than large ones. We can push this further with $\sigma(s) = \operatorname{ReLU}(s)^p$. The signal stays the same, since $1^p = 1$, while an interference term with similarity $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ shrinks to $d_k^{-p/2}$. The $M$ interference terms add up like a random walk, so the interference-to-signal ratio is
$$\frac{\norm{\text{interference}}}{\norm{\text{signal}}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{M}{d_k^p}}.$$
This means the capacity is about
$$M \approx d_k^p$$
memories, geometrically more than before!
To check this, we run the same experiment as before for five choices of $\sigma$:
Since the interference grows like $\sqrt{M}$, the lines are nearly parallel on a log-log plot. Only their height changes, and with it the capacity, where each line crosses 1:
• Linear: the capacity is $M \approx d_k = 64$.
• ReLU: zeroing the negative similarities shrinks the interference by $\sqrt 2$, so the capacity grows to $M \approx 2d_k = 128$.
• Squared ReLU: each interference term shrinks from about $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ to about $1/d_k$, so the capacity grows to $M \approx 2d_k^2/3 \approx 2700$, about 40 times the linear store’s.

• SwiGLU MLP, with the gate sharing the input projection’s weights as in the squared ReLU, $\sigma(s) = \operatorname{Swish}(s)\cdot s = s^2/(1 + e^{-s})$: its capacity nearly matches the squared ReLU’s.
• Cubed ReLU: each interference term shrinks to about $d_k^{-3/2}$, so the capacity grows to $M \approx 2d_k^3/15 \approx 35000$.
Self-attention as a non-parametric memory store#

Raising the weights to a power increases the capacity to about $d_k^p$. But what if we could push this to the limit? Rather than pick one power, we can use infinitely many of them. Indeed, the exponential is a weighted sum of every power,
$$e^{\beta s} = 1 + \beta s + \frac{(\beta s)^2}{2} + \frac{(\beta s)^3}{6} + \cdots = \sum_{p=0}^{\infty} \frac{(\beta s)^p}{p!},$$

with the sharpness $\beta$ setting the weight on the higher powers. Here is the same experiment with $\beta = \sqrt{d_k}$, the value self-attention uses,6 for the exponential and its series truncated after 2, 3 and 4 terms:

With 2 terms, the capacity is about 40, below the linear store’s, since the constant term gives every key a weight of about 1. With 3 terms it’s about 450, and with 4 terms about 3,100, close to the squared ReLU’s. The full exponential stays far below the dashed line, so its capacity is past the edge of the chart.

To find the exponential’s capacity, we query with a stored key $k_j$, so the target memory has similarity 1 and weight $w_j = e^{\beta}$. Every other memory has weight $w_i = e^{\beta s_i}$, where for random unit keys the similarity $s_i$ is roughly Gaussian with mean 0 and variance $1/d_k$. With random values of similar lengths,
Setting the ratio to 1 gives a capacity of
$$M \approx e^{2\beta(1 - \beta/d_k)},$$

growing exponentially with $\beta$ as long as $\beta$ is well below $d_k$, rather than polynomially in $d_k$ like before! With $\beta = \sqrt{d_k} = 8$, the capacity is about $e^{14} \approx 1.2$ million memories, nearly 20,000 times the linear store’s. A longer run of the same experiment puts the capacity at about 1.2 million too.

In practice, we may not want to naively exponentiate numbers in our implementation, since small numbers can underflow and large numbers can overflow. Fortunately, the interference only depends on the ratios between weights, as the chain above shows, so we can divide every weight by their sum without changing the interference-to-signal ratio, while ensuring numerical stability:
$$f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i\,\frac{\exp(\beta\,k_i\transpose x)}{\sum_j \exp(\beta\,k_j\transpose x)} = V\transpose \operatorname{softmax}(\beta K x).$$
This is self-attention.7

Unlike an MLP, whose keys and values are trained weights, self-attention computes its keys and values from the tokens in its context. Each token stores one memory, so the number of memories $M$ is the context length. That’s what makes self-attention non-parametric: its memories aren’t parameters, and the store grows with the context.

Here’s the bar figure again, starting with softmax. At $\beta = 8$, recall never fails within the slider’s range, so lower $\beta$ to 2 and raise $M$: recall fails after a few dozen memories. Each doubling of $M$ needs a bit more $\beta$ to keep recall working, which is the idea behind the next section.
Handling many key-value pairs in long context#

Since $\beta$ determines how hard we suppress less similar keys, we can increase $\beta$ as the number of key-value pairs increases. Why not just make $\beta$ huge? As $\beta \to \infty$, softmax becomes a hard argmax that picks only the most similar key, which isn’t differentiable, and a very large $\beta$ already makes training work poorly, since the softmax saturates and the gradients to every other key vanish. So we raise $\beta$ only as much as $M$ requires. Scaling the attention logits with $\log M$ is a trick for long contexts that does this. There are a few versions of it, and each sets $\beta$ relative to a fixed reference length $L$, usually the training length, so that $\beta$ keeps its trained value when $M = L$:

• Su (2021) derives a scale of $\log M$ from keeping the attention’s entropy constant as $M$ grows, normalized to match standard attention at $M = L$. The logits are multiplied by $\log M / \log L$ at every length. Scalable-Softmax has the same form, multiplying the logits by $s \log M$ with $s$ learned.
• The original Qwen models use LogN-Scaling, which applies the same factor only once the context is longer than $L$.
• Qwen2.5-1M uses YaRN’s attention scaling, which multiplies the logits by $(0.1 \log(M/L) + 1)^2$, so it grows like $(\log M)^2$.
Here’s how each rule does in our experiment, with $\beta = \sqrt{d_k} = 8$ at $L = 1024$ memories:

Qwen’s rule and Su’s rule coincide past the reference length $L$, where the interference-to-signal ratio falls as the store grows, to about 0.004 at 2 million memories. YaRN’s faster-growing scale pushes the ratio down to about $10^{-4}$. In each case, scaling $\beta$ with $\log M$ allows for essentially an unbounded number of memories with distinct keys to be stored.
Closing thoughts#
Here are the memory stores we visited, with their capacities when we query with a stored key and the keys and values are random:

We started from a heuristic memory store, the outer-product memory, and gradually built our way up to all the standard layers we see today in modern transformers. This perspective also allowed us to estimate how they differ in their capacity, their ability to act as vector-valued key-value stores.

I should mention that this capacity estimate is only one way to look at the architecture of modern neural networks. Our capacity estimate only counts how many random vectors a single layer can recall before the interference dominates the signal. In fact we haven’t actually considered the training data at all, which affects what actually is being represented in the keys and values! There are other works which account for the trained layers, measuring stored information in bits. Morris et al. estimate that GPT-style models memorize about 3.6 bits per parameter, and find that once a model fills its capacity, it starts to generalize and memorizes less of each training example. Allen-Zhu & Li find that language models store about 2 bits of factual knowledge per parameter, even when quantized to int8.
From here, there are many related directions which are also fascinating:

• How much information a layer can store: Nichani, Lee & Bietti, Barnfield et al. for linear stores, and Dugan et al., Garcia et al. for explicit fact-storing MLPs, and Zhong et al. which inspired the interference-to-signal ratio estimates here.

• Hopfield networks and memory stores with exponential capacity: Krotov & Hopfield on dense associative memory, Demircigil et al., Ramsauer et al., who connect it to attention, and the review by Krotov et al..
• Huge but sparse parametric memory stores to supplement or replace our MLPs: product-key memories, Memory Layers at Scale, UltraMem, Mixture of A Million Experts, and Engram.
• Nonparametric memory stores that grow by appending memories outside the weights: kNN-LM, RETRO, Memorizing Transformers, and growing nonparametric networks.
• Finding and editing the memories inside trained models: Geva et al., Bietti et al., and ROME and MEMIT.
• Compressing short-term memory, or turning it into long-term memory: KVzip, gist tokens, Cartridges, and attention matching
• Continual learning methods like sparse memory finetuning
I’ve always been drawn to memory, maybe because I viscerally feel how limited my own is. Perhaps part of me hopes that by understanding how machines remember, I’ll learn something about myself too.

• Sometimes this accumulation of keys and values is called “Hebbian learning”, since the strength of the synapses (weights) is increased by inputs (keys) and outputs (values) that fire together (are correlated). ↩︎

• This outer-product memory store is used for the state of linear attention, also called fast weights: each token stores the memory $(k, v)$ by adding $v k\transpose$ to a matrix that later tokens query (Katharopoulos et al.; Schlag, Irie & Schmidhuber). ↩︎

• This is for recalling a clean value vector. If each value only needs to point toward the right answer among a fixed set, like selecting the most likely token, a recall just has to land closer to the right answer than to the wrong ones, and a $d\times d$ matrix can hold about $d^2$ facts (Nichani, Lee & Bietti). ↩︎

• We can also use this regression objective to design short-term memories that a sequence model writes during the forward pass, like linear attention and self-attention. See my work on test-time regression. ↩︎

• For random keys, a ReLU reduces the interference by a factor of $\sqrt 2$. A random key’s similarity is equally likely to be positive or negative, so the ReLU zeroes about half of the weights and leaves the other half unchanged. That halves the interference’s variance, the sum of the squared weights, so the interference itself shrinks by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$. See Zhong et al. for a full derivation. ↩︎

• Transformers divide the similarities by $\sqrt{d_k}$ rather than multiplying. But their queries and keys have length about $\sqrt{d_k}$, so a matching pair has $q\transpose k \approx d_k$. Our keys and queries have unit length, so a matching pair has similarity 1. Hence we scale by $\beta = \sqrt{d_k}$ . ↩︎

• In transformer notation, the similarity is $k_i\transpose q$ with $q = W_Q x$, scaled by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$. I fold $W_Q$ into the keys. Keys and queries in a transformer have length about $\sqrt{d_k}$, so that scaling matches $\beta = \sqrt{d_k}$ for unit-length keys like ours. ↩︎

latimes.com/politics/story/2026-10-16/tr.headline: Trump's team is in chaos as midterms enter final stretch
latimes.com/politics/story/2026-10-16/tr.author: Michael Wilner

paragraphs.text: WASHINGTON — President Trump bypassed his White House chief of staff last week in selecting Katie Zacharia as his press secretary and chief messenger, triggering days of scathing headlines about her credentials and abilities before her ignominious resignation on Friday.

Susie Wiles, that senior-most aide ostensibly in charge of the president’s team, is facing his scrutiny over a different set of problems: widespread public anxiety over corruption in government under the Trump administration. The issue has surpassed the economy as the top concern of voters entering next month’s election, according a Fox News poll released this week.

Marco Rubio, the president’s secretary of state and national security advisor, has been silent on Trump’s decision to cut a deal with Moscow on diesel sales that could fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine. The president’s poll numbers have been below water across the board, but especially so on foreign policy, where over two-thirds of Americans disapprove of his job performance and support Kyiv’s fight for freedom.
And on Thursday, the president was forced to reverse course set out by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Pentagon to live-stream the execution of a convicted mass shooter by firing squad.

In the final stretch of the 2026 midterms, nearly two weeks out from Election Day, a White House that has enjoyed relative stability over the past two years has returned to the state of disarray that characterized much of Trump’s early political career, anticipating sweeping losses to Democrats in the House and Senate.
Staff upheaval is expected as officials brace for a blame game over Republican performance, with some distancing themselves from a fading political movement.

Polls suggest that Republicans are likely to lose control of the House, setting up two years of relentless congressional probes through the twilight of the Trump era, and could even flip the Senate, winning in ruby red states from Ohio to Alaska.
It is historically a time for closing arguments, when politicians deliver their final pitches to voters in neat, disciplined packages.

Yet Trump’s campaign blitz across the country in recent weeks has generated a muddled message, dismissing the importance of the election itself at risk of depressing Republican votes, overshadowing local candidates seeking distance from his record and touting an economy unrecognizable to most Americans.
The president’s selection of Zacharia, who lasted just five days on the job, raised fresh questions about his message discipline in the final stretch.

And infighting within the White House has reinforced a narrative among political pundits that Democratic gains are a fait accompli, despite Zacharia, in her first and only press briefing, foretelling of Republican energy and excitement “never seen before in the history of midterms thanks to President Trump.”
Election officials across the country fear that, anticipating inevitable losses, Trump may be laying the ground to challenge the authenticity of the election results themselves.

“You know, this is the only guy that — it’s ‘promises made, promises kept,’ but he did more things than he promised,” Trump said Thursday, referring to himself in the third person. “I think we did. We did much more than we promised.”
The extent of the coming West Wing shakeup could be extensive, reaching into a cabinet that has had far less turnover than Trump experienced in his first term.

Zacharia is the second senior official forced out by Trump in just three days, after Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former fiancé of one of Trump’s sons who served as U.S. ambassador to Greece, was revealed by the Wall Street Journal to have asked a Trump donor to pay off her $100,000 credit card bill.

Now, the president has begun asking political allies and donors about Wiles’ job performance, according to a recent Politico report, and several top administration officials are vying for her role anticipating her resignation after the elections next month.

The conclusion of the midterms will also kick off the start of the 2028 presidential election season, when Republican hopefuls — including many from Trump’s cabinet — are expected to launch exploratory committees.

“We have to get through the midterms first,” Trump said at the end of August, asked about Hegseth reportedly considering a run. “I bet there’s a lot of people considering it that you don’t know about. You have a lot of people.”
The party of incumbent presidents regularly loses seats in midterm elections, and it is common for presidents to shake up their staffs halfway through a term.

But the last time a term-limited Republican president faced voters in midterm elections, in 2006, Democrats swept into power in both houses of Congress — and President George W. Bush’s political capital never recovered.
That year, 37% of voters said they approved of Bush’s job performance. Polls published this month by AP and Reuters have found Trump already below that threshold.
In the GOP presidential primaries that followed, candidates jockeying to replace Bush distanced themselves from his legacy. He ultimately left office with an approval rating of 25%.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/replit-is-no-l.headline: Replit is no longer working with Anthropic, CEO says
techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/replit-is-no-l.author: Lucas Ropek, Kirsten Korosec

paragraphs.text: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that its was no longer with Anthropic.

“I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was it was a decision based on both cost, you know, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”

Replit sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. Under its partnership with Anthropic, Replit used the AI lab’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly.

Masad’s comments were met with some pushback from insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

There is some evidence that Replit was using Anthropic products as recently as September. For instance, a blog post in September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment.
TechCrunch reached back out to Replit for clarification and will update this story if we hear back.
Masad shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.

“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”
Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.

“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”

Lucas is a senior writer at TechCrunch, where he covers artificial intelligence, consumer tech, and startups. He previously covered AI and cybersecurity at Gizmodo. You can contact Lucas by emailing [email protected].

Kirsten Korosec is a reporter and editor who has covered the future of transportation from EVs and autonomous vehicles to urban air mobility and in-car tech for more than a decade. She is currently the transportation editor at TechCrunch and co-host of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast. She is also co-founder and co-host of the podcast, “The Autonocast.” She previously wrote for Fortune, The Verge, Bloomberg, MIT Technology Review and CBS Interactive.

The Norte fire in south Orange County broke out amid strong Santa Ana winds on Friday morning, triggering mandatory evacuations in San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano.
The fire has burned roughly 250 acres as of 2 p.m., according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. It has also burned multiple homes.
Evacuations
Mandatory evacuations were ordered for San Juan Zones 4, 5, and 10 and San Clemente Zone 12. “If you are in one of these zones, leave immediately,” the Orange County Fire Authority wrote on X.

The evacuation zones include a swath of hillside neighborhoods bordered by the 5 Freeway, Ortega Highway and Avenida La Pata. It also extends down into neighborhoods closer to the coast and bordered by the 5 Freeway and Camino Los Mares.
You can find a map of the evacuation zones on the Orange County Sheriff’s Department website.
School Closures
The following Capistrano Unified School District campuses are being dismissed early because of the fire:
• Bernice Ayer Middle School
• Clarence Lobo Elementary School
• Concordia Elementary School
• Harold Ambuehl Elementary School
• San Clemente High School
• San Juan Hills High School
• Shorecliffs Middle School
• Truman Benedict Elementary School
• Vista Del Mar TK-8
Shelters
Shelters have been established at the following locations:
• San Juan Capistrano Community Center at 25925 Camino del Avion, San Juan Capistrano.
• San Clemente Community Center at 100 Calle Seville, San Clemente.

cnbc.com/2026/10/16/midterm-election-fun.headline: 5 midterm money takeaways: Democrats have candidate cash. Republicans have Elon Musk
cnbc.com/2026/10/16/midterm-election-fun.author: Luke Fountain

paragraphs.text: One of the last big campaign-finance snapshots before the Nov. 3 Election Day is now available, and both political parties found something to like. But campaign cash is flowing in very different ways — and, on balance, points to an environment more favorable for Democrats.
On one side, Democratic candidates have turned into absolute cash cows, raising oodles more than their Republican rivals across Senate and House battlegrounds.

Republicans, however, still have a leg to stand on from an unprecedented flood of outside super PAC cash, bankrolled by a tiny circle of billionaires led by Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. The deluge of capital could be enough to stave off the worst of what has otherwise been a treacherous political environment for the GOP amid stubbornly high inflation and drooping approval ratings for President Donald Trump.

A flurry of Federal Election Commission filings Thursday at a key deadline detailed what candidates raised and spent from July through September and give insight into many of the outside groups backing them. More of the outside-money picture comes next week with another deadline for additional filings.
Here are CNBC's five takeaways:
Democratic grassroots strength
If Democrats want a financial case for a blue wave, start with the candidates themselves.

Democratic Senate nominees put up gaudy third-quarter totals. James Talarico raised $60.2 million in Texas, Jon Ossoff brought in $33.1 million in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed raised $30.7 million in Michigan. Sherrod Brown brought in $23.1 million in Ohio, while Troy Jackson raised $20.4 million in Maine, Mary Peltola $14.1 million in Alaska and Roy Cooper $12.2 million in North Carolina.
Even in reliably red Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton raised $9.4 million.

In several of those races, the Republican numbers were not even close. Ken Paxton raised about $10.2 million in Texas, Mike Rogers $9.7 million in Michigan, Susan Collins $5.2 million in Maine and Jon Husted $4.8 million in Ohio.

Candidate dollars are especially potent in the final stretch because campaigns control where they go and qualify for lower television advertising rates than super PACs do. In other words, Republicans may be able to make up a $1 fundraising gap with outside money — but it can cost them more than $1 to do it.
The same fundraising edge stretches into the House.

Democratic candidates outraised their Republican opponents through September in 13 of the 21 House races currently rated Toss Up by Cook, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. In North Carolina's 11th District, for example, Democrat Jamie Ager raised $2.1 million in the third quarter, compared with roughly $313,000 for Republican Jennifer Balkcom.

The fundraising surge coincides with a shifting map: the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter projected last week that Democrats could gain two to six Senate seats — enough to put the four-seat majority threshold within reach — and nine to 19 House seats, which would flip the chamber.
Republicans' ace in the hole
While Democratic candidates dominate direct donations, Republicans are countering with overwhelming outside spending.

The Senate Leadership Fund, the GOP's main Senate super PAC, raised a record $272.9 million from July through September, roughly $122 million more than its Democratic counterpart, according to FEC filings. On the House side, the Congressional Leadership Fund raised a record $94.4 million during the quarter and entered October with $156 million in cash, according to its FEC filing.

That outside money is functioning as a financial backstop for GOP candidates who trail badly in direct fundraising. Texas is the most extreme example: the SLF funneled $158 million into Texas PAC, the super PAC backing Paxton, according to FEC filings.

Elsewhere, Republicans have committed $15 million through the SLF to defend Sen. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska, The Wall Street Journal reported this week. Outside groups account for roughly 80% of all ad buys in Alaska, where the SLF has spent $14 million backing Sen. Dan Sullivan, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data.

The blitz allowed Republicans to hold an aired-ad advantage in seven of eight top Senate battles and 25 of 42 contested House seats rated "Toss Up" or "Lean" Republican or Democrat by the Cook Report as of Oct. 9, according to AdImpact.
But polls have shown little movement in recent weeks, despite the advantage.
Musk fights for Texas
No donor better captures the scale — or the leverage — of that outside-money advantage than the world's richest person, Musk.

He pumped more than $276 million into federal political groups during the third quarter, making him the biggest known individual donor of the midterms. His disclosed giving included $158 million to Senate Leadership Fund and another $89 million to his America PAC, according to FEC filings.
Most of that capital was earmarked for a single rescue mission: Texas, the state that's his primary residence and headquarters of his businesses.

Musk gave the SLF $75 million on Sept. 9 and another $83 million on Sept. 23. Both times, the SLF transferred the exact same amount to Texas PAC the following day. The group, which is backing Paxton, reported no other donors through the end of September.

Until now, many national Republicans had been reluctant to sink resources into the Lone Star state's expensive media market while fighting across an already expanded Senate map. Musk effectively erased that trade-off, supplying enough money to build a dedicated financial firewall around Paxton without forcing the party to pull resources from other battlegrounds.
Democratic megadonors get off the sidelines

For months, Democrats worried over the reluctance of traditional megadonors to write checks following the 2024 election cycle with presidential contest drama at the top of the ticket. The latest filings suggest that freeze is thawing — though much money is still bypassing the Democratic National Committee.

Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and his wife, Cari Tuna, put about $16 million into the midterm fight this summer, according to FEC filings, while LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, who had also withheld money from the DNC this cycle, poured $11.5 million into the super PAC backing Talarico earlier this year.
The renewed megadonor money gives Democrats another source of firepower for the final weeks that can be quickly redirected if needed.
Already, Democrats' Senate Majority PAC raised a record $151 million in the third quarter and ended September with $112 million in cash, even as its Republican counterpart raised substantially more.
Record-breaking money
All the spending is feeding an election on track to shatter spending records.

AdImpact projects $11.6 billion in political advertising during the 2025-26 election cycle, which would make 2026 the most expensive cycle on record — surpassing both the $8.9 billion spent during the 2022 midterms and the $11.2 billion spent during the 2024 presidential cycle.

The congressional fight alone has already put $3.8 billion in advertising on the air, more than $870 million ahead of the comparable point in 2024, according to AdImpact. Senate races are helping drive the surge: the firm projects $3.4 billion in Senate advertising by the end of the cycle, up 48% from 2022.
But as the amount of money rises, some of it is becoming harder for voters to trace back to its original source.

Thursday's filings showed millions flowing into super PACs from nonprofits and other entities that are not required to disclose their own donors, leaving the original source of some of the cycle's biggest checks hidden.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.headline: Timothy Busfield child sex abuse charges thrown out, judge orders
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.author: Alexandra Del Rosario

paragraphs.text: A New Mexico judge on Friday ruled in favor of Emmy winner Timothy Busfield, tossing out multiple child sex abuse charges against the actor.

During a hearing, Judge Joseph A. Montano granted Busfield’s motion to dismiss his indictment, citing prosecutorial misconduct and errors that undermined the grand jury process. According to the order, “the prosecuting attorney failed to act in a fair and impartial manner” and proceedings thus far “were conducted in a manner that violated grand jury statutes designed to protect the structural integrity of our grand jury system.”

State prosecutors had indicted Busfield in February and charged him with four counts of criminal sexual contact of a child. The since-dismissed charges stemmed from his alleged behavior with two actors, who are brothers, on the set of the Fox crime drama “The Cleaning Lady.” The actor, known for “The West Wing” and “Thirtysomething,” has pleaded not guilty to those charges.

While a legal representative for Busfield did not immediately respond Friday to The Times’ request for comment, a spokesperson for the Bernalillo County District Attorney’s Office said prosecutors are “evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed.”

A New Mexico judge issued a warrant for Busfield’s arrest in January, citing two counts of criminal sexual contact with a minor and a single count of child abuse. Busfield was accused of inappropriately touching the child actors during his time as an actor, director and producer on “The Cleaning Lady,” according to an affidavit filed by New Mexico officials.

One child actor alleged Busfield first touched his “private areas” multiple times on set when he was 7 years old, according to the complaint. He said that Busfield touched him inappropriately again several times when he was 8. The affidavit also detailed a police interview with Busfield in which he suggested that the boys’ mother might have sought “revenge” on the director for “not bringing her kids back for the final season.”

Busfield filed his motion to quash the indictment in June, alleging the court refused to provide members of the grand jury with additional information and that prosecutors refused to allow jury members to hear from other witnesses, among other claims, according to court documents.

“The State treated the grand jury not as an independent body, but as the arm of the prosecution our courts have forbidden,” the motion says. “The resulting indictment must be dismissed.” Prosecutors rebutted Busfield’s allegations in a response to the dismissal and asked the court to deny his motion.
Before Friday’s order, a jury trial was scheduled to begin May 10, 2027.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-16/.headline: City Controller subpoenas financial records from '28 Olympic organizers
latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-16/.author: James Rainey

paragraphs.text: Los Angeles City Controller Kenneth Mejia issued a legal demand Friday for the organizers of the 2028 Summer Olympics to disclose more information about the organization’s finances — including bank statements, detailed plans for venue construction and the size of contracts with outside vendors.

Mejia’s subpoena, issued under his City Charter authority, came two and a half weeks after officials at LA28, the Olympic organizing committee, rejected his previous request to disclose the information.
Mejia demanded the information, much of which was also requested by The Times, as required in the 2021 contract that defines the working relationship between LA28 and the host city of the 2028 games.
LA28 officials had no immediate comment.

Leaders of the Olympics organizing group have said previously that while they had not disclosed all of the information in their annual reports — as required by the so-called Games Agreement — they had provided the information to other city officials, including Mayor Karen Bass and the city administrative officer and chief legislative analyst.

“LA28’s refusal to comply with my Office’s request after years of withholding information that they are contractually obligated to provide to the City of L.A. is unacceptable,” Mejia said in a statement. “My responsibility is to protect taxpayer dollars, and I will use my full authority under the City Charter to assess the City’s financial exposure of hosting the 2028 Games.”

The information that Mejia wants is supposed to be contained in annual reports that LA28 issues to its officially designated city “liaisons” — the mayor, city attorney, and top administrative and legislative officers.

The Times found in its own review that LA28 had given vague and sometimes incomplete information. Among the missing details: progress on roughly two dozen venues around Greater Los Angeles and details about contracts of more than $1 million for services such as security and pre-production work for the opening and closing ceremonies.

Mejia’s office said in a press release Friday that it needed those details and more “to ascertain the financial status of the 2028 Olympic Games.” The statement added: “As the City’s accountant, auditor, and paymaster, the Controller has a responsibility to protect City of L.A. taxpayers from the impact of the LA28 Olympic Games.”

Under the city’s agreement with LA28, Los Angeles will be obligated to cover any losses, should the Olympics fail to break even or make money. The city would cover the first $270 million of losses, the state of California the next $270 million and the city any losses of more than $540 million.

Because of that potential financial liability, Mejia’s office said that “Angelenos deserve full transparency from LA28 related to all spending and revenue incurred in the process of planning and executing the 2028 Olympic Games.”

LA28 officials have reported that they have collected revenues — particularly from corporate sponsorships and ticket sales — that exceed projections. They have said the games remain on track to turn a profit, with excess funds promised to youth sports programs in Southern California.

The City Council has received and accepted multiple annual reports from LA28, raising a few questions but no major objections. The council did not intercede, for example, two years ago when LA28 stopped its previous practice of naming contractors that it had paid more than $1 million.

But the city’s chief administrative officer and chief legislative analyst in September asked for more details, calling information about the contracts “limited.” The two top City Hall bureaucrats said LA28 previously objected to disclosing the contract details, saying the disclosure could be “financially detrimental and a risk to its future competitive contracts partnership and sponsorship activities.”

Section 217 of the City Charter grants the controller and other city officers the power to order individuals to produce documents and to attend hearings, with subpoenas issued via the City Clerk’s office.

Other city officials mostly have remained quiet in the dispute about LA28’s financial reporting. But Mayor Karen Bass said in a statement prior to the controller’s subpoena that she backs the release of more financial information.

City Attorney Hydee Feldstein Soto’s office said in a statement to The Times last month that she “supports the Controller’s efforts to obtain the financial information necessary to understand the full scope of LA28’s finances and the City’s potential fiscal exposure.”

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.headline: Gone to the dogs: racing fans mourn closure of ‘Wenty’, Sydney’s historic greyhound track
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: The end of an era has fallen upon an Australian sporting landmark as the greyhound races at an inner-city track kicked off for the very last time.
Thousands packed into Wentworth Park in central Sydney on Friday night, where greyhound races have been held since 1932, for the last race meeting before the track’s planned demolition.
The final race of the night was the richest in the world – the Million Dollar Chase – and was won by Magical Ang.
For Geoff Rose, the closure was a sign of the times – the land in the inner-west suburb of Glebe is worth a fortune in a city where growth will not slow down.
But the NSW Greyhound Breeders, Owners and Trainers Association chair remained sad to see the park go.
“It is quite heartbreaking to a lot of people,” he said.
Another spectator mourning the closure was Jeff Collerson, a veteran greyhound writer who first set foot on the track at Wentworth Park in December 1962 as a 17-year-old cadet journalist.
Now 81, he was trackside as the dogs raced around the circuit, nestled against the Sydney city skyline, for the final time and reminisced about his career.
He said the closure of what locals refer to affectionately as “Wenty” was tragic.
“I remember saying to my wife years ago, I want you to cast my ashes in front of the winning post at Wentworth Park, but I told her not to do that now,” Collerson said.
“Wentworth Park’s got a special aura about it that the other tracks won’t have … it’s got a special buzz to it.
“That will be lost forever because having a city track is just fantastic.”
All buildings are slated for demolition after October 2027, and the site is planned to be returned to parkland under the auspices of Sydney’s council.
Wentworth Park was created between 1876 and 1880 using silt dredged from Sydney’s harbour. Greyhound racing began in the park in 1932, and by the 1970s, the sport was attracting large crowds.

Greyhound Racing NSW, the state’s regulator for the sport, announced this week it had chosen the existing Richmond race club, about an hour north-west of central Sydney, as the replacement site for the industry.
Rose said his association was also exploring another option, which could see it establishing race meetings at a site near Appin, south-west of Sydney.

Either way, the state’s racing minister, David Harris, has previously promised $10m in government funding to help the industry find a new home – a move criticised by those calling for the industry to be shut down altogether.
Some have welcomed the track’s closure as a move towards the whole industry’s end.
A crowd of protesters stood outside the park as punters filed in, chanting that the sport kills dogs, and calling for an end to taxpayer dollars propping up the industry.
Aleisha Kernan and Kirsten Lambros work for Greyhounds as Pets, which helps facilitate the adoption of retired racing dogs.
Kernan said the sport’s potential new facilities would “open new avenues”.
“I think people should look at the future as well,” she said.
But for one young punter, Harry Dunlop, nothing would replace what he described as a “prominent piece of Australia”.
“It’s very unlikely that we’ll be going out to Richmond,” he said.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv98zw1k8kp3o.headline: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad killed suspect
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv98zw1k8kp3o.author: Sareen Habeshian and Nardine Saad

paragraphs.text: An Oregon teacher threw her mobile phone before she tackled and tried to wrestle away a shotgun from the arms of a teen suspect who opened fire on a special educational needs class.
As she tussled with him on the floor of the class - where three children and a teacher were killed - a bystander ran inside. Armed with a .40-caliber pistol, he opened fire and killed the teen.
The bystander, a dad of two girls at the school, had been driving past Silver Rail Elementary in Bend when he saw the suspect firing in the car park then shooting through a window to enter.
The details of the Thursday attack were confirmed by police, who said the 16-year-old suspect was a prior student at the school.
Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.

"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence, and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said on Friday.

Police offered more information on the attack at at a news conference on Friday, where they identified two of the four victims. They include five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.
The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.
Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.
Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school saved lives.
He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman was not hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
He identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, who previously attended the school and was a special educational needs student there.
A search warrant has been executed at the suspect's home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.
Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but police are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun. A motive is also not clear.
Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.
But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.

The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school then shoot through a window and go inside.

Police said he had a legally concealed .40 caliber in his vehicle and his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him.
In a statement to the BBC's partner CBS News, Giamanco's family said he is a "lifelong resident of Bend" and that he "is not seeking recognition".

The family said Giamanco wants to express his "gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support". He and his family "respectfully ask for privacy".
US President Donald Trump praised the bystander's actions on Friday, calling him a "great hero".
Addressing reporters at the White House before departing for Georgia, Trump said the situation could have been "much worse" with no intervention.
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said.

Without naming the bystander, Governor Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions stopping further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well".
Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvgdn3d656vo.headline: Trial of German steakhouse heiress Christina Block that sparked a huge spy scandal
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvgdn3d656vo.author: Bethany Bell

paragraphs.text: It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.

Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.
There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.
In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.

Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.
There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.

Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.

Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.
They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.
The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.
On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.

The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.
Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.
Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.
All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.
The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.
Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.
In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.

A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.
In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.
He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.
She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.
She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.

The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.
Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."
The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.

Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.

However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers.
Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.
Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".
Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.
The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.headline: Mortgage repayments are now cheaper than rent in some Australian suburbs. Is yours among them?
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.author: Luca Ittimani

paragraphs.text: High rents and falling property prices have opened a rare window for Australian tenants to become homeowners, with mortgage repayments cheaper than rent in dozens of suburbs. Guardian Australia’s analysis of Cotality data shows that median rents in inner-city Melbourne, suburban Canberra and Darwin are now nearly matching weekly home loan repayments.
In one in 10 suburbs and towns across the country, repayments are less than $200 a week higher than rent, for the typical property. In some suburbs, they are actually cheaper.

Australia’s median rent prices rose 5.5% over the year to September to reach $713 per week, Cotality data shows. The median property price across houses and units was flat over the year, after six months of steady falls.
The typical rent for a Melbourne apartment was $628 a week after rising 4.8% over the last year.
The typical repayments for a Melbourne flat were $211 more, or $839 a week, based on a median value of $624,740 in September, down nearly $25,000 from a year earlier.

The analysis assumes a new 30-year loan of 95% of the value, at a 6.2% interest rate. It does not account for any additional costs. Smaller loans made with bigger deposits would make repayments even more affordable compared with rents.
Owner-occupiers purchasing with a 5% deposit would typically do so through the government’s low deposit scheme, which is designed to help first home buyers.
Repayments were cheaper than rent for the typical property in Carlton, Melbourne CBD, Notting Hill, Travancore and Southbank.

Repayments on new loans had risen overall in the last year for most suburbs, as lower values were offset by interest rates rising 1 percentage point. Where values had fallen more than 10%, though, repayments were likely lower.
Clint Waters, a Melbourne mortgage broker, said home buying interest had dropped but renters were inquiring in strong numbers as they weighed lower house prices against higher rents.
“They’re certainly doing the maths … [and] the equation at the moment is starting to narrow,” Waters said.
Waters, director at Axton Finance, said a stable or growing number were looking to buy direct from their landlord, making the switch without moving.

“Landlords are getting slammed left, right and centre, and going ‘screw this, I’m going to offload,” Waters said. “Tenants will ring us up and say, ‘I need to work out if I’ve got the capacity to buy this thing.’”
New apartments pushing down prices
In Sydney, repayments were just $100 a week more than rents in inner-city Ultimo and western suburbs Warwick Farm, Rosehill, Liverpool and Granville.
In the Canberra suburbs of Belconnen and Phillip, repayments were less than $75 a week more than rents. If only apartments are included, Braddon, Lyons, Gungahlin and Harrison join the list.

Gerard Burg, Cotality researcher, said areas with significant apartment development tended to be cheaper to buy than rent, especially where flats were being sold direct to owner-occupiers and not rented out.
“That just [shows] this influx of supply pushing down the value of the purchase, while comparatively tight rental availability had led to this increase in rents,” Burg said.
But such areas were “anomalies”, he said. Houses remain generally more expensive to buy than rent.
“If it was a sustained thing that you could buy a property more cheaply than renting it, then everyone would buy and everyone would exit the rental market,” Burg said.

It was cheaper to buy in a quarter of suburbs in Darwin, where rents have risen 11.6% in the year. Most areas where buying was cheaper than renting were mining or resource project areas in which fly-in fly-out workers temporarily rent rather than buy, Burg said.
Burg said mortgage repayments would likely fall if the Reserve Bank held rates steady and values kept falling, as expected by financial markets, potentially narrowing the gap with rents.
“[With] rents continuing to increase or … go sideways, that could occur.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g18ljjd8do.headline: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g18ljjd8do.author: Sarah Rainsford

paragraphs.text: Italy's defence minister has said it is a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.

In a BBC interview, Guido Crosetto warned that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace.

US officials have said Trump has not asked for the slowdown of internet speeds the US provides to Ukraine and which are vital for its war effort. Trump has also denied that the US has stopped sharing early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks with Ukraine.
Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice", and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine.
Trump agreed the deal with Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices.
Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table.
"Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome.
Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war.
"If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side – and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness – then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned.
"I think that is completely wrong."
Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid.
The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified.

In our interview, the defence minister vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached.
The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners.

That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground.
At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian".
Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with".
But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia.

"When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said.
But Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy.
During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms, instead of education.
Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs."
In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices.

Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the Ixè institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%.

There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too.
But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow – targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia".
"In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued.

"It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining."
Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe.
The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity".
A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us.
But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response.
"You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said.
With additional reporting from Rome by Davide Ghiglione.

astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-st.headline: Your Book Review: Storm Of Steel
astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-st.author: Scott Alexander

paragraphs.text: [This is one of the finalists in the 2026 book review contest, written by an ACX reader who will remain anonymous until after voting is done. I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked]

All Quiet on the Western Front ranks as the definitive anti-war novel of World War I, perhaps for all wars, and to some the most important war novel of all time. It was widely banned in the inter-war period yet went on to sell more than 20 million copies and has three film adaptations, the most recent the acclaimed 2022 version. It’s so famous, so prominent, so dominating, that the novel I think is the best war novel ever written can only point back at it from a ‘see also’ link on Wikipedia. That novel is Storm of Steel, by Ernst Jünger.

You may recognize that name from 2023’s ACX book review, On the Marble Cliffs. It was my first serious look at Jünger as well; he is described as a “serial killer” and a “sociopath,” the kind of modern psycho who nowadays would take glee in uploading videos of drones blowing people up, someone perhaps who sees war as the chance to visit death upon human beings with the state’s permission. I had heard of Storm of Steel, heard the acclaim for it, but never read any of his works. What kind of man was this?

The Wikipedia page is light on details, but it’s beyond impressive1. Jünger fought throughout World War I in the thick of it, starting as a private and ending as a company-commanding Lieutenant. He saw action at the Somme and Cambrai, the Battle of Arras then the Third Battle of Ypres and finally the Ludendorff Offensive. He was wounded 14 times, sometimes quite severely, and came out of it with the Pour le Mérite (the most prestigious Prussian officer’s decoration) alongside numerous other awards. Storm of Steel is, basically, his diary of his time in the war. After the war he was a very famous writer, and if you want to know more about him you should read the previous ACX review which covers his story more and is interesting in its own right.

So there was nothing to do but read it myself. Storm of Steel is not a very long book by page count. What I will call it is dense. It is not a diary that Jünger used to explain his theories, his ideas or his politics except as cursory asides. It is a book about WAR, hundreds of pages of it, from the mundane to the bloody to the idyllic. Storm of Steel is, in my humble opinion, the best war novel ever written.

I did not say that it is the best _anti-_war novel; I also did not say that it is a _pro-_war novel, although in some places and versions Jünger claims war can be glorious or make someone stronger in a rising-to-the-challenge sense. It is at its core an account of a war, a war more bloody and terrible than any of us could imagine, written by someone intelligent and gifted in writing who happened to see much of it and survive to tell the tale. It is by turns harrowing, riveting, insightful, terrifying, humorous, disgusting and soul-shaking. I had read All Quiet and Storm of Steel years ago, and for this review I read both again, then got a different version and translation of Storm of Steel to read it yet again; I can say that it was all worth it. There is nothing like it, and I hope that nothing like it will come ever again.
The Elephant in the Room
