theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.headline: Mimicking populists will not ease cost of living or boost productivity, Mathias Cormann warns
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.author: Kat Wong

paragraphs.text: Australia’s mainstream political parties are being warned not to adopt populist policies such as migration caps to address voters’ grievances over the cost of living.
Instead, Australia’s longest-serving finance minister Mathias Cormann is urging politicians to deliver housing, real wage growth and lower energy costs by boosting productivity.

Now the secretary general for the influential Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Cormann will deliver an address to the Centre for Independent Studies on Saturday night spruiking productivity as the only way to reliably lower the cost of living over the long term.

Though not directly named in his address, One Nation – which largely runs on an anti-immigration platform – has surged in popularity since the 2025 federal election, with its primary vote reaching 25%, according to the latest Guardian Essential Poll, rising above the Coalition’s 22%.

While populist parties may have gained popularity by speaking to real grievances over rising energy bills, homeownership and real incomes going backwards, Cormann is expected to warn Labor and the Coalition not to follow suit.

“Mainstream parties that respond to a populist surge by adopting its economics do not recover their voters. They lose twice: once to the original, which the electorate will always prefer to the copy, and once to the centre, which has nowhere else to go,” he will say in his address.
“The lesson is consistent: deliver homes, lower energy costs, real wage growth and a credible budget, and the populist tide recedes.
“Mimic the populists, and you simply confirm that they were right all along. The way to defeat populism is to solve the problems it feeds on.”
Cormann will point to “arbitrary migration caps” imposed regardless of their effect on business, hospitals, aged care, or universities.
He will acknowledge more Australians now than any time in 20 years say the migration intake is too high and may support such policies, with many attributing their concerns to housing.
But the answer is to address housing supply, infrastructure, services and the composition of the migration intake, he will say.

According to OECD research across Australia’s regions, in places where more migrants arrived, employment among Australian-born workers grew faster, not slower, with no measurable effect on their wages.
Without migration, Australia’s working-age population would decrease as the number of older people grows.

“An ageing country that chooses to shrink its working-age population while promising to spend more on health, care and defence has not developed a plan – it has put forward a contradiction,” Cormann will say.

Tariffs, which have been imposed by US president Donald Trump and proposed by One Nation, would also fail to address the cost of living and could instead raise costs for farmers, miners and builders, Cormann says.
He believes Australia can only grow its way out of the issue through productivity.
“There is no shortcut to a lower cost of living. There is no populist shortcut, through tariffs and caps and state banks,” he says.
“There is only the long way round: an economy that produces more, competes harder and grows faster than its costs… anyone offering you a quicker route is offering you a poorer country.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/15/business/tesla-ro.headline: Tesla Debuts 2026 Roadster ‘Flying’ Electric Sports Car
nytimes.com/2026/10/15/business/tesla-ro.author: Jack Ewing

paragraphs.text: Sales of electric vehicles are booming in much of the world as people look for ways to avoid gyrating fuel prices at the mercy of geopolitics.
But automakers are aiming a new fleet of electric cars at people who are not worried about prices at the pump and normally have garages full of vehicles with brawny, gas-guzzling engines.

At an event in Texas on Thursday, Tesla unveiled the Roadster, an incarnation of the company’s first car, but this time equipped with thrusters that allow it to go from zero to 60 miles per hour in less than a second and leave the ground for short distances.

“I'm not sure it will be legal in all jurisdictions,” Elon Musk, Tesla’s chief executive, joked after the car used the thrusters to hop over a row of other Tesla vehicles, executing a roll as it did so.
He did not name a price, but the Roadster will certainly cost hundreds of thousands of dollars when it goes on sale in 2028.

The debut of the Roadster came a week after Jaguar, once famous for powerful 12-cylinder engines, showed off a 1,000-horsepower battery-powered beast it calls the Type 01, which starts at $130,000. The vehicle is the first new model from the British luxury brand, a unit of Tata Motors, since it decided to focus exclusively on electric vehicles.
The Type 01 and the Roadster are bets that well-heeled aficionados will buy electric vehicles for their silent, fast acceleration and road handling, rather than gas savings.

Electric motors and batteries use energy more efficiently than internal combustion engines. They accelerate more quickly, require less maintenance and vibrate less. Heavy batteries give the cars a low center of gravity and improve handling.

When Jaguar was looking for a way to reinvent the brand, the decision to go electric was “obvious,” Rawdon Glover, the company’s managing director, said last week in an interview with The New York Times.
The Type 01 will be the first of several new models, including some that will be more affordable.
“A Jaguar should be fast, it should be comfortable, it should be luxurious, and in that context E.V. is the best mix of those elements,” Mr. Glover said.

The new high-end models from Jaguar, Tesla and others are part of an effort by Western automakers to distinguish themselves from Chinese companies that dominate the market for affordable electric cars in much of the world except the United States.

But this is a risky strategy. Buyers of ultraluxurious vehicles and sports cars are some of the most passionate fans of large combustion engines, their vibrations and their sounds. Some of these drivers have eschewed electric vehicles, saying driving them is as thrilling as using an appliance.

Several high-priced electric vehicles have faltered. Sales of Porsche’s electric Taycan, which starts at $112,000, slumped 31 percent globally in the first nine months of the year, the company said this month. Porsche has scaled back its electric vehicle plans and said this month that it would focus more on higher-priced sports cars, most of which run on gasoline.
Lucid, which makes electric sedans and sport utility vehicles that start at $70,000 but can go for as much as $250,000, reported a 7 percent decline in sales for the third quarter.

Ferrari’s electric Luce, which starts at more than $600,000, enraged many of the Italian company’s fans when it was unveiled in May, though the model has reportedly sold well. Ferrari’s archrival, Lamborghini, has postponed plans for an electric car.

Next year, Bentley, a unit of Volkswagen, plans to begin selling the Torcal, an electric S.U.V., with a starting price around $220,000. Even Rolls-Royce, a unit of BMW, sells an E.V., the $400,000 Spectre II.

Mr. Musk has acknowledged that the Roadster is unlikely to generate much revenue. The number of people with more than $200,000 to spend on a car is very small. Buyers must put down a $50,000 deposit to reserve a Roadster.

Some analysts have questioned why Tesla devoted resources to a costly project when sales of its mainstay Model Y and Model 3 are slipping. But other experts say the vehicle allows Tesla to burnish its status as a technology leader in electric vehicles.

“I think Tesla wants people to know they are able to deliver the highest-performing vehicle as an E.V. and go up against those brands, so they won’t be viewed as just a mass-market company,” said Ben Rose, president of Battle Road Research, who covers Tesla.

The two-seat Roadster offers features that other high-end sports cars don’t, assuming Tesla can produce it in significant numbers. Suction fans under the car keep it on to the road during stunts, such as when it to drove upside down on a parabolic ramp during the Thursday event.
The thrusters under the car and in the rear were developed in conjunction with SpaceX, Mr. Musk said, bolstering speculation that he plans to merge the rocket company with Tesla. He controls both.

The first generation of luxury electric vehicles was rather bland, Mr. Glover said. To avoid that, Jaguar engineers drove classic Jaguars to figure out how to give the Type 01 the same road feel and handling of those earlier models. The Type 01 will be able to go from zero to 60 in 3.1 seconds.

The silhouette of the Type 01 echoes classic Jaguars like the XKE, with an elongated hood (or “bonnet,” as the company’s British designers call it) and a voluptuous “hip” in the rear. Designers moved some battery cells from under the seats, where they are typically placed in most electric cars, to the front. That allowed a more low-slung profile.

Electric propulsion enables some features that are nearly impossible with gasoline cars. The wheels on the Jaguar, powered by three electric motors, can be tuned to roll at slightly different speeds to enhance handling.
Predictably, the online reaction among Jaguar fans was polarized. Some called the car beautiful, and others said it was “menacing and evil.”

“There is going to be a group that says it doesn’t have the voluptuousness the old ones have,” said Mark Mayuga, president of Jaguar Clubs of North America. “My answer is, ‘Let’s do something new, something fresh.’”

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.headline: Mexican judge sentences three men to 158 years in prison for murders of Australian and US surfers
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.author: Kat Wong

paragraphs.text: A Mexican ⁠judge ⁠has sentenced three men to 158 years ⁠and nine months in prison each for ⁠the murder of two Australian brothers and their American friend during a 2024 surf trip to the state of Baja California.

The defendants were declared guilty a week ago of homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft ⁠with violence, crimes committed against Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their American friend Carter Rhoad.
Rhoad and the Robinsons were shot dead in Baja California state in a suspected robbery while travelling through Mexico.
Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons.
Two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were also found guilty and have also been sentenced.
The brothers’ parents, Martin and Debra Robinson, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.
They have established a foundation in their sons’ names to carry on their legacy.
The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”.

Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.
More details soon …

techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/mark-wahlberg-.headline: Mark Wahlberg wants to take on the longevity-startup crowd with an affordable gym concept
techcrunch.com/2026/10/16/mark-wahlberg-.author: Connie Loizos

paragraphs.text: Mark Wahlberg has started companies of his own and backed plenty of others. But the gym he’s opening in December, he says, has him more excited than anything he’s done in his entire career. It also goes after a corner of the market where venture money keeps flowing: pricey, diagnostics-heavy wellness.

Speaking with us at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, the actor said the first Municipal Gym opens in December. It’s a 32,000-square-foot club outside Las Vegas with blood work, epigenetic testing, recovery gear, compression therapy, cold plunges, and a café that serves up protein muffins, among other things. He’s pitching it as the affordable alternative to the longevity clubs that charge tens of thousands of dollars a year for much the same thing.
It’s the second part of a scheme that was, in some ways, first hatched seven years ago, with a casual sportswear line.

The clothing brand Municipal launched during COVID, which Wahlberg volunteers “was not a good idea.” (Clothing was a lousy business to enter in 2020, with retailers from J.Crew to Brooks Brothers going bankrupt.)

It grew out of what he’d been seeing as a celebrity fitness spokesperson. He’d done collabs with various brands, and other companies kept approaching him to be their brand ambassador, but they all seemed to want the same thing, he said. “Everybody just kind of wanted to sell T-shirts and sneakers. And I was like, well, I want to kind of have a bigger impact on people’s lives as a whole.”

By that, he meant what people eat, what supplements they take, how they train, and how they recover. Clothing was just the start. “We figured, okay, we’ll start in the apparel space, and then we’ll build from there.” He says he only takes swings at “things that I’m very passionate about and things that are a direct extension of who I am.”

Even without a pandemic, clothing is a brutal business, as we pointed out, citing Lululemon’s repeated quality-control challenges. But Wahlberg didn’t seem fazed, talking instead about why the gym fits his vision. He thought it “always could be great for the brand” in part because it gives people a place to “actually feel and touch the clothes” before they buy. Besides, he continued, how people exercise is “another big part of people’s lives.”

Most in the space have been laser-focused on the high end. Fountain Life, the longevity company co-founded by Tony Robbins, raised $18 million last year to expand its centers for wealthy clients, and a full subscription runs $21,500 a year, according to reports. The Estate, a company co-founded by Robbins and hospitality executive Sam Nazarian, is still mapping out plans to charge $35,000 memberships to its wellness centers. Equinox is similarly taking names for a $36,000 longevity add-on that it plans to launch atop a traditional gym membership.

Wahlberg says Municipal aims for that same luxury tier but for a lot less. “We have a better price point than our competitors, and we’re going to get far more results,” he said. For $99, he said as an example, members will receive three rounds of blood work and an hour with a doctor to flag what they’re predisposed to. Supplements and hormone therapy are also “right there.”

When we asked whether the gyms double as storefronts for his other products (he owns a supplements brand), he said “kind of.” What he’s really building, he said, is a “health and wellness ecosystem” with “everything there, soup to nuts.”

He didn’t put a number on how many gyms he wants, but he called the growth strategy “aggressive,” telling us that “landlords and developers who toured the Las Vegas site have offered “AAA locations at very favorable terms, with great TI” (tenant-improvement allowances that help pay for the build-out).

Wahlberg’s record in fitness might scare off someone else. We told him we’d recently watched “Wahl Street,” his reality show, in which an early episode shows him getting deeply involved with the fitness chain F45 in 2019, and that we wanted to warn him about what was coming. “How did you know about the pandemic?” he joked, to laughs from the crowd. He bought into the company, known for its 45-minute classes, at a $450 million valuation. It went public in 2021, then was delisted from the NYSE in 2023 after its stock collapsed. Wahlberg said he learned a lot from the experience.

“I think the biggest takeaway was just making sure that I’m involved with people that share the same approach that I do.” He also said he always thought big box was the better model. F45’s classes suit people who are short on time, but he wants members to hang around Municipal for hours. Plenty of gyms run on a “join up but don’t show up” model, he said, adding: “I can’t understand that philosophy.”

The name Municipal is very intentional and clearly means a lot to Wahlberg, who grew up poor in Boston, one of nine kids, playing on public basketball courts and golf courses. “You learn a lot on the blacktop,” he said. “You learn to win, to lose, to compete, and hopefully to get back up and do it again.”
He has never hidden his rough youth. (He was sentenced to two years for assaults as a teenager and served 45 days.)

In fact, earlier in the afternoon on Thursday, surrounded by friends and business associates in a seating area backstage — this is the man who inspired the show “Entourage” after all — he said he was turned around by two people, including Father Jim Flavin, a Boston-area parish priest who has been in Wahlberg’s life since he was 13.

He wants the gyms to carry that same spirit. “It’s a place to work, but have fun and support each other and create community and really challenge people to be better versions of themselves,” he said. It’s personal, he said outright. “I’ve come from next to nothing to being in an amazing position,” Wahlberg said. “I try to constantly remind myself that I can inspire other people growing up in similar situations, especially inner-city kids and at-risk youth, that there is a way to overcome your circumstances if you’re willing to go out there and do the work.”

At 55, he added, his goals have changed; while he was once focused on looking good, “I just want to feel good when I wake up in the morning,” he said. “I want to be able to conquer all the things that I have planned for the day.”

He also said his plate is exceedingly full right now, between the gym, a film role as Pete Rose, and his daughter’s equestrian career. He’s so eager for the gym to open, he said, that visiting the construction site feels like “literally watching paint dry.” Indeed, asked if he was open to taking on new ventures, he shrugged. “I’m not out there hunting, looking for the next thing for sure.” But he wouldn’t rule it out, he added quickly. “If something amazing were to come along, obviously I wouldn’t turn it down.”
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

latimes.com/business/story/2026-10-16/as.headline: As Hollywood warms to AI, Culver City fills with AI studios
latimes.com/business/story/2026-10-16/as.author: Nilesh Christopher

paragraphs.text: The heart of Screenland is cozying up to artificial intelligence.
The open space in Culver Steps typically hosts community events and movie nights. But on Wednesday, it turned into a job fair for companies looking to hire talent for AI studios.
Companies showed off their life-like AI videos, urging emerging talent — and out-of-work creatives — to join them as they worked to reinvent traditional filmmaking.

“It’s a great breeding ground for this new filmmaking,” Dave Clark, cofounder of AI film production studio Promise, said about Culver City. “To the independent filmmakers here, it’s time to take back power.”
The event was part of LA Tech Week, a citywide event organized by venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.

Culver City is already home to big names in Hollywood and technology like Amazon MGM Studios, TikTok, Apple, and Sony Pictures Entertainment. Recently, a growing cluster of AI studios, including Promise, TrueShort, Native Foreign, and PhantomX, are expanding in the neighborhood.

Luma AI, a $4-billion Palo Alto startup that makes generative AI video software, opened a facility in Culver City last year. The company’s Dream Lab occupies a 7,000 square feet space and employs a team of 13.
“Culver City is the future of AI and filmmaking,” Caroline Ingeborn, Luma AI’s chief operating officer, said in a statement.

The companies said they are drawn by the legacy studios they hope to rival. The fact that space is available and affordable thanks to the general decline of the entertainment business in L.A. also helps.

Proponents of AI see it as an antidote to high production costs and say it allows creatives to make films that otherwise would never be made. However, many in Hollywood, its unions, and the public at large are suspicious of the surge in AI use, worried it is stealing the work of human creatives and taking people’s jobs.
The new wave of AI filmmakers have accepted the rise of AI as inevitable, and are forging ahead, increasingly in Culver City.
The city is not opposed to it.

“We’re a hub for the creative economy that is continuing to evolve,” said Adam Troy, Culver City assistant city manager, in a statement. “We look forward to what’s next in the space and what businesses see their future here in Culver City.”

TrueShort moved into Culver City last month, taking over most of a 5,000-square-foot office space near Amazon’s studio. The AI studio has raised $17 million and employs about 45 people. Around 75% of them are creatives: filmmakers, editors, sound designers and composers.

Its streaming app hosts short-form true crime audio and video shows that are fully AI-generated. On average, a 10-minute episode costs about $10,000 to make and takes about 10 days to go from idea to release.

“The next Netflix or the next Disney is going to come out of AI this time,” said Nate Tepper, cofounder of TrueShort. “And, in a way, it kind of needs to be a startup because the big incumbents are not going to move as fast. They’re going to be afraid of backlash.”
The company outgrew its Santa Monica office and is now located near Culver Theater.
“It is cool being next to the other bigger lots like Sony and Amazon, only because it’s inspiring,” Tepper said. “We want the lot. We want to become the big studio.”
Culver City-based creative studio Native Foreign makes AI commercials for brands that are more open than Hollywood about AI use. It has done ads for Virgin and Toys R Us.

It made one of the first AI-animated shorts, “Critterz,” using OpenAI’s software and planned to help make a movie based on it, but OpenAI pulled out of the project and canceled its video-making AI model.

“We don’t have the kind of opportunities that maybe some huge huge studios and companies have, so we are able to bag above our weight with these tools,” Nik Kleverov, co-founder of the company, said on a panel at LA Tech Week.

Google-backed Promise is another Culver City-adjacent AI studio that’s a proponent of hybrid productions, where human actors work with AI specialists. The company uses AI to generate backgrounds, visual effects, and synthetic humans for its slate of films, but a lot of the performances are shot on soundstages across L.A. using actors.

In late 2024, the studio acquired Curious Refuge, an online AI school that teaches traditional artists and newbies to use generative AI tools for filmmaking. Promise moved close to Culver from Venice in June.

Excitement about AI grows even as the industry puts up guardrails to contain it. The actors’ guild SAG-AFTRA has secured special protection against fully synthetic performers in the union contract signed this year.

However, some Hollywood veterans point out that the industry has fought over technology before. Alex Cancado, who spent years in visual effects and has worked on over 80 movies, now works in the AI Studios division of Amazon MGM Studios.
Pitching the crowd of creatives on Wednesday, he said the transition from practical effects to computer graphics was equally fraught.
“It was a challenge getting CG to be accepted by directors and producers,” Cancado said.
Much of the buzz around AI use for big productions started with a conference in Culver City called “AI on the Lot,” which started in 2023. It has since grown to thousands of attendees.

The organization also sponsored the job fair on Culver Steps and a networking happy hour for media AI companies in Culver City. It estimates that AI media companies with $2 billion in backing have converged on the city.

Mike Gioia, a founder of AI on the Lot, attends City Hall meetings and is trying to build momentum around the concept of a “Culver cluster” — bringing more companies and individuals working in AI to the neighborhood.
“We want to make Culver City the capital of AI media,” said Gioia.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxr5yvzv7rp0o.headline: Trump waives several Russian sanctions as new US law takes effect
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxr5yvzv7rp0o.author: Max Matza

paragraphs.text: US President Donald Trump has used his presidential authority to block numerous sanctions on Russia that were recently passed by the US Congress in an effort to punish the country for its war on Ukraine.

In an executive order on Friday night, Trump said that it is in the US "national interests" to withhold some of the sanctions. Trump signed the sanctions bill into law in September, and it was due to take effect on Sunday.

It comes days after Trump said the US would import Russian diesel in an effort to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections in November, which will decide which party controls Congress.
The plan shocked lawmakers, and has triggered a bipartisan backlash.
The US sanctions law is named for the late Republican South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, who was one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July.
The law took aim at Russian's economy, and gave Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.

Additionally, the law includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions.
On Thursday, a bipartisan group of 20 US lawmakers issued a letter calling on Trump to respect the new law, which is due to take effect on 18 October.
The lawmakers thanked Trump for signing the sanctions bill, and urged his "full and faithful implementation" of the law.

The lawmakers said it would be "decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously" and called on the Trump administration "to apply the Graham law's sanctions to their fullest extent and without delay".
Last week, Trump announced that he had held a phone call with Putin, and had agreed to purchase diesel from Moscow.
US allies criticised the move, anxious that it could help Russia in its war effort.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe8rzg6zl00o.headline: Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe8rzg6zl00o.author: Ione Wells, Joel Guinto

paragraphs.text: Brazil's government says deforestation rates in the country's Amazon and savanna regions have fallen to record lows ahead of a presidential election run-off where the rainforest's future is a key issue.

Left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, when he assumed office three years ago, pledged to end deforestation by 2030 in the Amazon. It had surged under his right-wing predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro.

On 25 October, Lula will face Bolsonaro's son Flavio in the run-off, with polls suggesting a neck-and-neck race. Flavio is expected to continue his father's policies if he wins, though he has pledged to fight organised crime in the Amazon.

Satellite data shows that in the year up to July 2026, the deforestation rate fell by 41.8% in the Amazon - the biggest drop since records began in 1988. The fall in the Cerrado, Brazil's savanna region, was 23.8%.
The Amazon rainforest - the world's largest - is a crucial buffer in the global fight against climate change and 60% of it is located in Brazil.
Why the Amazon rainforest is so important | What in the World podcast
Jair Bolsonaro promoted mining in indigenous lands in the Amazon and forest clearances soared at the same time as resources to protect the forest were cut.
During Bolsonaro's presidency from 2019 to 2022, the Amazon lost nearly 60% more in forest lands compared to the previous four years, AFP news agency reported, citing official data.

Lula reversed Jair Bolsonaro's policies and saw deforestation rates drop to a six-year low during his first year in office. Lula tightened up environmental monitoring and penalties for illegal logging.
"Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030," he said in a post on X on Friday.
Tropical rainforests like the Amazon are home to millions of species. In a healthy state they absorb vast quantities of planet-warming carbon dioxide, helping to keep the Earth cool.

But they have come under increasing pressure from decades of deliberate land clearance for agriculture and logging, as well as climate change, which scientists warn can create conditions for wildfires.
Brazil's Environment Minister, Joao Paulo Capobianco, described the decline in Amazon deforestation as "absolutely stratospheric".
It is a "historic achievement" for Brazil, said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima.
It shows that "with political will, it is possible to curb deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions", Astrini said.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3kgqjkzw29wo.headline: Three men jailed for 158 years each for murdering Australian brothers and US friend in Mexico
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3kgqjkzw29wo.author: Will Grant, Joel Guinto

paragraphs.text: A Mexican judge has sentenced three men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad to 158 years and nine months in jail each.
The Robinsons and Rhoad were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck on a secluded beach in Baja California in 2024 while they were on a surfing trip, the court heard during the trial.
The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico.
The guilty verdict was handed down last week. Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them".
The convicted killers' full names could not be given for legal reasons, and they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús.

In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo (alias "El Kekas"), was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.
The court heard that the bodies of the victims were found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads.
At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in the beach town of Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.
Ensenada has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.
The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.
Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week, when their families were able to identify them.

Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.

cbsnews.com/news/trump-waives-sanctions-.headline: Trump waives tariffs on largest buyers of Russian oil, days before Lindsey Graham-backed law was set to take effect
cbsnews.com/news/trump-waives-sanctions-.author: Joe Walsh

paragraphs.text: October 16, 2026 / 10:38 PM EDT / CBS News

President Trump prevented some new sanctions on Russia and hefty tariffs on large-scale buyers of Russian oil from taking effect late Friday, waiving portions of a bipartisan law aimed at pressuring the Russian government — as Mr. Trump seeks to ease prices by tapping Russian energy.

Tariffs of 100% on the world's five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas were set to take effect on Sunday under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act, which Mr. Trump signed late last month. But the law gives the president the authority to waive portions of the law if he certifies to Congress that halting the sanctions is "in the national interests of the United States," a provision that Mr. Trump invoked in an executive order Friday.
The president said he sent a notification to Congress.

He also waived the law's 500% tariffs on Russian goods, and halted certain other sanctions on Russia. He said the waivers will remain in place until administration officials "determine that further action is appropriate," and directed members of his administration to "monitor" countries that import Russian energy or evade sanctions.

The law — championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died before it was passed — largely took aim at the world's largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, including China, India and Turkey. The European Union has also historically purchased large quantities of natural gas from Russia, but it has cut imports significantly in recent years.
The Friday night waivers came one week after Mr. Trump eased sanctions on Russian diesel and announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import diesel to the U.S. market.

The moves mark an about-face for the United States, which has imposed tight restrictions on Russian oil and gas for years — and urged other countries to follow suit — in an effort to prevent Putin from using his country's energy wealth to finance his invasion of Ukraine.
But as oil prices remain high after spiking due to the Iran war, Mr. Trump has increasingly turned his attention to Russia and Ukraine, arguing that war in Ukraine has pushed up energy prices.

Mr. Trump pressed both countries to stop attacking each other's energy infrastructure last weekend, announcing an "energy ceasefire." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy initially said he was willing to abide by an energy ceasefire, but after Russian attacks continued, he said earlier this week that Ukraine would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries.
The U.S. president has lashed out at Zelenskyy, saying he is "not a big fan."

The decision to ease sanctions has drawn pushback in Congress. Earlier this week, a bipartisan group of senators called the diesel waivers a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine," and urged Mr. Trump to enforce the sanctions and tariffs laid out in the Graham law.

"These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict," they wrote.

cnbc.com/2026/10/17/ai-workplace-tokenma.headline: Some companies give AI to everyone. This CEO is doing the opposite
cnbc.com/2026/10/17/ai-workplace-tokenma.author: Lindsay Dodgson

paragraphs.text: At London-headquartered payments technology company Paysend, access to artificial intelligence tools has to be earned.CEO Ben Chisell told CNBC he is a “very cynical man” about the hype around the technology, though he still sees value in it.

Chisell, who previously worked at Amazon, eBay and Starling Bank, estimates that Paysend can now deliver around 25% more engineering work with the same-sized team, but argues that getting results isn’t as simple as handing everyone the latest tech.
I know it sounds very unglamorous and unsexy as an approach given the world of tokenmaxxing and AI, but I think it’s really, really importantBen Chisell Paysend

Instead, he limits AI tools to his highest-performing employees, often only after they’ve proved what they can do with them. In the wrong hands, he said, AI can magnify bad habits such as laziness and poor judgment.
His broader rule is to resist the “fear of missing out” and focus on customer problems.
“I know it sounds very unglamorous and unsexy as an approach given the world of tokenmaxxing and AI, but I think it’s really, really important,” Chisell said.
Companywide AI rollouts
The pressure to demonstrate AI’s value is growing, from the legal sector to software engineering and finance, and many companies are responding by putting the technology in as many hands as possible.

London-based Lloyds Banking Group has rolled out 40,000 Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses, with 97% of employees who have one actively using it, the bank said. Newcastle-headquartered software company Sage said its AI coding tools had saved hundreds of thousands of work hours, while London-based professional services firm Grant Thornton UK has encouraged all of its staff to use Anthropic’s Claude as part of a £500 million ($660 million) investment in AI.

These figures do not necessarily translate into gains on the bottom line, however. U.K. government research published in January found that three-quarters of businesses using AI said it had improved workforce productivity, but 77% said revenue had not changed.
Read more from CNBC Work

Like Chisell, Lokdeep Singh, CEO of British enterprise software company Unily, sees AI as a “superpower” best reserved for high-performing employees. He is also wary of companies giving it out to everyone as a way to reduce costs.

“I personally believe you should use it to expand your ambition rather than make the team smaller,” he told CNBC. “But the reality is that in many industries, again, because of the macro environment, it is being thought as: ‘OK, can I cut costs? Can I cut employees?’ The truth is probably somewhere in between.”
Measuring AI value
At Paysend, Chisell wants employees to demonstrate what a tool actually contributes. New hires get a month to experiment with AI tools and explain what they have achieved.

He recently put that policy to the test with a new search engine optimization lead who requested access to Claude. A month later, the employee told Chisell he no longer needed it. All he found it useful for, he said, was producing briefs more quickly. So instead of a general-purpose AI tool, the employee suggested building a dedicated content-brief agent, which he is now working on.

At software company CoreView, the approach has been different. London-based CEO Simon Azzopardi told CNBC the company was initially “very gung-ho” on AI, initiating a widespread rollout for its software engineers. They first used AI to investigate problems by correlating logs, events and data, as well as to produce technical documentation and onboard new engineers faster.
You feel more efficient, but you actually aren’tSimon AzzopardiCoreView

Now, he said, developers increasingly coordinate teams of AI agents handling tasks including back-end and front-end coding, quality assurance and documentation. Azzopardi said work that previously took weeks could now take days.
However, AI-generated work isn’t necessarily productive if employees use it to build things outside their expertise, Azzopardi warned. “You feel more efficient, but you actually aren’t,” he said.

Still, when onboarding a major customer in the U.K.’s National Health Service, CoreView only needed to add one engineer while continuing to deliver its other projects, he said. The company has been hiring rather than cutting staff, using the extra capacity to take on more work.
Jobs after automation

As AI takes on more of people’s existing responsibilities, the question is what happens to the employees who used to do these tasks. Chisell believes companies will thrive if they help employees move into new roles, rather than replace them once their work is automated.

Customer-service workers, for example, have spent years resolving complex issues — a skill that’s valuable across a business, he said. For Chisell, technology should never replace human responsibility.
“Having a human in the loop shouldn’t mean human CC’d,” he said. “It should mean human ownership.”

cnbc.com/2026/10/16/us-budget-deficit-20.headline: U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year
cnbc.com/2026/10/16/us-budget-deficit-20.author: Alex Harring

paragraphs.text: The U.S. finished the 2026 fiscal year with a budget deficit of nearly $2 trillion, the latest measurement to underscore the extent of the country's financial stress.
The $1.992 trillion figure was about 12% higher than the $1.775 trillion deficit in the prior fiscal year, the Treasury Department reported Friday.

It's the third-highest annual deficit in U.S. history, behind only 2020 and 2021, when the federal government was doling out trillions of dollars in financial stimulus amid the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2026 fiscal year saw record sums for both receipts and outlays, according to a Treasury Department official.

With Friday's release, the U.S. officially recorded its 25th straight fiscal year operating at a deficit. The government last recorded a surplus — meaning its revenues were larger than debts — in 2001.

Friday's report offers fresh evidence of how the U.S.'s fast-growing debt pile has dragged on the nation's overall financial health. The rising debt bill has helped exacerbate angst among bond traders, who sent the 10-year and 30-year U.S. Treasury yields to 24-year highs last week.
Where the debt comes from
Social Security amounted to the biggest slice of government spending at nearly $1.7 trillion for the full fiscal year, up modestly from the roughly $1.6 trillion spent in 2025.
Medicare was the second biggest contributor, costing almost $1.1 trillion for the fiscal year. By comparison, the government-run healthcare program required slightly under $1 trillion in fiscal 2025.
Net interest – a calculation of the Treasury's gross interest minus the interest it receives – also topped $1 trillion for the fiscal year. In the 2025 fiscal year, net interest totaled $970 billion.

Individual incomes taxes helped lessen the total deficit by bringing in more than $2.8 trillion, an increase of about 7% year over year. Corporate income tax provided $381 billion in receipts during the 2026 fiscal year. That was a decrease of about $70 billion from fiscal 2025 stemming from the tax cuts included in the One Big Beautiful Bill act passed by Congress last year.

In the 2026 fiscal year, the U.S. shelled out more than $1.3 trillion in interest on the national public debt. The total owed exceeded $40 trillion earlier this year and has more than doubled over the last decade.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC in August that the U.S. can "grow our way out of" its increasing debt pile.
"Our message to our allies, our trading partners, is that global growth is the way to take care of this mountain of debt," Bessent said in August.

President Donald Trump pitched his plans for broad and steep tariffs as a way to drive up revenue and shrink the government's debt. The White House has pushed forward with its strategy of increasing levies on trading partners despite the Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that many of those instituted by Trump were unconstitutional.

The Treasury saw a record high for gross customs duties in the 2026 fiscal year, according to a department official. But the total revenue from customs took a hit due to refunds required following the Supreme Court ruling, which sent billions of dollars back to retailers.
The Treasury also reported Friday that September's monthly deficit came in at $27 billion, a reversal from the prior year, when the department saw a surplus of $198 billion in the month.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/17/couple.headline: ‘I cannot carry all of this alone’: the couples kept apart by the war in Gaza
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/17/couple.author: Aseel Mousa

paragraphs.text: Wijdan Abu Matar, 43, was forced to leave Gaza in November 2023 with her eight children for medical treatment, while her injured husband, Hatem, remained behind.

Wijdan and her family were living in the Nuseirat refugee camp when the Gaza war began with the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. Ten days later, on 17 October that year, an Israeli strike hit the al-Muhandseen tower, near their home, injuring Wijdan and every member of her family.

“We were sitting together, just about to start lunch when the bombing happened,” Wijdan recalled. “The ceiling collapsed over our heads. Everything went dark. I couldn’t see anything. I just started screaming the names of my sons and daughters.”

Her daughter Nour, 15, suffered the most serious injuries, including a fractured skull and bleeding in the brain. Five-year-old Amna suffered severe burns to her chest. The family was initially separated after the strike.
Nour spent about 33 days in intensive care, with Wijdan by her side. Amna and Aysel, three and a half, were at a different hospital for 15 days.

On 30 November 2023, Wijdan travelled with Nour to a hospital in Egypt for treatment. For months, the family remained scattered across Egypt, receiving medical treatment and staying with other relatives.
“I felt completely helpless,” Wijdan said. “There was a fire in my heart because I was away from my husband and my family was scattered.”

Eventually, Wijdan managed to bring her children together in an apartment in Egypt. Three years on, however, she is still separated from her husband, who remains in Gaza. “I have become both the mother and the father to my children,” she said. “The responsibility is exhausting me, and I am constantly worried about my husband.”

Hatem suffered a serious leg injury that limits his mobility and is now displaced in a tent in Nuseirat. Even speaking to him is difficult because of Gaza’s unreliable internet connection. “When he manages to get online, he calls me and the children. He tells me, ‘I am counting the days until I can see you again.’ I can see the tears in his eyes,” Wijdan says.
Wijdan has no regular source of income and relies on donations. Hatem stopped receiving a salary 10 months ago and his injury prevents him from working.

In Egypt, life is difficult for Wijdan and her family. She says she cannot afford transportation to send five of her children to school. “I see my children’s future slipping away in front of me, and there is nothing I can do.”
Nour still requires medical treatment, but Wijdan often cannot afford her medication. She sometimes considers returning to Gaza to be with Hatem, but fears exposing her children to further suffering.

“I dream of getting my children the treatment they need, and I hope we can reunite with my husband as soon as possible so he can also receive treatment,” Wijdan said. “I cannot carry all of this alone. Psychologically, I am exhausted. I have lost 35 members of my family in this war.”

Since the war began with Hamas’s attack on Israel that killed 1,200 people, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the health ministry. Earlier this year an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continues to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.
Sami Abu Tabaq, a 29-year-old Palestinian photojournalist, was forced to leave the Gaza Strip in April 2024, leaving behind his family and his fiancee, Ola.
“Loneliness kills me every day,” he said. “Life away from the woman I love and my family is incredibly hard. I’m desperately waiting for the day God brings us together again.”

Sami became engaged to Ola five months before the war began. They had met by chance when he chose her family’s home as a location for a photoshoot. Before the war, they saw each other constantly. They went to the sea, had dinner at restaurants in Gaza, and spent months preparing the house where they planned to live after their wedding, which was scheduled for November 2023.

Sami and his family fled their home in Tal al-Zaatar, Jabaliya, early on in the war. Their home was badly damaged and later destroyed, along with the house Sami and Ola had been planning to move into once they got married.
When his sister decided to flee south with her children, Sami accompanied her but he could not reach Ola to say goodbye.

The separation became unbearable. Days, sometimes weeks, passed without Sami knowing whether Ola was alive. Once, he saw reports that an entire residential block near her home in Gaza City had been bombed. “I almost lost my mind. I had never felt so helpless,” he said. Unable to return north, he asked his brother to check on her. Eventually, his brother confirmed that she and her family were alive.

Sami continued working as a photojournalist from southern Gaza. Four journalists who had shared his tent were later killed, including Hamza al-Dahdouh, a son of the Al Jazeera journalist Wael al-Dahdouh.

As Israel threatened a ground invasion of Rafah in 2024, Ola began urging Sami to leave Gaza, fearing he would be killed. Sami paid a company coordinating exits at the time for both of them to cross into Egypt. But Ola could not reach southern Gaza to travel through Rafah. “She told me, ‘You go, and I’ll follow you,’” Sami said. “And here we are, still waiting, nearly two and a half years later.” They still have not managed to get married.

By his second day in Egypt, Sami was overwhelmed by guilt. “The overthinking kills me,” he said. “I felt ashamed to turn on the lights or eat proper food while my fiancee and my family were struggling to find the most basic things.”

In Egypt, his life has become dominated by loneliness and sleeplessness. “There is safety in Egypt and there are beautiful places, but I stay home. Happiness has no meaning without her. I cannot enjoy anything while she is not here,” he said.

Despite the war, Ola completed her bachelor’s degree in nursing at the Islamic University of Gaza. She has also endured enormous loss: her cousin, the journalist Ayat Khadoura, was killed, along with about 50 other members of her extended family.

From Egypt, Sami tries to create moments of happiness for her. For her latest birthday, he contacted her brother in Gaza and secretly arranged a cake, gift and flowers. “When she woke up and saw everything, she was so happy. I love her reaction when she’s happy.” The only problem was the flowers. “They were artificial,” he said. “I wasn’t happy with them, but natural flowers can’t get into Gaza because Israel does not allow them in.”
Sami says he has tried every possible way to get Ola out, without success. She is now applying for scholarships abroad, hoping education might provide a route to evacuation and, eventually, to him.

Sami recently travelled to Mecca for Umrah, where one prayer remained constantly on his mind. “I prayed, ‘God, please bring us together soon,’” he said. “But one thing I know for sure: I will wait for her for the rest of my life, until God brings us together.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8vgxwq4q5r2o.headline: Judge tosses child sex abuse charges against actor Timothy Busfield
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8vgxwq4q5r2o.author: Sareen Habeshian

paragraphs.text: A judge in the US state of New Mexico has thrown out charges against Emmy-winning actor Timothy Busfield on Friday, saying there were issues with how prosecutors presented the case.
The West Wing and Field of Dreams actor was indicted in February on four counts of criminal sexual contact of a child. Busfield has denied all allegations.
The charges stemmed from accusations brought by child actors he worked with on the Fox series The Cleaning Lady, which he directed and produced.
The judge said on Friday that the prosecutor "failed to act in a fair and impartial manner". The district attorney's office said it is evaluating options on how to move forward.
State District Judge Joseph Montano granted the defence's motion to dismiss the indictment on Friday, citing mistakes that undermined the grand jury process.

"Our office has received the order and is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed," a spokesperson for the Office of the Second Judicial District Attorney in Bernalillo County told the BBC on Friday.
The BBC has contacted a legal representative for Busfield.
The actor surrendered to state authorities in January when a warrant was issued for his arrest. A judge later ordered his release pending trial.
Busfield had originally been taken into custody in Albuquerque on two counts of criminal sexual contact with a minor and one count of child abuse.

The indictment against him, reviewed by the BBC, said that on or between 19 October 2022 and 10 September 2023, Busfield "touched or applied force to the intimate parts" of one of the unnamed boys when he was under the age of 13.

The Thirtysomething actor's defence team submitted more than 70 letters from people vouching for his character and said that he underwent and passed a polygraph test pertaining to the allegations against him.
In a warrant for Busfield's arrest, prosecutors had said the parents of the boys alleged that he groomed and sexually abused the youngsters while working on The Cleaning Lady.

Authorities claimed the boys referred to Busfield as "Uncle Tim" and alleged that he "would tickle them on the stomach and legs". Both boys told authorities they were touched inappropriately for years, his arrest affidavit stated.
Busfield's lawyers had said the actor was being accused as an act of revenge after the children were fired from the series, which angered their mother.
The BBC's Nardine Saad contributed to this report.

Demonstrators began rallying across France on Saturday against rising living and fuel costs, building on weeks of student-led protests for better school conditions that have heightened a sense of fiscal and social crisis in the country.

Some of the calls for demonstrations were made by social media accounts associated with the “yellow vest” protest movement that roiled France nearly a decade ago with its roadside demonstrations against high gas prices, among other complaints.

Officials expected protesters to march at some point on Saturday in about 80 locations and hold rallies in another 250. The protests marked a convergence between a student-focused movement that has spurred unrest in hundreds of schools, and a broader social movement that appeals to French citizens of different ages.

Hundreds of people have been injured since the student protests began last month amid escalating clashes with riot police. Thousands have been arrested, most of them minors, law enforcement officials said.

The protests erupted in a heated climate, as the government tries to pass a belt-tightening budget and as France approaches presidential elections next year. The French government has acknowledged that some of the students’ demands are legitimate but has condemned “urban violence.” It has also accused the far-left party, France Unbowed, of stoking the demonstrations, an accusation that the party has rejected.
Here’s what to know:
Why are the students demonstrating?

Students are frustrated by crumbling infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms, overloaded schedules, a shortage of teachers and staff and underfunded schools, according to the student union that is one of the movement’s main organizers.
Some are also calling for the abolition of state-run admissions platforms for higher education and universities that they call unfairly selective.

“Classrooms are not ventilated and we can barely open the windows,” Issam Makhloufi, 15, a student at Rosa Parks High School in Seine-St.-Denis, a working-class suburb of Paris that is a center of the protest movement, told The New York Times.
Unions and left-wing parties have seized on the protests as part of a wider expression of discontent as President Emmanuel Macron, who is limited to two terms, nears the end of his time in office.

“The public education system is in a catastrophic state after 10 years of Emmanuel Macron,” Sophie Vénétitay, the leader of a teachers’ union that has joined the students’ protests, said on the sidelines of a recent march. “It is lacking everything.”
Have the protests become violent?

Many of the demonstrations began peacefully but escalated as protesters fired mortar-style fireworks and attacked schools and other infrastructure, resulting in millions of dollars of damage, officials said.
At least 24 schools have been ransacked or set on fire, Édouard Geffray, the education minister, told France 2 in early October.
Rights groups, including Amnesty International, criticized the use of tear gas and stun grenades to disperse minors.

Prosecutors and a police watchdog are investigating at least 34 accusations of police misconduct during the protests. The cases include a 15-year-old boy whose left hand was ripped off, officials said, likely by the explosion of a police stun grenade; and a 14-year-old boy who was hit by a tear-gas grenade that an officer had fired at close range.
Nearly 8,000 people have been arrested, and about 900 police officers, as well as more than 350 students and staff members, have been injured, according to French officials.
France has a long history of youth protests that sometimes have turned violent, including student-led protests in 1968 that nearly toppled the government and helped transform French society.
How have the authorities responded?

The French government has condemned the violence and responded forcefully. Gérald Darmanin, France’s justice minister, said this month that he had directed prosecutors to pursue criminal charges where possible and to hold parents liable for damage.
But the government has acknowledged some of the students’ grievances. It quickly scrapped plans to increase some higher education registration fees announced as part of the 2027 budget.

It has also vowed to quickly deploy 3,000 substitute teachers to high schools hit hardest by staffing shortages and announced plans to do a better job of including students in decision-making related to schools. The education ministry set up an anonymous national online survey for high schoolers to voice their concerns — and Mr. Geffray, the education minister, said on Thursday that nearly 100,000 had done so.
But student leaders have largely dismissed the government’s proposals, calling them insufficient fixes for longstanding structural problems.
Reporting was contributed by Giulia Imbert, Catherine Porter and Ségolène Le Stradic.

nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/bend-shooting-.headline: School Shooting in Bend, Ore., Has Heroes and Pain, But Few Answers

paragraphs.text: The 16-year-old who killed three children and a teacher with a shotgun at an Oregon elementary school blasted his way through a side entrance before a teacher’s heroism and a father’s quick thinking prevented even more carnage.

As the makeshift memorial in front of Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., grew Friday, with donations of flowers, stuffed animals and candles, police and school officials began offering a clearer picture of how the attack unfolded — and how much worse it could have been.

They identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, a former special education student at Silver Rail who lived with his mother, Shauntai May Nickerson, a half-mile away from the school. He carried a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun that was registered to Ms. Nickerson, according to a law enforcement official who was granted anonymity to discuss details of the case.

The teenager approached the school on foot a little before 1 p.m. Thursday — picture day at Silver Rail — from an undeveloped and partially wooded lot on the side of the 11-year-old building, which featured modern school safety features at the front entrance.

A man in a red pickup truck was driving by and saw the teenager throw his shotgun over the fence and start to climb it, the police said. The driver “verbally confronted” the gunman, who paused to open fire at him, pelting the truck with shots. The man was not injured.
The teenager then got over the fence, shot through glass panes in a set of doors on the playground side of the building and went into a special education classroom just inside the school.

Inside, he killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher, Megan Lambert, who family members described as a young educator thrilled to be working in her hometown. He also wounded a 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher.
Another teacher in the room threw her cellphone at the shooter and then tackled him, Chief Mike Krantz of the Bend Police Department said.
Outside, Kaylub Giamanco, a father of two girls at the school, had seen the red pickup get shot while driving by on his lunch break. He swerved onto the sidewalk and ran inside.

He found the gunman wrestling with the teacher who tried to stop him and shot him several times with a .40-caliber handgun that had been legally secured in his truck, the police said. The suspect, who died, was carrying 44 more rounds of ammunition.
At a Friday afternoon news conference, Chief Krantz confirmed the I.D. of the suspect and then pledged that he would “not say his name again.”
He said the Bend community should give thanks to everyone who worked to stop the shooter.

“I don’t think we can underestimate or underappreciate that courage,” Mr. Krantz said. “When someone is willing to risk their own lives for others? A teacher who is willing to stand and fight for her children? Incredible.”

News of the heroism didn’t do much to soften the pain in Bend, a fast-growing city in central Oregon known for mountain biking, beer making and the ski slopes of nearby Mount Bachelor. The city is also familiar with gun violence: In 2022, a 20-year-old man killed two people and himself at a grocery store just three miles from Silver Rail.
“It’s awful that we know what this is like already,” said Michael LaMaita, the father of a preschooler who lives across the street from Mr. Giamanco. “It’s so weird to have it happen twice.”

Many Bend schools, miles away from Silver Rail, went into lockdown briefly on Thursday after the shooting, and thousands of people attended a candlelight vigil that night. School and recreational activities were canceled citywide Friday, so libraries and businesses that cater to families offered special programs for residents seeking community.
Carissa Honeycutt brought her 9-year-old son, Wallace, to a local park to practice skateboarding in an effort to “keep him busy, keep our minds occupied with other positive things today.”
Wallace attends Ponderosa Elementary but has still asked if it was safe to return to his own classroom. Ms. Honeycutt has reassured him, she said, even though she is also nervous.
Many parents talked of finding counseling for their children, and almost 200 people showed up at the city’s main library Friday morning seeking mental health support.
Sean Fink’s 10-year-old daughter is a fifth grader at Silver Rail and said she was in a classroom one floor above the attack.
“She told me she heard the teacher screaming for her life,” Mr. Fink said, adding that he’ll lean on the close-knit community around the school and its collection of young families to help her.

Derek Cox, another father of a Silver Rail student, said he planned to seek a therapist for his daughter in fourth grade, whose classroom was almost directly above the special education room where the shooting occurred.
“She heard it all,” he said, of his daughter. “I think she’s handling it as well as you could at that age right now, but this is going to have a long-term impact for sure.”
Brian Jolly, the grandfather of Rhoam Summer, a 5-year-old boy killed in the attack, said “the whole thing is senseless, and a shock.”

Mr. Jolly lives in Bend and said he saw his grandson often. “He was in my house a lot, and in my garden with me, and wrestling with me on the couch,” he said. “He was very bright and very mischievous and very fun-loving, and totally without fear.”

Investigators plan to keep the school roped off as a crime scene into early next week, and they still have a number of questions they are trying to answer. Among them: What motivated the shooter, and how did he gain access to the shotgun and ammunition?

The suspect’s mother, Ms. Nickerson, told a local television station in September 2020 that she was grateful her son, then 10, could return to in-person instruction following the Covid-19 school closures. He had struggled with learning from home, she said.

On Friday morning, Ms. Nickerson sat on the deck of her second-floor apartment, smoking and weeping. In a brief conversation, she said that her son “was a good boy,” and that she had seen no warning signs that he might commit violence.
“If I could have prevented this, I would have,” she said.

Investigators have searched the apartment, according to the law enforcement official who spoke anonymously. His mother was cooperative, the official said, and investigators seized the boy’s electronic devices under a search warrant.

The police said the shooter had attended Silver Rail for at least some of elementary school, though they were not able to provide details of when he was a student there or whether he knew any of the teachers he shot. He was not enrolled in the Bend-La Pine school district at the time of the shooting.

Superintendent Steve Cook said the school district will conduct its own investigation to determine how the shooter entered the building, which parents said had an updated front entryway designed to prevent just this kind of attack. Silver Rail had a school resource officer, but the officer was responsible for a half-dozen campuses and was not at Silver Rail on Thursday afternoon.
“Rest assured,” Mr. Cook said Friday, “we will take a hard look at everything we have done.”
The 7-year-old girl who was shot was in serious but stable condition after being airlifted from Bend to a children’s hospital in Portland, Ore., officials said.

She was also the beneficiary of a teacher’s bravery: Heidi Penington, a friend of the girl’s family, said another special education teacher, identified as Becky Drury by Ms. Drury’s husband, threw herself on top of the child as the gunman fired.
A bullet went through Ms. Drury’s arm and the girl’s face, Ms. Penington said. Both are expected to survive.
Jacey Fortin, Livia Albeck-Ripka, Madison Malone Kircher and Mimi Dwyer contributed reporting.

nytimes.com/2026/10/16/nyregion/cornell-.headline: Cornell Board Presents United Front Amid Crisis Over Sexual Assault Allegations

paragraphs.text: In protests, statements and open letters, some Cornell students and faculty members continued to express outrage this week at how the university had handled allegations of a gang rape at a fraternity house two years ago.
But inside the meeting halls where the university’s powerful board of trustees gathered on Thursday and Friday, there were no visible cracks in its unity.

One board member, who shared details of what was talked about behind closed doors on the condition of anonymity, said that discussions of how to plot a path forward for the university dominated the board meeting on Friday.

The trustees’ prevailing concerns, this person said, appeared to be about quickly getting clarity on how the university was addressing the fallout from the allegations made by the former undergraduate, Jane Doe, and about creating additional support for students — and not about anger or a push for a no-confidence vote in Cornell’s president, Michael I. Kotlikoff.

The multiday board meeting, and a small protest held by students on Friday outside of where board members gathered, came at the start of an unusually subdued homecoming weekend at Cornell, as the campus continues to grapple with the aftermath of a lawsuit filed by the former undergraduate against Cornell, the fraternity, her sorority and the seven men who she alleged sexually assaulted her in October 2024.

Cornell canceled its annual drone and laser show to respect a moratorium on student events that had been passed by Ithaca’s town council in the wake of the lawsuit. Student organizers canceled a concert out of respect for survivors of sexual violence. Rainy skies appeared to leave some events on Friday sparsely attended, like an opportunity to rappel down the side of the football stadium.

And there were no outward fireworks from the board, which has the power to force resignations over the Jane Doe case. Three brief meetings open to the public between Thursday and Friday — the longest of which lasted 25 minutes — provided a glimpse at an assembly determined to present itself as collegial and unfazed.

None of the university’s 64 trustees were willing to speak on the record to the media during the meetings, some using even umbrellas to block a photographer’s view of them on a rainy day. Earlier in the week, Board Chair Anne Smalling appeared with Dr. Kotlikoff during an interview with The New York Times, an implicit endorsement of his leadership.

The board has stuck with Dr. Kotlikoff though other crises — the divisive student protests over the Israel-Hamas war, the university’s $60 million deal with the Trump White House, and an embarrassing incident in which he bumped into protesters with his car. There seemed no immediate sign that they were going to change horses this time.
While the campus’s faculty senate is debating a resolution of no confidence in the administration, some alumni and donors are clearly standing behind Dr. Kotlikoff.

John S. Dyson, a trustee emeritus and a major Cornell donor, said that the trust was because he and others felt Dr. Kotlikoff — who served as provost for nearly a decade before rising to the presidency in 2024 — had taken appropriate steps in the immediate aftermath of Jane Doe’s allegations and through the recent fallout. He felt it was the district attorney who dropped the ball.

“Mike is taking these kind of steps with a lot of advice from people on the board,” he said, mentioning in particular a recent decision by Cornell to ask for help from the state police in investigating sex crimes. “If you bring in some guy from the outside, where does he start?”
“It’s a very simplistic idea that you replace him,” he added.
The board’s only public hint at the current crisis came from Harriet P. Schleifer, the university relations committee chair.

“As you know, we have had some difficult times at Cornell and the broader community,” she told fellow trustees at an open meeting on Thursday. “I do think it’s important that we are all together here today.”

A special committee of the board has already announced that it has retained Sally Yates, a former deputy attorney general, to lead a comprehensive independent review of how the university prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus. That review could take months.

In addition to asking that those answers be presented with urgency, the trustees also asked administrators for more clarity on a host of fronts related to their current response to the woman’s lawsuit, including for more concrete details on how a recently announced ban on fraternity parties would be carried out, according to the trustee who provided details.
Outside the meeting hall, protesters on Friday drew attention to what they saw as the dire failings of the board and Dr. Kotlikoff in Jane Doe’s case.

Using megaphones and displaying the faces of the president, other administrators and the accused men on stakes, about 60 protesters held a mock trial, finding the seven men accused by Jane Doe guilty of all charges. In reading out their allegations against Cornell, they focused particular ire on its decision to expel only two of the men accused.
“There’s a great deal of mistrust and disappointment in the way the university has handled this case,” said Kaori Quan, a member of the graduate student union.
The accused men have all denied wrongdoing and none have been charged with a crime.

After about an hour, the protest escalated. A row of students, banging on pots and pans, faced off against the Cornell police guarding a trustee event at Barton Hall. But they dispersed in the rain, and no arrests were made.

Among the alumni coming to campus for homecoming, the mood varied. At tented tables outside Collegetown Bagels, a popular student hangout, several recent graduates explained how the campus felt unusually sad, even somber. But inside the Statler Hotel, at a summit for alumni volunteers, there was more of a circle-the-wagons spirit.

Lee Hendelman, a volunteer who studied business at Cornell, said that he had continued to donate and be involved with Cornell even after being upset with how it had handled the divisive protests after the Oct. 7 Hamas-led attack on Israel. And he would do so again.
“The only way to make things better is to be part of the solution, not to run away,” he said. “And so I feel the same way about this, as difficult as it is.”

Susan Littman, another alumna at the summit, said she had heard a variety of opinions on the administration’s actions from fellow alumni, but that the volunteers on campus this week were supportive overall.

“A lot of us even know the administrators because we’ve been going to these events, and they’re, by and large, really good people,” she said. “They’re trying really hard to deal appropriately with a very delicate situation.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/16/nyregion/cornell-.headline: When a Social Media Mob Came for Cornell’s Jane Doe

paragraphs.text: The online campaign to unmask Jane Doe began with pleas on X.

“Please help me discover the Cornell girl,” Aidan Thompson, a 23-year-old man who regularly praises Hitler and disparages women on the social media platform, wrote in one of the first posts. “I have a good lead, but I need your help.”

Within hours of Mr. Thompson’s post, another user had offered a bounty of $5,000 for the name and photos of the woman who had sued Cornell University under the pseudonym, claiming she had been gang raped at a fraternity party. Within a day, commenters were circulating a woman’s name and images of her from a social media account.
On the fringes of the internet, bigots, attention-seekers and trolls have long seized on polarizing legal cases to air anger and disgust at women — and boost their following.
Now they were coming for Jane Doe.

A little more than a week after Mr. Thompson’s post about the former Cornell student, more than 11,000 accounts had made almost 25,000 posts that purported to name her, according to an analysis by an online analytics company, Gudea, conducted at the request of The New York Times.
The analysis showed that the posts had begun on X and spread to Bluesky, 4chan, Discord, Telegram, Rumble and other platforms, their numbers growing by the hour.

Many of the posts included hateful or antagonistic language. Some used misspelled words, such as “sIut” instead of “slut,” in apparent attempts to evade the platforms’ text filters, or added videos of far-right influencers like Nick Fuentes, the white nationalist and antisemite, to drive engagement. Often they traced similar themes: Jane Doe had actually consented to the sex; the men she accused were the true victims.

The former student’s lawsuit, filed on Sept. 16, named seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity and said they had sexually assaulted her at a party on Cornell’s campus in Ithaca, N.Y., in October 2024.
All of the men have denied wrongdoing. None have been charged with a crime.

Details that emerged after the lawsuit — including that Jane Doe had willingly drunk alcohol on the night of the party and said she had initially agreed to sex with two of the men — have touched off anger and debate over questions of consent and accountability on college campuses, but also about who deserves anonymity in sexual assault claims.

A lawyer for Jane Doe, Thomas Giuffra, said she had initially wanted to file her lawsuit using her real name but that he had advised against it. He added that the harassment she was facing had taken a severe toll.
“The backlash of trying to identify her and the threats have made this much more difficult for her,” he said. “It’s scary.”

After her lawsuit gained attention, the men she accused also became targets of online harassment. In one Instagram video, a woman posted their names and photos and invoked a female serial killer who had murdered seven men in Florida, saying she hoped they got what they deserved. The video was viewed more than 240,000 times.

Separately, after Jane Doe’s lawyers mistakenly identified the wrong man as one of her assailants, the family of that man, an active-duty Marine, received so many death threats that law enforcement officers had to be stationed outside of their home.

Still, it is common practice in the justice system for courts to permit people who say they were sexually assaulted to pursue civil claims anonymously, to ensure their safety and protect them from stigma. That anonymity, however, is not guaranteed. Judges must decide on a case-by-case basis whether an accuser’s request for privacy outweighs the public’s right to transparency, and the court has yet to rule on that question in Jane Doe’s case.

In the meantime, the online vitriol directed at the former Cornell student could have a chilling effect on other women who are weighing whether to come forward with claims of abuse, advocates for sexual assault victims said.

Catharine MacKinnon, a feminist legal scholar whose work helped establish federal Title IX protection for college students facing sexual harassment, said that an online push to identify someone who had filed an anonymous sex assault claim amounted to an attempt to silence that person.

“It’s to communicate to every woman to whom this has happened that this is what is waiting for her — public shaming, stigma and a spoiled identity,” Dr. MacKinnon said. “This is why people say it takes courage to come forward.”
The people posting about Jane Doe online saw things differently. She had tied the names of seven men to an alleged sexual assault, exposing them to rancor and embarrassment.
Now it was her turn.
An Opportunity
Mr. Thompson, the right-wing provocateur, had been involved in controversy before.

In 2024, he resigned as treasurer of the Kansas Young Republicans amid criticism over his interactions with Mr. Fuentes. (The same group was later embroiled in a scandal after leaked texts showed some of its members participating in a racist, misogynist and antisemitic group chat.)
Since then, interspersed with shirtless selfies, Mr. Thompson has posted a steady stream of racist, homophobic, antisemitic and misogynist content on X.

“Hitler? Hitler, can you can hear me? Yes, there’s a problem. We need you Hitler. You’re our only hope,” he posted on Sept. 20, above a photo shared by a Texas state senator depicting a multicultural group gathered to watch a college football game.
“Hard not to hate women as you sleep with more of them,” Mr. Thompson posted four days later.
Most of these posts received only modest engagement. But the Cornell case, he told The Times in an interview, presented an opportunity.
Fifteen hours after sending the call out for Jane Doe’s identity, he shared a woman’s name and photos, calling it “BREAKING NEWS.”
