“They have a right to face their accuser,” he wrote of the seven men, “and we have a right to publish her identity if we discover it.”
This time, his post ricocheted across X, shared by users and amplified by the platform’s own recommendation algorithm. It has since accumulated more than 19 million views.
A spokeswoman for the platform, which is owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, did not respond to requests for comment.

In the interview, Mr. Thompson described himself as a “white male” who has had “histrionic women lambasting” him “as like a Nazi” his “entire life.” He defended the men in the Cornell case, saying that their names and photos had been widely circulated, and adding that they had already been “adjudicated guilty by the public.”

“A lot of parties are incentivized to boost this,” Mr. Thompson said, comparing himself to Stephen Miller, the Trump administration official who, as an undergraduate student at Duke University, made a name for himself defending lacrosse players at the school who had been wrongly accused of rape.
“I’m not lacking in self-awareness,” Mr. Thompson added. “I understand that I’m dramatically opportunizing off of this.”
Mr. Thompson said he had used information included in Jane Doe’s legal complaint to try to ferret out her identity.

His “BREAKING NEWS” post was followed by a torrent of messages directing anger and hate at the woman he named. Some called her a whore. Others made vulgar comments about her body. Still others went further.

One series of posts on X included not only a name, but also an address, phone numbers and information about the woman’s apparent relatives. The posts, which violated X’s rules on sharing private information, racked up more than 1.4 million views, before being removed a few days later.

Savanah Hernandez, a commentator for Turning Point USA, who has more than 700,000 followers on X, shared a woman’s name and photo and wrote that the accuser “was so embarrassed about everyone at Cornell knowing she was such a huge HOE.”
She deleted the post not long after, but then wrote of the men: “I do think if they’ve been named, so should she.”
‘Don’t Blame Me’
Soon after Mr. Thompson claimed to have unmasked Jane Doe, Michael Tracey, an independent journalist with more than 350,000 followers on X, was preparing a post of his own.

Mr. Tracey, who had earlier gained notoriety for questioning the veracity of a prominent Jeffrey Epstein accuser, had recently fixated on people who file anonymous legal complaints making what he called “reputation-destroying claims” about others.
By Oct. 2, Mr. Tracey announced to his followers on X that he, too, had confirmed Jane Doe’s identity.
His post on X listed the name and photo of the woman Mr. Thompson had identified.
Separately, on Substack, Mr. Tracey posted a screenshot he said had come from a state court website that also listed the name in relation to the Jane Doe case.
Because the name had been revealed on a public docket, he said, it was fair game.
“Don’t blame me — the New York court system just posted it,” he wrote.
But it appeared Mr. Tracey had been duped.

The site he referred to had no connection to the New York State court system. Instead, registration records show, it appeared to have been created by a 33-year-old man in Michigan who described himself on social media as a “digital creator.” That man did not respond to requests for comment, and the site is now offline.
Amid cascading criticism, Mr. Tracey deleted the posts with the woman’s name later on Oct. 2, arguing that “the principle has been served.”
“I don’t believe she’s the main ‘villain’ here,” he wrote in another post on Substack, saying he was instead calling out “sleazebag lawyers.”

In an interview, Mr. Tracey defended his initial decision to connect a name to Jane Doe, claiming it was in the public interest. He said he had not relied on the third-party website, and had instead verified her identity through other means.

“There are situations where you report on the information of somebody that they or others would like to not see reported,” he said. “That is what I did, but apparently that’s doxxing or that’s some great offense against humanity if you do it with respect to a litigant in a civil action that’s had all these far-reaching reverberations.”
Before he deleted his posts, though, others on social media had already begun citing them as their own justification to attach a name to the woman.

One streamer on Rumble, a right-wing version of YouTube, soon broadcast the name to followers, using a screenshot of Mr. Tracey’s post on X. In the days that followed, right-wing influencers on YouTube amplified the name to still more viewers, decrying the amount of harassment facing the men.
On Instagram, the same name was soon automatically labeled a “popular” search subject.

A spokeswoman for Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, said such posts were prohibited by company policy and that the social network had removed some of the material. The company also removed the name from the ranked results on the platform’s search function.
YouTube, too, took down videos that claimed to identify the woman, saying they violated its harassment policies, a spokesman said.
Representatives for Rumble did not respond to a request for comment.
For his part, Mr. Tracey, having removed his posts about Jane Doe’s identity, said he and his family had themselves become victims of online mobs.

“There are maniacs on the internet,” Mr. Tracey said. “So, yes, I’m aware that anybody who’s involved in a matter of public controversy can probably expect to receive some deranged messages from people on the internet.”
Real-World Consequences
As the online furor mounted, it appeared that at least some people on the internet had indeed learned Jane Doe’s true identity.

On the evening of Oct. 6, a man called the police and said he had shot his mother and was going to kill his sister next. He gave as his location the address of Jane Doe’s family home, police records show.
An officer sped to the house, approached a truck as it was backing out of the driveway and drew his gun. He ordered the two men inside — Jane Doe’s loved ones — to the ground.
More officers arrived, and they soon determined that the call was a hoax. When they entered the house, they found the former Cornell student inside.
She told them she had been inundated with phone calls and messages threatening her and her family’s lives. She said she was panicking because her phone would not stop ringing.
As the police were interviewing her, a man called their department again, said he had an assault rifle and that he was heading toward the house with plans to kill everyone inside.
It would be a good idea, the police told Jane Doe’s family, if she just turned off her phone.
Georgia Gee, Kirsten Noyes, Kitty Bennett, Duy Nguyen and Dylan Freedman contributed research. William K. Rashbaum contributed reporting.

nytimes.com/2026/10/16/technology/meta-m.headline: Meta Withdraws $25 Million from Its Midterms Push

paragraphs.text: Meta’s effort to shape the midterm elections has quietly become $25 million smaller.

About a year ago, the Silicon Valley company announced an ambitious effort to elect state politicians who are friendly to the artificial intelligence industry, eventually outlining a $65 million budget for the operation. The subtext, heard loud and clear in states debating A.I. legislation, like California, Illinois and Texas: Meta’s political team was watching, and to be feared.

But this summer, with no announcement, Meta received $25 million of that cash back from political groups it had funded, according to filings made public this week. That made the company’s campaign budget about 40 percent smaller than at the outset.

In the world of campaign finance, where outside groups often carry cash from cycle to cycle, returns of tens of millions of dollars are rare outside of scandals. Meta, one of the world’s largest and wealthiest companies, also does not need $25 million to add back to its cash reserves, which recently stood at more than $90 billion.
A company spokesman said in a statement that the refunds were part of “adjustments.” He declined to answer additional questions about why they had taken place.

“More than 90 percent of the candidates we supported won their primaries, and we are now focused on supporting candidates in the general election,” the spokesman said. “We will continue to make adjustments as we evaluate the best ways to support candidates we hope will be great partners in supporting America’s technology leadership.”

The refunds came primarily from the American Technology Excellence Project, a political committee that Meta funded with $45 million in September 2025. In July and August, the group issued two returns to Meta for a total of $22 million, according to the new filings with the Internal Revenue Service on Thursday.

Separately, Meta has a California-specific advocacy group, Mobilizing Economic Transformation Across (Meta) California, which the company backed with $20 million in August 2025. The group refunded $3 million almost exactly a year later, according to a state filing.

Much has changed in the world of tech regulation since Meta announced these efforts. The company is navigating a public that has become skeptical of A.I., and some A.I. industry donors have been reassessing their political efforts. Despite Meta’s smaller budget for politics, its statement suggested that it remained committed to engaging in campaigns and elections.

Meta’s money was spent primarily in Democratic and Republican primaries. The American Technology Excellence Project transferred about $3.2 million to its Democratic affiliate and about $4.1 million to its Republican affiliate. The Republican group was particularly active in Texas and the Democratic group in Illinois.

The tech giant, which owns Facebook and Instagram, scored some victories in legislative races in Texas and Illinois, along with engagements in Florida, South Dakota, Georgia, Alabama and Ohio. A notable loss came in Texas’ comptroller race, where Meta’s Republican group spent about a $500,000 for Kelly Hancock, who was defeated.

Meta’s entity in California, its home state, spent more than $9 million through September in state politics, not counting the refund to the parent company. About $1.2 million went to support Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor.

nytimes.com/2026/10/16/science/leap-seco.headline: The Leap Second Has Been Canceled

paragraphs.text: Every few years since 1972, computers, financial institutions, communications networks and other systems have had to reset their clocks by a single second.
On Thursday, the international authority on timekeeping voted to abolish this contentious quirk of global synchronization. The change will take effect in 2027.

In a meeting of officials from the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, or B.I.P.M., in France, the group axed the leap second, which had been established to align our clocks with Earth’s rotation.

The practice was similar to that of the leap year, when an extra day is added to our calendars to keep us in sync with Earth’s orbit around the sun. Leap years are predictable, happening every four years. But leap seconds account for seemingly random irregularities in how fast Earth rotates, which has been causing trouble for timekeepers, including the looming possibility of needing a “negative leap second” because Earth’s spin is getting faster.

“This decision has become particularly timely because recent changes in the Earth’s rotation have raised the possibility of a first-ever negative leap second, which has never been experienced and that could create additional risks for critical infrastructures,” Noël Dimarcq, president of the B.I.P.M.’s committee for time and frequency, said in a statement.

In lieu of the added second, humankind will wait until an entire hour is needed to bring us back into synchronization with the planet’s spin. This new practice is “just easier” to keep track of, said Patrizia Tavella, director of the bureau’s time department.
It’s unclear when this extra hour may be needed, but it might not happen for centuries.

“It’s really just taking the problem well, well into the future,” said Andrew Novick, an electrical engineer and manager of the time and frequency division at the National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST, in Maryland. “It could be thousands of years before this leap hour happens.”

For much of history, “the Earth was the best available clock,” Duncan Agnew, a geophysicist at Scripps Institution of Oceanography in California, explained during the meeting. Keeping time mostly involved ways of dividing how long it takes Earth to complete one rotation on its axis: Earth rotates at about 1,000 miles per hour, on average, so a day equals 86,400 seconds.

By the mid-20th century, humans needed more timekeeping precision to support the advent of computers, international communications systems and space exploration. Enter atomic clocks, which measure time by tracking the tiny changes atoms undergo at regular intervals. These ultraprecise clocks ushered in a global way of keeping time: Coordinated Universal Time, or U.T.C., which was adopted in 1963.
“You only know how good your clock is when you get a better clock,” Mr. Novick said.

Sometimes gravitational interactions with other celestial bodies or the movements of air, water and rock on our dynamic planet can affect its rotation speed. Once clocks became more precise, these subtle shifts in Earth’s rotation became more noticeable, which is why we adopted the leap second. In recent decades, though, the added second posed two main problems for our digital systems.

For starters, it can be a hassle to change the time by a single second and could even cause time-linked systems to temporarily shut down. Some tech giants such as Google adopted a “leap smear” instead, temporarily slowing down their clocks rather than adding the leap.

What’s more, Earth’s rotation isn’t always lagging behind. The same forces that slow it down can also work in reverse, meaning that one day we might have a negative leap second. And while most of the digital systems that rely on U.T.C. are prepared to jump ahead, far fewer have the code built in to handle a move backward in time.

Since the 2000s, Earth’s rotation has been speeding up, driven by a combination of changes to Earth’s core and surface phenomena like the melting polar ice caps. This makes the need for a negative leap second more likely, and, in part, drove timekeepers to their decision to end the leap second.
The vote was not unanimous. Delegates from Russia, whose satellites often have a built-in system for handling leap seconds, voted against the measure, and those from Belarus abstained.

The differential between our clocks and Earth’s rotation is currently hovering around zero, meaning the next leap second could have easily been a negative one, Mr. Novick said. Still, Mr. Novick and other scientists said they will miss this little idiosyncrasy in the way we keep time.
“It’s the one time you could almost assure that NIST would be on the news,” Mr. Novick said, “because it gets people thinking about the Earth’s rotation, and about time.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/math-ai-terenc.headline: Terry Tao Is on the Front Lines of the Debate Over AI and the Future of Math

paragraphs.text: Terence Tao is typically described as one of the world’s greatest living mathematicians, but right now he is doing very little math.

“I’m on a war footing,” he said while grabbing coffee during a two-day math workshop at the University of California, Los Angeles, that was rife with talk about the existential crisis that artificial intelligence has created in his field.
Days earlier OpenAI had announced that it had solved the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven “Millennium Prize problems” that had stymied the greatest minds in math for nearly a century.

“There are no rules any more,” Dr. Tao, 51, said in an interview before the workshop in his modest office on the U.C.L.A. campus, his home since 1996, when he arrived after completing his doctorate at Princeton at the age of 20. “I’m just numb to what would have been jaw-dropping events for me a year ago. At some point, maybe I’ll get hit by a whole wave of PTSD.”

Instead he was hit by a bigger bomb on Oct. 6, when OpenAI released more than 350 findings in nearly every subfield of the profession, including algebra, number theory, theoretical computer science, mathematical logic and topology. Stunned mathematicians, some who were close to solving problems they had worked on for years, found themselves beaten in an instant by A.I.

Dr. Tao, who has been a tenured professor since the age of 24, said senior academics like himself are not as threatened by A.I. as those starting out. But the math world is looking to him for answers. He has accepted that his celebrated status has made him an unofficial spokesman for the field, a job that for now is consuming most of his time.

Until recently his job was as a bridge between the slow-moving world of higher math and the scorching speed of A.I. Dr. Tao, who uses A.I. as an assistant to run calculations, write code, search vast troves of literature and brainstorm ideas, has been experimenting with OpenAI’s models since 2023. He was an enthusiast for a “best of both worlds” future.
OpenAI’s releases have now left him feeling used. “As recently as a year ago, I had a pretty good relationship with many employees at OpenAI,” he said in a recent phone conversation.

“A lot of people I interacted with shared a very common vision of how A.I. should be used — you know, to empower scientists.” But the rush to publish new findings, he said, shows their true purpose. They “used math for what they needed, which was to evaluate their models,” he said. “At this point, I don’t see a way to constructively engage.”

His anger was clear in a post on the widely read math blog Proofs and Prompts after OpenAI’s Oct. 6 release. “I am horrified by the many person-years” of research, particularly by young mathematicians, “being casually disrupted or destroyed,” he wrote.

“Much as one cannot unhear a movie spoiler or a crossword clue, one cannot explore a problem as profitably and richly once one is aware of an existing solution.” He mourned, he added, “the path not taken, and the opportunities lost in the frantic race to develop this technology.”
As Much Art as Science

At the heart of the crisis in the profession is a menacing question. If solving hard problems is a mission of math, what happens when machines can do it faster? So much of higher math — hiring, promotions, graduate training and acclaim — is based on the difficulty, quality and the impact of papers (the written documents explaining proofs) that a mathematician produces.

The consensus is that A.I.-assisted problem solving is the inevitable future, but no one knows exactly what that new world will look like. “Deep uncertainty will persist in these next years,” a draft report by a group of mathematicians meeting at Harvard on Ph.D. education concluded last month.

A.I. does offer “exciting new possibilities” the report reassured. But implicit in its pages was the sense of loss among humans drawn to math for the intellectual adventure of problem solving — often deeply frustrating, sometimes thrilling and euphoric if a personal breakthrough leads to an advance in the field.

“You’ve had epiphanies, right?” Ravi Vakil, a prominent Stanford mathematician and the president of the American Mathematical Society, asked in an interview. “Suddenly everything in the room becomes clear.”

Theoretical, or “pure” math — the math of Dr. Tao — is loved as much for its art as its science. Its primary goal is to add to the understanding of the vastness of math itself. Unlike applied mathematicians, who have generally embraced the power of A.I. to help them solve practical problems in engineering, finance, weather forecasting and other sciences, pure mathematicians study shapes, structures, numbers and abstract concepts.

Still, pure math ultimately has led to, among many other advances, the creation of the internet, microchips, GPS, cybersecurity, encryption, CT scans and other medical procedures. In 2006 Dr. Tao and three partners created the mathematical theory of compressed sensing, which sped up the scan times of MRIs. Today MRIs can produce real-time images of the beating heart, and many children can be scanned without sedation.
‘Screaming for Help’

He may say he is battle ready, but Dr. Tao hardly projects as a warrior. In his office, he spoke softly in a lilting Australian accent, was self-deprecating, occasionally funny, upset about the relationship he once had with OpenAI and far from the stereotype of a tortured, brooding math genius. He is known for his sunniness in the rarefied realm of pure math, and students remark on his modesty.

He was dressed in faded blue jeans and a loose polo shirt that seemed to hang absent-mindedly from his slight frame. A blackboard that ran nearly the length of the room was covered with computations by one of his three current Ph.D. students, Ben Goldman. Nearby was the bike Dr. Tao had ridden to work, with his lunch from home in a plastic bag strapped onto the rack over the back wheel.
“It’s leftovers from three days ago,” he said.

He spends much of his time in what he calls “community organizing” — pulling together groups of mathematicians, strategizing, responding to the media, delivering lectures on A.I., counseling. “It’s someone screaming for help,” he said. “I can’t help them because I have no bandwidth, but I can identify somebody else they can talk to.”

His own 20-year-old blog has become math’s front page, filled increasingly with guest posts from others but also notes from the graduate class he is teaching and breaking math news. The day he posted a statement he signed along with 24 other winners of the Fields Medal, math’s version of the Nobel Prize, that called OpenAI’s math “detrimental” to the field, his blog shot to 100,000 views.
“My wife says I’m The Huffington Post,” he said.

His lightheartedness faded as he talked about appearing in a promotional video for OpenAI earlier this year. Its roots were in the Trump administration’s suspension last year of $600 million in research grants to U.C.L.A. that threatened the existence of the university’s Institute of Pure and Applied Mathematics, where Dr. Tao is director of special projects.

Dr. Tao reached out to OpenAI as part of an emergency fund-raising drive, and the lab agreed to sponsor a workshop at the institute for what Dr. Tao said was $60,000 to $70,000. It was held in March, when OpenAI conducted an hourlong video interview with him in which he talked about the benefits and risks of A.I.

He expected the entire video to be posted. OpenAI instead cut it to one minute: “I think it’s ready for prime time,” Dr. Tao says of A.I. as he writes rapidly on a blackboard and a soundtrack of joyful music seems to urge him on.
He gave OpenAI permission to use the ad, he acknowledged in his blog. But in retrospect, he wrote, he should have “pushed back harder.”

An OpenAI spokesman, Laurance Fauconnet, said in a statement that “we value our engagement with Terence and the wider mathematics community.” The lab, he said, is “working with the community to turn progress in A.I. into deeper human understanding and new discoveries, and we will continue to act on its feedback.”
(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Dr. Tao was not impressed with the writing in OpenAI’s proof of the Navier-Stokes problem. “It is technically readable,” he said. “But no expert I’ve talked to has actually understood the whole argument.” He said the writing is better in the latest release, though he called it a “mixed bag.” Some papers appropriately cited his work, he said, and seemed to have advanced it in a way he thought was plausible. Still, “there is no author that I can have a real conversation with about the results.”
Dr. Tao was aware last month that OpenAI was working on the Oct. 6 release and at the time called the coming results “toxic waste.” Now he calls them “maybe treated waste.”
A 760 on the Math SAT at Age 8

The first day of the math workshop — the topic was the field of partial differential equations “in the age of A.I.” — got underway in a small auditorium at 9 a.m. The institute’s director, Dimitri Shlyakhtenko, welcomed several dozen academics, including a batch from Harvard, Princeton, the University of Tokyo and Sandia National Laboratories, the home of the nation’s nuclear stockpile testing. The room was expectant, waiting to hear from Dr. Tao on what he thought A.I. might have in store for them.
“Our first speaker does not require introduction,” Dr. Shlyakhtenko said.

Indeed he did not. As Dr. Tao popped up from his seat to take his place at the lectern, it is safe to say that most in the room already knew him as a legend. Born to Chinese immigrant parents in Australia, he taught himself to read at the age of 2, scored 760 on the math portion of the SAT at 8 and won his Fields Medal at 31.

The medal was for his advances in harmonic analysis — the study of breaking down complex waves into simpler ones — but also for work in partial differential equations and the fields of additive number theory and combinatorics. The Fields Medal Committee cited Dr. Tao for his most famous work, with the mathematician Ben Green, on what is known as the Green-Tao theorem, which proved that there are arbitrarily long, evenly spaced sequences of prime numbers — a monumental achievement in the field.

Up at the lectern at U.C.L.A., Dr. Tao began with an apology. His plan, he said, had been to spend the summer developing a “living spreadsheet,” or network, built and maintained by A.I., of academic results about explicit analytic number theory, an unforgiving subfield of math. “But I’ve been a bit distracted in the last few weeks, and I have not actually devoted as much time to this project as I wanted to,” he said.
He finished with another apology. The network was not complete. He had budgeted all of September to get it done, but “some things happened in the meantime.” The crowd chuckled knowingly.
The most intense discussion on A.I. came after lunch. Sometimes it seemed like a group-therapy session.

“As we soul-search about what the role of the human mathematician is, shouldn’t we go back to where mathematics came from?” said Tatiana Toro, the director of the Simons Laufer Mathematical Sciences Institute at the University of California, Berkeley.

Andrea Bertozzi, a U.C.L.A. professor of math and mechanical and aerospace engineering, said that one thing she liked about college math was that “you sat down with your pencil” and coffee and paper, “and you could prove things.” She brought up the cost of solving Navier-Stokes, which OpenAI said took a swarm of 10,000 agents 88 hours to produce a 165-page proof. Was it “something like $6 million?” she asked.
“More like 22,” someone in the audience said.
This led to a round of comments that the cost of A.I. is undemocratic, particularly to mathematicians in developing nations. “Half the world is going to fall behind,” Dr. Toro said.

Dr. Tao, who had the last word, agreed that the field needed to do some soul-searching. But, he mused, given how fast things were moving, maybe he was doing “soul-searching at gunpoint.” At that point, the room laughed.
‘The Elephant in the Room’

Mr. Goldman, like Dr. Tao’s two other Ph.D. students, is facing an ambiguous future. He is 25, a graduate of the University of Chicago and now in his fourth year of a five-year program. He doesn’t know what he wants to do after he gets his doctorate, but he said he has long been drawn to the creativity of math research.

“I’m not saying I was necessarily trying to prove the thing that’s going to be in every textbook 30 years from now,” he said. But he would be happy with a proof “that feels like the argument is me somehow, that has my DNA in it and that people will at least for that one result want to know the way I thought about something.”

After the latest OpenAI release, Mr. Goldman said he was plowing ahead with the research for his dissertation, “even if it can be made obsolete by some messy manuscript released by these companies in the next coming months.” He was upset, he said, “to see a field that I love being sort of strip mined.”

Siddharth Mulherkar, a fifth-year Ph.D. student of Dr. Tao, is applying for postdoctoral research jobs for next fall, the next step on the long pursuit of a tenured professorship. Dr. Tao has given him, like the others, the OK to use A.I. in his work. And yet when he discloses on a job application that A.I. helped with the proof he submitted, how will he himself be evaluated?

“Obviously I don’t want to just be pushing buttons and getting answers to problems,” said Mr. Mulherkar, 27, who was born in California but moved to India with his parents and lived there until he arrived at U.C.L.A.

OpenAI’s latest release, he said, has made him even more uncertain. “I’ve spent quite some time training to become a research mathematician in the traditional sense,” he said. He knows he’ll need new skills, but what they are and “what this career is going to look like and what it will value is completely unclear to me.”

Arian Nadjimzadah, 26, another fifth year Ph.D. student of Dr. Tao, said he was shocked by OpenAI’s latest release claiming to have solved the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture and other problems related to his own work. “I had to take a couple days from working on math,” he said.

He was particularly frustrated, he said, with the writing in OpenAI’s proof explaining the conjecture. “The result is extremely difficult to read and uses very unfamiliar jargon to us in the field,” he said. “That’s the nice thing when a person posts a result. They’re accountable. They give talks about it, and they help people understand.”

Mr. Nadjimzadah is studying this academic quarter at the Institut Mittag-Leffler outside of Stockholm and is looking for a postdoctoral job. At the advice of Dr. Tao, he is including in his job applications how OpenAI’s Oct. 6 release connects to his current work and future plans.
“He just said it’s important to address the elephant in the room,” Mr. Nadjimzadah said.
Therapy Sessions

To Dr. Tao, the next few years will require the reinvention of math, or at least of math education. The Harvard report recommended, essentially, that math become more human-centric: Doctorate degrees should not be rewarded primarily on the text of a dissertation, as they are now, but more on a rigorous in-person defense. Students should regularly show professors they can speak fluently about their work.

Dr. Tao went further last week when he presented what he sees as the future of math in a lecture at the California Institute of Technology. Despite OpenAI’s releases, he said, most problems at the frontiers of math are unsolved, math remains infinite and the difficulty of problems is therefore boundless. Since A.I. has given mathematicians the ability to collect data on such a vast scale, they will increasingly work in large groups collaborating on once-unimagined projects.

Dr. Tao, who sees each of his three students once a week, said every meeting is “increasingly a therapy session more than technical guidance.” His answer to them is that “if you focus on only the things you could do before, it looks bleak.”

So he has offered hope with advice that amounts to acceptance born of necessity rather than fighting a war. Problem solving is not a destination but a journey, and lessons learned along the way are often more important than the answer itself. Rather than solving a single problem on their own, they can use A.I. to solve 10 problems and find new patterns and more questions to ask.
“They will have to use their imagination,” he said. “This is a time for creativity, and I do hope students rise to the challenge. They didn’t ask for it. But I think many of them will surprise us.”

livescience.com/technology/communication.headline: New 4,300-mile-long internet cable will shuttle data along the ocean floor at 1 million gigabits per second
livescience.com/technology/communication.author: Owen Hughes

paragraphs.text: A new 4,300-mile (7,000-kilometer) undersea fiber cable will shuttle data between the U.S. and France at breakneck speeds of up to 1 million gigabits per second (Gbps) — enough to move around 125 terabytes of data every second, or roughly 25,000 HD movies, each 5 gigabytes large. The cable, called Petal, will be funded and operated by Facebook and Instagram parent company Meta.

When it comes online in 2029, the ocean-spanning cable will be the first to deliver petabit capacity — double the capacity of existing subsea cables of this length — across transoceanic distances, Meta representatives said in a statement. That's enough to allow 75% of the world's population to stream music at once.

Petal will also be the first commercial subsea cable system to use multi-core fiber technology, according to the statement. Whereas conventional fiber strands typically contain a single core, each of Petal's fiber strands will contain two cores that carry optical signals in opposite directions, allowing a single strand to provide the capacity that would conventionally require a pair of single-core fibers.

Each fiber strand is roughly as thick as a human hair, measuring just 125 micrometers in diameter. Petal will contain 24 pairs of dual-core fibers, giving it 96 individual fiber cores in total and enabling it to carry as much data as 48 conventional fiber pairs, Meta engineers said.
Japanese technology company NEC will be responsible for the overall design and construction of Petal, while Sumitomo Electric will provide the fiber itself.

"Achieving petabit-per-second capacity across a transoceanic submarine system represents a major technological milestone in the history of global telecommunications," Eduardo Mateo, chief strategy officer of the Submarine Networks Division at NEC, said in the statement.
Bedrock of the internet

Subsea cables are among the most critical layers of internet infrastructure, carrying around 99% of the world's internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, the United Nations agency for digital technologies.

Installing thousands of miles of fragile glass cable on the ocean floor is an engineering feat in itself. Equally challenging is ensuring that these cables can carry the tiny pulses of infrared light that transport fiber-optic data across such huge distances without impacting performance.
This is typically achieved through repeaters — amplifiers installed at regular intervals along the cable that use lasers to boost the optical signals.
A 4,300-mile subsea cable typically needs about 100 of these repeaters to amplify the signals along its length, Meta representatives said.
Related stories

Petal will incorporate something called "fan-in/fan-out" technology. As each two-core fiber strand enters a repeater, an optical interface routes the signal from each core into a separate single-core fiber strand so that each can be amplified independently. The amplified signals are then routed back into the two cores of the dual-core fiber before continuing along the cable.

Combined with its dual-core fiber, this feat of signal engineering will enable Petal to double its data-carrying capacity without requiring a proportional increase in power, Meta representatives said.

Petal is one of many subsea cable investments by Meta in recent years, including Marea in 2018, Amitie in 2023 and Anjana in 2025. Marea, the company's first transatlantic fiber instalment, supports 192 Tbps, meaning Petal will offer more than five times that capacity.

npr.org/2026/10/17/g-s1-147874/hospital-.headline: Sidewalk sleepers: They have nowhere else to stay while a loved one is in the hospital
npr.org/2026/10/17/g-s1-147874/hospital-.author: Sajad Hameed

paragraphs.text: DELHI, India — At 2 a.m. on the sidewalk outside one of Delhi's best-known public hospitals, Shabana Kumar gently wakes her husband. They sleep in shifts of about an hour at a time because their 6-year-old son is a patient in the oncology ward, being treated for leukemia, a cancer of the blood and bone marrow. They are afraid that if they are both asleep, an urgent call could come about their son's condition and they might miss it.
The Kumar family lives more than 600 miles from Delhi in the state of Bihar. Arun, 32, works as a farmer. Shabana, 30, is a homemaker caring for their only son.

They made the trip to Delhi because they could not afford the cost of their child's cancer treatment in Bihar. The All India Institute of Medical Sciences, or AIIMS, subsidizes expenses for families in need.

But for many families, there is one challenge they must bear on their own — finding a place to live in Delhi during the days, weeks, even months of treatment. Like the Kumars, families who can't afford to rent lodging often set up a temporary dwelling on the sidewalk.

On a night in August, dozens of families were sleeping on blankets or sheets spread directly on the sidewalk. Some tie mosquito nets to railings to protect themselves and their kids. They keep their bags and other belongings beside them as they sleep.

During the day, families move between the sidewalk and the hospital for appointments, tests, medicines and consultations. They carry their most important belongings with them while leaving less valuable items at their sleeping spot. One family member often stays behind to keep an eye on their things.

Like the family from Bihar, people who've accompanied a patient may sleep outside while the patient is housed in the hospital. In other cases, the person receiving care is seen during the day but does not have a bed, so they sleep on the sidewalk as well.

At night, the sidewalk dwellers return to the pavement, where a small ecosystem has grown around the families. Women cook rice over makeshift brick stoves. Volunteers distribute food. Nearby shops sell medicines and other necessities. Nearby tea stalls not only serve beverages but let families charge their phones.
Once strangers, they exchange information about doctors, tests and where to find a free meal or, when none is available, an affordable one they can pay for.
Vishnu Singh, 38, runs a tea stall outside AIIMS.
"I see poor people sleeping here every day, so many that I cannot even count them," he said.

At AIIMS and Safdarjung Hospital, which is associated with Vardhman Mahavir Medical College, we interviewed families who had traveled from across India, often hundreds of miles from home, to seek medical care. The two hospitals stand opposite each other, treating patients with illnesses ranging from cancer and heart conditions to intestinal disorders and other serious ailments.

Some families had been there for a week, others for a month or longer. For many, returning home between hospital visits was impractical, so patients and the relatives accompanying them stayed in Delhi for the duration of their care.
The families we spoke with described their experiences spending days or weeks in Delhi while navigating appointments, tests, consultations and treatment.
When treatment means living outside

It is a startling contrast — a hospital that provides critical care, that, according to its annual report, gives subsidies to thousands of poor families for treatment — and that is ringed by folks who traveled great distances to find care for a loved one and who cannot afford a place to stay.
NPR reached out to the hospital by email to ask about the issue of accommodations and the community of sidewalk dwellers. The hospital did not respond.

AIIMS' website notes that its Medical Social Service Unit provides financial assistance for medical treatment and travel costs for some patients coming from outside Delhi. It also states that the unit helps arrange accommodation for out-of-town patients and their family members and caregivers at dharamshalas, traditional charitable lodging facilities affiliated with AIIMS, or other low-cost accommodation.

The website does not say whether AIIMS pays for those accommodations or provides financial assistance specifically for the lodging costs. Shalini Yadav is one of the patients who sleeps on the sidewalk with her parents.

Yadav is a second-year college student from Piprat village in Tikamgarh district, Madhya Pradesh, in central India. She had been preparing for the state civil service examination. Her plan was to become a government officer.

Now she is spending her days reading Gunahon Ka Devta (The God of Sins), a famous 1949 Hindi tragic romance novel written by Dharamvir Bharati, on the pavement outside AIIMS, waiting to find out when her treatment will begin and when she can go home.

Yadav says she has been dealing with an intestinal illness for five or six years and has already undergone two operations. Her family had sought treatment elsewhere before relatives and neighbors advised them to travel to Delhi in search of better treatment at AIIMS — a trip of roughly 370 miles. "We thought AIIMS was the best hospital in India," she said. The cost of staying in Delhi was also a burden: Her family could not afford a room and had already spent thousands of rupees on travel and other expenses.
When we interviewed her on Aug. 3, she had been there for about three weeks with her parents, Surendra Singh Yadav, 47, a farmer, and Kalpana Yadav, 45.
"We thought the facilities would be good, the doctors would be good, and everything would happen quickly. We never imagined that we would have to sleep on the road," she said.
For her, the pavement is not just uncomfortable, it is also frightening. During the day, she says, she can manage. At night, she worries about the people around her.
"There are all kinds of people here," she says. "Some are good, but some drink or use drugs. There is shouting and fighting. As a girl, I feel very uncomfortable here at night."
But the family has little choice. They cannot afford a room in Delhi, she says. "We have decided that we have to sleep on the road because there is no other option."

During the day, Yadav goes into the hospital for appointments, tests and checkups, then returns to the pavement while waiting for the next step in her treatment. Everything is on hold — her college education, her hopes of qualifying for a government job, her father's farming work.
"It feels like we are being forced to live like this," she says.
"I just pray that I can meet a doctor"

Lakhi Bai, 62, from Ramnagar in Maihar district, Madhya Pradesh, in central India, about 500 miles away, came to Delhi seeking treatment for diabetes and a condition that she says causes numbness and a loss of sensation in parts of her body.

She says she could sometimes sustain an injury without feeling pain. When we met her, she had been sleeping outside Safdarjung Hospital for about 20 days. During that time, she says, she had been going to different doctors and departments for consultations and tests but had not yet received a treatment plan.
Bai is a farmer and describes herself as a homemaker. She said she has three sons but is no longer in contact with them. She came to Delhi alone.
"I cannot afford to bring someone with me," she says. "If I bring someone, I have to pay for their food and accommodation, too."
It's been a difficult period. "Sometimes I don't even get food," she says. "I sleep with an empty stomach."
Sleeping outside is also stressful. The heat is hard to endure, she said, as is rainwater.
"When it rains, water comes here," she said. "There is nowhere to go."
AIIMS did not respond to requests for comment about her account or the experiences described by other families interviewed for this story.
Bai did not know how much longer she would have to remain in Delhi. "I have no place to stay," she says. "I just pray that I can get the treatment I need and something can be done."
A month outside awaiting a child's heart treatment
In August, Balraam Singh, 35, a brick-kiln worker from Meerut, Uttar Pradesh, had been sleeping outside Safdarjung Hospital for about a month with his wife and their 7-year-old son, Munna Singh.
Munna has a heart condition that his father describes as a "hole in the heart."
They had come from about 50 miles away seeking further medical evaluation and treatment at Safdarjung Hospital.
"We came with a lot of hope that we would find a doctor and my son would be treated," he says. "But now it feels like we may have to go back without knowing what will happen next.
For Singh, who can earn $5 to $7 a day at the kiln where he works, staying in Delhi means not only a loss of income but the need to spend money on food and other daily needs.
Six months of saving for another hospital visit

Gulshan Bano, 38, had come to Delhi from Bihar with her 60-year-old mother, Asma Khatoon, and her 6-year-old daughter, Fiza. They had been sleeping outside Safdarjung Hospital for about a week when we met them in August.

Bano says her mother has had a heart condition for several years and was receiving treatment in Bihar. Her mother had undergone checkups and tests there, but the family felt she needed further evaluation and care.
Relatives also advised them to seek treatment in Delhi, and the family decided to travel for further consultations and tests.
Bano said doctors have told them that her mother has a heart problem and have prescribed medication rather than recommending surgery.
The family returns to Delhi for checkups about every six months. To pay for the trips, Bano works in domestic jobs in Bihar.
"I work for months and save whatever I can, and then I come here," she says. "Whatever little money remains has to be used here."
Bano said her husband does not contribute to her mother's medical expenses and she has little choice but to keep making the journey to Delhi.

A visit can last about a month, Bano said, as the family waits for scheduled consultations, tests and follow-up care. Because they cannot afford other accommodation, they sleep outside the hospital between appointments and tests rather than return home and make another journey to Delhi.
"Where should I go?" she said. "I have to come here because my mother needs treatment."
For families like Bano's, charities and volunteers can provide some of the practical support they need while they wait outside the hospitals.

Rajiv Ranjan, who works with the Delhi-based Donate A Meal Trust, said his organization regularly helps patients and their attendants staying outside AIIMS and Safdarjung Hospital by distributing food, clothes and rations.
He said the organization has seen many families remain outside the hospitals while seeking treatment or caring for relatives inside.

"We come here for people who sleep outside while they or their family members are receiving treatment inside the hospital," he says. "They have nowhere else to stay, so we try to help with whatever we can." The group distributes about 100 meals a day, Ranjan says.
Food, however, is only one of the needs.

"People need shade from the sun, and during the rainy season they need somewhere to stay dry," Ranjan said. "Some of them take shelter under the Delhi Metro, the city's rapid-transit rail system, when it rains."

For Shalini Yadav, the 20-year-old college student from Madhya Pradesh who traveled to Delhi for treatment, the food distributions and other help have become part of life outside the hospital. She said people arrive to help in whatever way they can, but the assistance does not reach everyone.
"Sometimes we get food. When we don't, we buy it nearby. But there are many people here who don't get anything to eat."
For families, treatment means returning to Delhi again and again
Suhana Bano, 47, from Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh, has been bringing her 18-year-old son, Mohammad Sameer, to Delhi for treatment for about two years.

Sameer has irritable bowel syndrome. He was in seventh grade when this digestive ailment forced him to leave school. The family first sought treatment at several hospitals in Bareilly, about 155 miles from Delhi, before traveling to Safdarjung Hospital.
Suhana Bano said the family turned to Delhi after seeking treatment locally, hoping to find the specialized care Sameer needed.

The family travels to Delhi whenever Sameer is due for a consultation or tests. Typically, they stay one to two months, Bano says. While in Delhi, the family sleeps outside Safdarjung because they cannot afford a room.
Aamar Singh, 60, a farmer from Hathras, Uttar Pradesh, had been sleeping outside AIIMS for about a week when we met him in April.

His 35-year-old daughter, Neelam, was admitted to the AIIMS intensive care unit with a respiratory problem, he said. His 40-year-old sister, Rashima, stayed outside with him. At night, they sleep alongside stray dogs that also gather on the pavement.
Singh does not know how long his daughter will remain in the ICU after being admitted for treatment and therefore does not know how long he will have to remain outside.
Food is not always available, he said, and some days they go hungry.
"Sometimes you eat, sometimes you don't," he said. "My daughter is inside, so I have to stay here. What else can I do? This is our situation."
So Aamar Singh waits on the pavement for news about his daughter until he can take her home.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

Sajad Hameed is an India-based journalist and multimedia storyteller focusing on South Asia. He writes about politics, human rights, health, business, the economy and the impact of climate change, with particular focus on the region's evolving social and political landscape.

Rehan Qayoom Mir is an independent journalist whose work has appeared in outlets including Al Jazeera English, The Guardian, Nikkei Asia, The Progressive, Jacobin and more. He reports from across India and South Asia, with a focus on ground reporting and human-interest stories.

npr.org/2026/10/17/nx-s1-6004276/trump-t.headline: Trump promised a swing district blitz. He's going to a lot of very red states
npr.org/2026/10/17/nx-s1-6004276/trump-t.author: Tamara Keith

paragraphs.text: 📲Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App

Early in September, President Trump gathered Republicans running in competitive races for a dinner in the White House Rose Garden. Prime aged beef burgers were on the menu as the president made a pledge to spend the final month before the midterms campaigning for the approximately 30 Republican candidates in attendance.
"I'm going to go to every one of those 35 places and we're going to see if we can get everyone elected," Trump said confidently.

The White House hasn't clarified which 35 places the president was talking about that night. Since then, Trump has campaigned with fewer than a third of those candidates. Rather than focus on swing states and swing districts as the president said he would, his travel schedule has taken him to a lot of Republican territory.
Trump's itinerary is both a reflection of where he can help (and where he can't) but also of a shifting landscape where even red state Republicans need a boost.
On the tarmac between rally stops in Arizona and Montana this week, Trump attempted to spin his visits to states he won decisively just two years ago as a matter of gratitude.
"So, I do it to thank them," Trump said. "I also do it because we have some great people there that are running and I want to make sure they win."

He went on to bemoan the drop in Republican turnout in years when he isn't on the ballot, something Trump and his team are trying to counteract with an October campaign rally blitz that has taken him to Ohio (twice), Texas (twice), Oklahoma and even Tennessee.
"What the hell am I doing in Tennessee?" Trump mused from stage to wild cheers.

Earlier this week, the president took an eight hour flight to Alaska to campaign for Republicans, Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Rep. Nick Begich, both of whom face races that are too close for comfort in a state Trump won by 13 points in 2024.
"This is worth the 8 hours in a plane," Trump said to an adoring crowd. "And don't forget I've got 8 hours going back. Give me credit for that."
In fact, he made two more stops on the way back and spent the night at the Trump hotel in Las Vegas.
The Republican National Committee has announced he'll be campaigning in Kansas Monday, which has a toss-up U.S. Senate race, something few would have anticipated even a month ago.

Republicans are on defense in a lot of states where they've traditionally won without much trouble. Trump's team is picking locations where he can activate the Republican base in places where he's done well in the past.

"Just a lot of excitement, a lot of momentum building up on the ground here," said RNC Chairman Joe Gruters in a call with NPR from a Trump rally in Arizona. "It's turnout, turnout, turnout. How do you get the base to show up? You put the president on the ballot. You put him out there."

Trump frequently implores his supporters to vote as if he were on the ballot. It's a novel political strategy that runs counter to the norm for unpopular presidents whose parties face significant midterm headwinds. Trump claims the polls are wrong about his underwater approval rating.

As for Trump's message, it doesn't change much from stop to stop. There are the greatest hits: his past election wins, his One Big Beautiful Bill, and a walk down memory lane from right before he launched the war with Iran when gas prices were cheaper. He teases a $5,000 dividend to every American adult if Republicans win the House and the Senate, an idea he first rolled out at the unconventional Republican midterm convention, but has faced resistance from elected Republicans. On most stops he talks about a specific project or deal he has planned for the state.

On Tuesday, Trump is set to campaign in Greenville, North Carolina. Republican campaign committees have already started canceling ad reservations meant to help Trump's handpicked Republican Senate candidate there, Michael Whatley. It's a sign they see that race as moving out of reach.

There's also a congressional district in Eastern North Carolina that was redrawn to favor Republicans as part of Trump's mid-decade redistricting push. It shouldn't be competitive, but it's now rated a toss-up by the Cook Political Report.

"I think it's going to backfire on them this year in every way shape and form," said Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party. "He's trying to drum up any amount of support that he can at the last minute. But I don't think that North Carolinians are going to fall for it again."

npr.org/2026/10/17/nx-s1-5976921/grocery.headline: Weddings are expensive. How about a grocery store cake?
npr.org/2026/10/17/nx-s1-5976921/grocery.author: Stephan Bisaha

paragraphs.text: Going to a specialty baker to craft your dream wedding cake can cost you more than $1,000.
Or you can order a few half sheet cakes from Costco for about $30 each.
"We love Costco, first of all," said Anna Holleran, who got married in California's Bay Area this year — and, yes, picked up her wedding cake from the grocery wholesaler.
"Their cakes are so good," she said. "How can you go wrong?"

Weddings are one of the most expensive days in many people's lives, costing on average about $36,000, according to the wedding-planning website Zola. The Bank of America Institute reports wedding spending among its customers was up 8.5% in May from a year earlier.

Some of that is by choice, with couples deciding to splurge on the venue or chasing the latest TikTok reception trend. But there are less controllable economic factors too, from inflation driving up the price of suits and catering to tariffs bumping up the cost of imported flowers and bridal gowns.

And according to Emily Forrest, head of communications at Zola, one place where couples are willing to trim costs is the cake. About a third of couples surveyed by Zola said they'd consider spending less on cake and dessert.

"When it comes to a wedding, every couple always has to sit down and say, 'Where are we going to save, and where are we going to splurge?'" said Forrest. "And cakes just don't seem to rise to the splurge occasion for a lot of couples."
What couples aren't willing to do is ditch the cake tradition entirely.
"You can't skip the cake!" said Lily Alana Stewart, who got married last year in central Alabama. "Everybody looks forward to a cake at a wedding."
To save money, she ordered her cake from Publix, a grocery chain in the South.

Stewart used baby's breath for decorating the venue, and Publix incorporated that into the cake design. Her co-workers who attended were surprised to learn where the cake came from. "They said, 'Wait, wait, wait. Your wedding cake was from Publix?'" Stewart said. "And they were still mind blown."

While the average wedding cake costs about $5.50 a slice, according to Zola, a slice of Publix cake is about $1.50 cheaper, while still pulling off that classic three-tiered, white-frosted wedding cake look. The chain also offers couples a tasting flight, so they can sample four flavors — including red velvet and carrot — before they order.

The wedding cake business has grown at Publix. The stores around Birmingham, Ala., sell about 50% more than they did before 2020, according to Jeff Brancato, a Publix retail improvement specialist. A chocolate cake with fondant that can serve 94 people costs $388, according to the price guide for the Birmingham area.
"There is definitely big savings when it comes to it," Brancato said.

Still, you do get what you pay for in a grocery store cake, including fewer options than what a specialty baker might offer — like more flavors or more customized decorations. While Publix touts its wedding cake business, Costco doesn't even list its half sheet as a wedding cake. It works out to about 70 cents per slice. (Costco did not return NPR's request for an interview.)
Holleran's priority was saving money where she could. Her wedding was near her home in California wine country — a region that's a destination spot for other couples and where venues are expensive.

Holleran said the culinary details of her cake weren't what mattered. "The real point is that you're sharing a dessert for the first time with somebody that you love," she said. "It's kind of symbolic of all the sweet moments that you're supposed to share in a marriage."

npr.org/2026/10/17/nx-s1-6004887/no-king.headline: No Kings turns its focus to voting this weekend. Here's what we know
npr.org/2026/10/17/nx-s1-6004887/no-king.author: Ava Berger

paragraphs.text: No Kings, the coalition known for organizing anti-Trump protests, is trying a different democratic tactic: increasing voter turnout.

On Saturday, grassroot groups across the country will hold over 3,000 "No Kings: Vote Early" marches and other events. Organizers say these events are a nonpartisan effort to promote early voting in the midterm elections, and will involve helping people check their voter registration, make a plan to cast their ballot and understand their voting rights.
The voting push effort marks a pivot for the No Kings coalition, which comprises hundreds of partner organizations, including the American Civil Liberties Union and Black Voters Matter.

No Kings has previously held three days of nationwide protests since the start of Trump's second term because organizers say Trump's actions in office are more akin to those of a monarch than a democratically elected head of state. Trump has previously rejected the idea that he is behaving like a monarch.

"The first three No Kings were designed to send a message," says Ezra Levin, the co-founder of Indivisible — one of the major organizations within the No Kings network. "We're done sending a message."
Now, he says, they want people to vote.
There are two main goals for the event, says Levin, the first is to help facilitate what he hopes will be the largest number of midterm early voting numbers in the country's history.

The second goal is No Kings groups getting volunteers trained as poll watchers, an endeavor Levin says is in response to efforts by the Trump administration that he views as threats to election integrity. Levin points to the failed SAVE America Act that would have required voters to show a document proving their U.S. citizenship, such as a passport or a birth certificate, when registering to vote. He also raises concerns that federal immigration officers will be sent to the polls, and President Trump's attempted restrictions on voting by mail.
What do organizers expect nationwide?

Saturday's events vary widely across the country, from block parties to cookouts to rallies. In Golden, Colo., a "Paws to the Polls" event invites people to bring their dogs on a march. Organizers in Everett, Wash., planned a "concert for democracy," featuring an environmental troubadour.
All events will share similar restrictions, Levin says, including a rule against political endorsements and inviting current candidates to speak.

Superhero capes and masks will be a staple of Cammy Dunford's event in Frisco, Texas. Dunford, a co-leader of Indivisible Frisco, plans to hold a "voting is your superpower" gathering. She will be wearing a red and blue cape (to embrace the political spectrum of voters) and will give away other superhero capes and masks.

"I don't care if you're an independent, first-time voter, Democrat, Republican," Dunford says, "if you are eligible to vote, you need to get out there and vote. Because without everybody voting, we don't have a democracy."

Early voting in Texas does not start until Oct. 19, but Dunford and a group of her neighbors put together 500 mini goodie bags to hand out — filled with QR codes linking to voting information and voting resources. They will also wave bright signs with superhero-shaped images urging people in passing cars to vote.

Dunford says that her group has two people already trained as poll monitors and is hoping to recruit more on Saturday. She says poll monitors are trained by Common Cause, a government watchdog group that equips them to answer questions from voters. They have T-shirts that identify them at the polls, she says, so voters can find them and ask questions.

At a Wyandotte, Mich., event, Christy McGillivray, the executive director of Voters Not Politicians, a nonpartisan advocacy organization, is scheduled to speak to a No Kings crowd about the history of fighting for democracy in the U.S. She says the organization of grassroots events across the country is inspiring.
"It makes people feel like they're a part of something bigger than themselves," she says. "And that's what democracy is. Democracy is about working with each other and for each other."

cnbc.com/2026/10/17/trump-waives-russia-.headline: Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act, citing national interest
cnbc.com/2026/10/17/trump-waives-russia-.author: Azhar Sukri

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving parts of a recently enacted package of sanctions aimed at curbing Russia's ability to prosecute its war against Ukraine.
"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States," Trump wrote in Friday's order.

The House passed the Russia sanctions bill on Sept. 16, and Trump signed it into law two days later. The bill was introduced over a year ago, and its primary backer was the late Lindsey Graham, a veteran Republican senator who represented South Carolina.
Titled the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, the legislation targeted Russia's economy, intending to penalize the country over its continued full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The act required the president to increase duties on all Russian goods imported into the U.S. by up to 500% no later than 30 days after enactment. It also required Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries including China and India that are among the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas.

Trump's latest order waives these two parts of the Graham Act and comes two days before the law's implementation deadline. However, the order preserves existing sanctions on Russia under earlier executive orders.
The law could also sanction Russian leaders, officials, and financial institutions, and expand sanctions on Iran.
Oil sales revenue is critical to funding Russia's war effort.
The move also comes a week after the Trump administration temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027 to ease a supply crunch caused by the war in Iran.
High fuel prices are a sensitive issue for voters ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.
A 'historic moment'
"The suspension of some of the provisions of the Graham Act marks an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's economy envoy, said in a post on X.
"The U.S.-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue," Dmitriev added.
But Trump's opponents have criticized the move.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat who also drafted the Graham Act, condemned the latest waiver.

"Donald Trump confirms again that he stands on the side of a bloodthirsty thug & the enablers of Russia's war machine & against the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, & our European allies," Blumenthal said in an X post.

Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that the U.S.-Russia diesel agreement could set a precedent for further sanctions relief, while highlighting Ukraine's continued reliance on U.S. military technology and intelligence despite efforts to develop alternatives.
"Sanctions will be lifted after gas," Zelenskyy said. "They will be lifted on something else. Then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemical industry."

Earlier this week, reports emerged that Ukraine has restricted SpaceX's Starlink military application, Starshield. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X that the U.S. government and president were ultimately responsible for any curbs on the network.

persuasion.community/p/eliot-cohen.headline: Eliot Cohen on Why America Keeps Losing Wars It Should Win
persuasion.community/p/eliot-cohen.author: Yascha Mounk

paragraphs.text: Eliot A. Cohen is the Arleigh Burke chair in Strategy at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. His latest book is The Strategist: How to Think About War and Politics.

In this week’s conversation, Yascha Mounk and Eliot Cohen discuss what genuine strategic thinking requires, why America’s war with Iran represents a failure of strategy rather than of military capability, and what Winston Churchill’s wartime memoranda reveal about what good strategy actually looks like.
This transcript has been condensed and lightly edited for clarity.

Yascha Mounk: Why is this term “strategy,” which people throw around in all kinds of contexts, often very loosely, actually very important if you’re trying to understand the world, and if you’re using it rigorously?

Eliot Cohen: Well, I think you have to go back to the origins of the word, which come from the Greek, strategos, general. We live in an age of war. I suppose that’s really my central point. I begin the book by saying you undoubtedly live in a state that may be at war, or whose borders have certainly been shaped by war. That’s true of pretty much all of us. And strategy is at the heart of what war is all about. I think what’s happened is that the word “strategy” has gotten so diluted, and the considerations of it really so bloated, that people have in some ways lost the ability to think about it. So what I wanted to do was to write a book, a relatively brief book, that would not be a massive tome, to try to focus people on the original meaning of the word. Because if there’s one thing particularly Americans have learned, but plenty of others have as well, you can have the most advanced weapons, you can have very professional and skilled soldiers, you can have perfectly sound tactics, and you can still fail. The reasons for the failure are at the level of strategy, usually not at the other levels of tactics and so forth.

Mounk: Perhaps I’ll start with that, and we might be able to come back to it, because I want to get into some of the interesting, meaty theoretical concepts in your book. But what’s striking about the Iran war at the moment is that America continues to be militarily supreme compared to any of its competitors—certainly compared to any of the competitors that have been fighting in the Iranian theater. China may be catching up to the United States on various military metrics, but China’s not directly involved in this war. And yet, despite the fact that very few American soldiers have died, America has superior planes, superior operations, is able to carry out these very impressive, technologically sophisticated operations—this looks like one of the biggest humiliations for the United States in a long time, and it comes after other humiliations, from the Iraq War to the Vietnam War and so on. So, should we lay the fault for all of that at the feet of strategy? Is it Trump’s total lack of strategy going into this war which explains this?

Cohen: The fact that American installations suffered as much damage as they did, that American aircraft suffered as much damage on the ground as they did—that is really more of a kind of military-technical result of people failing to take precautions which, in some ways, you just can’t understand. And there are operational failures here too. But it does seem to me that the big failures have really been at the strategic level, in a whole bunch of ways. Failing, I think, to operate within a real strategic context. The Trump administration goes into this war having alienated almost all of our allies, when actually you really do need their support if you’re going to be in this conflict. It goes in, I think, failing to understand the Iranian regime—I’m not sure even now that it does. I think it’s failing to have thought through what are the means it can really bring to bear to achieve what it wants, and really without having a clear—what I call—a theory of victory, an explanation for how all this is supposed to work. Now, you could have had a much better strategic approach to the war, and that doesn’t necessarily mean that you succeed, but you have a much better chance.

I guess I would also just say, on the Iran war specifically, we still don’t know what the final outcome is. I do think a lot of people have been surprised by the way in which Trump has not simply walked away from it, which many friends of mine who share a similar view of the president that I do really expected—that he would, in the now-stock phrase, “chicken out.” He hasn’t quite, which is an interesting thing. So the end of the story has not been written. But yeah, I would say fundamentally, the major missteps that we’ve seen are very much strategic missteps.

Mounk: I wrote an ill-timed article back in January arguing that Trump doesn’t have a doctrine, but he has a playbook. And the playbook is that he goes for these rapid strikes, spectacular actions, that don’t risk many American lives, don’t cost a lot of money, and by the time people wake up, it’s kind of over. Very true for the first round of strikes against Iran, and very true, of course, for the spectacular capture of Nicolás Maduro. It’s very much not true for this. So the question is, why is that? Now, I think I’m going to slightly defend my ill-timed article and say I think they believed it would be similar. They believed they had a plan that’s very similar to Venezuela, where they’re going to go in, use massive force, and decapitate the Iranian regime. They seem to have believed they had some kind of deal with Ahmadinejad, who was going to be able to go in and take over in the same way that Delcy Rodríguez had taken over in Venezuela. Presumably they thought, if it somehow doesn’t work, we just retreat—we’ve destroyed a bunch of Iranian facilities and planes, and that’s the end of it. But they don’t seem to have reckoned with the Iranian ability to close the Strait of Hormuz. Now, ironically, Trump is in the same situation that he has repeatedly criticized George W. Bush for, which is to get into a war for which you don’t have an exit plan.

Cohen: I would say I mostly agree with that, but not entirely. Let me spell out—well, first, I would say I agree that he does not have a deep understanding of military affairs, and I do think the Venezuela episode influenced how he thinks about this. There have been other cases like that too—the assassination of Qasem Soleimani in the first administration; he actually has a record there. What are some of the things that are different, though? I think one is his antipathy to the regime is qualitatively different than his attitude to just about any other country on earth. Part of that is for the rather simple reason that they have tried to kill him. Even now they’re threatening not just to kill him but members of his family. People do take that kind of thing personally.
Mounk: Of all the different strange things that Donald Trump takes personally, this seems like a very reasonable one.

Cohen: Yeah, I was going to say—I think even you or I would really take it personally. I think he does take the nuclear dimension quite seriously as well. What’s the reason for that? I suspect that, with Trump, a lot of his basic views of politics were formed in the eighties, roughly the early eighties. He thinks of that regime in particular in that framework, and they were a particularly threatening kind of regime when they were first created. That’s one thing—his view of them is different. I think the second thing, though, that is surprising—if he simply followed that playbook, it would be the “TACO” bet. “Trump Always Chickens Out,” which I tend to modify as “Trump Always Chickens Out Sometimes,” which makes it a little bit less useful.

We hope you’re enjoying the podcast! If you’re a paying subscriber, you can set up the premium feed on your favorite podcast app at writing.yaschamounk.com/listen. This will give you ad-free access to the full conversation, plus all full episodes and bonus episodes we have in the works! If you aren’t, you can set up the free, limited version of the feed—or, better still, support the podcast by becoming a subscriber today!
If you have any questions or issues setting up the full podcast feed on a third-party app, please email leonora.barclay@persuasion.community

What they’ve decided to do instead is to maintain a distant blockade of Iran, which has been successful—a return to a very intense sanctions regime, and doing things quietly which enable a fair amount of oil to get out through the Strait of Hormuz. I was just looking at the news today, and people are saying somewhere between ten and twelve million barrels—it fluctuates down from seventeen million, but that’s not zero. He’s adopted a military course of action which is different from the one that one might have expected. What I think they certainly didn’t expect, though, is that this war would begin to expand in the way that it has, particularly with the Houthi successes in Yemen, and the Iranian connection there. He’s not a strategic thinker, he’s not a geopolitical thinker really, and I think they’re finding themselves surprised on that score. On this one, I think he has departed somewhat from the playbook.

Mounk: I agree with you. I think there’s a way you can make that argument less awfully wrong than it seems on a superficial reading. I think fundamentally it’s true that this goes against a lot of the other things he said. He said in his second inaugural, “I want to be measured by the wars I don’t start.” It’s striking—it’s really a strange irony—that he rose to prominence in good part by beating up on his Republican predecessor, George W. Bush, as well as, of course, by his nativist attacks on Barack Obama. Now he is facing a terrible shellacking in his second-term midterms, about to be a huge lame duck, and a big part of the reason for that is an unpopular war of choice. I think those wars have different contexts, and I don’t want to equate them, but it is really a very strange echo of history—and particularly ironic, given how gleefully cruel he was to and about George W. Bush—that he has not emulated any of the better things about George W. Bush, but very much emulated some of the shortcomings of George W. Bush.

Cohen: Yeah, well, he’s not the only one who’s been cruel to George W. Bush. It is striking, and I think it does show—if I can use the word “seriousness” with reference to Donald Trump, which seems like a bit of a stretch—look, if he were really primarily concerned about the midterms above all else, he would have declared victory and gone home. Said, “We destroyed the nuclear program, obliterated it”—or “reobliterated” it, depending on your point of view—and disengaged. That really would have brought diesel prices down, I suspect. The markets would certainly have reacted to that if we’d said, “Okay, no more violence in the Persian Gulf.” He hasn’t done that. On the other hand, I think you’re right that part of his self-conception is that he’s the only guy who can settle wars, and that accounts for two fits of vituperation: one against Volodymyr Zelensky, which is really pernicious and unwarranted, and the other against the hapless Norwegians on the Nobel Prize Committee, who he went after for not giving him the Nobel Prize. I think that is because he’s dealing with that sort of internal, psychic conflict between his ideal self, I suppose, in which he sees himself as the dealmaker, peacemaker, and the real world, in which he’s conducting a war which has expanded and could expand further.

Mounk: That’s fascinating. His obsession with winning the Nobel Peace Prize is itself a fascinating psychological case study. I think it’s partially that he has this very strange competition with Barack Obama, and he can’t brook the idea that Obama won the Peace Prize, of course, hugely prematurely and strangely—but Obama did, and he himself is not going to. I want to go into some of the deeper concepts in the book, and then perhaps we can come back to some of those more contemporary questions about strategy and other things. What does it look like to have a good strategy when you go to war? What does that tell us about some of the failures that we’ve seen in recent American military history?

Cohen: In the book, as people always ask, “So what does good look like?”—it’s one thing to be critical—I try to give an example. What I do is I take the memoranda that Winston Churchill wrote as he’s sailing across the Atlantic, immediately after Pearl Harbor, to meet with Franklin Roosevelt. I say, this is as good as it gets. He’s been prime minister for a couple of years, since May of 1940. He has all of his subordinates around him. He has eight days with no distractions. He has been at the top of the British government for a very long time, and he’s a very, very distinguished military historian.
