bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c61m4zkx47vlo.headline: Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c61m4zkx47vlo.author: Aleks Phillips

paragraphs.text: A rare pink diamond is going on display in France for the first time since it was stolen almost 100 years ago to the day - the last time it was shown to the public.
The nine-carat, pear-shaped gemstone known as the "Grand Condé" was pilfered in an overnight raid on the Château de Chantilly in October 1926 and concealed in a hollowed-out apple.
The diamond - one of few royal jewels to survive the French Revolution - was recovered a few weeks later when a hungry maid at the hotel in which the thieves were staying took a bite of the apple.
It will once again be on display in the Condé Museum at the Château de Chantilly until 3 January.
The museum's director Mathieu Deldicque said that while the apple story may sounds far-fetched, it was widely covered by newspapers at the time.

Deldicque has faced questions about whether the exhibition may be tempting fate, especially given the string of heists on European cultural institutions in the past 12 months, including the daring daylight robbery of jewellery from the Louvre museum in Paris.
While he declined to reveal to CNN how much the diamond was insured for, he noted that extensive academic study into the properties of the diamond had taken place to make it uniquely identifiable.
The results of this analysis, as well as previously unseen archive material about the gem's history and theft, form part of the exhibition, according to the museum.

Naturally occurring pink diamonds are exceptionally rare and often sell for tens of millions of dollars. The highest price ever fetched for one at auction was $71.2m (£53.6m) in 2017, according to Sotheby's.
The exact origins of the Grand Condé remain a mystery.
It was first mentioned in 1740 in an inventory of Louis Henri de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, drawn up following his death, the Château de Chantilly said.
It then became part of the collection of Queen Marie-Amélie of Bourbon-Sicily, the wife of French King Louis Philippe I, and then her son, Prince Henri of Orléans, the Duke of Aumale.

He bequeathed it to the Institut de France, which now owns the Château de Chantilly, 50km (31 miles) north of Paris, along with thousands of artworks and manuscripts which became the Musée Condé collection.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwly3zd1r45ro.headline: Actress Selma Blair says she 'did not intend to harm anyone' in plane altercation
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwly3zd1r45ro.author: Nardine Saad

paragraphs.text: US actress Selma Blair has spoken out after being accused of assaulting multiple people on a flight to New York.

A publicist for the Legally Blonde star said she "did not intend to harm anyone" and that there was "much more to this story". Blair "experienced a medical emergency on the flight" and is still fighting multiple sclerosis (MS), a statement read.
Blair's publicist said that the 54-year-old had a neurological disorder that "bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her".
The star pleaded not guilty to charges that she assaulted an officer and a nurse after being removed from the flight. She was also accused of assulting two flight attendants on board.
Blair's team said the public account of what happened to her aboard a Delta Airlines flight to New York had been "built almost entirely on a police statement and a decade-old headline".
They also denied media reports that she had attempted to open the door of the aircraft.

The publicist noted Blair's fight against multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic illness the actress revealed publicly in 2018. She announced in 2021 that she was in remission for the disease, but the statement noted that the Hellboy and Cruel Intentions star "still has bad days".

It added that she also has pseudobulbar affect (PBA) - a disorder that develops in the context of a brain injury or underlying neurological dysfunction, according to the US National Institutes of Health.
The disorder affects emotional expression that can result in sudden involuntary and out-of-control episodes of laughing, crying or anger that do not match how a person actually feels.
Blair's publicist described the actress's physical achievements since her MS diagnosis as "nothing short of a miracle" and said she still lives with pain daily.

"Selma had never been arrested before Sunday night," she said. "There is much more to this story than has been reported and we ask to consider the entirety of the facts before rushing to judgement, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion."

The incident happened on a flight travelling from Los Angeles to New York on Sunday evening. New York airport officials responded to a call about "a physically abusive passenger" on a Delta Airlines flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.
A pilot asked for medical help, describing "a bloody nose" and "some bite marks", according to audio recorded on air traffic control obtained by CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

Blair was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons by the FBI for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US that relates to the on-board altercation.
The two additional charges of assault were filed in state court after she was taken off the plane. She has pleaded not guilty to those charges and was released on bail.
Additional reporting by Rebecka Pieder

npr.org/2026/10/17/nx-s1-5987671/south-a.headline: Decades after apartheid, South Africans seek justice for crimes of the past
npr.org/2026/10/17/nx-s1-5987671/south-a.author: Kate Bartlett

paragraphs.text: SHARPEVILLE, South Africa – Paulina Mathinye gestures with anguish at the rows of garbage-strewn graves, overrun with weeds, in the cemetery where her father is buried.

"Look at that, where they sleep," she says of the dozens of Black protesters buried here, all of whom were killed when police opened fire on March 21, 1960 in what became one of the bloodiest days in apartheid history.
"Why are they dirty? It's a disgrace," says the 71-year-old grandmother, who wears a floral dress and a smart sunhat.

The cemetery, like much else in this visibly poor township about an hour's drive from Johannesburg, has been left to decay. But Mathinye notes that for one day a year at least, when South Africa's political elite descend to commemorate the massacre, the graveyard is spotless. The anniversary is a public holiday known as Human Rights Day.
"I'm still angry. My anger comes out because that's the day my father was shot," says Mathinye, who was just five years old at the time.
She says her father's part in what became a turning point in the struggle against apartheid has not been sufficiently recognized by the current democratic government.
And she says she wants justice – however delayed.
That's why she's signed up to take part in a potential class action lawsuit 66 years later, along with Sharpeville survivors and the families of Sharpeville victims.
At least 69 people were shot by police that day. They had been demonstrating against the country's pass laws – which restricted black people's movements and where they could live and work.
While it's unclear if any perpetrators are still alive, those taking part in the case hope it could lead to reparations.

But first, the group's lawyers must challenge an apartheid-era law that continues to block their efforts to seek legal redress. The law remains in force decades after apartheid ended and a Black-majority government took power.

In September they filed an application in the Gauteng High Court challenging the continued existence of the Indemnity Act 61 of 1961. If the court finds the law unconstitutional, and also certifies a class action for survivors and dependants of those killed, then claims for individual damages could follow.
Mathinye says the repercussions of that day in 1960 have affected her whole life.
Without her father, the main breadwinner, she couldn't finish school. That, in turn, affected the lives of her children and grandchildren.
"So we struggled a lot. And we are still struggling now, because nothing has been happening," she told NPR.
If the case goes ahead and succeeds, Paulina says she'll use any money from reparations to fix up her modest home and pay for her four grandkids' educations.
Part of a wider trend
The Sharpeville case is just one in a new wave of legal efforts that are seeking truth, accountability and reparations for apartheid-era crimes before it's too late.

"It's crucial that these issues of deep injustice are properly dealt with and that South Africa confronts them and does not sweep them under the carpet," says Daniel Leader, an international human rights lawyer advising the South African legal team representing the Sharpeville survivors and families.
Other cases include a court ruling last year that found South Africa's first Nobel Peace Prize laureate, Chief Albert Luthuli, was beaten to death by apartheid police in 1967.

Luthuli, the former leader of the African National Congress — Nelson Mandela's party — had previously been ruled to have died after being struck by a train. The new ruling overturned the finding of an earlier inquest.

The inquest into the 1985 killings of four anti-apartheid activists known as the "Cradock Four" has also been reopened. The activists were abducted and killed by apartheid security forces near the Eastern Cape town of Cradock. Although the officers involved are all dead, the victims families hope the inquest will establish who ordered the killings.
And the inquest into the torture and death of Steve Biko, the iconic Black Consciousness leader who died in police detention in 1977, has also returned to court.

"It's very clear that the murder of Steve Biko was exactly that, murder," Biko's son Nkosinathi told media in September at the reopened inquest. "We hope that this inquest will eventually get to this very certain, unambiguous finding."
The original inquest in 1977 heard from members of the security branch who said Biko had fallen and hit his head in a "scuffle with security police."

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), a court-like restorative justice body set up in the 1990s to uncover the truth about human rights violations during apartheid, re-examined the Biko case.
It denied amnesty to security officers who testified, saying they hadn't been truthful. That essentially cleared the way for possible prosecutions, but they never happened.

In fact, hundreds of the TRC's recommendations for prosecutions were delayed or never pursued. Last year, President Cyril Ramaphosa established a formal inquiry to investigate whether the recommendations were deliberately shelved.

The inquiry is looking into whether there was a secret deal between the old leaders of the apartheid regime and the country's new Black leaders not to prosecute cases in the interests of reconciliation. Its findings are due in December.
Back at the Sharpeville cemetery, Paulina Mathinye and three other descendants of those killed in the massacre, pause in front of a memorial plaque before exiting the graveyard.
Vincent Thamae, from the NGO, Voices of Sharpeville which works with survivors and descendants asks that they take leave of the dead.
"We ask of those who are sleeping here to be with us as we pursue justice for them," he says.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/17/uae-ye.headline: UAE agrees with Saudi Arabia to re-enter Yemen conflict amid Houthi gains
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/17/uae-ye.author: Patrick Wintour

paragraphs.text: The United Arab Emirates has agreed to re-enter the Yemen conflict by resuming payments to some government forces fighting Iran-aligned Houthis in the south, according to sources in Yemen. In return, Saudi Arabia has agreed to provide air cover for the anti-Houthi force.

The new cooperation agreement is the first tangible signs that the deep rift between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen’s future is starting to be healed – if only because the advance by Houthi forces across Yemen has alarmed all the rival Gulf state rulers.
Saudi Arabia is facing daily drone and missile attacks and is struggling to maintain an atmosphere of normality, as Houthi strikes immobilise its airports and some of its energy infrastructure.

Southern forces – mainly in the Giant Brigades – were previously trained and funded by the UAE, and are regarded as some of the most effective in the disjointed anti-Houthi military coalition. But the UAE quit operations inside Yemen in January, cutting off its funding supply line.

Neither Saudi Arabia nor the UAE have responded to a demand this week by southern Yemen separatists for a referendum on secession, a move that would restore the 1967-1990 borders, when Yemen was two separate states.

The separatist Southern Transition Council has also not yet agreed for its troops to fight outside the borders of the old Southern Yemen, but an explicit agreement by Saudi Arabia to allow a referendum would be likely to lead to the lifting of that restriction.

Yemen’s UN-recognised government, based in Aden, declared last week a counteroffensive to drive Houthi forces from the capital Sana’a, but so far the military drive has met with limited success around Majzar near Marib and the Bab al-Mandab strait.

There is also no direct contact between the STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, and Saudi officials. Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi in January after a failed STC attempt to take charge across the south and announce a referendum on separation in two years’ time. In response, the Saudis bombed UAE arms shipments for STC forces.
The UAE then announced it was quitting all involvement in Yemen, and the Saudi-backed government said it would seek to try Zubaidi for treason.

UAE officials are deeply concerned by the state of the conflict. Despite massive losses, the Houthis are determined eventually to capture Taiz and Marib, the two remaining cities outside the boundaries of the old Southern Yemen.
On Friday two missiles fired by the Houthis struck the airport of Aden while a passenger plane was preparing to take off. No casualties were reported.
The missiles landed about 500 meters from the Yemenia Airways aircraft, and approximately 100 meters from the midpoint of the runway, said Yemen’s information minister, Moammar Al-Eryani.
The strike came a day after at least five people were killed and 16 injured in a Houthi attack on a presidential palace in Aden.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fattah el Sisi, said he was convening an emergency session of parliament to grant his country’s military the powers to take action in defence of Saudi Arabia. He stressed Egypt would not be taking any offensive action, and would only defend Saudi Arabia.

In the UK, discussions are continuing about a Saudi request for further military aid. The UK has sent an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft, but regional diplomats are pressing for the UK to do more. Some concern is being expressed over whether Riyadh should be engaging closer with other Gulf States, including Oman and Qatar, on the issue.

The legal implications of a blanket UK backing for the largely Saudi air campaign is also being considered, since the court of appeal in 2019 found the UK had acted unlawfully in issuing arms export licences during a previous Saudi bombing campaign of Yemen in 2015-16. The Campaign Against Arms Trade said the UK had made no proper assessment of potential Saudi breaches of international humanitarian law, forcing the UK to revise its procedures.

Saudi Arabia claims to have revised its methods substantially since then, and certainly argues that it is acting in self-defence in line with the UN charter. The UN security council on 15 October adopted a UN presidential statement on 15 October asserting Saudi Arabia’s right to act in self-defence in line with international law.

No accurate death toll in the war since August is available, but more than 200,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN, which is placing increasing pressure on Aden-based humanitarian groups.

livescience.com/planet-earth/plants/cali.headline: California redwoods are struggling in the heat — and it's not clear how much damage is being done
livescience.com/planet-earth/plants/cali.author: Sarah Wild

paragraphs.text: When temperatures spike, California redwoods slow down photosynthesis, new research has found. This finding has serious implications for the long-term survival of the iconic trees in a warming world, and their role in storing carbon from the atmosphere.

California redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) forests are among the largest aboveground carbon stores on the planet. These towering trees are native to central and northern California, and evolved to take advantage of the region's historically mild weather. In recent decades, their range has contracted significantly. But climate change is threatening the health and function of these forests.

The region has seen significant warming in recent decades, and faces more frequent extreme heat days, with temperatures spiking above 100 degrees Fahrenheit (37 degrees Celsius). Now, in a new study, published Sept. 22 in the journal JGR Biogeosciences, a team of researchers has shown that California's renowned redwoods are struggling to photosynthesize in the heat.
Photosynthesis is the process used by plants, algae and some bacteria to turn sunlight into energy. It chemically converts carbon dioxide and water into sugars and oxygen.

"These trees adapted to grow in really temperate environments, so no one had really looked at the impact of heat on photosynthesis," study first author Lily Klinek, a doctoral candidate in the Plant Optics Lab at the University of California, Davis, told Live Science.

From 2022 to 2024, Klinek and colleagues measured how the leaves of redwoods in Garcia River Forest in Mendocino County responded to the heat. Once or twice a month, the researchers took three different California redwood leaf samples and measured their fluorescence and temperature.

A plant's molecules can use absorbed light in three ways: for photosynthesis, dissipated as heat, or reflected as light (florescence). Fluorescence is a proxy measurement to understand photosynthesis in the plant, Klinek said.

The researchers wrapped a fourth leaf in tinfoil for 20 minutes to put it in a state of "rest" before taking the same measurements. "When they're in a state of rest, we expose them to a pulse of light that’s in the wavelength they would use for photosynthesis to see what would be their maximum photosynthetic rate," Klinek said.

They found that on hot days, the leaves exposed to sunlight were up to 18 degrees Fahrenheit (10 degrees Celsius) hotter than the air temperature. "That's a huge difference and indicates that the leaves are stressed to the point where they can't thermoregulate effectively," Klinek said.

Many plants' leaves manage their temperature and photosynthesis by opening or closing their stomata, which are tiny pores on their surface. These stomata (from the Greek word for mouth) regulate the amount of carbon dioxide entering the plant, and how much oxygen and water vapor it releases. Lower carbon dioxide intake leads to reduced photosynthesis, meaning the plant has less energy.

The large differences between air and redwood leaf temperatures suggest that the leaves had closed their stomata to avoid losing water from evaporation during hot conditions and consequently overheated, Klinek said.

To further investigate the impact of heat on leaf physiology, the researchers took California redwood leaf samples back to the laboratory and exposed them to a range of temperatures while they were in water. Despite their access to water, the leaves still photosynthesized less as they got hotter, even though their stomata were open, Klinek said.

This shows that heat imposes direct limitations on redwood photosynthetical capacity, rather than indirectly decreasing that capacity by causing stomatal closure, the researchers wrote. The finding indicates that redwoods' ability to photosynthesise and store carbon will decrease as temperatures rise.

"It is not only stomatal closure that is causing reduced photosynthesis," Lucy Rowland, an ecologist at the University of Exeter in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email. "These trees are already suffering from the direct effects of heat on their photosynthetic systems."
Related stories

The finding has serious implications for the future of redwoods and similar plants. "The points at which this damage becomes irreversible remains really poorly understood, but is something which is really essential to understand if we want to predict how our future climate is going to impact plants," she said.
The next step in Klinek's research is to move beyond leaf physiology to understand these thresholds on the trees and their ecosystems as a whole.

"We're not sure to what extent the effect that we saw is a reversible stress response and if they are sustaining damage from this constant stress," she said. Researchers need more data to "really get a better sense, beyond the leaf scale, how these ecosystems are responding to heat and drought," she added.
Campaign spending for these midterm elections passed 10 billion dollars this week, according to the tracking group AdImpact.
Maybe we should repeat that number: $10 billion dollars.

The senate race in Ohio, for example, has already cost more than $460 million in combined ad spending. The Texas Senate race has surpassed half a billion. Then there's $260 million more in the Maine Senate race.

The most expensive House race in the country isn't in California or New York, but Michigan's 7th congressional district with nearly $60 million in ads. Contests in Iowa and Florida are just under $50 million apiece.

There are limits on personal campaign contributions in the United States--but, since the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision in 2010, no limits on donations to "super PACs," which can publicly support or oppose candidates but can't directly coordinate with campaigns. Rich donors have used that ruling to steer hundreds of millions of dollars to support both parties, up and down the ballot. Elon Musk alone has given $276 million to Republican groups, just since July. George Soros has given more than $100 million dollars to Democrats this election cycle.

Meanwhile, voters, whom politicians are trying to win over with all these ads, tell pollsters and reporters that their top issues this fall are the economy and the cost of living. Inflation is up; gas prices have spiked since the start of the Iran war; groceries cost a third more than they did in 2019.

It is hard not to wonder: what could those hundreds of millions of ad dollars accomplish if they went toward food, gas, or shelter for those in need, or to help people with health care costs? Could some of it pay for school nurses, music teachers, and librarians? Subsidize addiction care? Clean up public parks?

Maybe a candidate could win support these days by declaring, "And I vow to spend less money on my campaign than my opponent!" After all, as the Los Angeles Dodgers might remind us this week, spending the most money doesn't always deliver victory.

cbsnews.com/news/vance-cbs-town-hall-tak.headline: Vance says it'll take time to see economy improve: "We're turning the ship around"
cbsnews.com/news/vance-cbs-town-hall-tak.author: Joe Walsh

paragraphs.text: October 17, 2026 / 7:54 AM EDT / CBS News
As Americans express frustration with the country's economic outlook, Vice President JD Vance told CBS News this week it could take some time to see improvement.

"I'll be the first person to tell you that just as this country wasn't broken in one presidential term, it's gonna take more than 18 months to fix things and turn them around," Vance said during a town hall in Michigan that will air Saturday evening.

Vance was responding to a question from a woman who said her small business is struggling. Polls show that most Americans are dissatisfied with the state of the economy and frustrated with inflation, and the majority of voters blame the Trump administration's policies.
President Trump is more positive, giving his administration an "A+" on the economy.

Asked about Mr. Trump's characterization of the economy by "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil, Vance said: "I think that what the president is saying is that we are seeing all of these massive new investments come into our country. But he would be the first person to tell you that you gotta build the factories first, before you can employ the workers working in those factories."
"I think what we're doing is, we're turning the ship around," the vice president continued.

Watch CBS News' "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance" on Saturday, Oct. 17 at 8 p.m. ET/PT on the CBS Television Network or stream it on Paramount+. The one-hour special will also be available to watch afterward on CBSNews.com, YouTube and CBS News 24/7.
Vance says it's going to take time to turn around the economy

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe9lx54g7x9o.headline: Nursery owner in China jailed for life after hundreds of children poisoned
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe9lx54g7x9o.author: Rorey Bosotti

paragraphs.text: A nursery owner and five members of her staff have been jailed after they were found to have poisoned more than 200 children with lead-tainted food.

Li Huifang, who operated the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Tianshui, in the Gansu province, was sentenced to life in prison for producing and selling toxic and harmful food, according to Chinese state media.
In July 2025, 247 pupils and staff at the nursery were found to have abnormally high blood lead levels after children began falling ill.
A report into the incident found that chefs at Heshi Peixin had used inedible paint to "enhance the look" of its meals to attract more students - despite the paint being being clearly marked as such.
In addition to the sentence, the Lanzhou Intermediate People's Court also ordered the confiscation of 500,000 yuan (£56,200; $74,700) of Li's personal assets, state broadcaster CCTV reported.
Nursery executive principal Zhi Jinglin was sentenced to 15 years in prison and fined 300,00 yuan.
Four other members of staff who worked in the nursery's kitchen received sentences of between six to eight years, according to state media.
The court found the four had been instructed by Li and Zhi to add toxic and harmful ingredients to food served to children and staff.
Food samples were later found to contain lead 2,000 times in excess of China's national safety limit.
The investigation into the poisoning began after 235 children from Heshi Peixin nursery had to be treated for lead poisoning after eating steamed red date cakes and sausage corn buns.

Investigators found that the red date cake and the corn sausage rolls had lead levels of 1052mg/kg and 1340mg/kg respectively, both of which far exceed the national food safety standard limit of 0.5mg/kg.
Lead poisoning is "particularly harmful to young children" and can "severely damage the brain and central nervous system", according to the World Health Organization.
Officials later found that dozens of provincial officials and hospital staff attempted to cover up the incident by tampering with blood tests and accepting bribes from a nursery investor.

China has since published a set of national guidelines for the provision of meals on campuses. Among the measures is the requirement for every new batch of food to be tested, and for flour, rice and cooking oil to be purchased from centralised procurement points only.

theatlantic.com/culture/2026/10/catholic.headline: Another Battle Between the Catholic Church and the Trump Administration

paragraphs.text: Several winters ago, a few weeks before Christmas, I went to confession. The parish close to work was hosting a reconciliation service, meant to prepare the faithful to celebrate the birth of Christ. A dozen or so priests were scattered across the cathedral. Penitents lined the aisles. Whispers of contrition and pardon filled the air.

The Catholic Church counsels believers to seek confession regularly—at the very least, once a year. I hadn’t been back in a few. So in addition to feeling spiritually unmoored, I was worried about how the priest would react to hearing about my hiatus. But when I told him, he simply smiled and said, “Welcome back.” His response put me at ease then, and it helped change how I approach the sacrament now: less as a nerve-racking ordeal, more as a moment of mercy.

Sacraments such as confession are central to Catholicism. Through them, the Church teaches that simple actions—having a conversation with a priest, eating bread and drinking wine—are, with grace, tangible encounters with God. For the past year, the Trump administration has been making it harder for Catholics at migrant-detention centers to have those encounters.

The most recent example came to light this month, when the Archdiocese of St. Louis filed a federal lawsuit over the visitation policy at Saint Genevieve County Jail in eastern Missouri. According to the claim, the 10 priests who minister at the jail aren’t allowed to celebrate Mass. The suit also alleges that priests are permitted to visit migrant detainees just once a week, during a four-hour period, and that the jail’s “no contact” security policy lets the clergy speak with detainees only over the phone, through a glass partition. As a result, the approximately 150 migrants at the jail at a given time—most of whom are Catholic, according to the archdiocese—have been going without their religious needs for weeks. Since the middle of 2025, according to the lawsuit, Saint Genevieve has housed approximately 3,000 people.
[Read: The Catholic Church’s new schism]

This isn’t the first time that Catholic clergy have complained that the government is preventing them from ministering to detained migrants. Last year, the Florida detention facility known as “Alligator Alcatraz” kept priests from visiting or offering Mass to detainees for a month, until an agreement was reached between the Archdiocese of Miami and state authorities. In May, after a six-month legal fight, a Catholic nonprofit won a preliminary injunction to let Catholic priests celebrate Mass and administer sacraments at the Broadview ICE processing center outside Chicago. And the administration’s immigration crackdowns seem to be hurting the Church more broadly. Dioceses across the country have reported decreased Mass attendance among Spanish-speaking parishioners who fear detention. ICE has reportedly conducted raids near Catholic churches during Mass hours.

The Department of Homeland Security has denied allegations of wrongdoing at Saint Genevieve. In a statement to multiple outlets, the agency said that the jail is not an ICE facility—although Saint Genevieve is listed as a detention facility on ICE’s website—and that it “ensures detainees are accommodated with religious services.” As described in the lawsuit, however, those accommodations disregard the religious significance of the Catholic sacraments.

Consider confession. The suit claims that at Saint Genevieve, conversations between detainees and priests are not private, and the phone lines that they use to talk may be monitored. These policies may be in place for security reasons, but confession is meant to be a private exchange between penitent and priest, who acts in persona Christi—in the person of Christ. Confession is “one of the most intimate, profound acts that someone can do,” David Inczauskis, a Jesuit priest who ministers at the Broadview ICE facility, told me. He added, “To state very specifically the sins that they have committed and to ask humbly for pardon and for peace” requires a “level of vulnerability” that is “very high.”

An even bigger problem comes up with the sacrament of the Eucharist, or Communion. The complaint includes an email from a deputy at the local sheriff’s office suggesting that priests “provide an unopened, individually wrapped Communion wafer” to a member of the detention center staff, who could then hand it to a detainee. This way of distributing the Eucharist would be “sacrilegious,” as Archbishop Mitchell Rozanski of St. Louis recently told Reuters. The Church teaches that the Eucharist is the “Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity” of Christ—not a symbol, but God’s real presence. For that reason, Inczauskis said, the Church distributes the Eucharist through either ordained ministers or specially trained laypeople.
[Read: The Catholic Church and the Trump administration are not getting along]

For much of the past quarter century, many conservative figures have taken up religious liberty as an essential cause. The Trump administration purported to continue these efforts when it established a commission last year meant to identify “emerging threats” to the exercise of faith. In June, the commission released a draft report claiming that “in recent years, Americans from all religious backgrounds have faced increasing persecution for their religious beliefs.” Some of the issues discussed in the report include rising anti-Semitism, how gender and sexuality is taught in schools, and conscience protections for health-care workers who object to participating in abortions or assisted suicides. The report said nothing about the administration’s migrant-detention practices.

When the commission was announced, my colleague Elizabeth Bruenig wrote that “Christians shouldn’t conclude” that it would “necessarily defend their interests.” That warning seems prescient a year and a half later. At Alligator Alcatraz, Broadview, and Saint Genevieve, the Catholic Church has shown that it believes that detainee access to the sacraments matters deeply. Given the choice between restricting immigration and protecting the religious liberty of migrants, the administration, too, has demonstrated where its values lie.

cnbc.com/2026/10/17/bending-spoons-wants.headline: Bending Spoons wants to revive software castoffs. Berkshire is backing the plan
cnbc.com/2026/10/17/bending-spoons-wants.author: CJ Haddad

paragraphs.text: At the time of its Nasdaq debut in July, Bending Spoons was a little-known holding company out of Italy that owned older internet names like AOL, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Evernote.

Less than four months later, the Milan-based firm has emerged as a surprising home for former high-flying software startups that have been thrust aside by the artificial intelligence boom. Its M&A plan got a major boost this week from the most famous holding company on the planet: Berkshire Hathaway.

Berkshire, which Bending Spoons describes as a "longstanding inspiration" for its strategy, has now invested over $900 million in the company, including a $330 million stake disclosed on Wednesday. Wall Street loved the deal, sending Bending Spoons' stock up 41%, though some of those gains were lost later in the week, leaving the company with a market cap of about $30 billion.

"Berkshire's decision to add to its position just a few months after the IPO and at these levels provides another vote of confidence in the Bending Spoons model from one of the world's most respected long-term investors," wrote analysts at Mizuho, in a report after the announcement.

The other big news out of Bending Spoons this week underscores the flipside of the business: job cuts. In August, Bending Spoons announced it was buying workflow software provider Airtable for about $1.3 billion, or almost 90% below the company's peak valuation from late 2021. Bending Spoons said Monday that a "large portion of the pre-acquisition team" from Airtable would be leaving with "substantial separation packages." Layoffs were previously implemented at Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer and others in the portfolio.

For the technology industry, Bending Spoons' moves represent the latest example of how quickly fortunes are turning in the AI era, as new agents powered by large language models displace software developers and the products they built. With Anthropic and OpenAI marching toward trillion-dollar valuations, businesses are putting more valuable work in their hands at the expense of a host of software-as-a-service names, creating a phenomenon that's become known as the "SaaSpocalypse."

Shares of Intuit, HubSpot and Adobe are all down at least 30% this year, and a long list of private SaaS companies that were once venture darlings are now struggling to find capital, with the public market showing no appetite for IPOs. Last month, Bending Spoons agreed to buy collaboration software vendor Miro, once valued at $17.5 billion, for $1.36 billion.

"You're either like a hot thing or you're nothing," said Ethan Kurzweil, founder and managing partner at Chemistry VC and a veteran software investor. Kurzweil said he uses Airtable, and said there are plenty of good SaaS products on the market led by solid teams, "but they're not on the frontier anymore."
An app turned acquirer

Bending Spoons was launched in 2013 by friends Luca Ferrari, the CEO, Matteo Danieli and Francesco Patarnello. A mobile app they'd created called Evertale failed to take off, and they used the $40,000 they had left to build an operating company instead of "products nobody wanted," according to the IPO prospectus.
Bending Spoons has announced all of its biggest deals in the last few years, beginning with Evernote in 2022, followed by Brightcove in 2024, and Vimeo, AOL and Eventbrite in 2025.
The company held its IPO on June 30, raising about $1.7 billion at $29 a share, and hit the Nasdaq the next day. The stock closed Friday at $47.07.

Prior to Bending Spoons' recent jump into enterprise software, some of the leading acquirers in the space over the past decade were private equity behemoths Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity Partners. Those firms were aiming to buy what they viewed as undervalued SaaS companies and, through a combination of cost cuts, efficiency improvements and rollups, turn them into assets that could be sold or taken public at a higher price.

Bending Spoons is using a different playbook. The company isn't looking for eventual exits but rather wants to generate profits from the businesses it buys, similar to the Warren Buffett model. But unlike Berkshire, Bending Spoons' focus is technology, and it's taking a hands-on approach with its own software, operations and personnel decisions.
Nick Mehta, former CEO of cloud software vendor Gainsight, said private equity firms are limited now because "they got their nose bloodied."
"They paid much higher prices and have so many troubled companies that it's difficult for them to take swings now," said Mehta, who sold Gainsight to Vista in 2020.
Thoma Bravo and Vista didn't respond to requests for interviews. Bending Spoons told CNBC in a statement that it hadn't been outbid for a target in "several years."
As the company started jumping into SaaS, Mehta said "Bending Spooned" became a verb in Silicon Valley, referring to companies getting scooped up for pennies on the dollar.
"Unfortunately, a lot of my friends in that game are stuck," Mehta said. "Investors want out but there are no buyers. Anything pre-ChatGPT is legacy now."
Lloyd Walmsley, an analyst at Mizuho, said Bending Spoons' model is distinct from the older buyout approach.

"I think there aren't a lot of people that do what these guys do in terms of the depth of operations and the willingness to make substantial product changes," Walmsley said in an interview. "It's not typical of traditional private equity firms to make anywhere near this level of change."
For customers of the companies that Bending Spoons buys, sudden price hikes can follow.

In April 2023, months after the Evernote acquisition, Bending Spoons lifted the annual personal subscription price to $130 from $70. Later, the company changed its offerings, charging $100 for its so-called starter plan and $250 for "Evernote Advanced," compared to the $170 it had been charging for the pro plan.
"My first reaction was like, Oh man, I guess I have to switch to OneNote," said Walmsley, referring to Microsoft's notetaking app. But he said he stuck with Evernote.
"They're really savvy at finding these things that they provide a lot of value, and the switching costs are really high," Walmsley said. "The price isn't that high relative to the switching cost."
Bending Spoons uses the profits from its portfolio companies for future growth, the "overwhelming majority" of which comes from doing more deals, Ferrari told CNBC in an interview on Thursday.
"There are certain opportunities for improvement we can unlock over the first few years, and then the business will have whatever organic growth is intrinsic in that market," Ferrari said.
For Berkshire and its fellow Bending Spoons investors, the bet is still unproven.

The products have to remain desirable enough that customers are willing to pay up at a time when AI is squeezing margins across much of the software sector. In its first earnings report as a public company in August, Bending Spoons said revenue more than doubled from a year earlier to over $700 million, with growth almost entirely driven by acquisitions, while net income climbed 171% to $177 million.

That was before the Airtable deal had closed and Miro had yet to be announced. In the coming quarters and years, Wall Street will get a clear picture of whether the firm's structure can revive software.
On the earnings call in August, an analyst asked whether Airtable represents a long-term shift in the M&A strategy towards enterprise.

Ferrari said that about half of Bending Spoons' revenue already comes from professional businesses, largely through Brightcove and Vimeo, which has an enterprise component. The focus on software of late, he said, has more to do with where he's finding value after a hefty selloff.
"Most enterprise SaaS businesses were valued at irrationally high levels until somewhat recently," Ferrari said. "We never saw those prices making any sense."
— CNBC's Ari Levy contributed to this report.

paragraphs.text: Fri, October 16, 2026 at 3:25 PM PDT 1 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC has quietly presented its own draft AI safety bill to US lawmakers with a plan for regulating artificial intelligence safety and security, according to a Politico report.
Most Read from Bloomberg

According to Politico, the proposal suggests the government could block the release of an AI model if it's determined to imminently risk killing or injuring more than 50 people or causing more than $1 billion in damages. The threat must be a result of the model creating or releasing a biological weapon, the AI going beyond human control or a cyberattack, Politico reported.
The bill also proposes that independent evaluators would routinely review Anthropic and its AI models, said Politico, citing a draft it had reviewed.
The draft proposes many of the the ideas Anthropic first proposed in its Advanced AI Framework this June.
The report did not specify which lawmakers or how broadly Anthropic has pitched the proposal so far.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Carmen Arroyo

paragraphs.text: Fri, October 16, 2026 at 3:08 PM PDT 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- OpenAI has hired SpaceX's Graham Seamans to lead sales for the firm's cybersecurity business, the latest in a string of hires from Elon Musk's artificial intelligence venture.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Seamans, who had led xAI's sales team since August 2025 and was part of the firm's renewed push to sell the Grok chatbot to Wall Street, said he's joining the developer behind ChatGPT to work on the cyber team. Seamans is the latest sales executive who OpenAI has hired from SpaceX's AI units. Before joining xAI last year, Seamans had worked at MongoDB Inc. for about eight years, according to his LinkedIn.

Since September, OpenAI has also hired Brian McCarthy and Ismail Elmas in Europe, both of whom had worked for coding automation startup Cursor, which was acquired by SpaceX for $60 billion in August. OpenAI has also hired other staffers from SpaceX's AI compute team, including Uday Ruddarraju and Brent Mayo.

OpenAI is trying to expand its commercial reach by boosting sales from enterprise customers and creating new revenue sources such as advertising ahead of a potential public listing. Musk lost a lawsuit against OpenAI, which he helped form, arguing that the AI lab betrayed its mission to the public by changing to a for-profit business. He started a competing AI developer, xAI, which he then merged with SpaceX.
OpenAI declined to comment.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: UK’s Healey Backs Heathrow Third Runway in Clash With Burnham
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Philip Aldrick

paragraphs.text: Fri, October 16, 2026 at 2:30 PM PDT 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey has backed plans for a third runway at Heathrow, setting up a possible Downing Street clash with Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Speaking to reporters at the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings in Bangkok the chancellor made his support for the project clear, saying "the case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth."

Burnham has refused to state whether he would back expansion of the UK's premier airport, arguing that "it's a matter for London and Londoners," and that he is "open minded" about the £49 billion ($65 billion) plan.

Healey is backing the current scheme and voted for the third runway in a parliamentary vote on new capacity in 2018. Their contrasting positions are the first sign of potential tensions between the chancellor and his more illustrious neighbor at 10 Downing Street.

Approving a third runway at Heathrow was the centerpiece of former Chancellor Rachel Reeves' plan for growth and investment. She committed to the long-awaited, much debated project in January last year when Keir Starmer was prime minister. She said at the time she wanted planning to be "signed off" before the next election, due on 2029.

Reeves set a target of completing Heathrow expansion by 2035, but airport chiefs have said it may not be up and running until 2039. Thomas Woldbye, Heathrow's chief executive, said it would be a "huge missed opportunity" if the runway was not built. The investment would simply go elsewhere in the world, he said.

The Department for Transport estimates that an expanded Heathrow would create 60,000 local jobs and deliver as much as £42 billion of benefits to the UK. The UK's Climate Change Committee is being consulted on how to ensure expansion is consistent with the net zero framework.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Alberta Early-Voter Surge Suggests Edge for Anti-Secession Side
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Iain Boekhoff and Derek Decloet

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- More than 1 million people have already cast their ballots in Alberta's referendum on separation from Canada, signaling strong voter turnout that pollsters say may favor the "remain" side.
Most Read from Bloomberg
A spokesperson for the province's election agency said more than 525,000 people voted in the first three days of in-person advance polls and 491,000 mail ballots have been processed.

The official voting day is Monday, but those who want to cast their ballot early can do so until Saturday evening. Residents of the energy-rich western province will weigh in on whether they want to remain part of Canada, or begin a process that could eventually lead to independence. If they choose the latter, a second vote would be held.

Public opinion surveys have suggested the "remain" side is well ahead, including a recent poll from Leger that found 70% of Albertans wish to stay in Canada. But pro-Canada campaigners have pushed to get people to voting centers, fearing that complacency and low turnout would benefit the separatist cause.
There were roughly 3 million eligible voters in the province as of last year. About 1.8 million voted in the last provincial election in 2023.

Fresh polling data from the Angus Reid Institute shows that Albertans who want their province to stay in Canada are more likely now than a couple of months ago to say the referendum is "very important" for the future of Alberta.
"The vote motivation is significantly higher among remainers," Shachi Kurl, the polling firm's president, said in a phone interview. "They are seized with the gravity of the moment."
Angus Reid's latest survey, released Friday, puts the remain side at 66%, while 34% favor going further down the secession path.

Among those who choose the second option, however, 60% are motivated by "sending a message to Ottawa" and just 37% are motivated by actually wanting separation, the polling firm said in a news release. The poll was an online randomized sample of about 1,000 Alberta residents, taken from Oct. 13 to 15.

Political leaders are using the last few days before the vote to make their final push for national unity. Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Calgary on Thursday campaigning for Canada and plans to give another speech Friday night in Edmonton, the provincial capital.
Conservative Party Leader Pierre Poilievre — who, like Carney, grew up in Alberta — called for its residents to "lock arms" with their fellow Canadians and reject the secession movement.
"Our real goal should not be separation. It should be restoration," he told a Calgary audience on Friday. "It should not be to tear down our country, but to build it up."
Poilievre argued the frustrations Albertans have with the federal government in Ottawa are shared across the country.
"Canada is more than a government. It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise," he said.

While much of the debate around separation has focused on the ways the Canadian government has failed Alberta, the Conservative leader said leaving would deprive the province of the opportunities that come with being part of a larger country that has three coasts and more than 41 million people. He pointed to the large number of people who move to Alberta from other parts of Canada and make it a new home.
"Quitting is the easy way out and Albertans are not quitters," he said.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Investors Prepare for Data Dump That Will Determine Canada’s Rate Path
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Erik Hertzberg

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Two key economic data releases Monday could make or break the case for a Bank of Canada interest-rate hike later this month.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Statistics Canada will release September inflation data at 8:30 a.m. Ottawa time, and the central bank will publish its latest business and consumer outlook surveys shortly after. They will be the final major clues to how the economy is weathering oil-driven inflation risks and the fallout from escalating trade tensions before policymakers make their next rate decision on Oct. 28.

Officials have held the benchmark rate steady at 2.25% for the past seven decisions. But policymakers have signaled they're worried that the longer gasoline prices remain elevated, the more likely firms will raise prices on other goods and services.

Dovish forecasters are pointing to September labor data, which showed job losses and a rising unemployment rate. But that might not be enough to keep policymakers from raising rates if Monday's data releases show persistent price pressures and a steadying economy.

"If you get a hot inflation print and the business outlook survey is strong, then an October hike is on the table, even with the weak jobs number," Benjamin Reitzes, a Canadian rates and macro strategist with the Bank of Montreal, said in an interview.

The latest inflation data will be especially crucial to the bank's decision. The headline yearly change in the consumer price index has held near 3% for months, which Governor Tiff Macklem has called "too high." Annual core inflation metrics are close to the bank's 2% target, though the more recent trend in price pressures has accelerated.
The big question is whether inflation is at risk of flaring up further.

Robert Both, a macro strategist at TD Securities, said he'll pay particularly close attention to monthly changes in the bank's trim and median core measures and the share of CPI components rising at 3% or more.
"I'd be concerned if we were seeing more inflation coming through core goods," he said, describing products other than food and energy, like clothes and furniture.
The bank's business outlook and consumer surveys will help gauge Canadians' outlook for inflation and spending.

If they show evidence that firms and households are resilient, despite slower immigration and the tariff war with the US, it would ease worries about growth. If firms plan to pull back on hiring and investment spending, however, it could give the bank pause and suggest that the second quarter economic rebound growth won't last, said Taylor Schleich, director of economics and strategy at National Bank of Canada.
"They seem to be pretty confident that businesses have adapted," he said. "We'll see."

Officials will be concerned if the surveys express even higher inflation expectations. The central bank may also ask firms about their pricing behavior, including whether they expect to pass higher input costs on to customers.

Markets put the odds of a hike at the end of the month at about 30% as of Friday morning. Most economists don't see the central bank tightening borrowing costs just yet, though the consensus suggests hikes are likely to start sometime in 2027.
On Saturday, Macklem will speak to reporters from International Monetary Fund and World Bank meetings in Bangkok.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: US Interest Costs Hit Record $1 Trillion, Risking Debt Snowball
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Yash Roy

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The US government's debt interest burden reached a record high for fiscal 2026, eating up a growing share of federal revenue and risking a snowballing of borrowing that could leave the country more vulnerable to economic shocks.
Most Read from Bloomberg

For the year through September, net interest costs came to $1.05 trillion, up more than 8% from the $970 billion in fiscal 2025, Treasury Department data showed Friday. The Peter G. Peterson Foundation, a research group, sees the costs reaching 3.2% of gross domestic product, surpassing the previous record, reached in 1991. GDP figures for last quarter are due later this month.

The increase reflects both that there's a lot more debt to pay interest on — one key measure exceeds $32 trillion, some $10 trillion more than just five years ago — but also much higher interest rates. The average rate the government paid on marketable Treasuries was 3.52% at the end of September, more than double the 1.47% five years before.

What's worse is that current yields are even higher, with the current gauge from Bloomberg's US Treasuries index now around 5%. The rise in rates has prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent into extraordinary steps to contain the move, though economists argue the nation remains distant from crisis. Demand at debt auctions has proved solid, and higher borrowing costs aren't hindering credit flows.

"It doesn't seem like a crisis — it's kind of a slow eating away" of fiscal capacity, said Louise Sheiner, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and former economist at the Federal Reserve. What's unknown is the point at which "some lenders are going to decide not to lend to us — and if that happens, that could lead to a fiscal crisis," with the Treasury losing access to raise money from markets, she said.

Gennadiy Goldberg, head of US interest rates strategy at TD Securities, said one thing staving off deeper concerns for now is that the nation's nominal GDP growth rate — which is key for things like corporate revenues and tax receipts — is higher than US Treasury yields. The nominal year-on-year GDP gain for the second quarter was 6.3%. "A fiscal apocalypse is not upon us just yet," Goldberg wrote in a recent note.
Managing, for Now

"Somehow we're managing, even with interest rates going up," Congressional Budget Office Director Phillip Swagel said in an Oct. 8 event in Minneapolis. At the same time, he cautioned that deteriorating fiscal dynamics do leave the nation increasingly prone. "Anytime there's a negative shock, interest rates rise for whatever reason" there can be a "turbocharger effect."

In that scenario, the shock of higher rates "feeds into the deficit, feeds into the debt, feeds back into interest rates to the economy," said Swagel, whose agency in February projected that the debt-to-GDP ratio will hit a record surpassing 106% in 2030. The former Treasury official also said that, while he's been delivering the same fiscal message for a long while, the past two years, market participants have been more interested.

Interest costs are now one of the top three biggest item on the list of federal outlays, after having more than doubled since just 2022. It's only exceeded by Social Security and Medicare, the giant federal programs for older Americans, whose costs escalate each year as beneficiary rolls climb by the million. The Defense Department and Medicaid round out the top five.

The last time interest costs as a share of the debt were around current levels, American politics girded to address the challenge. President George H.W. Bush famously reneged on his no-new-taxes pledge by signing a package of increases in 1990, just before the interest-cost ratio peaked. His successor Bill Clinton went on to boost levies further in 1993.
Waiting on Catastrophe?

The end of the Cold War also saw a slump in spending on defense, bolstering the fiscal picture. By the late 1990s, a pickup in economic growth amid the diffusion of the internet and personal computing was propelling revenues.

Today, Bessent and other Trump administration officials have been touting the artificial intelligence boom as a growth stimulus that will help bring down the debt ratio. Budget experts, however, are skeptical. Spending on defense and entitlement programs appears set to keep climbing, while GDP gains aren't likely to be fast enough to stoke revenues sufficiently, they say.

"The problems only getting worse, so we shouldn't be debating whether to wait for the catastrophe — we should be working on it now," Brett Loper, executive vice president of policy at the Peterson Foundation. "It's going to be really hard to climb out of this problem."

This year's increase in net interest payments, at $81.4 billion, could be dwarfed if rates keep rising. The Fed is expected to hike its overnight benchmark rate — currently at 3.75% to 4% — at least once more, which would drive up the costs of the short-term debt Bessent has increasingly favored.
A 100 basis-point rise across the yield curve would drive up 2027 interest costs by $310 billion, according to calculations by TD Securities.

"I don't think a fiscal crisis is imminent, we still have a pretty strong economy," said Karen Dynan, a Harvard University economics professor who served at the Treasury in the Obama administration. And rates still aren't back to levels from three or four decades ago, she noted.

At the same time, "with debt so high, net interest payments really matter — they will lead to a snowballing of debt," she said. "The increase in interest rates and in interest payments relative to GDP, that may bring public pressure for action."

finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/uk-pay.headline: The UK Is Paying More Than Ever to Steady a Straining Power Grid
finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/uk-pay.author: William Mathis and Jessica Shankleman

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Britain's power grid came under unexpected pressure this week on what should have been a fairly unremarkable day.
Most Read from Bloomberg

There were no major, unexpected power-plant failures or extreme weather, and plenty of wind power was being generated in Scotland. But bottlenecks on the network meant not enough electricity could reach London and southeast England, forcing the grid operator to take emergency action on Monday to secure additional imports from France.

The episode exposed a longstanding shortcoming in Britain's electricity system: The country can have enough power overall and still struggle to get it where it's needed. The UK has built much of its growing supply of wind power far from where electricity demand is concentrated — and is adding wind farms faster than it can construct the infrastructure needed to carry that power south.

That mismatch is becoming increasingly expensive. In September, the UK paid a record of just over half a billion pounds to balance its power system, according to data compiled by LCP Delta. October could prove even more expensive, with actions taken on Tuesday alone costing £38.4 million ($51.2 million), a single-day record, the energy consultancy found.
"This is something we'll keep seeing," said Shivam Malhotra, head of power trading at LCP Delta. "We will see these records broken."

The mounting bill reflects what the National Energy System Operator pays to balance supply and demand and keep the network operating smoothly. A large part of that involves managing constraints: paying wind farms in Scotland to switch off because there isn't enough transmission capacity to carry their power south, and then paying far more for gas plants closer to major cities to fire up instead.

"These wind farms were built with very limited consideration of where that electricity would be consumed," said Jason Mann, senior managing director at FTI Consulting. "Those costs are locked in for generations."

This week offered a stark illustration of the problem. Britain had plenty of electricity. It just wasn't in the right place. Transmission infrastructure in southeast England that had been expected to return to service remained unavailable, according to NESO, further limiting the amount of electricity that could be moved into the region. Even as NESO sought additional supplies from France, electricity continued flowing out of the south of England to Belgium, the Netherlands and France through other connections.

Ultimately, consumers pick up the tab. Windy and sunny conditions can push wholesale power prices lower, but those savings can be eroded when grid bottlenecks force NESO to pay gas plants elsewhere to switch on.

The UK's Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh acknowledged the shortcomings of the current system at a parliamentary hearing this week, calling it "candidly not fit for purpose." But she pushed back against concerns that the strains could threaten supplies, saying she was "100% confident the lights won't go out this winter."

The resilience of the system has nevertheless come under scrutiny. Ofgem is investigating NESO's handling of an incident during a period of extreme heat in June, when tight power margins put the grid under pressure. No customers lost power, but the regulator is examining whether relevant security standards were met.
What's less clear is how quickly the underlying problems can be fixed.

Many of the grid's current issues can be traced to a policy implemented in 2010 under then-Energy Secretary Ed Miliband known as "connect and manage," according to FTI's Mann. The policy allowed renewable power projects to connect before all the grid infrastructure needed to carry their electricity to consumers was in place.

Successive governments of both major political parties then subsidized a rapid expansion of wind generation without a comparable buildout of transmission infrastructure. The result is a growing gap between where electricity is generated and where it's needed — and an increasingly costly job for NESO to bridge it.

The risk was identified even before the policy took effect. In 2008, John Mogg, then chairman of energy regulator Ofgem, wrote to Miliband warning that allowing more renewable generation to connect in Scotland before transmission capacity was expanded could cause constraint costs to "increase significantly."

Back then, Mogg cautioned that the cost of constraints had reached some £300 million. This year the figure could be 10 times that amount, based on data published by NESO and the grid operator's forecasts.

Last year, in a second stint as Energy Secretary, Miliband rejected a switch to a zonal electricity market, which would have introduced different power prices across Britain to better reflect the physical limitations of the grid. Higher prices in the south, for example, could signal gas plants there to switch on and electricity to flow into Britain through interconnectors when needed, rather than leaving NESO to correct for those imbalances after the market has settled.
With that reform off the table, the UK is instead relying heavily on building more transmission capacity between the north and south.

"The long-term choice for the UK is between investing once in modern grid infrastructure or continuing to pay for imported fossil fuels year after year," said Benj Sykes, UK chair of Danish offshore wind company Orsted A/S. The government and transmission operators need to accelerate grid upgrades, storage and other forms of flexibility, he said, both to improve energy security and "tackle the energy affordability challenge" facing consumers and businesses.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Burnham Finds His Plans to Focus on Britain Blown Up by Trump
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Alex Wickham and Chloe Chaplain

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Prime Minister Andy Burnham's bid to break from Keir Starmer's premiership by focusing more on UK domestic policy and less on global events is proving near impossible in Donald Trump's world.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The US president's latest gambit in the Russia-Ukraine war — striking a diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin and pressuring Kyiv to stop drone strikes on Russian oil refineries — has pushed foreign policy to the top of Burnham's agenda just three months into the job.

In a show of support to Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the premier hosted Ukraine's president in London this week and publicly vowed to help "repair bridges" between him and the US administration. Privately, however, UK officials described their view of a darker reality: Trump is simply not on their side on the fundamental issue of European security.

That's brought the "special relationship" between the US and UK to its lowest point in recent memory, leaving Burnham with a challenge that will define his premiership, according to one senior official, who like others for this story, was granted anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic matters. Any premier, even wartime leader Winston Churchill, would find the circumstances difficult and Burnham is a novice by comparison, the official said.

Burnham's first meeting with Trump in New York last month was a case in point. While the president was polite in front of the cameras, praising his counterpart as a "natural business person," behind-closed-doors conversations were more difficult as he railed against Britain's lack of support for his war in Iran, according to UK officials familiar with the matter.

Another example was the recent alleged plot targeting a British airbase used by the US. Trump said there was a joint US-UK intelligence operation tailing the suspects, while reports cited officials close to the White House as suggesting the threat related to plans for a spectacular drone attack. Neither reflected reality, British officials said.

"President Trump had a good meeting with Prime Minister Burnham at the United Nations, and our countries will continue working together on areas of mutual interest," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in an emailed statement.

Kelly said Trump "has done more than anyone to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to a close" and that by selling American-made arms to NATO allies, Trump is "generating billions of dollars for U.S. industries while getting Europe to take primary responsibility for its own defense."

Trump's latest pivot toward Russia leaves questions Burnham's government is struggling to answer, about how to handle the president and ensure Ukraine isn't pressured into accepting an unjust outcome to the war.

While Burnham has sought to focus on the issues voters say they care about the most, such as immigration and the cost of living, failure on the international stage could harm his popularity, according to Chris Hopkins, political director at pollster Savanta.

"The public tend to see foreign affairs and diplomatic relations as a fundamental part of the job, and therefore appearing strong and statesmanlike is the minimum expected," he told Bloomberg. "Appearing weak on the global stage, therefore, can have a calamitous impact on public perceptions, even when global issues generally do not drive public opinion."

That reinforces the importance of the US relationship. On taking office Burnham decided to follow Starmer's approach, espoused by the UK's National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, that Britain's unique relationship with the US means it is best served by pursuing quiet diplomacy to persuade Trump to take less hostile positions toward Europe, people familiar with the matter said.

Advocates of this strategy point to counterfactual scenarios that would have been much worse: Trump did not try to take Greenland by force, he hasn't tried to leave NATO or end all military and intelligence support for Ukraine, nor has he fully sided with Putin to impose defeat on Zelenskyy.

The starker truth is Britain has no credible alternative to trying to keep Trump onside, the people argued. Its security is more inextricably linked to US support than other European countries to the point that achieving fully sovereign capabilities is not realistic. In better times the relationship has helped Britain punch above its weight. Now it leaves it uniquely exposed, they said.

The UK's key foreign policy aim beyond the Ukraine war is ensuring the transatlantic alliance does not collapse because that would realize Russia's overarching strategic objective, an official said. Burnham's role is even more important now French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz are declining in influence, they said.

Yet with Ukraine saying it temporarily lost full access to the Elon Musk-owned Starlink system this week and Trump renewing his public criticisms of Zelenskyy, it's hard to argue the British strategy is having better than mixed results.

One difficulty reported by officials is that the change of UK leadership in July means diplomatic relationships have had to be restarted from scratch. Number 10 has detailed no phone calls between Burnham and Trump since the president's diesel deal, nor any call between the premier and other western European leaders. Officials also noted the lack of progress under the so-called Coalition of the Willing format of Ukraine's allies in recent months. UK pledges to secure more air defenses for Ukraine, including from the US, have yet to deliver results.

To be sure, Britain does not yet see the situation as dire. The US appears to have restored Starlink, officials said, and the UK will continue to argue that Trump should not cut off access to a key US early warning system that helps Ukraine defend against Russian attacks.

Zelenskyy also retains the ability to launch drone attacks on Russian oil refineries without US support, officials said. Russia is militarily and economically weak and desperate, and that is why Putin is so keen for Trump to increase pressure on Ukraine, they added. The UK is sending more long-range Storm Shadow missiles to Kyiv so it can continue to hit military targets inside Russia.
Longer-term, Burnham is looking to a post-Trump world and believes there will be a progressive resurgence in Europe and potentially the US.

"We've had a decade of populism that isn't working for people," he told Bloomberg in Kyiv in August. "The change I sense in Britain possibly is a change that's going to come a bit more around the world," he said. "The pendulum has to swing back."

While Trump faces his own domestic troubles with the mid-terms looming, Burnham is stuck with him as he tries to navigate a potentially decisive phase of the Ukraine war. An adverse outcome would hardly be his fault but it might end up being the story of his premiership.

finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/trump-.headline: Trump Waives Russia Energy Tariffs, Sanctions in Graham Law
finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/trump-.author: Alicia Diaz

paragraphs.text: Fri, October 16, 2026 at 5:49 PM PDT 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump waived massive tariffs linked to Russian energy exports mandated in a law that he signed last month, as the measures complicated his push to lower diesel prices ahead of the US midterm elections.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Trump on Friday invoked a waiver clause under the law, which was championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham as a way to punish Russia for its invasion of Ukraine.

"I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act. I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," Trump said in an executive order.

The measure gave Trump 30 days to impose 100% tariffs on all goods from the top five buyers of Russian crude. It would also slap sanctions on numerous Russian entities and impose 500% tariffs on all US imports of Russian energy products. That one month deadline was set to expire on Oct. 18.

Those provisions conflict with his plan — announced last week — to work with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release the country's diesel supplies into global markets. Trump is seeking to lower US diesel prices that are hovering at record highs weeks before the Nov. 3 elections.
