latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-17/.headline: SoCal braces for more Santa Ana winds as firefighters battle blazes
latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-17/.author: Iris Kwok, Ruben Vives, Karen Garcia, Hannah Fry

paragraphs.text: Firefighters are bracing for another day of Santa Ana winds and extreme temperatures as they continue to battle a blaze that destroyed six homes in south Orange County.

The Norte fire, which has burned more than 460 acres in the area of San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano, remained at 0% containment as of Friday evening, according to Orange County Fire Authority Fire Chief TJ McGovern. About 6,000 homes, and 16,000 residents, remain under an evacuation order.
“Our current objective is keeping the fire within its current footprint,” he said.
Firefighters were also dealing with fires on Camp Pendleton and in Malibu.

A red flag warning, indicating potentially hazardous fire weather, will remain in place through Saturday evening for many parts of Southern California. But forecasters say the most dangerous conditions could be behind us.

“In terms of winds, right now is the peak,” Chandler Price, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service San Diego office, said on Friday afternoon. “And then winds will gradually decrease early Saturday morning into the afternoon before finally calming.”

Last weekend, south Orange County received about an inch to an inch and a half of rainfall, but vegetation didn’t have enough time to absorb the moisture. Combined with low humidity, the dry vegetation is catching fire more easily and supported the Norte fire’s rapid spread early on.
The fire burned intensely through grass and chaparral, UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist Daniel Swain said Friday afternoon.

“We were talking about how the fire risk here was somewhat less, at least than it was in some other parts of Southern California where the rain had not occurred as recently,” Swain said in a livestream on YouTube. “But in this case, clearly the conditions have already dried out enough for significant, relatively high-intensity fire spread.”
Swain said this Santa Ana wind event doesn’t compare to those that fanned the flames of the Palisades and Eaton fires.
“It did rain last week, but it is still dry enough and windy enough for this to be a problem,” he said.
Officials are prepping for more potential fires Saturday.
The Los Angeles Fire Department has extended red flag parking restrictions in the city through Sunday morning.
The restrictions are intended to keep parked vehicles out of the roadway, providing access for first responders and people trying to evacuate in the event of a fire.
The Norte fire is burning in a hilly area in San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano, fueled by intense winds.
It moved so rapidly that some people had to flee with what they could quickly grab.
Linda Verraster was on the deck behind her home in San Clemente, just south of the evacuation zone, on Friday afternoon, watching for signs it might be time to leave.
Temperatures in the area were in the mid-90s and winds howled with gusts of up to 35 mph, a less-than-ideal situation for firefighters.
Verraster had already filled her cars with gas and began preparing what she would grab if the fire kept growing.
“We’re watching the wind. I’m getting my cat carriers ready just in case,” she said. “It’s not great.”

San Clemente Mayor Rick Loeffler said his city has been preparing ahead of fire season, deploying goats to chomp at brush on hillsides and ensuring a steady water supply is available for crews and helicopters.
“We’ve been cognizant of what can happen in the coastal city with canyons and Santa Ana winds,” he said. “So we’ve been working really hard to prepare ourselves as best we can.”
Loeffler encouraged people not under an evacuation order to stay home so the roads are clear for first responders.

“We want to be able to have the people that have to evacuate, and our public safety partners be able to get around the city. So the less traffic on our streets, the better. Hunker down, and I think we’re going to be OK,” he said.
U.S. Rep. Mike Levin (D-San Juan Capistrano) said his family was among those evacuated from their home due to the Norte fire.

“This is an incredible community, and I cannot tell you how grateful my wife and my mom and our two kids are ... for all the firefighters who worked hard today and every day. For all the sheriffs, for all the first responders. You saved our entire neighborhood today.”
Firefighters in Malibu are still dealing with a fire that broke out Thursday.

Containment on the Bryson fire, which has scorched 147 acres near Encinal Canyon Road since igniting, increased to 39% Friday evening, according to officials with the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection.

marketwatch.com/story/meet-the-home-buye.headline: Meet the home buyers totally unfazed by 7% mortgage rates

paragraphs.text: Individual investors and second-home buyers accounted for 1 in 5 home purchases in September - the highest share in a little over a year
While mortgage rates over 7% have everyday house hunters pulling back from the market, data suggest that real-estate investors are sticking it out.
In June, real-estate investor Justin Smith closed on a duplex in Roscoe, Ill. - about 90 miles west of Chicago - for $250,000. The rate on his 30-year fixed mortgage was 7%.

Smith, a 34-year-old real-estate broker who also owns three apartment buildings in Roscoe and nearby Rockford, told MarketWatch that smaller Midwestern cities in particular offer an easy way into real-estate investing, because the barrier to entry - namely, home prices - is relatively low. The average home value in Rockford, Ill., is about $185,000, according to Zillow's (Z) (ZG) estimates, compared to a national median value of about $366,000.
More importantly, "we have such a strong rental population," Smith said, meaning that many people in the area rent instead of own.

Smith isn't the only real-estate investor who's buying right now. While surging mortgage rates over 7% have everyday house hunters pulling back from the market, data suggest that real-estate investors are sticking it out.

In September, individual investors and second-home buyers accounted for 20% of home-purchase transactions - the highest share in a little over a year, according to the National Association of Realtors.

"Investors tend to pull back less than noninvestor buyers when conditions deteriorate," Hannah Jones, a senior economist at Realtor.com, told MarketWatch. "So their share of total buyers rises as higher mortgage rates squeeze out more noninvestor buyers." (Realtor.com is operated by News Corp subsidiary Move Inc.; MarketWatch publisher Dow Jones is also a subsidiary of News Corp.)

"There are opportunities for investors today that we haven't seen in years. Inventory is rising, sellers are cutting prices and negotiating leverage is shifting toward buyers," Michael Carbonare, another real-estate investor, told MarketWatch.

In September, the total for-sale housing inventory in the U.S. jumped to 1.6 million units, the highest level since November 2019, NAR said. About 43% of sellers were cutting prices as of Oct. 12, according to separate data from ParclHQ.
"It's a good time to be looking for motivated sellers, buying right and structuring deals that make financial sense," Carbonare said.
Related: U.S. wealth has shifted to stocks from homes. There are big reasons to worry.

Relatively small-time real-estate investors - those who own three to nine properties - have been more active than large landlords. About 14.5% of home purchases made in August were by smaller real-estate investors, which was up from 13.6% a year ago, according to Cotality, a real-estate data-analytics company.
In contrast, 9% of purchases were by medium-sized investors, and 2% were by large investors.

One factor driving some investors to buy houses now is strong rental demand. Rents nationally are trending upwards: In September, the typical rent rose 2.7% from the same time a year ago to around $1,900, Zillow found in an analysis.
"Elevated mortgage rates have pushed home shoppers straight into the arms of rentals," Kara Ng, a senior economist at Zillow, said in the report.
The company estimated that demand for single-family rentals rose nearly 22% in September from the previous year, and 10% for multifamily or apartment rentals.

In Chicago, where the typical rent grew 4.7% in September from last year to about $2,200, according to Zillow, 66-year-old Tom Moran is putting down $500,000 for a $2 million, six-unit apartment building in the city - the latest addition to his portfolio of 18 other buildings.

The mortgage rate was 6.625% for the bank-portfolio loan Moran used to finance the purchase, though he said the rate wasn't a concern for him. "It's just a number," Moran, a real-estate investor and broker who is now under contract on the property, told MarketWatch.

"Interest rates go up, interest rates go down - but in general, real estate is a long-term buy," he said. "I look at real estate as basically like a little business ... so I'm not worried about the initial return."
Having bought his first property in the late 1980s when the 30-year mortgage rate averaged over 10%, Moran said he's accustomed to high-rate environments.

As part of his due diligence before his latest purchase, Moran called up a few mortgage lenders for quotes before he pulled the trigger. The rates he was quoted ranged from mid-6% to over 7% - but he said he was unfazed.

"People freak out" when they see the 7% handle, Moran noted. On the loan he was pursuing, the rate going up a quarter point, from 6.875% to 7.125%, amounted to a roughly $250 hit per month for him. "It's not a deal-breaker," he said.

Do you have questions about real estate and home-buying that you would like to see covered in MarketWatch? We'd love to hear from you. You can write to us at readerstories@marketwatch.com. A reporter may be in touch to learn more. MarketWatch will not attribute your answers to you by name without your permission.

latimes.com/politics/story/2026-10-17/bi.headline: Big assertions, sharp exchanges, little clarity define DOJ election battle with California
latimes.com/politics/story/2026-10-17/bi.author: Kevin Rector

paragraphs.text: First came the letter from acting Deputy Atty. Gen. Trent McCotter — just three weeks before the Nov. 3 election — demanding that Los Angeles County’s top elections official launch a sweeping investigation into thousands of voters the Trump administration alleges are “likely noncitizens” and withhold their ballots in the meantime.

The letter arrived with a thumb drive purporting to contain the list of voters in question, and a handwritten note providing the password. Dean Logan, head of the L.A. County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk’s office, said accessing the device broke security protocols, and he wouldn’t open it.

Then came an Excel spreadsheet, listing some 20,000 voters by name, date of birth and address. It appeared to contain voters from across the state of California, not just L.A. County, and provided no information on the Trump administration’s methodology for questioning those voters. Logan’s office again pushed back.

“We cannot withhold or refuse to count ballots based solely on unverified allegations, nor can we disregard the legal requirements governing our election — and we certainly have no authority to act on records that are outside of our jurisdiction,” Logan said.

On Friday, the back and forth escalated yet again, when the Justice Department warned in a letter to L.A. County attorneys that county elections officials who tabulate ballots from the flagged voters could face criminal prosecution for being “aiders and abettors to a federal crime.”

For the last week, Trump administration officials and California election leaders have been locked in a fiercely contentious standoff over alleged election fraud that independent elections experts say is like nothing they have ever seen before.

The battle — which escalated into a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by the Justice Department against the state, Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Logan — features striking assertions of official misconduct. They include willful indifference to systemic election fraud among California officials, as alleged by Trump officials, and a nefarious effort by the administration to “lay the groundwork” for questioning any unfavorable election results next month, as alleged by California leaders and independent elections experts.

With little public clarity around the voters whose registration is being contested and how the administration came to question their eligibility, the debate has centered instead on the efficacy of vetting voter rolls right before an election and the increasingly bitter claims of political meddling from the many federal, state and local officials involved.
“More dangerous nonsense from a President losing his grip on reality,” Gov. Gavin Newsom posted on X.

“No, Governor. You are violating federal law by facilitating voting by noncitizens,” responded First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, whose office is leading the lawsuit.

“Mail ballots are already in most voters’ hands, and Election Day is less than three weeks away. Every count, recount, hand count, lawsuit, and audit has found that there’s no widespread voter fraud in the U.S. The Trump Admin’s last-minute demands are meritless, and we look forward to making our case in court,” California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta wrote on the same platform.

“We produced a list of 20,000 noncitizens on your voter rolls, and your response is ‘it’s too late’ because you already mailed the ballots. Not good enough,” Essayli shot back. “It’s a violation of the U.S. Constitution and federal law for California to dilute the votes of American citizens.”
Both sides have accused the other of being unreasonable and of ignoring practical concerns about voting and election security, though in very different ways.

Trump administration officials have said their effort “should not be controversial,” and reflects a common-sense approach to election oversight. “The law is clear, aliens in the United States cannot vote in federal elections,” McCotter said.

In its lawsuit, the Justice Department argued it is “not practicable or feasible” for the federal government to investigate “thousands, let alone tens of thousands, of individuals” before the November election alone, so California and local officials should be required to help them do it.

California officials — joined by independent elections experts — have accused the Trump administration of breaking the law to bolster a grand election conspiracy the president has propped up for years without evidence, including by trying to purge voters from rolls right before an election.

David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, said the National Voter Registration Act prohibits states from conducting systemic maintenance of voter lists within 90 days of an election, and that the U.S. Supreme Court recently affirmed that limit.
Bonta said the timing of the Justice Department’s demands “reeks of desperation and bad faith.”

State officials and election experts also have questioned why Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested California had some 190,000 noncitizen voters on its rolls as recently as July if the number now stands at 20,000.

“What happened to the 170,000? You just got those wrong?” Bonta said. He also noted with derision that the administration’s lawsuit repeatedly hedges its assertions by saying that federal officials “believe” that noncitizens “may be” registered in California.
“You believe, or you know?” Bonta said. “They may be or they are?”

Kiersten Pels, a Justice Department spokesperson, said the 20,000 flagged voters “are the ones that have been manually verified” as ineligible, but that number “can and will go up” as federal authorities continue their work. She referred additional questions about the figures to Homeland Security, which did not respond to questions.

Becker said the administration’s figures “should be treated with serious skepticism,” given similar claims falling apart elsewhere. He cited a Homeland Security claim of about 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada voter rolls dropping to 185 voters before Nevada officials investigated and found every single one of those voters was a citizen.
California officials have not shown a similar interest in launching their own investigation.

In a letter to McCotter, Weber wrote that treating the 20,000 voters on the Justice Department’s list as “ineligible until proven otherwise” would not only violate the 90-day quiet period before an election, but amount to “an unprecedented suspension — and even denial — of voting rights.”

She said if the Trump administration has any proof for its claims, California would “review that evidence and any supporting data or methodology” and “take the appropriate steps in compliance with federal and state law” to address any problems. “However, I will not disenfranchise thousands of Californians — or order any county elections official to do so — based solely upon an unsupported and likely inaccurate ‘belie[f]’ that certain voters are ‘likely’ noncitizens.”

A spokesperson for Logan’s office said Friday that it was reviewing the Justice Department’s spreadsheet — in part to determine how many of the voters are actually in L.A. County — but had yet to receive requested information on the methodology used for flagging those voters.

Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar, chair of the Democratic Assn. of Secretaries of State, said the Trump administration’s efforts in California are “another attempt by the federal government to harass and intimidate elections officials,” and that their timing is “obviously a political attempt” to prevent voters — particularly Latino voters —from holding the Trump administration accountable for its failed leadership.

But he also said that California officials — to the extent they can under the law, and working closely with Bonta — should work to refute the Trump administration’s claims through their own review of the data, just as Nevada officials did.
“We are not afraid to defend our elections,” he said. “And California should take that same approach. You cannot be reactive to these situations. You have to be strategic.”

latimes.com/business/story/2026-10-17/el.headline: Elon Musk just showed off a flying car. Here's what to know about the Tesla Roadster
latimes.com/business/story/2026-10-17/el.author: Caroline Petrow-Cohen

paragraphs.text: Nearly a decade after Tesla first announced its second-generation Roadster, the company debuted the car in a flashy demo that seemed to challenge the laws of physics.
The sleek white sports car drove upside down, thrust itself into the air and performed a flip over a lineup of other Tesla vehicles.
It accelerated from 0 to 60 miles per hour in under a second, with Tesla Chief Executive Elon Musk saying it will eventually be able to travel as fast as half the speed of sound.

“Let’s take it to the limits and way past the limits,” Musk said at Thursday’s event in McGregor, Texas. “You’re gonna see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company.”
Here’s what to know about Tesla’s latest electric model.
When will the Roadster actually be available to customers?
At the demo event, Musk said production will begin in 2028.
The second-generation Roadster, a nod to the company’s first-ever car, was originally unveiled in 2017. The plan then was for production to begin in 2020.

“Delaying something for nine years, if that was Mazda, no one would stand for that. Tesla just seems to get a pass on everything like that,” said Brian Moody, an analyst at Capital One Auto Navigator.
The original Roadster hit roads in 2008 and was discontinued in 2012.
Tesla does not have a good track record of meeting its own deadlines. Musk has long promised to perfect self-driving technology and make it available in existing Tesla models.

Since 2017, Tesla has collected numerous deposits of $50,000 from customers who wanted to reserve their Roadster. Many of those customers have taken to social media to complain that the wait has been too long.
Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, posted a series of screenshots on X in 2025 that showed him asking Tesla for a refund of his Roadster reservation. His email to the company bounced back.
“I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays. But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait,” Altman wrote on X.
Will the Roadster really be able to fly?
At the Texas demo, the Roadster didn’t exactly soar through the air — it thrust itself off the ground for brief moments using thrusters on the bottom of the vehicle.
The version of the car that’s capable of leaving the ground won’t be publicly available and does not have approval for use on public roads.

Dubbed the “Rocket” package, the thruster-enabled Roadster will be sold only to invited customers. It will seat one person and be equipped with a multi-mode suction system and cold-gas thrusters that can boost it into the air.
The technology is a collaboration between Tesla and SpaceX, both run by Musk.
“A tease like that has a little bit more reality to stand on when it’s coming from a company that can send things to the moon and bring them back intact,” Moody said.
The “Thrust” package, which will see a limited release, comes with thrusters positioned on the rear of the vehicle that can propel it forward at record speeds.
“It’s gonna crush every track record that’s ever existed,” Musk said Thursday.

Customers can now reserve a “Performance” version of the Roadster that can be driven on regular roads. Musk did not announce a price for the vehicle, but it is expected to cost hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Could the Roadster boost Tesla’s faltering sales?
Tesla’s electric vehicle sales have been falling, and Musk has made clear he’s orienting the future of his company around AI, self-driving technology and robotics.

The company recently discontinued its Model S and Model X electric vehicles, and in turn unveiled the Cybercab, a golden robotaxi that can carry two passengers and lacks driver’s parts like a steering wheel and gas pedal.
The new Roadster demo gave Tesla shares a short boost, but they quickly came back to Earth. Its stock price fell 2% Friday to trade near $355.
Like the original Roadster, the new version isn’t intended to be a mass-market vehicle, said iSeeCars.com analyst Karl Brauer. It’s likely to cost more than $250,000.
“This car, like most exotic cars, does not pay the bills,” Brauer said. “They’re supposed to be attention-getters. They’re supposed to reflect the advanced capabilities of the company.”
The Roadster could generate new excitement around the company, but it won’t make revenues surge.

Though Tesla has die-hard fans, Musk’s reputation was battered in 2025 when he briefly led President Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency. An overall cooling of the electric-vehicle market under the Trump administration has also slowed sales of mainstream Tesla models.
“His last all-new vehicle, the Cybertruck, everyone has pretty much agreed that’s an official flop,” Brauer said. “From a reputation point of view, Musk does need this one to be a hit.”

latimes.com/food/story/2026-10-17/takeou.headline: Where to find the best takeout sushi in Los Angeles
latimes.com/food/story/2026-10-17/takeou.author: Jenn Harris

paragraphs.text: So much grab-and-go sushi has an instantly recognizable stench. A sharp, sweet, slightly sulfurous aroma that involuntarily wrinkles the nose. It’s the same scent regardless of the contents in your plastic clamshell. If swiped from a refrigerated case, the California roll and the pieces of rubbery nigiri all smell the same. Even the stuff from the best Japanese markets (and a few chain sushi restaurants) will supply that familiar whiff to varying degrees.

I braced myself for the smell when I walked into the new Tiger’s Den, a Japanese market and restaurant that opened in the center of Koreatown in May. Behind a long counter, a cluster of chefs slice fish for nigiri, and splay more tiles of tuna and salmon over boxes of sushi rice for chirashi. As soon as a roll or row of sushi is formed or cut, it’s packaged and placed in an open refrigerated case near the register.

You jockey for position with other people in line to peruse the minute’s selection. The last time I was in, the four people in front of me demolished the case. But a few minutes later, there was more.

The chefs make sushi throughout the day, and the assortment varies. There might be futomaki, delightfully oversized rolls of crisp, lightly pickled vegetables, tuna and salmon. Or slices of torched salmon over sushi rice. What you won’t find is that familiar takeout sushi smell.

“We use Nishiki premium rice and we control it at every step,” says owner Sam Koo, a veteran chef who opened his first sushi restaurant more than two decades ago. “That’s why the shari doesn’t have that smell,” referring to the seasoned, vinegared rice that forms the foundation of sushi.

Koo’s team has decades of experience making sushi, with the greenest employee boasting 15 years behind a sushi counter. The nigiri mirror the meticulousness found at some of the city’s most lauded restaurants. Pieces of fish are hand sliced to the ideal thickness and length, and beautifully adorned with garnishes that dazzle the eye and strategically heighten every bite. A tiny heap of yuzu and black salt sits atop each piece of sweet shrimp. Hot, sharp yuzu kosho is dotted over tender octopus.

The shari is balanced, lightly sweet and subtly salty with a savoriness that enhances whatever fish is draped over its surface. And the quick turnover ensures that the rice’s temperature never dips too chilly. It keeps its texture, squeezed between fish and nori in the maki, with grains that don’t clump together or mush.

You could view the sushi case at Tiger’s Den as a meditation on the omakase format, with Koo’s history and tastes revealed through the selection on the shelves. There is no spicy tuna roll, because Koo doesn’t eat them. He sources his fish daily from two local wholesale seafood distributors, filling the case with whatever is freshest, and his favorite.

A negihama roll brims with chopped yellowtail studded with scallions, and enough fish to nearly obscure the rice. Fatty tuna collapses on the tongue, with salty pops of caviar and green onion. Lightly torched salmon belly is slightly smokey and ultra buttery.

The chef’s special chirashi boxes are striking, opulent collections of the day’s bounty. Recently a box showcased sweet, custardy amaebi, salmon belly, chum ikura, uni, toro, Hokkaido hotate, octopus and kizami wasabi adorned with various flowers and pickles.

The casual setup and price points at Tiger’s Den swing the sushi pendulum away from ultra luxury and back toward its origins in Japan as a quick, working-class meal. I shy away from using the word “affordable” when evaluating the price of any meal out, because it’s relative. Instead, I will say that the pricing feels just. The chirashi boxes range from $23 to $55, while the rolls start at $5.

Hidden at the back of the dining room, along the wall of Japanese pantry products and behind a display of snacks is a narrow display of bento. Here, you’ll find musubi filled with squares of Spam and fluffy tamago, and golden nuggets of karaage that taste of ginger and soy under an uber crunchy coating. Or grilled mackerel, eel and salmon over rice with tsukemono, and caramelized yellowtail and salmon collars. Everything is priced between $4 and $11.

“It’s important to sell good quality stuff for a good price,” says Koo, who decided to lean into the hybrid restaurant and market model after closing all five of his former restaurants during the pandemic. “Most people are having a hard time surviving right now. I’m trying to keep lower prices so more customers can come and try my food.”
Koo credits his good vendor relationships with helping him control expenses. He also refuses to spend any money on advertising or marketing.
“A lot of my friends who own restaurants told me that you need to court influencers,” he says. “But if the food is good and reasonably priced, then someone coming will tell their family and friends.”
Consider this me telling my family and friends.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/st.headline: 'Sense and Sensibility' review: Succeeds on strength of its sisters
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/st.author: Glenn Whipp

paragraphs.text: The days are growing shorter, and, in between heat waves and Kelvin waves, you can almost feel autumn in the air and with it, the chance to put the kettle on without fear of heatstroke and cozy up to the idea that there’s yet another wave of Jane Austen adaptations upon us.

Austen will never go out of style because we’re not going to reach a point when we stop worrying about money, status and the gobsmacking difficulty of telling someone you love them. Earlier this year, BBC One gave us a “Pride and Prejudice” spinoff, “The Other Bennet Sister.” In December, Netflix will present a six-episode limited series of the novel itself. And in between, we have a new film version of “Sense and Sensibility,” which dares to trod on the same hallowed ground as the 1995 Ang Lee movie, a film that won Emma Thompson a screenplay Oscar, introduced most audiences to Kate Winslet and confirmed that there are few things more pleasurable than a flustered Hugh Grant.

How do you top that? You don’t. But more than 30 years on, there’s still room for another check-in with the Dashwood sisters. If you haven’t already met, that’s Elinor (Daisy Edgar-Jones), prudent, practical, the “sense” of the family, and Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles), passionate and impulsive, the “sensibility.” Of course, as Whitman and Bob Dylan have noted, people are not just one thing. They contain multitudes, and so too do the Dashwood sisters. Much of the pleasure of Austen’s novel and this new adaptation, directed by Georgia Oakley and written by Diana Reid, comes from watching the fiercely bonded young women navigate their temperamental differences and arrive at a place of mutual understanding.
With due respect to the Dashwoods’ suitors (save for that scoundrel Willoughby), this is the love story of Oakley’s “Sense and Sensibility,” the one between the sisters. And it is deeply felt.

If you know your Austen, you know that financial insecurity drives the narrative. Mrs Dashwood (Caitríona Balfe) and her three daughters, Elinor, Marianne and mischievous young Margaret (Bodhi Rae Breathnach) are forced to leave their sumptuous Sussex estate and move to a humble cottage in Devon after Mr. Dashwood dies and their property passes to the sisters’ half brother (Tom Brooke) and his greedy wife, Fanny (Stacy Martin, relishing every wicked moment). It’s not fair. But them’s the rules in Regency England.

Oakley delights in the move to the country and gives her “Sense and Sensibility” more of a windswept, autumnal Brontë feel than we saw in the actual Brontë adaptation, Emerald Fennell’s “Wuthering Heights,” earlier this year. Oakley favors natural lighting and minimal makeup, lacing the film with shots of critters and insects going about their business. Plenty of bees, plenty of bonnets — though, thankfully for the women, no overlap between the two.

Love is buzzing in the air too, with Marianne falling for the cad Willoughby (Frank Dillane), despite it being obvious that you couldn’t trust him with an unattended farthing, and Elinor waiting (and waiting) for the shy Edward (George MacKay) to declare his intentions. (If you measure your Edwards by the force of your desire to leap at the screen and shake some sense into him, MacKay is aces.) Also waiting — or more accurately, lurking — in the background is the brooding Col. Brandon (Norwegian actor Herbert Nordrum), who deeply admires Marianne’s passion but is too stiff and silent and, frankly, weird to declare his intentions. Nordrum (“The Worst Person in the World”) makes you really root for the big lug.

The supporting cast, which also includes Fiona Shaw stealing every scene as the gossipy, generous Mrs. Jennings, is terrific. But the success of any “Sense and Sensibility” depends on the rapport between the sisters, and both actors deliver. Edgar-Jones makes us feel the yearning beneath Elinor’s calm reserve and Creed-Miles dazzles, conveying Marianne’s open-hearted abandon. (She’s the daughter of Samantha Morton, so this is quite the year for the family.) No, they don’t look at all alike, but their sibling dynamic feels fresh and alive.

Will this new adaptation win the hearts of those who consider the 1995 film a sacred text? Maybe? Thompson’s screenplay used precious few lines from Austen’s novel; she preferred to mimic the author’s style. This “Sense and Sensibility” takes itself, and Austen’s novel, a little more seriously. It stands apart. Diehards might find fault with something or other, but, to quote the author, you’d have to possess a “most forbidding, disagreeable countenance” not to be charmed.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/st.headline: 'La Bola Negra' review: Sprawling epic charts gay-related stories in three eras
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/st.author: Mark Olsen

paragraphs.text: A self-consciously grand, sweeping epic about some of the most intimate and personal aspects of people’s lives, “La Bola Negra” explores the strands that bind generations together in unexpected ways. Using the history of gay male desire in different time periods — dangerous, clandestine, outlawed and at long last fitfully accepted — the film examines legacy and what gets handed down across time.

The story takes place during different time periods in Spain, opening in 1937, skipping back to 1932 and leaping ahead to 2017, then moving as a time-tumbling tale among the three strands with fluid transitions becoming a defining trait of the film’s storytelling. (The ping of a Grindr app notification when we first enter the modern world is both cheeky and uniquely ties the eras together.)

Directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, known collectively as Los Javis, are prolific television creators and media personalities in their native Spain, with “La Bola Negra” their second feature film following the 2017 religious-themed musical comedy “La Llamada.” This latest project is co-written with Alberto Conejero, whose play “La piedra oscura” was a point of inspiration along with the life and work of gay dissident poet and playwright Federico García Lorca.

The film opens in 1937 during the Spanish Civil War as a small rural village prepares to welcome Italian comrades but is instead met by gunfire and bombs. A young trumpet player, Sebastián (played by the singer-songwriter known as Guitarricadelafuente, making his film debut), is soon conscripted to fight for the fascists. Earlier, in 1932, a young man named Carlos (Milo Quifes) wants to be accepted by an exclusive men’s club, but his membership is repeatedly rejected because of suspicions that he is homosexual. Then in 2017, Alberto (Carlos González), a failed playwright turned historian, receives an unexpected inheritance from a grandfather he never knew.

All three stories are revealed to be connected in some way to Lorca, who was murdered at the beginning of the fighting. The film reimagines the circumstances around his unfinished play, “La Bola Negra,” transforming it into a connection bridging generations.

As the three strands begin to come together, the movie truly hits its stride, once Alberto begins to understand the importance of the historic papers he has been left and how they came to be in his grandfather’s possession. The story gains a sense of momentum and inevitability as these disconnected tales suddenly become part of a continuous thread.

Los Javis, working with editor Alberto Gutiérrez, keep things moving, and the film’s two-and-a-half-hour running time moves at a surprisingly brisk pace. Penélope Cruz arrives for a few scenes as a wartime cabaret singer — her performance for a group of cheering soldiers is a burst of bawdy energy. She also has some insightful words of wisdom for Sebastián. Glenn Close, speaking in Spanish, later arrives briefly as an American literary historian who understands the importance of Alberto’s discoveries. Actor and comedian Julio Torres also brings a lively presence to his few scenes as Alberto’s boyfriend.

Along with a crafts team including cinematographer Gris Jordana, production designer Roger Bellés and costume designer Ana López Cobos, Los Javis have an eye for bold, distinctive images, often evincing a sense of curiosity and desire: what it is to look at something with wanting eyes. But many of the film’s most evocative images, often involving groups of soldiers, handsome and glistening and in varying stages of undress, remain just that — images without a strong connection to the larger storytelling.

“La Bola Negra” rolls in amid a wave of expectations that has been rising ever since it received a rapturous 20-minute ovation after its premiere at the Cannes Film Festival, where Los Javis also picked up the directing prize. Now the film arrives as Spain’s entry for the Academy Awards and with a commitment for an unprecedented extended theatrical release from its distributor Netflix.

Which could all be just empty awards-season positioning were it not for the fact that the film does have such a rhapsodic and tender way about it. Los Javis use the present to shine a light on the past — and the past to help explain the present. The movie is about how history can be not only a cycle but an evolution, moving us toward a better understanding of ourselves and each other.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/st.headline: 'You Can See Everything' review: This combative doc draws blood
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/st.author: Amy Nicholson

paragraphs.text: In the mindbending documentary “You Can See Everything,” comedian Nathan Fielder and professed inventor Elizabeth Holmes sit in her beach house staring at each other like gunslingers. Fielder is the creator of the TV series “The Rehearsal” and “Nathan for You” who constructs discombobulating sham realities that include bogus businesses such as Dumb Starbucks. Holmes is the former billionaire CEO of Theranos who pretended she’d built a revolutionary blood testing machine to squeeze investors for a few dollars more.

Each is an expert in the con. But Fielder is deadpan and cold where Holmes is earnest and warm — and he’s been nominated for Emmys while, in May of 2023 when the film begins, she’s about to serve an 11-year sentence in federal prison. As the camera cuts between close-ups of his narrowed eyes and her big, blue ones, Fielder tries to suss whether he can trust the famous fibber to be honest with him. The showdown is riveting.
“You’re being real right now?” Fielder asks, dubious.
Holmes beams. “I’m always being real,” she swears with a smile.
Her charm hits Fielder in the gut. His face stays neutral yet you can see his own confidence bleed out across the screen.

Co-directed by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim (“Primetime”), “You Can See Everything” is the closest Fielder has come to making a traditional documentary. A thrillingly cringe-tastic interviewer, he blurts out blunt questions like a bungee jumper leaping off a bridge, including asking Holmes’ romantic and business partner Billy Evans, the heir to a San Diego boutique hotel chain, whether it’s possible a woman convicted of fraud might be with him for his money.

At nearly three hours long, “You Can See Everything” won’t bore you for a minute. The hook is right there in the title, Fielder’s challenge to the audience: Here’s how Holmes held up to his scrutiny — do we think she’s telling the truth? But be alert. Fielder remains a trickster. One shot in particular proves you can see everything while being blind to what you’re actually watching.

In the first half of the movie, Holmes and Evans, the father of her two young children, give the small crew complete access to their lives during her last weeks of freedom, including inviting Fielder to sleep in their guest bedroom. It’s an act of “radical transparency,” Evans says. As evidence, there’s a fully nude shot of Evans in the shower, testifying to the intimacy the subjects claim they’re granting the team and the confidence they have that the documentary will make them look great. (Evans also boasts that he’s “excellent” in the sack.)

Holmes maintains both her innocence and her eerie smile, a rictus of empathy. She constantly nods, subliminally snake-charming the listener into a sense of agreement. That assessment might be fair or it might be her reputation making you over-analyze her tics. Doubling down, she even insists she’s never told a lie in her life — a claim that momentarily leaves Fielder at a loss for words.

Yet at times, Holmes really does appear to be sincere. Once she surrenders herself to the Bryan Federal Prison Camp in Texas (where, in an unmentioned coincidence, Epstein collaborator Ghislane Maxwell is also incarcerated), the tone shifts into film noir as Fielder struggles to reconcile Elizabeth Holmes’ dual identities. Is she the sweet-natured scientist, the only version of her he’s ever met, or a femme fatale who may still be running a scam?

“It’s personal,” Fielder says of his fixation. How frustrating that he of all people — the dark prince of pranks — may be Holmes’ latest patsy. Composer Ari Balouzian borrows bits of Bernard Herrmann’s violin score from “Vertigo” while cinematographer David Bolen makes the audience hold its breath by framing an image of Fielder and Holmes like they might kiss.

When the movie’s style gets weird, that’s when Fielder is most in his wheelhouse. Stop reading now if you want to preserve the surprise. Micro-analyzing his encounters with Holmes, he reenacts them with an actor, Amanda Seyfried, whose emotional intensity blows into the film like a gust of fresh air. Seyfried, of course, won an Emmy and a Golden Globe for playing Holmes in the 2022 miniseries “The Dropout.” The twists to come, however, feel as much like last year’s naughty hit “The Housemaid,” the domestic thriller in which Seyfried played a shady wife with a marriage made of lies.

Evans initially seems to think they’re participating in a project closer to Netflix’s glossy portrait of Meghan Markle and Prince Harry. The couple doesn’t know much about humor, pop culture or Fielder himself. Fumbling to figure out what makes him tick, Evans attempts to neg the provocateur as someone who lacks the passion to think differently. (Evans may also be the person who used Holmes’ social media account to write a flattering post calling JD Vance “Lisan al-Gaib,” revealing he’s entirely missed the point of “Dune.”)

But thinking differently is Fielder’s awkward superpower. Sooner or later, all of his projects circle around to his concern that he’s simply wired to be unpleasant. His interactions with Holmes are pure cringe comedy, like when she starts to cry perhaps a bit on cue and he stiffly sputters, “Do you want, like, a tissue?” For the record, he brings her one.

As a viewer, the biggest strike against Holmes is this documentary’s very existence. Whether or not you think she’s guilty of fraud, she is about to be separated from her infant and toddler until they’re in grade school. Who on Earth would genuinely want Fielder, the human equivalent of a skunk, to crash their last moments with their loved ones as he does his darnedest to stink up the place?

Fielder is most comfortable as the film’s villain, shooting himself lurking in the couple’s house like “Halloween’s” Michael Myers. At times, his presence does feel monstrous. In one scene, he needles Evans about whether he thinks his soulmate has ever lied to him while Holmes is on the phone in the next room, tearing up as she asks how often she’ll be able to bathe in prison.

The film doesn’t drill into the technical details of Theranos beyond one dizzying scene where Fielder tries to pin Holmes down on exactly what she meant when she said her machine can run hundreds of different tests. She means it just as I would if I bragged I can benchpress a beer keg — that is, once I strength-train beyond my piddly 5 lb dumbbells.

Instead, it tilts into becoming a caper flick as Seyfried’s commitment to understanding her character’s motivation inspires the actor to invite herself along. The drama they uncover is psychological, as befits an era where Silicon Valley CEOs are closer to cult leaders than engineers, making their cash from being televangelists for their IPOs. And both are attuned to the moments when Evans lets his aggravation slip. One scene is a doozy.

Ultimately, suspicion reigns. “You Can See Everything” is an absorbing study of public presentation and private doubts, a documentary that asks more questions than it answers. I hope Fielder will smile and nod approvingly at me if I say I left the film distrusting him, too, especially Seyfried’s re-staging of a long monologue Holmes delivered in prison where recording devices aren’t allowed. Can we believe that Holmes really did say, “I’m tired of having other people speak for me,” or was that laugh line written by the master manipulator himself? I’m now as paranoid as he is — and what a pleasure.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/tv/story/.headline: 'VisionQuest' review: Intellect over emotions, not unlike a synthezoid
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/tv/story/.author: Robert Lloyd

paragraphs.text: Regular readers of this space will know that I don’t pay much attention to the Marvel Cinematic Universe, or the comic books that inspire it, there being way too much to remember, especially since they keep rebooting the timeline and redesigning characters, canonically, except as is necessary to review Marvel’s television shows, which I greet with anticipation and watch with approval.

Where the movies are big, loud, overpopulated machines, the TV series are full of interesting ideas, weird notions and good comedy and give their characters room to breathe. IP cross-references aside, they can stand on their own. They don’t always last long, even some of the best of them — that’s show business, now more than ever — but you can be more or less sure that another will come along soon enough.

Premiering Wednesday on Disney+, “VisionQuest” is a sequel to “WandaVision,” the first of these shows — it began the MCU’s Phase Four, if those words mean anything to you. It’s not a bad idea to familiarize yourself with the former show to take the full measure of this one; there are also some elements of the spun off “Agatha All Along,” which I had forgotten completely. It might answer some questions you’ll have during “VisionQuest,” but the dramatic intentions and character relations are plain enough.

As a story of artificial intelligence, “VisionQuest” has some currency, though past the idea that these systems can work for good or bad, it’s not really about that — nobody is talking about guardrails here, which in this genre would just be a case of closing the pen after the electric sheep have got out. The androids, or synthezoids, here are presented for the most part in human form, which is easier on the eyes, the budget and the actors, and gives them room to act. (They don’t act like robots, either.) The show’s big themes are personal, not political: identity, love, loss, fathers and sons, family freedom, connection and being “real.”

Anyway, I’m not going to pass on any series that features both Emily Hampshire (Stevie Budd on “Schitt’s Creek”) and Diane “Cunk” Morgan in its cast. (No offense to the rest of the cast. Everyone does their bit.) Also attractive was the fact the show was created by Terry Matalas, a director and showrunner on “Star Trek: Picard,” another fine series about organic and synthetic life-forms, and creator of Syfy’s “12 Monkeys” series (in which Hampshire starred).

To catch you up, Vision (Paul Bettany) is a synthezoid and the late lover of the witch Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen). In “WandaVision,” a grieving Wanda cast a spell on a New Jersey town based on a sitcom idea of perfection — the early episodes featured pastiches of “The Dick Van Dyke Show,” “Bewitched” and “The Brady Bunch” — and installed a reborn Vision there as her husband; they had twins, Tommy and Billy. This didn’t prove to be such a great idea (though it made for excellent television), and in the end she removed her hex on the town and Vision dissolved into the ether.

Somehow he has de-dissolved, and we find him working in an Edinburgh pub, looking like an ordinary Englishman, rather than a mechanical man. (A “W+V” inside a heart, carved into the furniture, remains from a scene in “Avenger: Infinity Wars.”) Still, something is off: “I have his memories but not his feelings,” Vision says of his earlier self. “I have his face, but not his virtue. All I can feel is the weight of him. His legacy, his worthiness, his name.” But he’s a caring sort, even if he’s going through the motions, who believes that “integrity and respect and honesty are the key measures of character.”

At the same time, he lives in a world inside his … I guess you’d call it his head … in a big house with a staff of avatars, “sentient autonomous AIs who have complementary personalities that are conducive to problem-solving,” in the tradition of Doc Savage or the Impossible Mission Force or the animated emotions in “Inside Out.” Their names are represented onscreen in capital letters, with periods, as though they were acronyms, but let’s leave that alone; they read as people. J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy) is the Alfred of the house, who reminds Vision that “I was created first and I can still tie a better Windsor knot” (“The older sibling card,” says Vision, “it never gets old.”). (Like Vision, he is very British.) F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), as in “girl Friday,” possibly, helps with Vision’s socialization and humor; E.D.I.T.H. (Hampshire) is an adventurer; she sees herself as “the fun one.” D.U.M.-E. (Henry Lewis) and U. (Jonathan Sayer) are comedy “maintenance men,” in the spirit of Laurel and Hardy, or Chuck McCann and Bob Denver in Sid and Marty Krofft’s “Far Out Space Nuts.” Some of them have appeared in Marvel movies.

Also in the house is, of all synthezoids, Ultron (James Spader), Vision’s genocidal nemesis — frenemy would be the better word here — held as a sort of prisoner in a loft space filled with art and television sets. (Just what he’s doing there is not explained, but the proximity is important.) Spader voiced the character in the movies, and you’ll recognize the voice before the face, hidden by a big beard, looking a little like Paul Giamatti (or, when he wears a top hat, Dr. Demento). It’s a very Spader-y performance, arch, ironic, low-key, recalling his scenes with William Shatner in “Boston Legal.” But he’s also a philosophical aesthete, who dreams of visiting the Louvre, and offers Vision some solid life advice. And he’s lonely.

Meanwhile, out on the streets, young con artist Thomas Shepherd (Ruaridh Mollica) and pickpocket Lisa Molinari (Lauren Morais) are running petty scams. Thomas, you might realize, is Tommy Maximoff from “WandaVision,” the son of Vision and Wanda, whose soul was transplanted into the body of a drowned London teenager, which he’ll get around to understanding after a very mixed-up spell. Meanwhile, says Thomas, “I get to wake up every morning and be whoever I want to be,” to which Lisa responds, very much in the spirit of the rest of the show, “If you don’t ever get to be the real you, you might as well be invisible.” (So true.) They’re the series’ lovable young lovers.

Eventually, after an arrest and escape alongside Lisa, Tommy will meet Vision, who will find his paternal instincts emerging (“I’ve noticed you don’t use your indicator, and you haven’t adjusted your rear view mirror,” he tells his son). Complicating matters, Vision is being sought by one Paladin (Todd Stashwick), a relentless bounty hunter working for a mysterious client; Morgan plays his nameless remote handler. And there’s a murder mystery, surrounding what the press has dubbed the Butcherbird Killer. (Vision’s house is remodeled into a police station, with a murder board, and CCTV examined for clues. There’s a “Scooby-Doo” reference, as well.) Another episode, set at a gala, has notes of James Bond. T’Nia Miller plays Jo Carrington a.k.a. Jocasta, about whom I can say nothing that won’t register as a spoiler.

I found it highly entertaining and fun, if more intellectually than emotionally moving. (An observation, not a criticism — maybe even a compliment.) The inner and outer realities can get confusing, not that it particularly matters. It goes on a little long — well, most everything does these days — so that by the end the beginning may have grown blurry. (Take notes.) Points are made repeatedly; you will not be allowed to escape the references to “Pinocchio” and “The Wizard of Oz.” (The working title for the series was “Tin Man.”) Things go to the brink of disaster as often as a Pearl White serial.

But it’s worth your time, even if you follow Marvel even less than I do. The production design is excellent, the humorous details of Vision’s metaphorical manse and the externalization of computer processes clever. The show, which can certainly be tense, spends more time on being funny than violent. Enemies may often become allies — one of my favorite narrative tropes. Despite their intentional and collateral damage, even the bad guys get a break, which is to say, they may not be all that bad, by their own reckoning at least. They might even be allowed a measure of satisfaction. It’s a kindhearted show. “I believe in second chances,” says Vision, because people are complicated, and synthetic people are people, too.

theguardian.com/books/2026/oct/17/isabel.headline: Isabel Allende wins €1m Spanish literary prize under pseudonym
theguardian.com/books/2026/oct/17/isabel.author: Emma Loffhagen, Ella Creamer

paragraphs.text: The Chilean-American author Isabel Allende has won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio Planeta, one of the world’s most lucrative literary prizes, under a pseudonym, with a sequel to her celebrated debut novel, The House of the Spirits.

Allende, 84, won the 75th edition of the award on Thursday with La hora antes del alba, which returns to the characters of her 1982 novel, a multigenerational family saga set against political upheaval in a country inspired by Chile.

The new story follows Alba, the granddaughter of Esteban Trueba and Clara del Valle, as she tries to recover from imprisonment and torture during Pinochet’s dictatorship, according to Reuters. Allende said the book would bring the universe of The House of the Spirits to a close. The 1982 novel is often read alongside Daughter of Fortune and Portrait in Sepia as part of a loose trilogy of interconnected family sagas.
Speaking at the award ceremony in Barcelona, attended by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, Allende said it was “like winning the Nobel”.
“I had never entered a competition because I wanted to avoid the embarrassment of coming last,” she said. “At my age, there is very little to lose.”

She said she had been prompted to write the sequel by decades of readers asking what happened to Alba. She also drew parallels between the political circumstances surrounding the novel and the contemporary rise of extremism. Allende was forced into exile after the 1973 military coup led by Augusto Pinochet that overthrew the Chilean president Salvador Allende, a cousin of her father. Allende had been Latin America’s first democratically elected Marxist leader. Under Pinochet’s regime, an estimated 40,000 people were tortured and more than 3,000 killed.
“Now that I see so many democracies threatened by authoritarianism, extreme nationalism and even fascism, I feel again the fear that led me to leave my country,” she said.

Allende is one of the best-known writers in the Spanish-speaking world, whose books have sold more than 80m copies worldwide and been translated into more than 40 languages. The prize is open to unpublished manuscripts, with the option of submitting under a pseudonym, and Allende entered under the name Luz Ventura, with the fictional title Los que faltan.

However, the judges may have been able to pick up on Allende’s style. “I’d be very surprised if the judges did not know that it was Isabel Allende,” said Prof Duncan Wheeler, the chair of Spanish studies at Leeds University and president-elect of the Association of Hispanists of Great Britain and Ireland. “You have to bear in mind that the Planeta prize is one of the most generously remunerated in the Spanish-speaking world, but definitely not the most prestigious.”

The prize has at times faced criticism over the choice of winner. In 2021, the prize was awarded to La bestia, a thriller published under the pseudonym Carmen Mola, which had been marketed as the identity of a female author. At the awards ceremony, it was revealed that Mola was in fact three male writers – Jorge Díaz, Agustín Martínez and Antonio Mercero.

The prize is run by Planeta, one of the largest publishing groups in the Spanish-speaking world, and includes the condition that the winning book be published by them. Allende has been published by Plaza & Janés, an imprint of Penguin Random House, since The House of the Spirits, so this marks a significant coup for Planeta.

Despite the option to submit pseudonymously, the prize has a history of favouring established writers and TV figures: past winners of the prize have included prominent Spanish-language authors such as Juan Marsé and Manuel Vázquez Montalbán, and the controversial TV personality Juan de Val.

Asked about the perceived trend of awarding the prize to figures known for appearing on TV shows, José Creuheras, the president of the Planeta Group, said, according to the Spanish newspaper El País: “I’m not in a position to say whether the Planeta Prize has more or less prestige than it did in the past. We have some of contemporary literature’s biggest names among our winners and finalists. The prize’s reach, as measured by the figures, speaks for itself, and the number of people taking an interest in the Planeta is growing.”
The runner-up was the Spanish writer and screenwriter Sergio Hernández, whose historical novel La añoranza won €200,000.

thebignewsletter.com/p/how-the-federal-r.headline: How the Federal Reserve Secretly Raises Your Electric Bill
thebignewsletter.com/p/how-the-federal-r.author: Matt Stoller

paragraphs.text: In D.C. and Wall Street, it’s an article of faith that the only solution to high prices and inflation is to have the Federal Reserve increase interest rates. A few days ago, the Wall Street Journal profiled Fed official Beth Hammack, a 30 year veteran of Goldman Sachs before joining the central bank in 2024. Like the rest of her colleagues, she’s struggling with an inflationary economy, and trying to figure out the right policy approach to bring down the rate of price growth. While she doesn’t mention it, keeping the stock market up is also likely on her mind.

Hammack’s specific concern that too many businesses have pricing power, which is leading to excessive wage growth. She’s known as a monetary ‘hawk,’ which means her view is that the Fed needs to hike rates, and ultimately throw the economy into a recession so wages stop growing. Only then will prices stop rising so quickly. Few people noticed the article profiling Hammack, or the fact that her goal is to suppress wages. It’s not noticeable, since it’s just how we’ve become accustomed to thinking about the role of the Fed, which is to punish ordinary people under the veil of technocratic inflation-fighting.

Critics of the Fed are generally brushed aside as irrelevant, since we are unwilling to make the hard choices to control consumer prices. And yet, the Fed has been raising rates for years now, with a limited impact on consumer price increases. After the pandemic, the Fed missed the huge surge of pricing pressure, and then began a radical increase in 2022 before almost crashing markets in 2023. Then it paused, due to fear that investors might be hurt. It soon began cutting rates as Donald Trump demanded they do so to help speculators. In the last few months, they have begun their interest rate hikes again, though they are keen to pause at any point that the AI bubble wobbles.

These choices are consistent with a model of monetary policy assuming the only way to lower prices is to reduce demand, bounded by the political reality that they must keep asset prices high to placate their stakeholders on Wall Street. But what if there’s a theoretical problem, not just a moral one, with this approach? What if higher interest rates aren’t reducing prices, but increasing them? In at least one sector, that’s what’s happening.

Early last year, Con Edison filed a docket to New York state regulators asking to raise prices on consumers, arguing the “main challenge” was the company’s “ability to earn a fair rate of return.” Among other factors was “a volatile interest rate environment” that “expose the company to the risk that it will not be able to earn its cost of capital.”

But one key new excuse was the “volatile” interest rate environment, aka the Federal Reserve increasing rates. Basically, let us raise rates on consumers to pay Wall Street lenders, who are demanding higher returns due to the Fed’s actions.

And Con Edison is not alone; last month, Otter Tail in Minnesota made the same request - pay us more because interest rates are up. And Oncor in Texas got a rate bump as well, justifying it in part because “Interest rates have significantly increased.” Indeed, we’re starting to see utilities more broadly plan to ask for rate hikes as a result of higher interest rate costs.

Now, it’s important to note the villain here in this particular case isn’t actually the utilities. They are engaged in a bit of bad behavior, attempting to use interest rates to justify higher equity returns, but they are right that higher bond rates do drive up costs. If the rate they have to pay on their bonds goes from, say, 4% to 7% to finance new plants and equipment, they have to get that amount from customers. And since that interest rate is just what they are paying to bondholders, they aren’t making extra profit here, it’s pure pass-along costs to lenders. (As a technical matter, make their profits on returns on equity, not debt.)

In other words, in the utility sector, what is happening is that a higher interest rate is driving higher consumer prices, not lower ones. That’s the opposite of what the Fed models used by people like Hammack assume. And it’s not just utilities, a bunch of areas have a similar dynamic. Municipal bond costs are going up as interest rates rise, which means property taxes have to increase. The costs of farm inputs, notably the financing for equipment, livestock, and crops, is increasing with the price of money. Any business with working capital has to pay more. Credit card prices, auto payments, mortgage payments - all of these are consumer prices, and they are going up.

BIG is a reader-supported newsletter focused on the politics of monopoly and finance. It’s entirely financed by you. As politics gets weird and the AI bubble pops, honest information is more important than ever. If you are not yet a paid subscriber, please consider becoming one. BIG is journalism and advocacy that challenges power. You can always get lies for free. The truth costs a few bucks, but in the long run it’s much cheaper. You can subscribe here:

In other words, the conventional wisdom that higher borrowing costs is the route to reduce inflation seems to be wrong, at least in these areas. That said, there is a real rejoinder. If people and businesses have to pay more as a result of high interest rates, ultimately they will have to cut back and the economy will slow, possibly into a recession. Enough companies will go bankrupt to dry up demand, leading to cheaper inputs and more unemployment, and that will reduce inflation. And that is correct, but the cost is high.

What the Fed’s model does is not slow investment to gently bring down inflation, but starkly break enough balance sheets to create a private credit shock. It is that credit shock is what leads to economic restraint. It’s a brutal approach, and it requires a crash. And sure a crash will bring down inflation, but it’s very much a “destroy that village to save it” mentality.

Still, if that were the only way to address inflation, well, then it would be a tough decision, but justifiable. But is it? The other possibility is something few consider today. We could simply have the government put in rules to charge different interest rates for different purposes. Utilities would get a lower rate, so would municipalities and mortgage holders. That would keep a lid on costs. Speculators would get a higher interest rate, so would areas of the economy that we think need to slow. Basically, we’d channel capital directly with regulations.

Believe it or now, that’s how things used to work. The specific mechanism is that America had different banking sectors, such as thrifts for mortgages, commercial banks for commerce, and investment banks for speculative and corporate purposes. They all had different regulatory schemes, and they didn’t co-mingle, so it was possible to loosen credit for mortgages without loosening credit for corporate lending, or vice versa. It was only after deregulation that the Fed simply set “THE” interest rate, as if buying a fridge and buying shares of SpaceX on margin needed to be handled in the same money market.

When I was researching the history of monopoly power, I noticed that’s how Democrats used to understand interest rates and central banking. Populist Congressman Wright Patman, who was in office from 1929-1976, absolutely hated high interest rates. Today, we tend to defer the choice on interest rates to the ‘independent’ central bankers at the Fed, but that anti-political stance is a relatively new development. In 1964, the Democratic party platform, for instance, insisted on “the importance of low interest rates.”

Patman was the leader of the low interest rate faction, arguing that higher rates led to higher prices. Higher rates are “like pouring gasoline on a fire,” he said in 1966. “It makes prices higher, not lower…. Builders can’t afford to pay those high rates to build homes and people can’t afford to pay even higher rates for mortgages.” He compared inflation during World War II, the government paid just 0.375% on short-term debt, by 1966 that had gone up to 5.04%. “In 1946 it cost the taxpayer $3750 to borrow a million dollars.” In 1966 it cost $50,470. In other words, it’s costing nearly 13 times more.” And inflation was much higher in 1966 than during World War II. That’s not because there weren’t inflationary pressures, but because we used credit controls, rationing, and regulation to move capital into markets where we needed production.

That is not the world we live in today. During Covid, I made the point that big banks and investors got access to credit because their institutional setups worked well, whereas small businesses and individuals didn’t have much access to banking. That’s called the Cantillon Effect, and it shows that how we deploy monetary policy is not neutral in terms of its effects on inequality. I’d add that prices don’t go up uniformly, that bigger firms can keep a lid on the inflation they must pay, while smaller ones have to pay more. And of course asset prices, like stocks and real estate, which are the prices that speculators and the superrich care about, well, those matter too. Inflation, like monetary policy, isn’t neutral.

Indeed, what deregulation was really about was bringing us a world where monetary policy makes the rich richer. Today, the only way to restrain inflation is to foster a crash and lower wages. But that’s not inherent to a market-based society, it’s a particular regulatory scheme that privileges holders of capital over the rest of us. We could do things differently, but actually imposing clear rules on the financial sector and breaking it apart requires a massive reallocation of political power.

As Americans revolt against high prices and inflation, the main institution in D.C. tasked with taming consumer costs, the Federal Reserve, is still living in a world where they assume regulation can’t happen. Maybe they are right. But as your utility bill goes up, know that the reason is the nerds at the Fed who can’t imagine any monetary policy model except one that holds down prices by overcharging you until you go bankrupt, and then nodding approvingly over the wreckage.
