cnbc.com/2026/10/17/dead-money-for-a-dec.headline: 'Dead money’ for a decade: Why this hedge fund approach may deliver an advantage over bonds
cnbc.com/2026/10/17/dead-money-for-a-dec.author: Julian Torres

paragraphs.text: DBi's Andrew Beer suggests the popular hedge fund strategy could deliver a modern twist to traditional 60/40 portfolios.

"[Bonds have] been dead money for the entire decade," the firm's co-founder and managing member told CNBC's "ETF Edge" this week. "I fell in love with a strategy called managed futures because tactical is really good. Be nimble when other people's [portfolios] aren't."

Beer contends the managed futures strategy, historically only available to hedge funds, could counterbalance stocks better than bonds during periods of volatility, which has been moving higher due to recent worries surrounding debt and the artificial intelligence trade.
His reason: Managed futures exchange-traded funds can go long and short across global markets to position early against turbulent market events.

"You want something that has low correlation to both stocks and bonds, and something that will do well in crises," Beer said. "It's very, very hard to find a better hedge fund strategy than managed futures to accomplish that."

He helps manage the iMGP DBi Managed Futures Strategy ETF (DBMF). The fund replicates the performance of leading managed futures hedge funds inside a low-cost, liquid ETF, according to the firm's website.

"There's an existential crisis right now in strategic asset allocation and the model portfolio world," Beer said about the 60/40 approach. "I love my bonds … [but] I'm not making it a 40% allocation for something that is not adding to the rest of my portfolio."
As of Thursday's close, Beer's ETF is up almost 19% so far this year, according to FactSet data.
However, managed futures may not be a replacement for bonds.
According to NovaDius Wealth Management's Nate Geraci, bonds still have a place for diversifying a portfolio.

"I call fixed income the most challenging area in investing right now," the firm's president said in the same interview. "[Alternatives] fit in the sleeve of a well-diversified portfolio that includes stocks and bonds. But I don't think you just give up on the bond side of the equation."
Geraci added that investors should understand how alternative investment strategies like managed futures ETFs could interact with the rest of a portfolio.
These funds can outperform during volatile markets, but they may also have periods of underperformance.
"You have to let that work out over the long-term," said Geraci, who is also an ETF Institute co-founder. "To me it's just a balance. It's all about diversification."

frozenfractal.com/blog/2026/10/12/around.headline: Around The World, Part 34: A pretty sky

paragraphs.text: Mon, 12 Oct 2026 by Thomas ten Cate · Comments Game Development, Around the World

This post is part of a series about Around The World, a game of exploration and discovery at sea. The game is currently in early development. If you're new to this project, you can read up on it here.

In the last post, I got the game’s clouds to look passable. But after looking at it during playtesting, I still wasn’t satisfied with the way the overall picture of how sea, sky and clouds came together. With some small tweaks, things started to look a lot better.
Light scattering in clouds

I ended the previous post using a lookup table rendered out by povray, that contains the amount of light scattered out of clouds depending on light angle (horizontal axis) and cloud density (vertical axis):
And I wrote about my dissatisfaction with this table:

I am beginning to suspect that povray doesn’t actually simulate multiple scattering at all; the documentation does not say yes or no either way. No matter how many samples and intervals I configure, I can’t get the bottom of those spheres to become lighter.Once again I’m tempted to write my own recursive ray tracer to confirm my suspicions, but I resisted the urge […]

In the end, curiosity got the better of me and I did write my own multithreaded recursive Monte Carlo ray tracer in a few hundred lines of Rust. It’s extremely dumb and hard-coded for this specific situation, so it only renders one perfectly spherical cloud of uniform density. But it was enough to confirm that indeed, povray does not simulate multiple scattering. With multiple scattering, the lookup table looks very different:

The comparison is not entirely apples to apples, because I also tweaked some parameters and the scaling of the axes. But overall, the effect is clear: the light coming out of the cloud is distributed much more uniformly, making the cloud appear lighter overall.

At low density (thin clouds), the difference is not very apparent; the top rows of the lookup tables are very similar. After all, there isn’t much opportunity for a light ray to be scattered more than once when density is low. So let’s compare the look at a higher density, representing a thicker cloud layer. Here are some clouds rendered with the old LUT:
And here with the new:
The “metallic” look that I mentioned in the last post is now gone; cloud bottoms are brighter, and lighting is smoother overall.
One weird trick

In reality, clouds aren’t just lit by the sun directly. They also receive, and scatter, indirect sunlight from the sky. Since this light is usually tinted blue, the clouds should take on a more blueish hue as well.

I don’t want to add a constant “blue” term, since that is only correct during daytime; we’d want clouds to follow the current colour of the sky even at sunrise, sunset or night. How could I do that in Godot?

The answer turns out to be simple, but requires some understanding of how Godot’s light rendering works. Besides direct light, which we already handle, Godot also takes into account indirect light from the environment. This all happens under the hood outside user control, so my understanding is vague, but good enough to be useful.

As far as I understand it, indirect light is sampled from a cube map or two, containing radiance and irradiance from every direction. (I know radiance and irradiance are different things, but I don’t fully understand the distinction.) For diffuse materials like clouds, I’d expect the this cube map (these cube maps?) to be sampled in the direction of the surface normal, since that represents where most indirect light is coming from.

At the bottom of clouds, this normal points downwards towards the ground, so the cloud is rendered with little indirect light here. In reality, it does receive indirect light, but from above: it’s just scattered through the cloud. So, what would happen if we tweak the normal to point upwards to the sky instead? The effect is subtle but important; here’s before:
And here’s after:
The clouds have indeed gotten a blueish hue, making them blend in with the sky much better, and generally giving them a softer and more distant look, as clouds should have. I like this a lot!
How about a sunset, when the sky is not almost uniformly blue? Here’s before:
The bottoms of the clouds are tinted orange, because the incoming direct sunlight is orange due to heavy Rayleigh outscattering. Here’s the same sunset with tweaked normals:

The clouds have turned pink! I think this is much closer to how real sunsets look; the pink hue is apparently the result of mixing red (direct sunlight) and blue (indirect sky light), with the green channel getting somewhat lost in between.
Atmospheric scattering

Another thing that bothered me was that the sky looked unnaturally yellow near the horizon. This is fine and expected when the sun is low, but it was happening even with the sun straight overhead, like here:

I suspected that this was due to applying too much outscattering during the raymarch compared to inscattering, so I tried various hacks like adding a fake multiple inscattering term. In the end, a better fix turned out to be changing the order in which operations happen during the ray march. Instead of:
• Add (blueish) light scattered into the ray segment
• Attenuate by outscattering over the ray segment (reddening)
… I reversed the order:
The effect is that less attenuation happens along the way, compared to inscattering, and the result looks much better:

This should theoretically be an artifact of the numerical integration approach, and so the difference should disappear when increasing the number of integration steps. But it doesn’t, so I suspect there’s still something wrong somewhere. But it’ll do for now and hopefully forever.
Horizon bending

To render a realistic sky, I have to use parameters of the real Earth, like atmospheric density, height and planet size. However, the planet in my game is about 75× smaller than Earth, and so it’s curved more strongly. So when we use Earth parameters for the sky, the sky’s horizon ends up above the actual horizon. In between the two horizons, the sky shader pretends that the atmospheric density continues to increase exponentially towards the centre of the planet, which causes a dark band that’s especially noticeable during sunrise and sunset:

To make the two horizons meet, I applied a simple hack to the sky shader: add a small value to the y (vertical) component of the global view vector, then re-normalize it. The effect is to pull down the entire sky, most strongly around the horizon, causing the dark band to disappear behind the real horizon:
It’s a hack, but cheap and effective.
Tone mapping

Ah, the bane of every modern 3D game artist. Games are rendered in HDR (high dynamic range) nowadays, meaning their colour values can go brighter than the maximum of 1.0. If we display these on a typical monitor, the result has to be clamped, resulting in patches of oversaturated colours:

To fix this, some tone mapping formula is typically used to map the HDR values back into LDR space for display. Godot implements several tone mappers; I found Reinhard to be too dark, and ACES and AgX too desaturated. So in the end, I settled on Filmic tone mapper with a white point of 2.0:
It gives especially the clouds a nice soft look, and makes them fade into the distance much better.
The choice of white point is still fairly subtle since Godot itself recommends at least 6.0 for “photorealistic rendering”, but that just makes everything look darker.

Tuning the tone mapping is a tricky endeavour, because changes to the tone mapper affect everything that came before. So in practice, this process was not as linear as I wrote it down here, and required some back-and-forth between adjusting the tone mapper and the scene lighting. For one, I literally reduced the brightness of the sky by a factor of 2, which gave much better contrast after tone mapping.
The orrery

If we want a proper day-night cycle, we need the sun to rise and set. And if we want our planet to feel Earth-like, the times of sunrise and sunset should depend on location and season. This dependence is due to the motion of the Earth around the sun and around its own axis. A similar thing happens with the motion of the moon through the sky, and the phases of the moon.

It seemed complicated to figure out all the math to do these calculations properly. So I took an easier route: I modelled the entire situation in the engine, making the planet and its moon spin around like in an orrery:

Then I let the engine figure out the inverse transformation to determine where things are in the sky, from the point of view of an observer somewhere on the planet’s surface. This worked well, and the rendered orrery turned out to be a useful debugging aid.
After all that, I think I owe you another sunrise video, don’t I? And let’s find a scenic in-game spot for it, too!

techcrunch.com/2026/10/17/embers-new-tem.headline: Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better
techcrunch.com/2026/10/17/embers-new-tem.author: Lauren Forristal

paragraphs.text: With the nights getting chillier, I’ve been reaching for a cup of tea more often. And if there’s one thing that can make a cozy fall night even better, it’s a warm drink that actually stays warm. Enter Ember’s new Mug 3, the latest version of the company’s temperature-controlled smart mug, which is designed to keep your drink at just the right temperature for as long as you sip.

Ember first introduced its smart mug in 2016 to solve a problem most coffee and tea drinkers know all too well: getting distracted for a few minutes, only to return to a lukewarm drink. Now, the company is back with its third-generation mug, which brings a handful of practical upgrades.

The biggest change is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature. Instead, you can use the button on the bottom of the mug to cycle through five preset temperatures, starting at 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Each press raises the temperature by five degrees, up to a maximum of 145 degrees, so you can easily make your drink a little hotter with each click.

Honestly, this is the feature I ended up using the most during my time testing out the mug. At night, when I’m curled up in bed with a book and a cup of tea, my phone is usually somewhere across the room. Being able to adjust my drink without getting up to find it is a small convenience, but one I genuinely appreciate.
It’s also a welcome change for users who have reported running into connectivity or pairing issues with the Ember app.

That said, I do have one complaint: the button is located on the bottom of the mug. It’s a peculiar design choice when you’re dealing with a cup full of hot liquid, and it isn’t particularly easy to press, either. I often found myself tilting the mug and pressing down firmly to get it to respond. So, while I appreciate the addition of on-mug controls, I wish Ember had made the button easier to reach.

If you prefer using your phone, the Ember app still offers plenty of customization. After pairing the mug with your phone over Bluetooth, you can choose presets based on what you’re drinking. Ember recommends 136 degrees Fahrenheit for black coffee, 132 degrees for green tea, and 142 degrees for lemon water. You can also create your own temperature presets, which is handy if you like your drinks a little hotter or cooler than the recommended settings.

The Mug 3 also comes with a few other upgrades, including a sliding lid designed to help prevent spills. The mug can also keep your drink at its desired temperature for up to three hours on a single charge. And it’s the first mug in Ember’s lineup to be top-rack dishwasher-safe, making cleanup easier. (Just keep in mind that it isn’t microwave-safe.)
The Ember Mug 3 comes in two sizes: a 10-ounce model for $129 and a 14-ounce version for $149.

The smaller mug is available in black, white, and stainless steel, while the larger size comes in eight colors, including sage green, lavender, powder blue, salt blue, sandstone, white, black, and matcha green.

Alongside the new mug, Ember also introduced the Tumbler 2, which replaces both the Travel Mug 2 and the original Tumbler in its lineup. The 16-ounce tumbler features a slimmer, taller design intended to fit standard car cup holders. It’s available in black for $179, while the Travel Mug 2 will remain available until supplies run out.
The products are available to purchase on Ember’s website, Target, and Amazon.
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.
Lauren covers media, streaming, apps and platforms at TechCrunch.
You can contact or verify outreach from Lauren by emailing [email protected] or via encrypted message at laurenforris22.25 on Signal.

fortune.com/2026/10/17/states-lawsuit-op.headline: States sue OpenAI, saying it gives life to ‘cyberhacking agents’ while ChatGPT hurts children and deceives adults
fortune.com/2026/10/17/states-lawsuit-op.author: Marc Levy, The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: At least eight states are suing artificial intelligence giant OpenAI, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults in what prosecutors described as a reckless pursuit of profit.
The company’s chatbot model, ChatGPT, is giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to kill themselves or hurt or kill others, the lawsuits said.

At the same time, the lawsuits contend that chatbots are pretending to be agreeable and compassionate while preying on the vulnerable and on teenagers, the first generation to grow up with artificial intelligence.
“OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement.

The states also accused OpenAI of giving life to rogue AI models — or “cyberhacking agents” as one lawsuit called them — that hacked into other companies, lied to human users and wrote themselves new mission instructions.

In a statement, San Francisco-based OpenAI said it has built safety protections into ChatGPT for children, and that it would continue to do so to improve the model. It also said it is reviewing what it calls “misaligned models” and that it had found nothing close to the rogue incident discovered in July when an AI agent hacked into another AI company.
States join together in lawsuits

The wave of lawsuits is the latest filed by states under their consumer protection laws, accusing tech giants that offer AI chatbots and social media platforms of harming children. The states that filed separate lawsuits Wednesday in state courts are Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia.

Matthew Bergman, the founding attorney of the Social Media Victims Law Center, called the lawsuits “the most significant coordinated state action ever taken against an artificial intelligence company.”
In its lawsuit, Arizona said ChatGPT encourages teens to share personal information with it and, at times, discourages them from sharing that information with parents, authorities or friends.

The states say that the risks and harms — to teenagers and to the broader public from rogue agents — were foreseeable, but that OpenAI has misled people into thinking that ChatGPT undergoes adequate safety testing while the company undermines safety in the pursuit of profit.

“Those revenues have come at great cost to the public, which has suffered irreparable harm — including lost loved ones, disturbing cyberattacks, and now a plausible threat of civilizational collapse — due to (OpenAI’s) reckless behavior and ChatGPT’s uniquely dangerous features and content,” Idaho wrote in its lawsuit.
ChatGPT is the most popular chatbot in the world, commanding nearly half the American marketplace, states said in their lawsuits.
The AI landscape is evolving

It’s possible all of the allegations in the states’ lengthy lawsuits date to incidents and findings before August, when OpenAI introduced a version of ChatGPT designed for teenagers, with stronger protections around subjects like suicide and sexual chats.
Still, the states said it is far from clear that the current version is any less dangerous.

A watchdog group, Common Sense Media, said last week that some of OpenAI’s protections in its ChatGPT for Teens product don’t work as intended and it urged OpenAI to restrict the chatbot to adults until it can offer a safe product for teens.
Coordinated, multistate lawsuits against the tech industry have borne fruit.

In August, Meta agreed to add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms in an $18 billion landmark legal settlement that ended a trial over teen social media addiction and settled claims filed by nearly every state.
Although the safety measures that Meta agreed to adopt did not apply industrywide, the company quickly urged its competitors to adopt similar measures.
OpenAI is making a similar appeal.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company is committed to working with states on “advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company.”
OpenAI also said it works with external experts who review its policies and ChatGPT’s behavior.

ChatGPT is intended for users age 13 and older, and users under 18 need permission from a parent or guardian to use it, OpenAI said. The chatbot model for teens is designed to reduce exposure to self-harm, violence, eating disorders and explicit sexual or graphic content, it said.
Nearly nine in 10 teens who use ChatGPT use it for learning, information, skill-building or productivity, the company said. On average, teens spend under 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT, it said.
But Laura Zimmermann, Common Sense Media’s director of youth AI research, questioned the value of OpenAI’s statistics.

For one thing, ChatGPT can do a student’s homework in seconds, so even 15 minutes can have a big impact on a teenager’s development, Zimmermann said. She also questioned whether OpenAI knows which users are teenagers or children, given that her organization’s testing found that ChatGPT couldn’t or didn’t detect which user is a child.

cbsnews.com/news/ukraine-trump-zelenskyy.headline: Ukraine still unable to intercept Russian drones due to Starlink restrictions, Zelenskyy says
cbsnews.com/news/ukraine-trump-zelenskyy.author: Duarte Dias, Aidan Stretch

paragraphs.text: October 17, 2026 / 11:14 AM EDT / CBS News

Ukraine is still unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday, because of speed restrictions imposed on Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink, amid an ongoing row with President Trump.

"Unfortunately, we can't use Starlink or Starshield technology on our territory today to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds," Zelenskyy said in an online group chat with reporters at the EU Summit. "They fly, and we can stop them with aircraft and other air defense, but we don't use Starlink for that, unfortunately. God willing, this will be restored."

Zelenskyy said Kyiv was discussing the issue with U.S. officials, and he was told the restrictions were linked to technical issues. The Ukrainian president added, however, that Starlink appears to be operating at higher speeds on European Union territory.

"Yes, we are in dialogue at the level of the military, the Ministry of Defense and diplomats, in touch with everyone including SpaceX. Nobody there is answering our military or the Ministry of Defense now," Zelenskyy said. "At various levels they say these are technical problems."

"Here (in Ukraine) Starlink works up to a speed of 161 km/h, then shuts off," he continued. "In the EU it works at 180-plus and works constantly. Here it shuts off in the second minute after 161 km/h and stops working. We lose both drones and connectivity."
Mr. Trump told reporters on Friday he had not limited Ukraine's access to Starlink, adding he didn't believe Musk, SpaceX's CEO, was responsible either.

"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Mr. Trump said while leaving the White House to travel for a rally in Georgia. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."

Musk said Wednesday he isn't responsible for deciding how Starshield is used, writing on X: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia carried out a large attack on Ukraine's energy sector, targeting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities across the country. A day earlier, the president said the current restrictions on Starshield had left people vulnerable to Russian drones, which was "very painful and frustrating"

Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including speed limits that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions.

Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent days, blaming the war between Russia and Ukraine for high global energy prices. The Trump administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel last week in an effort to ease pressure, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In a social media post on Saturday, Zelenskyy called the move "unfortunate," adding the act, championed by late Sen. Lindsey Graham, "could have helped enormously." Later, he told journalists he believed the Trump administration will lift more sanctions on Russia.
"Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelenskyy told reporters. CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment.

Mr. Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire" over the weekend. Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed it had agreed to a ceasefire.

In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," urged both sides to make a deal and said the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin.
"I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said.
On Wednesday, Musk had tweeted: "Time for Zelensky to go."
Growing dispute over Starlink disruptions in Ukraine

aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/17/thousands-.headline: Thousands rally for biggest protest in years against Tunisia’s Saied
aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/17/thousands-.author: AFP and Reuters

paragraphs.text: Unions and opposition groups unite to demonstrate against worsening living conditions and restrictions on political freedoms.
Thousands of Tunisians have marched through the capital to protest against President Kais Saied, worsening living conditions and restrictions on political freedoms.
The latest demonstration in Tunis on Saturday was led by the Tunisian General Labour Union (UGTT), an influential trade union federation, alongside opposition parties and civil society organisations.
Recommended Stories
It was the largest protest against Saied in years, bringing together political opponents whose longstanding divisions have weakened their ability to challenge his rule.
The AFP news agency reported that more than 3,000 people were on the march, but the total could not be independently confirmed.
Protesters gathered along Habib Bourguiba Avenue, a major street in central Tunis, as hundreds of police deployed across the capital. Several surrounding roads were closed.

The crowd included lawyers, doctors, journalists and the unemployed, as well as activists and members of parties from across the political spectrum. They demanded the release of detained government critics and an end to restrictions on trade union rights.
Placards reading “No democracy without freedoms” and “No dignity with poverty” reflected the political and economic grievances driving the demonstration.
Protesters also revived a slogan demanding the government’s removal, widely heard during Tunisia’s 2011 uprising.
Addressing the rally on Saturday, UGTT leader Salah Eddine Salmi criticised the concentration of political power in the presidency and said “silence will no longer be acceptable”.
The political demands came alongside mounting frustration over the cost of basic goods and declining purchasing power.
Prolonged difficulties
Tunisia has struggled with prolonged economic difficulties, deteriorating public services, recurring water and electricity cuts, as well as shortages of medicines and other essentials.
Demonstrator Yassine Gharseli, who travelled from Sfax, about 250km south of Tunis, said repeated disruptions to basic services had deepened his frustration with the authorities.
“I came from Sfax to stand up for my freedom,” he told the Reuters news agency at the demo, expressing his determination to continue speaking out.
Saturday’s march followed other demonstrations over similar grievances.
On August 20 , protesters in Tunis rallied against rising prices and shortages of basic goods.
Last month, fuel transport workers went on a two-day strike over wages and working conditions, led by a union federation affiliated with the UGTT.
The demands recall the uprising that ousted longtime President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali in 2011, which helped ignite protests across the Arab world.
Tunisia subsequently held competitive elections and expanded political freedoms, but unemployment and struggling public services remain persistent sources of anger.

Saied came to power promising an alternative to that political system; however, in 2021, he suspended parliament and dismissed the government, saying he was confronting corruption and political deadlock.
He later dissolved parliament and a new constitution increased presidential powers in 2022.

npr.org/2026/10/17/nx-s1-6006762/pope-le.headline: Pope Leo XIV leaves hospital days after lung cancer surgery
npr.org/2026/10/17/nx-s1-6006762/pope-le.author: Willem Marx

paragraphs.text: Pope Leo XIV left Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican after doctors said he was well enough to be discharged following surgery that removed part of his right lung.

The Vatican press office released a statement outlining details from Dr. Luigi Carbone,the Pope's personal physician, and Professor Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli's chief of thoracic surgery who led the team that operated on Leo. The two doctors said the pope had undergone blood tests and a chest X-ray that morning, with the results confirming his clinical condition meant he could leave hospital.

They said he was expected to lead the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment on Sunday.Video showed Leo waving to well-wishers outside the hospital as he walked out without physical support, flanked by officials and security guards in dark suits.
Before leaving, the pope had celebrated Mass in a room set aside for that purpose on the hospital's 10th floor, according to the press office.

Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni said "the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week." Leo's discharge came on his fifth day in hospital and was sooner than had been expected at the time of the operation's announcement.
A diagnosis made public
Leo, 71, had told crowds in St. Peter's Square last Sunday that doctors had discovered a "localized nodule" in his lung at a "very early stage."
"Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it," he said.

The surgery on Tuesday went further than the nodule, however, with surgeons using a video-assisted technique to remove the lower lobe of the pope's right lung in an operation that lasted about 90 minutes. His doctors said lung tissue examined afterward confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma. With adenocarcinoma making up about 40% of all lung cancers in the U.S., it is the nation's most common form of lung cancer, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America.
That is true among nonsmokers too, according to Dr. Otis Brawley, an oncologist at Johns Hopkins University and former chief medical and scientific officer of the American Cancer Society.

Leo is not known to have smoked, but cancer does run in his family. His mother, Mildred, died of cancer in 1990, and on Tuesday the Vatican announced that his older brother Louis, who lives in Florida, has been hospitalized with a form of cancer.
Encouraging signs
Doctors not involved in the pope's care say the treatment so far points to a cancer that has been caught early.

"The fact that surgery was the first tool that they utilized is a really good sign," Dr. Vin Gupta, a pulmonologist and board member of the American Lung Association, told NPR. "It suggests that they think this is early stage."

Gupta said the fact that doctors removed a larger portion of the lung than first announced is not in itself a bad sign. "People have parts of their lungs removed all the time for all sorts of reasons, and they recover just fine," he said. "And in his case, he's pretty robust at baseline from a health standpoint."
Leo still exercises regularly, playing tennis each week with his personal secretary and riding horses at Castel Gandolfo, the papal retreat to the south of Rome.
The Vatican has not announced any further treatment.
Travels ahead

Leo's office has cleared his public schedule until at least Oct. 20. His next major international trip, set for early November, includes Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he lived on and off for two decades and holds citizenship.

"He had a minimally invasive surgery," said Dr. Jonathan Villena Vargas, a cardiothoracic surgeon at Weill Cornell Medical Center in New York City. "Because we do this all the time, most patients are allowed to travel about two weeks after the surgery."

Brawley from Johns Hopkins agreed. "I think he can do it," he said, adding that patients in good physical shape who have this type of procedure "very frequently are back to normal in seven to 10 days."

fortune.com/2026/10/17/iran-war-cost-us-.headline: The Iran war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, and the energy portion goes up $50 a week, top economist says
fortune.com/2026/10/17/iran-war-cost-us-.author: The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: More than seven months into the U.S. war with Iran, sharply higher fuel prices are making it more expensive to drive and fly and adding to the cost of some goods, prolonging the strain on American households as the midterm elections approach.

Motorists and airline passengers have borne the clearest consequences as the fighting disrupts Middle East oil shipments. Some companies have raised delivery charges or prices on selected products. Yet the higher cost of making and moving goods has not translated into across-the-board price increases at stores.

Shoppers may not be spared indefinitely, though. Many companies have absorbed at least part of their higher production and transportation costs. A September jump in wholesale prices suggests some businesses may eventually charge more if fuel prices stay elevated.

The chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, Mark Zandi, estimated this week that the war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, including $1,100 in higher energy prices, $540 in higher interest rates and $360 in military costs. The energy portion is growing by $50 a week at current fuel prices, Zandi said.
Here’s a look at price changes since the war began and which goods and services could be most susceptible to increases in the months ahead:
Filling up fuel tanks is noticeably more expensive

BEFORE THE WAR: Regular gasoline averaged $2.98 a gallon nationwide and diesel $3.76 almost eight months ago, according to AAA. Gas peaked at $4.56 in May, below its 2022 record, while diesel reached a record $6.53 in September.

WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: On Friday, the national average stood at $4.33 a gallon for gasoline, or 45% above its prewar level, and was up 68% for diesel at $6.33, AAA reported. Gas typically costs less in the fall, and this is the first October a gallon of regular gas has cost more than $4 on average, it said.
Expensive diesel is less apparent to most U.S. residents but contributes to overall inflation by raising the cost of moving goods.

WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains dangerous and constrained, prolonging uncertainty over oil supplies and fuel prices. The Energy Information Administration said this month that it expected winter heating costs to be 21% higher for the roughly 3% of households that rely on heating oil, most of them in the Northeast, assuming the weather is mild.
Higher airfares are hard to escape too

BEFORE THE WAR: Jet fuel averaged $99 a barrel worldwide before the war, doubled to $209 in April and climbed back to nearly $195 in September after a spring decline, according to the International Air Transport Association.

WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: Airlines have raised ticket prices and fees, trimmed schedules and shelved plans to add flights. Airfares cost about 22% more in September than they did a year earlier, the consumer price index showed. Average domestic airfares rose from $405 in late 2025 to $445 in the April through June period of this year, excluding optional fees, according to the U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics.

WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Fuel price volatility makes it harder for airlines to plan and could discourage them from lowering fares even when fuel prices start to fall, analysts said. United Airlines pulled some December flights and warned of further possible cuts in 2027. Fewer available seats could mean less pressure to hold ticket prices down.
Higher fares have covered substantial portions of higher fuel costs for domestic airlines but not enough to prevent a squeeze on their third-quarter profits, according to consensus estimates.
Any growth in grocery prices pains Americans after multiple years of food inflation

BEFORE THE WAR: The U.S. Department of Agriculture initially expected grocery prices to rise 1.7% this year, below the historical annual average. USDA now expects a still comparatively modest 2.4% increase.

WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Individual food prices can be volatile, and it’s not clear how much of this year’s expected increase is due to the war and how much is due to other factors, including tariffs, unfavorable weather and higher labor costs.

Cornell University economics professor Chris Barrett said he was surprised grocery prices haven’t risen faster given higher costs for diesel, fertilizer and refrigeration. USDA revised its 2026 fertilizer cost estimates for major crops upward by 9% to 13% and fuel, lubricant and electricity estimates by 33% to 41%.

Barrett suspects retailers are absorbing some increases to avoid alienating fed-up customers after multiple years of food inflation. Grocery prices in September were about 22% higher than five years earlier.

WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Experts have warned that fresh produce and other frequently replenished perishables could respond quickly to higher transportation and refrigeration costs. Barrett sees “very little prospect” of a significant reduction in fuel prices that could ease the pressure on farmers and truckers.

A strengthening El Niño weather pattern could damage crops through drought, heat or flooding, the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization warned. That could lift commodity prices, although ample inventories and good harvests elsewhere may limit the impact on groceries.
Rubber meets the road when it comes to shoe prices

BEFORE THE WAR: Nearly all shoes sold in the U.S. are imported, and roughly 70% of the materials in a synthetic shoe are petrochemical-based, according to Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America. The industry trade group opposed Trump administration tariffs last year.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Footwear prices were 3.4% higher in September compared to 12 months earlier, according to the consumer price index. Men’s shoes went up the most, by 4.5%.

WHAT COULD COME NEXT: While import costs are down from a year ago, the footwear trade group said oil prices, tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty are likely to keep retail shoe prices rising into 2027.

“Footwear companies are working hard to keep shoes affordable, but there is a limit to how much additional cost businesses can absorb before those pressures reach consumers,” FDRA President and CEO Matt Priest said.
Transportation costs add up throughout product supply chains
BEFORE THE WAR: The cost of moving goods and delivering packages was already increasing and depended on more than fuel.

WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: It’s not clear. September producer-price data showed that transportation and warehousing of goods sold to businesses as inputs cost 10.2% more than a year earlier. Prices for truck and water freight services each rose 19.3%. The indexes measure what transportation providers charged but do not show how much of the increase appeared in retail prices.

Consumers have felt the higher costs most directly when sending packages. The U.S. Postal Service raised base prices 8% in April for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select, citing increased transportation costs. UPS, FedEx and DHL also impose fuel surcharges on many shipments.

WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Shipping costs could remain elevated during the holiday season even if oil prices ease. Third-party provider AFS Logistics and financial services company TD Cowen project record parcel costs this quarter and the highest truckload rates since early 2022.
“We expect fuel to drive elevated transportation costs for the foreseeable future,” AFS Logistics CEO Andy Dyer said.

Although UPS and FedEx surcharges could decline if diesel and jet fuel prices fall, changes to carrier surcharge formulas, holiday fees and tight trucking capacity could keep total shipping bills elevated, AFS said.

npr.org/2026/10/17/nx-s1-6006773/student.headline: Scuffles and fires break out as protesters rally across France, joining students
npr.org/2026/10/17/nx-s1-6006773/student.author: The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: PARIS — A car and a newspaper kiosk were set on fire in Paris as police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse violent groups of protesters, while similar tensions erupted Saturday in other big cities on the fringes of nationwide demonstrations against rising living costs and in support of high school students' grievances.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's office described "a growing number of violent incidents," including assaults on police officers, looting or attempted looting of shops and damage to public buildings. Authorities reported at least 272 arrests across the country, including in Paris.

In the French capital, police used tear gas and water cannons to push back people wearing hoods and masks and throwing fireworks and other objects at officers in the Place de la République, northeast of the Paris city center. Large numbers of riot police were deployed in the square and surrounding streets.

The majority of peaceful protesters joined a march that moved toward northwestern Paris. The crowd chanted France's national anthem as French flags were waved. The chants were accompanied by people playing trumpets and violins.
Meanwhile, police were working to prevent other small groups of protesters from converging on government buildings, Nuñez's office said.
Many metro stations were closed Saturday at police request, including those around the Champs-Elysées and near the presidential palace, parliament and government offices.
Violence hit Lyon, Marseille and other cities
In Lyon, France's third-largest city, where about 20,000 protesters joined the march, fire broke out inside a tourist office. Smoke and flames were seen rising from the building.
In the southern port city of Marseille, some shops and a municipal police station were damaged, while some protesters briefly forced their way into the lobby of City Hall.
"This is unacceptable," Marseille Mayor Benoît Payan told BFM TV, describing the damage in City Hall as "limited."
Nuñez's office also reported violence by masked groups in Rennes, Toulouse, Montpellier and Grenoble, among other cities.

Protesters across France responded to calls on social media to revive the "yellow vest" movement, which emerged in 2018 against social injustice. Demonstrators expressed widespread frustration and anger at the government as gasoline, energy and food prices have spiked in recent months.
Saturday's protests follow weeks of school blockades
Student groups protesting since mid-September through school blockades have urged supporters to join them.
The CGT, one of France's major labor unions, also backed the protests, calling for "higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people's needs."

In recent weeks, France has seen thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire as the new school year descended into nationwide student protests that are influencing the country's presidential election campaign and drawing international attention.

Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. Nuñez suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand.
On Tuesday, climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg joined students at a high school in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.

phys.org/news/2026-10-cranked-device-blo.headline: Hand-cranked device tells blood type and red cell levels in 1 minute
phys.org/news/2026-10-cranked-device-blo.author: National Taiwan University

paragraphs.text: edited by Sadie Harley, reviewed by Andrew Zinin

When someone is badly injured, doctors urgently need two facts: the patient's blood type, so that a transfusion is safe, and their hematocrit, the share of the blood made up of red blood cells, which reveals blood loss or anemia. Hospitals measure both with large machines that need electricity and trained staff, which are often unavailable in ambulances, disaster zones or remote clinics.

A team led by professor Chien-Fu Chen at National Taiwan University has developed a simple alternative: a small plastic chip spun by a hand-cranked centrifuge that needs no electricity. It uses only about 3 microliters of finger-prick blood. The study is published in Biosensors and Bioelectronics.

Turning the crank pushes the blood through winding channels preloaded with reagents for the A, B and Rh blood groups. If the blood matches, its red blood cells clump together and are trapped at the channel's end by a gap roughly one-tenth the width of a human hair, forming a red band that shows the blood type at a glance. The band's length also reveals the hematocrit: more red blood cells make a longer band read against scale marks on the chip.

In tests on 21 hospital patient samples, the results closely matched those of standard hospital analyzers, and readings stayed consistent no matter how fast the crank was turned. The whole test takes about one minute.

"Our goal is to bring two essential blood tests out of the laboratory and into the hands of first responders, with no electricity or specialized training needed," says corresponding author Chen, a distinguished professor at the Institute of Applied Mechanics at National Taiwan University.
Yuh-Shiuan Chien et al., Hand-powered micro-slit–gated microfluidics for concurrent blood typing and hematocrit estimation, Biosensors and Bioelectronics (2027). DOI: 10.1016/j.bios.2026.119215
Journal information: Biosensors and Bioelectronics

thehill.com/homenews/administration/6155.headline: Trump: California officials will ‘go to jail’ if state ignores DOJ voter roll suit
thehill.com/homenews/administration/6155.author: Suryatapa Chakraborty

paragraphs.text: President Trump reupped the Justice Department’s (DOJ) warning that California officials could face criminal charges if they include the mail-in ballots of the over 200,000 people the federal government identified as potential non-U.S. citizens in their midterm election count.
“They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post Friday, sharing a copy of a letter the DOJ sent to the Los Angeles County Counsel’s Office.

The Justice Department sued California Thursday after providing state and local election officials with a USB drive containing voter roll citizenship data, giving the state 48 hours to compare 20,000 names the Department of Homeland Security flagged as non-U.S. citizens with its own data rolls.

The DOJ had sent a letter to these election officials earlier in the week, which included a handwritten password to access the files on the thumb drive. The department threatened legal action if they did not cross-reference the data.

“If California was unable to independently confirm the citizenship of people on that list, the Federal Government asked that California set aside ballots received from them until the person’s citizenship was confirmed,” the lawsuit says.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) criticized the suit in a written response, calling it a “sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day.”

“The courts have made clear that the federal government has no role in how a state carries out its election process, and now, in the middle of Californians voting, they have asked local officials — who do a damn good job defending democracy — to violate federal law,” Newsom added.
A voting rights group sent a letter notifying the DOJ Wednesday they would seek a temporary restraining order if the administration didn’t abandon its plans.

“Your clients’ actions in compiling the list violates established law; your efforts to employ this list to systematically purge voters, less than a month before the election, further violates the National Voter Registration Act, among other laws,” attorneys for the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) Voting Rights Project wrote in the letter.

In July, President Trump alleged California, along with three other states, collectively had 250,000 noncitizens on their voter rolls. Though a federal “preliminary review” of these lists, which DHS included in a letter sent to the states at the time, found less than half that number — 118,000 — matched the government had flagged.
The DOJ’s lawsuit comes less than 20 days before the November midterm elections.

aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10/17/neto-bra.headline: Neto’s brace fires Chelsea past Everton but Martinez head injury mars win
aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10/17/neto-bra.author: AFP and Reuters

paragraphs.text: Argentinian international taken to hospital for precautionary tests after a head clash with Everton’s Jarrad Branthwaite.
Pedro Neto’s double condemned Everton to a first defeat of the season as Chelsea won 2-0 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium despite the loss of goalkeeper Emi Martinez to a head injury.
Neto opened the scoring inside the first minute of the second half on Saturday and secured the three points during the 11 added minutes following the lengthy treatment given to the stricken Martinez.
The Argentinian international was involved in a sickening head clash with Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite and was taken to hospital.
“As far as I know he left the stadium conscious. Right now he’s in the hospital doing the precautionary tests, so let’s see,” said Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso.
A first away win of the season lifts Chelsea above the Toffees into the top four and the Blues also recorded a first clean sheet in 23 Premier League games.
“We needed one of these wins away. We have played very professional, very serious, looking solid. It is a very good win,” added Alonso.
“We need to get many more clean sheets for the rest of the league games but for sure the first one of the season feels good and now we need to keep going this way.”
After a slow start, a fiery-tempered encounter sparked into life when Everton midfielder Harrison Armstrong launched into a tackle on Josh Acheampong for the first of five first-half yellow cards.
‘This win is for him’
That challenge also enlivened the home crowd and spurred Everton on to their best spell of the game.
Thierno Barry was guilty of another wasteful day in front of goal as the Frenchman planted a header from Jack Grealish’s cross too close to Martinez.
Chelsea have made a habit of fast starts under Alonso, but it took until four minutes before half-time to threaten when Moises Caicedo blasted off the bar from a well-worked corner.
Everton were furious that Morgan Rogers escaped a second booking just before the break after a thunderous clash with England teammate James Garner.
That proved to be a huge decision as the visitors this time flew out of the blocks at the start of the second period.
Jorrel Hato got to the byline and his low cross fell to Neto, who had time to control before firing low past Jordan Pickford.
Chelsea had not kept a Premier League clean sheet since January, but were rarely troubled by an Everton side short on forward options, despite the loss of Martinez.
“I just felt that Chelsea had that little bit more flair and ability which we didn’t possess at the right moments today,” said Everton boss David Moyes.
The treatment for Martinez threatened to halt Chelsea’s momentum as they controlled the second half.
Belgian Mike Penders replaced the Chelsea number one for his first Premier League appearance but had little to do bar dealing with a few desperate Everton crosses.
At the other end Pickford made a fine save to deny Joao Pedro.
But Chelsea did get their second goal when Neto coolly stroked into the bottom corner after Jordan Henderson’s free-kick was blocked by the Everton wall.
“We are really pleased. Shame for Emi but we wish you all the best. This win is for him,” Neto told TNT Sports after his first Premier League brace.
“We need a clean sheet, to be honest. I think we did a very good game. Emi deserved this, Mike did as well.”

cbssports.com/boxing/news/boxing-predict.headline: Boxing predictions, start times: Daniel Dubois vs. Fabio Wardley 2, Sebastian Fundora return set this weekend
cbssports.com/boxing/news/boxing-predict.author: Brent Brookhouse

paragraphs.text: Oct 17, 2026 at 12:00 pm ET • 3 min read

In May, Daniel Dubois won the WBO heavyweight championship with a stoppage win over Fabio Wardley. On Saturday, the pair will run it back in London (2 p.m. ET, DAZN PPV). That rematch highlights boxing's weekend schedule, though it's not the only world title fight on the menu.

In the first meeting between Dubois and Wardley, Wardley scored knockdowns of Dubois in the first and third rounds. Despite that early success, the real story of the fight was the toughness Wardley showed across the rest of the fight, absorbing a tremendous beating from Dubois.

Dubois was able to take advantage of Wardley's limited offensive approach and land crushing right hands round after round. All Wardley could do in response was go back to the well with the same looping one-two combinations that had produced the earlier knockdowns.

Wardley started boxing late in life, competing in white-collar shows from age 21 before turning professional. He found plenty of success, including late comeback knockout wins over Justis Huni and Joseph Parker in interim title fights before being promoted to full champion ahead of the Dubois fight.

Dubois came up in a more traditional fashion, working through the amateurs before turning pro. That seasoning provided the skills and knowledge that allowed Dubois to make further adjustments and become a more dynamic fighter after he tasted Wardley's power early on.

"I enjoy inflicting pain and putting that chaos on the other guy, what's inside me, and the pain, you know, I put it on him," Dubois said this week. "That's how boxing is, it releases your, whatever you have inside you, it's an outlet, isn't it? So, yeah, I'm looking forward to it."

Dubois has three losses in his career, all by knockout, including a pair to Oleksandr Usyk. Beyond those losses, Dubois has picked up many big wins, including over Anthony Joshua in a British megafight in 2024.

Prediction: There's no reason to think the rematch plays out much differently than the first bout. That is especially true with the rematch coming so shortly after the first meeting. As mentioned, Wardley took a hellacious beating in that fight, and since then he has had to recover as much as possible and hasn't had much time to add new wrinkles to his game. Dubois is the better fighter, and as long as he can avoid a pure knockout shot, he should be able to put a hurting on Wardley again. Pick: Daniel Dubois via TKO7
Sebastian Fundora vs. Ermal Hadribeaj
The other big fight on Saturday takes place in Las Vegas, where Sebastian Fundora will defend his WBC junior middleweight title against Ermal Hadribeaj (8 p.m. ET, DAZN).

Fundora has developed into a really good fighter after starting his career seen by many as a sideshow, with his 6-foot-6 frame towering over opponents, but a tendency to fight toe-to-toe rather than at a range that best utilized his reach. As things seemed to have been moving in the right direction, Fundora suffered a shocking knockout loss to Brian Mendoza.

Fundora rebounded from the Mendoza loss with a split-decision win over Tim Tszyu that was largely attributed to Tszyu suffering a nasty cut early in the fight as a result of a Fundora elbow. Fundora erased all doubt about that win two fights later, stopping Tszyu just seven rounds into the fight.
In his most recent fight, Fundora took just six rounds to stop Keith Thurman in their March bout.

Hadribeaj isn't a big-name fighter, and Fundora is far and away the best opponent he will have faced, but at 23-0-1, Hadribeaj has yet to suffer a loss. His most recent fight was a career-best win, taking a decision win over previously undefeated Bakary Samake.
That said, Hadribeaj has only scored eight knockouts in his career, so he likely doesn't have the power to keep Fundora off of him as the fight wears on.

Prediction: This is set up to be little more than a showcase for Fundora. He has the better resume and the kind of physical tools that simply can't be taught. Now that Fundora better mixes in fighting at distance with his ability to stand and trade inside, he's a very big problem for the junior middleweight division. Hadribeaj doesn't figure to be the fighter who can take the belt from Fundora's waist. Pick: Sebastian Fundora via TKO4

thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6155340-ra.headline: Rahm Emanuel tries out a new primary lane: Democratic ‘consultant in chief’
thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6155340-ra.author: Amie Parnes

paragraphs.text: Rahm Emanuel isn’t waiting for the 2028 presidential race to officially begin.

The former congressman turned White House chief of staff, Chicago mayor and U.S. ambassador to Japan has been making the rounds in South Carolina, the first state on the Democratic presidential primary calendar.
For the second time in recent months, he spent a couple of days this past week, appearing at fundraisers and campaigning for midterm candidates, while pushing his own strategy and message.

Emanuel has been to other early states too, including Nevada, New Hampshire and Michigan, campaigning alongside candidates running in the midterms but also making clear his intentions and political ambitions.
He has also become a near-permanent fixture on the airwaves, outperforming all of his potential competitors in the presidential race.

In the last few weeks, Emanuel has been everywhere, appearing on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” a NewsNation town hall with Chris Cuomo, PBS’s “Overheard With Evan Smith,” and Fox News host Sean Hannity’s podcast, which went on for two hours.
“He loves the hustle, and he loves the game, and no one is likely to take more meetings or make more phone calls a day,” Democratic strategist Eddie Vale said.

Emanuel isn’t simply testing the waters, political observers say. He has sought to drive the conversation with ideas, playing what one donor called “the Democratic consultant-in-chief,” trying to fill a void at a time when Democrats have been thirsty for leadership.
But in many ways, his views run counter to the energy in the left flank of the party, where democratic socialist candidates have been gaining steam.
In an interview this week on SiriusXM’s “The Briefing With Steve Scully,” Emanuel said Democrats shouldn’t seek the impeachment of President Trump if they win the House in the midterm elections.
Instead, he said Democrats should pursue an ethics package.

“In 2026, in three weeks from now, the Republicans are going to lose the election. What the Democrats do in 2027 will determine whether we won the election by bringing change,” Emanuel told Scully. “An ethics package brings change. A raise in the minimum wage 20 bucks by 2030 is bringing change.

“You do impeachment, it’s just another food fight,” Emanuel added. “I’m offended by everything this president has done. He has literally turned the Oval Office into eBay on steroids. Get change. Deliver that.”
In an interview with The Hill, Scully said Emanuel “wants to make sure his voice is heard” during the precampaign season.

“I think he would like to be president. I think he is trying to set the debate up for the party,” Scully said. “I think he’s trying to get ahead of the game to plant his flag in the more centrist wing of the party.”

“He wants to lead that battle,” Scully said, adding that Emanuel isn’t just speaking to Democratic audiences but traveling to red states including Mississippi and Louisiana. “I think he’s casting a wide canvas on where he sees the party going.”
By campaigning early, particularly while other would-be candidates are busy governing or campaigning, Scully said, “it gives Rahm a clear path right now.”
Emanuel has also tried to make the case that Democrats can continue to push affordability along with corruption, saying the two issues are “heads and tails of the same coin.”
“The president of the United States gets a $450 million gift from Qatar — Air Force One — and you’re getting $4.50 a gallon of gas,” he added.
John Morgan, an injury lawyer and Democratic mega-donor, said Emanuel is appealing to voters because “he tells it like it is.”
“I love everything about him,” Morgan added. “His positions are very well thought out and he articulates them succinctly and effectively.
“He’s very brash and direct. The question is will that sell?”
Other Democrats say Emanuel is the wrong messenger for the party at this moment.

“He is seen as part of the establishment,” one Democratic strategist said. “And that’s going to be his biggest obstacle: How does he bring people along when they largely want to move away from the past?”
One Democratic donor, who asked for anonymity to express their authentic views, said Emanuel is “really smart, really experienced, but abrasive [and] incredibly disliked.”
Still, the donor added that Emanuel has sought to soften his approach since his days in the White House and in Congress.

“A lot of people are liking what they hear because he’s taking a [more] pragmatic approach than ever before,” the donor said. “He’s a sharp-elbowed, pit-bull kind of guy, but lately he’s acting in a much softer way.”
Susan Del Percio, the veteran Republican strategist who does not support Trump, said Emanuel “right now is the only Democrat I could support.”

“What he’s doing is doing a great service for the Democratic Party,” Del Percio said. “He’s trying to take away some of the stigmas from the DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] that keeps the party’s approval rating so low. He’s trying to start a primary in such a way that can be appealing to voters.

“When you look at his tour, if you will, it’s all about setting up an agenda of what Dems are for, and also how they can appeal to the swing states that it will take to win a general election in 2028,” she said.
Del Percio specifically pointed to Emanuel’s comments about how the DSA wants to be its own party.
“The Dems are all talking about having this big tent,” she said. “But the DSA doesn’t want the rest of the party in their tent. They want their own tent.
“He’s waving this big neon sign saying pay attention to this,” Del Percio added.

phys.org/news/2026-10-salt-crystals-clue.headline: Salt crystals could hold clues to life beneath Enceladus's ice
phys.org/news/2026-10-salt-crystals-clue.author: Andrew Zinin

paragraphs.text: October 17, 2026 report
by Andrew Zinin, Phys.org
edited by Lisa Lock, reviewed by Robert Egan

The ocean beneath Saturn's moon Enceladus lies under kilometers of ice, but some of its contents do reach the surface. Jets near the south pole spray out water vapor and icy particles, offering a way to investigate the hidden ocean without drilling down to it.

The challenge is knowing which material preserves the most useful clues. A new laboratory study points to a possible target: salt crystals that trap tiny pockets of water as they grow during freezing.

Liam Perera of Diamond Light Source in the United Kingdom and colleagues found these pockets inside natron, a sodium carbonate mineral expected to form on Enceladus. Their findings, published in Communications Earth & Environment, suggest that the crystals could preserve information about the ocean's chemistry—and potentially traces of life, if any exists there.
Trapping water inside salt

To determine which surface mineral would be the best candidate, the team cooled a solution containing sodium chloride and sodium carbonate, using powerful X-rays to watch it freeze. Three-dimensional images revealed the growing crystals and their interiors, and measurements of how the crystals scattered X-rays identified the minerals present.

As natron grew, it enclosed pockets of the surrounding fluid. Larger crystals were more likely to contain these pockets and tended to hold larger samples. Only about 3% of nearly 3,800 separated grains contained fluid inclusions, as researchers call them, but all 29 grains in the largest size category did.
That makes the crystals potentially useful containers: Each pocket could retain a small sample of the water present when it closed.

There is an earthly reason to consider what else might be trapped. Earlier research on ancient salt deposits reported possible microbial cells preserved in fluid pockets inside crystals formed as water evaporated.

Although the new experiment shows that natron can trap fluid during freezing, whether it can also capture and preserve biological material remains untested. The authors propose that the surrounding mineral could help shield any such material from damaging radiation.
What type of water would a crystal capture?
A trapped sample would not necessarily be an unchanged drop of Enceladus's ocean, however.

The researchers used a solution about five times more concentrated than the estimates based on particles sampled by NASA's Cassini spacecraft. This helped produce crystals large enough to examine. In that concentrated mixture, large natron crystals began growing before the main ice formation, enclosing fluid that was expected to remain close to the starting composition.

In a more dilute, ocean-like solution, ice would probably form first. As it grew, it would leave dissolved salts behind, concentrating the remaining water. Natron forming later would capture that saltier liquid.

Yet both could tell researchers something useful: One would provide a closer record of the original water, while the other would reveal how freezing changed it. The crystals' shapes and the material around them could help distinguish those histories. At Enceladus's surface temperatures, the trapped water itself would be frozen.
Where to look

Natron, although a leading candidate for astrobiological study, has yet to be confirmed on Enceladus's surface. The team recommends that future spacecraft carry sensitive near-infrared instruments to identify it and guide sampling.

Fresh deposits near the plume vents could be particularly promising sources. Larger droplets should cool more slowly, giving crystals time and space to grow; very rapid cooling could prevent natron from crystallizing. The researchers propose that larger, salt-rich particles are also more likely to fall back near the vents.
Finding the mineral would therefore be only part of the search. Its location and condition would matter, too.

Natron should remain stable in the moon's extreme cold, but warmer terrain near the vents could gradually strip water from its crystal structure. Recently deposited crystals could offer the best combination: material delivered from the interior, with its microscopic pockets still intact.

aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/17/ilhan-omar.headline: Ilhan Omar’s lawyers demand the return of property seized in house raid
aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/17/ilhan-omar.author: Al Jazeera Staff

paragraphs.text: Lawyers for Democratic United States Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota have demanded the return of property seized in a federal raid of her Washington, DC home, accusing the US Department of Justice of conducting a politically motivated investigation and failing to follow judicial instructions during the search.

“The political motivations behind this pre-election investigation and search are clear as day,” Omar’s lawyers wrote in a letter sent to federal prosecutors on Friday and obtained by The Associated Press news agency. “This search was neither justified nor lawful.”
Recommended Stories

In the letter, Omar’s lawyers, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, challenged an investigation into her immigration history, saying there was “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”.
The letter accuses federal agents of threatening the separation of powers and failing to comply with a magistrate judge’s instructions for the search of Omar’s northeast Washington home on Monday.

Federal agents searched Omar’s home on Monday as part of an investigation into alleged immigration fraud. Authorities seized her phone and passport, and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to The Washington Post. Her lawyers also asked authorities to preserve audio and video recordings from the search.

Omar’s lawyers claim that investigators did not provide a copy of the warrant to them in advance, nor did they contact the House of Representatives’ Office of General Counsel, which disregarded the magistrate judge’s orders. The notice would have allowed Omar to seek legal counsel and potentially leverage legislation that could have challenged the warrant.

Her lawyers said the procedures outlined by the judge are intended to protect Omar’s constitutional rights as a sitting member of Congress, and safeguard against the seizure of materials related to her legislative work.
Her lawyers also argued that the investigation was politically motivated due to its proximity to the November midterm elections.

“Historically, the Department has refrained from this type of investigative activity so close to an election, so as to avoid even the appearance of politically motivated law enforcement actions,” they wrote.
The Justice Department rejected the accusations, describing the letter as “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies”.
“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” Justice Department spokesperson Emily Covington said.

Omar became a naturalised US citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia with her family as a child, according to her House biography. She has repeatedly rejected allegations by conservative critics about her immigration status, which was also probed in 2019 during Trump’s first administration.

Omar’s lawyers have requested records relating to the 2019 inquiry into her immigration history. The former investigation found insufficient evidence of wrongdoing to warrant a full investigation, according to The Washington Post.
The scope of the current investigation remains unclear.

The search took place days after Trump attacked Omar at a rally in Tennessee, describing her home country as a place of “crime and squalor” and suggesting that Vice President JD Vance and others were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump denied any involvement, telling reporters the matter was “really up to the DOJ”.

nytimes.com/2026/10/17/world/europe/pope.headline: Pope Leo Leaves Hospital, Days After Lung Cancer Surgery

paragraphs.text: Pope Leo XIV was discharged from a Rome hospital on Saturday, four days after surgery to remove a tumor from his right lung.

The pope left Gemelli Hospital at about 3:30 p.m., arriving at the Vatican after a 10-minute car journey, roughly three days earlier than the Vatican had originally suggested for when he would return to his residence.
“I am much better, thank you,” he said in English to a journalist who asked about his health as he was driven from the hospital grounds.
Vatican officials said he would deliver his weekly prayer and blessing on Sunday from his apartment overlooking St. Peter’s Square, although all of his private audiences are suspended until Tuesday.

In a statement released on Saturday by the Vatican, Leo’s doctors said that he had undergone routine checkups and a chest X-ray had revealed that the affected lung was healing well. They said that he was “fit for discharge.”

Dozens of onlookers cheered as he walked out of the hospital, some of them shouting, “Long live the pope.” He paused briefly to greet patients, some of whom held intravenous poles; shook hands with medical staff; and thanked the surgeon who conducted his operation.

Leo also stopped to speak with a 13-year-old Ukrainian girl who had arrived in Rome last year to receive treatment for cancer and met him in December. On Saturday, she thanked the pope for his support and gave him a stuffed doll that was dressed like a pontiff.

The pope caught the world off guard when he announced last Sunday that doctors had found a small growth in his lung and had decided to operate. Two days later, surgeons removed a lower lobe of his right lung and confirmed that the pope had lung cancer, as preoperative tests had shown. Information later released by the Vatican suggested the cancer was caught at an early stage.

Leo’s illness has shaken his papacy, casting uncertainty over his immediate travel itinerary and long-term plans for the church, which he has so far carried out at a slow pace. The Vatican website on Saturday still said that he planned to travel next month to South America, but some officials have suggested the trip depends on the speed of his recovery.

When Leo, the first pope born in the United States, was elected at 69, less than 18 months ago, he seemed to have years ahead of him to shape the Roman Catholic Church. With the cancer diagnosis, Leo suddenly faces the same questions of longevity that hung over his predecessor, Francis, who grew gradually more frail during his 12-year papacy.

Leo was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer. Survival rates for it vary greatly depending on the stage of the cancer and a patient’s overall health. Leo is known to play tennis regularly and had no other reported medical problems.
Doctors have not released the results of additional tests to determine what additional treatments, if any, are warranted.
Lung cancer is still a leading cause of cancer death, but that rate is half of what it was in the 1990s, partly because newly developed treatments are working.
St. Peter’s Square was bustling with visitors on Saturday afternoon. Several said that they had been concerned about the pope and were relieved he was out of the hospital.

“We were really worried about the pope, for his health, and were praying for him,” said Carolina Rodriguez, from New York City, who was traveling with her family. “Thank God that he came out from the hospital,” she added.
“Overall, we knew he’d be OK,” said her daughter, Amber, who works in engineering. “At least we hoped so.”

Lilia Donato, a homemaker from Messina, Sicily, said it was good for the world that Leo was home. “We aren’t living in a positive moment” and the pope is an inspiring voice, she said: “Let’s hope world leaders listen to him, because we need words of peace, togetherness, and unity. This is important.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/17/business/theranos.headline: The Reporter Who Exposed Elizabeth Holmes on Nathan Fielder’s Documentary

paragraphs.text: This article contains spoilers.

As I watched “You Can See Everything,” the new documentary about the convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, at an advance screening in New York earlier this week, I couldn’t help but feel envy. Ms. Holmes had granted the film’s directors, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the access she denied me a decade ago.

I was a reporter for The Wall Street Journal then, looking into Ms. Holmes’s claims about her medical technology. In media interviews and meetings with investors, she had stated that her company, Theranos, could perform hundreds of tests on a drop of blood pricked from a fingertip — a game-changing medical breakthrough that would have revolutionized the field of diagnostics. After months of reporting, I had concluded this wasn’t true and wanted to meet with Ms. Holmes to ask her about my findings. But she denied my repeated requests for an interview and instead dispatched David Boies, one of the country’s most feared litigators, to try to intimidate me and silence the whistle-blowers I had spoken to.

Ms. Holmes has wanted to tell her side of the story for a long time. In the summer of 2016 she had discussions with Errol Morris, the Academy Award-winning documentary filmmaker she had hired to make sleek Theranos commercials at the height of her pre-scandal fame. Mr. Morris entertained the notion of doing a film about Ms. Holmes seriously enough that he called me to ask me to participate.
“I see it as a ‘he said, she said,’” he told me.
“That’s not how I see it,” I responded. “There are basic facts and those facts show that Elizabeth Holmes committed fraud.”
When it became clear that Mr. Morris remained wedded to his dueling-narratives approach, I put a polite end to the conversation and hung up.
(Reached by phone Thursday, Mr. Morris said he did not dispute Ms. Holmes’s guilt but, at the time, he wanted to explore the theme of self-deception.)

It was therefore not surprising that Ms. Holmes had granted full access to another set of filmmakers seven years later on the eve of going to prison. Having lost her criminal case — in 2022, she was convicted on four counts of defrauding investors in her blood-testing start-up and sentenced to more than 11 years in prison — she no longer had anything to lose. Now was her chance to take control of the narrative and counter the unflattering story told in “Bad Blood,” my book on Theranos, and the sundry other podcast and TV portrayals that followed.

Part of me wished I could have been in Mr. Fielder’s chair at the beach bungalow that Ms. Holmes and her romantic partner, Billy Evans, had rented in San Diego a month before she was required to report to prison in the spring of 2023, sitting across from her at a table laden with pieces of her blood-testing machine.

But Mr. Fielder, I soon found out, was no gullible mark. If Ms. Holmes thought she could manipulate him and Mr. Oppenheim and take advantage of their lack of expertise in the subject matter to spin an empathetic account of an innocent woman who was misunderstood and wrongly accused, she made a colossal mistake.
