Instead, something very different happened: By letting them train their ultra-long zoom lenses on her face while subjecting herself to Mr. Fielder’s polite but insistent questioning, Ms. Holmes handed them — and us — a microscope with which to observe and dissect her lies.

As Ms. Holmes denies to Mr. Fielder that she did anything wrong, one can spot her tells: the long, unblinking stares; the little nods of the head; the forced half-smiles beneath innocently lifted eyebrows; the tears manufactured on demand. The dishonesty becomes ever more obvious. She tells Mr. Fielder at one point that she’s never once told a lie. “Liz, what?” an incredulous Mr. Fielder exclaims.

One of the film’s many highlights is a sequence where Mr. Fielder shows Ms. Holmes Abbott and Costello’s famous “Who’s on First?” routine. Ms. Holmes says she’s not familiar with it, which is credible given that she was born in 1984, decades after the duo’s heyday. But after they watch it together, she claims to still not grasp the joke. When Mr. Fielder explains it to her, she says softly: “I didn’t get it.”

You would expect someone who hadn’t initially understood a joke to blurt out “Oh!” or show some flicker of recognition when it registers, but Ms. Holmes has no visible reaction. To me, it was another tell: She had understood the joke but was playing dumb.

Why would she do this? Because in a previous sequence, Mr. Fielder had floated the notion that she interacted with the world differently, which might explain why past statements she saw as innocent were viewed by her investors as lies. By pretending not to understand the Abbott and Costello routine, she was reinforcing that notion and casting herself as the neurodivergent entrepreneur who operated on a different wavelength.
But the performance was no more convincing than her denials of wrongdoing.

Another revealing moment occurs when Mr. Evans takes her to a photography studio. The idea is to capture Ms. Holmes’s face and body from dozens of camera angles to create a digital replica that he can show their two young children when she’s in prison. But when Ms. Holmes is asked to pose in front of the cameras, she suddenly breaks down. Through a flood of tears, we hear her say that the last time people in her entourage pushed her into the spotlight, it didn’t turn out well.

The scene may be poignant to viewers who aren’t well-versed in the saga, but I practically jumped out of my theater seat. Watch Mr. Morris’s promotional videos of Ms. Holmes, or her 2014 TED talk at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco, or her dozens of public appearances as Theranos chief executive and see if you can find someone who reluctantly embraced the limelight.
The proof is in some of Ms. Holmes’s private texts from that period, which came out during her criminal trial.

On April 25, 2015, nine days after she was featured on “CBS This Morning,” Sunny Balwani, her then-lover and second-in-command, texted her that Ron Conway, a Silicon Valley angel investor, thought there was “too much hype around Theranos and you,” adding: “I am worried about over exposure without solid substance which is lacking right now.”
Ms. Holmes’s response was dismissive. “On outside they are jealous,” she texted back.

Two days later, Jim Cramer interviewed Ms. Holmes on CNBC’s “Mad Money" and compared her to Steve Jobs. Afterward, she texted Mr. Balwani: “Press strategy we talked about is Bulls eye. I can feel it. We are building a movement.”
Mr. Balwani, setting aside his earlier concerns about overexposure, texted back: “You were flawless in mad money. Just perfect.”
“Loved seeing this so much,” she replied.

Ms. Holmes is charming around Mr. Fielder, even flirtatious. But you catch fleeting glimpses of the stone-cold chief executive who hit back forcefully against my reporting and went after my sources in 2015 and 2016. When Mr. Fielder asks her yet again whether she’s sure she did nothing wrong, we hear her snap: “I did not.”

Her stubborn denials reminded me of the judge’s words when he sentenced her in November 2022. “What is the pathology of fraud?” Edward Davila of the U.S. District for the Northern District of California asked. “Is it the inability or the refusal to accept responsibility or express contrition in any way? Now perhaps that is the cautionary tale that will go forward from this case.”

In Mr. Evans, Ms. Holmes has found a kindred spirit. He refuses to entertain the possibility that his partner might be culpable despite having no firsthand knowledge of the events that led to her conviction (they met in late 2017, two years after the Theranos scandal exploded), and he is willing to forge dubious alliances to promote their narrative.

Halfway through the film’s two-hour-and-55-minute run time, we find out that Mr. Evans has become chummy with Ryan “Egypt” El-Hosseiny, an eccentric self-promoter who claims to have rebuilt Theranos’s blood-testing technology from trial exhibits and patents and proved that it works exactly as advertised. (Evidence presented at Ms. Holmes’s trial showed that the Theranos machine could perform only 12 blood tests and that the results were riddled with errors.)

Last year, Mr. El-Hosseiny erected billboards in Los Angeles, New York and Miami proclaiming Ms. Holmes’s innocence. On some, he appeared alongside Ms. Holmes, wearing sunglasses and an ostentatious, rapper-style necklace bearing the Theranos logo. Around the same time, Mr. El-Hosseiny was stationing himself outside The New York Times building in Manhattan in hopes of intercepting me. He even tried to come up to the newsroom with a cameraman in tow before being turned away by security.

Mr. Evans doesn’t seem troubled by Mr. El-Hosseiny’s antics. In fact, the two appear to be in frequent contact. In one of the film’s most entertaining sequences, Mr. Fielder catches them talking on the phone. When Mr. Evans hangs up, Mr. Fielder asks him whether being associated with someone like Mr. El-Hosseiny, whom Mr. Fielder calls a “kook,” is good for Ms. Holmes.
“Probably not,” Mr. Evans admits.
You come away feeling that Mr. Fielder is the one who has Ms. Holmes’s best interests at heart.

Mr. Evans is a big part of the film and he does not come off well. At her trial, Ms. Holmes tried to put the blame for what happened at Theranos on her ex, Mr. Balwani, who was convicted and sentenced to nearly 13 years in prison in a separate trial for his role in the fraud. The jury didn’t buy it. But what’s true is that the irascible Mr. Balwani was a terrible influence on Ms. Holmes.

Mr. Evans doesn’t seem much better. We learn that he and Ms. Holmes are working on “Theranos 2.0,” which would be laughable if it weren’t for the fact that they’re actively pursuing the idea. Ms. Holmes’s parents look on nervously as she and Mr. Evans discuss holding weekly calls with patent attorneys from prison and going “from idea to working prototype in under 365 days.”
Mr. Fielder asks Ms. Holmes’s father whether it’s a good idea for his daughter to be getting into business with a romantic partner again. “I trust Billy,” Mr. Holmes responds.

It’s hard to understand why. At one point, Mr. Evans invites the camera crew to film him naked in the shower. At another, he tells Mr. Fielder that he doesn’t care if Ms. Holmes’s digital replica is used to make pornographic content. We later learn that he has obtained power of attorney from Ms. Holmes and is controlling her X feed, writing expletive-laden posts that she would probably never write herself.

Mr. Evans comes off at times like an angry young man. He has purchased a gun that he carries at all times, and we see him practicing at a shooting range. In one disquieting scene, he threatens to ruin the lives of everyone he thinks has wronged Ms. Holmes.
“I’ve got vengeance in my heart,” he says, adding ominously: “I’m pretty strategic and well resourced. I know people who can do just about anything.”

Given my history with Ms. Holmes, I found those statements disturbing. At the very least, they provide insight into why I was never granted the same access as Mr. Fielder and Mr. Oppenheim. Mr. Evans and Ms. Holmes wanted a friendlier audience they hoped to sway.
But like the lab tests produced by Theranos, the result is not what they intended.

nytimes.com/2026/10/16/weather/malibu-wi.headline: Firefighters Race to Control California Wildfires as Winds Threaten to Spark More

paragraphs.text: A fast-growing brush fire erupted in the tinder-dry foothills of southern Orange County on Friday, injuring two firefighters, damaging at least six homes and prompting dire warnings by officials, who ordered thousands of people to immediately evacuate.

The Norte fire, as that blaze was called, started about 11:30 a.m. on Friday, when local fire officials said it was just 10 acres. About four hours later, the blaze had exploded to more than 450 acres, engulfing a pocket of wilderness tucked in the middle of wealthy suburban neighborhoods with ocean views.
Strong winds fanned the rapidly spreading fire and firefighting efforts were focused on keeping it from becoming larger, Chief TJ McGovern of the Orange County Fire Authority said in a news briefing.

The fire had grown to 570 acres on Friday evening but receded to 465 acres just after midnight Pacific time on Saturday. However, about 8 hours later, the fire service was reporting that it had spread to 570 acres again.

Dramatic local news footage showed several large homes engulfed in flames, while images posted on social media by the fire authority showed glowing red fire lines and plumes of smoke churning through brown grass along trails, just over a ridgeline from winding cul-de-sacs lined by houses with red-tiled roofs.

Nearly 16,000 people in the cities of San Juan Capistrano and San Clemente have been ordered to evacuate, Chief McGovern said. About 400 firefighters had been deployed to the Norte fire and another 400 firefighters were on their way, he added.

The two injured firefighters were in stable condition in nearby hospitals, Chief Kevin Fetterman, the fire authority’s incident commander for the Norte fire, said at the news briefing on Friday evening. He did not specify the nature of their injuries. Capt. Steve Concialdi, a spokesman for the fire authority, had said earlier that a firefighter had been treated for heat exhaustion.

The Norte fire was just the latest in a string of blazes that have ignited in Southern California, as strong Santa Ana winds combined with dry air and hot temperatures to create especially combustible conditions that were forecast to last into Saturday.

Most were quickly contained, but the howling winds throughout the region have left residents and officials on edge; all it takes, as raging wildfires in recent years have shown, is one windblown ember to destroy an entire community.

And billowing smoke from wildfires can wreak havoc of its own. The Henderson fire in the Camp Pendleton area north of San Diego had burned roughly 2,080 acres as of Friday evening, but early evacuation orders had been lifted. Still, the smoke from the fire prompted the authorities to close Interstate 5, a major artery connecting San Diego and Orange counties.

Farther north, hundreds of firefighters had started to gain control of the Bryson fire, which was burning through dry brush in the Santa Monica Mountains north of Malibu, Calif. The Bryson fire ignited late Thursday afternoon and quickly spread to more than 140 acres and forced evacuations. On Friday afternoon, about 12,000 people were under evacuation warnings, according to a New York Times analysis.
Friday was delivering the hottest temperatures and strongest winds of the week, with highs in the 90s and winds up to 50 miles per hour in the valleys and up to 90 m.p.h. in the mountains.

Much of Los Angeles County and neighboring Ventura County will be under a red flag warning through Saturday, and mountainous areas of Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo Counties were under warnings through Friday evening. The warnings mean that experts are worried that fires could start more easily and spread quickly if they do.
Any new fires that start on Friday could “get really big, really fast,” said Ryan Kittell, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Oxnard.
At 3 p.m., the National Weather Service said the worst of the winds were likely over in the area of the Norte fire, but windy weather remained in the forecast into Saturday.
“We’re seeing the winds decrease already, but it’s going to be a slow progression for the next few hours,” said Jonathan Suk, a meteorologist with the Weather Service office in San Diego.
A wind advisory for parts of Orange County, including where the Norte fire was burning, was in effect through noon Saturday.
Southern California Edison preemptively cut power to more than 130,000 homes and businesses to reduce the risk that power lines knocked over by winds could send sparks flying.

Leaders in Los Angeles on Friday morning tried to reassure skittish residents of the county’s vast, hilly areas most prone to fires that they are ready for any blazes that might ignite, while also urging residents to stay vigilant.

“We know the uncertainty that comes with these fires, which is why it’s important for us to look out for one another and to stay prepared,” Lindsey Horvath, a Los Angeles County supervisor, said in a news conference on Friday.
“Know your zone, sign up for alerts, have your go bag ready, and if you’re told to evacuate, do so immediately,” she said.
More than 400 firefighters have been sent to battle the Bryson fire, which was about 39 percent contained as of Friday.
“Great progress was made by firefighters overnight,” said Anthony Marrone, the Los Angeles County fire chief.
Mr. Marrone said that no structures had been destroyed or damaged so far.

Residents of the remote canyon areas near the fire were ordered to evacuate, while other residents were under warnings. Nearby parks, roads and the Getty Villa, a museum perched above the Pacific Coast Highway in Malibu, were all closed preemptively.
California has had fewer fires this year, with only 300,000 acres burning since Jan. 1, compared with the over one million acres that fires would have typically burned by mid-October.

For Angelenos, Friday’s conditions called to mind the ones that helped lead to the Palisades fire and the Eaton fire last year, which together killed dozens of people and burned thousands of homes. Many residents who were displaced in Malibu and in the nearby Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles still haven’t returned. In the aftermath of those catastrophes, numerous reports found that the county and city were ill-prepared for wildfires of that magnitude.

This week, Los Angeles leaders — including Mayor Karen Bass, whose reputation never fully recovered after she was out of the country when the Palisades fire ignited — have emphasized that firefighters and equipment have already been sent out to high-risk areas, even if there is no active fire.
The Los Angeles County sheriff, Robert Luna, on Friday morning warned would-be burglars that deputies would be on the streets of the evacuated areas and that the department was adding extra patrols.
“If you think you’re going to come in and take advantage of these poor folks who have been asked to evacuate or don’t have power,” he said, they would most likely encounter officers.

nytimes.com/2026/10/17/dining/breakfast-.headline: Can Cereal Be Healthy? Big Companies Are Trying.

paragraphs.text: In hindsight, this year’s fiber-forward Super Bowl commercial starring William Shatner may have been a Hail Mary. Using the nickname Will Shat, Mr. Shatner passes around boxes of Raisin Bran while making puns about bowel movements. He even name-checked a Shih Tzu.

Cereal is in trouble. Despite a brief glimmer of growth during the pandemic, the nearly $13 billion business in the United States has gone soggy. Shoppers last year bought 13 percent less cereal than in 2021, according to Nielsen IQ. Despite price hikes, dollar sales are declining, too.

At a time when gut health, protein content and convenience drive food sales, many Americans view grabbing a breakfast bar or drinkable yogurt — or nothing at all — as easier and healthier than pouring milk over a bowl of ultraprocessed grains from a box. Younger people didn’t grow up with the same cultural or emotional attachment to breakfast cereals as earlier generations raised on cereal ads sandwiched between Saturday-morning cartoons.

“Generation Z in particular is not so enthusiastic about cereal for breakfast, and that’s hit the long-established players in the market,” said Richard Caines, a senior analyst with the market research company Mintel. “They are more enthusiastic about products that have functional health benefits.”

Mix in pressure from the “Make America Healthy Again” movement’s push for less-processed food, in addition to the rise of GLP-1 drugs and higher prices for what used to be a budget-stretcher, and you can understand why cereal executives are worried.

As it has many times since the first bowl was poured during the Lincoln administration, the industry is returning to cereal’s roots as a health food, born of a Victorian belief that bland grains softened in milk could restart sluggish digestive tracts and ease other maladies.

Classic cereal boxes are being redesigned to trumpet their fiber and vitamin content, or reformulated with more protein and less sugar. Granola is the new It cereal. In July, WK Kellogg Co., which the food giant Ferrero Group bought in 2025, introduced Kashi Gut Health Granola. A month later, Ferrero bought Purely Elizabeth, a granola company started by a Manhattan holistic-nutrition counselor, for $850 million.

“Now is the time to be deliberate and disruptive in continuing to make cereal culturally relevant,” said Doug VanDeVelde, chief growth officer at WK Kellogg, in May as the company rolled out a redesign for some cereals that covers a third of the box with simplified nutrition information, highlighting the ingredients in vogue with health-focused shoppers.

“Consumers are telling us that they want their cereal to work harder for them and to do more,” said Joan Kavanaugh, vice president for national buying of the global discount supermarket chain Aldi. “And while it does more for them, it needs to cost less.”
Like other grocery companies with their own private-label lines, Aldi is creating new cereals with added protein and fiber.

The four biggest cereal companies, which control about 80 percent of the market, are feeling pressure from the growing popularity of those house brands and from small protein-forward, no-sugar upstarts like Catalina Crunch and Magic Spoon, which began selling only online and are now in thousands of supermarkets.
Sweetening Sales

For all that, the towering wall of cereal boxes in any store is still dominated by Cinnamon Toast Crunch, Frosted Flakes and other sugary favorites that cereal makers euphemistically call “taste-forward cereals.”
But even those are getting a glow-up.

The Ghost supplement company joined General Mills this year to create a Lucky Charms-flavored cereal with 17 grams of protein per serving, which is a cup and a quarter. That’s more than four times the amount in the original version, with about 25 percent less sugar. A banner promising “high fiber to support digestive wellness” has been slapped across boxes of Frosted Mini-Wheats. Cheerios Cookies & Crème with Protein, which General Mills infused with protein powder from yellow peas, is a top seller on Instacart.

“It’s all about macros,” said Laura Jones, Instacart’s chief marketing officer, referring to macronutrients like proteins, carbohydrates and fats. “We’re looking for the intersection of health goals plus the emotional level of fulfillment that you can get from a comfort food like cereal.”
Four of the top 10 fastest-growing cereals on the Instacart site are high-protein, and three of those are versions of Cheerios.

Alyssa Buckalew, vice president for innovation, technology and quality at General Mills, said Americans still love cereal. “The category has been challenged and there’s a number of reasons for that, but we do feel that there’s still relevance for cereal,” she said.

Like other big cereal companies, General Mills is trying to entice more adults to eat its sugar-laden cereals, like Golden Grahams and Lucky Charms, with the message that they’re not just for breakfast. Cereal is being promoted as a dessert with benefits. It now comes packaged in tubes or individual pouches that can be tipped directly into the mouth — leaving, say, a gamer’s hands free of crumbs.

Last spring, Dairy Queen introduced shakes made with Fruity Pebbles and cones covered in crushed Cinnamon Toast Crunch called “cinnadust.” Kellogg’s has even started putting toys back in cereal boxes.
A Pantry Full of Kashi
Nyles Peterson and Megan Saia are exactly the health-focused customers the cereal makers aim for. The Atlanta couple bake focaccia on the weekends and think a lot about their macros.

Ms. Saia, 28, a lawyer, never ate cereal while growing up and didn’t think she ever would. Mr. Peterson, 31, an engineer, loved Cinnamon Toast Crunch so much that his friends sent him a carton of it as a joke when he was in college. His tastes have matured along with his health goals.
“Eating a bowl of cereal is pretty fast and easy and enjoyable,” he said. “To get protein and fiber from it is a big plus.”

They tried psyllium husks and other sources of fiber, but didn’t love the taste or how it made them feel. They hunted for a cereal with a simple list of ingredients, lots of fiber and none of the whey or pea protein add-ins that can give it a peculiar taste and texture.
Their mainstay is Kashi GO Original, whose 12 grams each of protein and fiber per serving are big selling points. More than a dozen boxes of various Kashi cereals sit in their pantry.

“Initially I didn’t want to eat it because I thought it was ultraprocessed, which I’m sure it is,” Ms. Saia said. “But it’s just so convenient and an easy way to get enough fiber that I don’t really care, and it makes me feel fine.”

They eat it with yogurt, whole milk or as a dry snack. And because cereal prices have risen about 25 percent since 2020, according to data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, they wait for buy-one, get-one sales to load up their cart.
Back to the Beginning

Breakfast cereal as we know it was created in 1863 by Dr. James Caleb Jackson, a physician in a Western New York sanitarium. His recipe was a dried mix of water and a coarse whole wheat flour championed by Sylvester Graham, an eccentric, health-obsessed Presbyterian minister who invented the graham cracker.

Dr. Jackson named his cereal granula, and it was so hard you couldn’t eat it unless it soaked overnight in milk or water. He and other evangelists for better nutrition believed that bland, unstimulating food would soothe the body’s digestive system and suppress sexual urges.

Two brothers, John Harvey Kellogg and Will Keith Kellogg, who were influenced by the dietary edicts of Seventh-Day Adventism and ran a sanitarium in Battle Creek, Mich., came up with cornflakes 35 years later. Around the same time, the businessman Charles William Post created Grape-Nuts.

Decades of advertising, food-science advances and mountains of sugar followed, transforming cereal into what the nutritionist Marion Nestle calls “vitamin-supplemented cookies” in her new book, “Sugar Coated: Unboxing the Hidden Forces Shaping America’s Favorite Breakfast Food.”

She wrote it with Lisa Sutherland, a former vice president for nutrition at the Kellogg Company and the interim president of Jacksonville University. “The more things change, the more things stay the same in the cereal industry,” Dr. Sutherland said. “They just keep cycling back to their roots.”

Cereal companies, which might introduce a dozen varieties of their most popular cereals every year, have two ways to catch a health wave. They can redesign packaging to emphasize certain nutrients that already exist, a process that can take a few months, or change the formula. That’s trickier, and can take a year or longer.

“When you change or add certain ingredients, they can have funky flavors to them,” Dr. Sutherland said. Vitamin D can add a metallic taste, and certain proteins lend a bitter or cardboard flavor and a chalky texture. “So then you have to figure out how am I going to mask the flavor and deal with the structural impact.”
Claims and Clashes

Companies most often turn to linguistic gymnastics to give their cereal a health halo, sometimes battling federal regulators and consumer groups. The fights come down to minuscule details like the font size on labels, the definition of words like healthy and nutritious, or larger scientific questions like whether cereal really can help you sleep better, improve a child’s attentiveness or prevent a heart attack.
In 1984, Kellogg partnered with the National Cancer Institute to claim that the fiber in cereal might prevent colon cancer.
“Once that happened, there was no going back,” Dr. Nestle writes. “Kellogg hadn’t discussed it with the F.D.A., and its officials were appalled. But the National Cancer Institute was thrilled.”

The most famous battle between cereal companies and the Food and Drug Administration came in the late 2000s, when General Mills mounted a vast marketing campaign claiming that the oat fiber in Cheerios could lower cholesterol by 4 percent in six weeks. The F.D.A. said that promoting the cereal with specific, clinically proven medical outcomes effectively reclassified Cheerios as an unapproved new drug under federal law. The company reverted to more generic claims, like “can help lower cholesterol.”
“If you give it a moment’s thought,” Dr. Nestle said, “you know that proving breakfast cereal prevents heart disease is ridiculous.”

To her mind, the worst misrepresentation came during the 2009 swine flu epidemic, when Kellogg executives added a prominent “immunity” banner on boxes of Rice Krispies and Cocoa Krispies, claiming that the cereals’ antioxidants could help keep children from getting sick.

Nutritionists and consumer watchdog groups called the move predatory and deceptive, pointing out that refined grain cereals that were nearly 40 percent sugar by weight weren’t exactly health foods. State attorneys general balked, and the Federal Trade Commission barred Kellogg from making health or immunity benefit claims unless they were backed by scientific evidence.
“They’re just desperate to find a way to sell,” Dr. Nestle said. “They never miss a trick.”
Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. Get regular updates from New York Times Cooking, with recipe suggestions, cooking tips and shopping advice.

nytimes.com/2026/10/17/us/politics/elect.headline: Trump Revives 2020 Election Conspiracy Theories as Midterms Loom

paragraphs.text: One of President Trump’s many false claims about the 2020 presidential election, which he has repeatedly, and falsely, claimed was rigged against him, was an assertion that there had been “thousands and thousands” of “crooked votes” cast in Wisconsin nursing homes.

The allegation was unfounded. Yet the view that American nursing homes are a hotbed of illegal voting, where aides regularly change the votes of unwitting residents, lives on in Trumpworld. And like a number of other enduring conspiracies about election fraud, the false claim has seeped into the mechanics of governance this year.

In July, the Department of Health and Human Services issued fresh guidance on the topic of voting assistance, “reminding facilities and their staff that they cannot engage in inappropriate coercion or other violations of residents’ rights.” Voting rights advocates decried the message for its potential to discourage nursing-home aides from providing lawful assistance to elderly voters.

The episode has heightened fears that the Trump administration plans to use the power and force of the federal government to cast doubt on the election, discourage participation or, in a worst-case scenario, try to delegitimize the results.

Election fraud in nursing homes is one of many conspiracy theories from years past that are haunting the 2026 midterms. Though some of the wilder schemes offered to support Mr. Trump’s effort to overturn his 2020 loss have been largely abandoned — there is little talk these days about unleashed Krakens, or the nefarious influence of Italian satellites — other 2020-vintage conspiracies have carried over into the present.
And this year, some of them carry the force of the executive branch behind them.

Among the most prominent are Mr. Trump’s unproven claim that significant numbers of noncitizens have made their way onto American voter rolls, and his baseless assertion that mail voting is “inherently corrupt.” Hundreds of investigators from several federal agencies have been dedicated this year to hunting for noncitizen voters, even though experts say the practice is exceedingly rare.

In September, the U.S. Supreme Court rejected a Trump administration plan that would have used the U.S. Postal Service to enact complicated changes to the way Americans vote by mail in the weeks before Election Day. The plan also called for the agency to deny mail services for ballot delivery in states that refused to comply, raising the specter of the disenfranchisement of millions of Americans.
Other administration efforts appear to stem from old conspiracies that live on today, including the idea that certain voting hardware is untrustworthy.

Last month, Markwayne Mullin, Mr. Trump’s homeland security secretary, asked the Justice Department to look into whether voting machines that tally votes with the aid of electronic codes can be trusted to create a verifiable record. Tina Peters, a Trump ally and former Colorado county clerk who was convicted in state court of tampering with voting machines after the 2020 election, recently met with the president, who had symbolically pardoned her, in the White House. Ms. Peters has raised concerns about voting machines that have foreign-made parts, and has said that she wants Mr. Trump to seize such machines.

“To have the federal government undermining the credibility of our elections is troubling,” said David Becker, a former voting rights lawyer for the Justice Department who now runs the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that works to support election officials in both parties.
To Mr. Becker, that effort is a “tired” one. He noted that conspiracists have failed, over the course of six years, to verify their claims. But he said there was still reason to be concerned.
“For the first time in our nation’s history, the federal government appears to be prepared to act as an active amplifier of disinformation,” he said.
Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, defended Mr. Trump in an email.

“Despite extreme Democrats and the media claiming it never happens, the evidence of voter fraud continues to pile up,” she wrote. “Anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable.”
‘Right about everything’

Critics of the administration fear that the embrace of conspiratorial ideas could be used to justify actions that may disenfranchise voters before the election. For example, the administration has encouraged states to use a database that goes by the acronym SAVE to check for noncitizen voters, even though the use of the database is known to have resulted in numerous errors.

Alternatively, critics are concerned that if state or local election officials decline to address dubious concerns about their voter rolls or voting machines, the administration could use their refusal to act to construct post-election arguments that the results are not valid.

In addition to creating opportunities for tactical advantage, however, the embrace of conspiracies also appears to be motivated by something more fundamental: the belief among some of Mr. Trump’s supporters that he “was right about everything,” as one of his signature ball caps once put it — especially his fantastical belief that he never actually lost to Democrat Joseph R. Biden Jr. in 2020.
“The core belief of the MAGA movement is we won the 2020 election,” Steve Bannon, the right-wing influencer and former Trump adviser, said in a recent interview with “CBS News Sunday Morning.”

The Wisconsin nursing home conspiracy, and recent executive branch moves that appear to be inspired by it, demonstrate how the conspiracy-promotion machine translates into actions that could affect midterm voters.

Mr. Trump alleged in a speech in Arizona in 2022 that “almost everybody” had voted in the state’s nursing homes in 2020 — an anomaly, he said, because only a “small portion” of such residents typically vote. A few days after the speech, the website Factcheck.org debunked the claims in a detailed post. “There is no evidence of fraud and voting rates in the state’s nursing homes were not out of the ordinary,” the post’s author wrote.

Four years later, with the 2026 midterms approaching, administrators for Mr. Trump’s Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services sent a memo to nursing home inspectors around the country that warned workers at the facilities about taking part in “inappropriate coercion or other violations of residents’ rights.”

That language replaced previous federal guidance that had “encouraged nursing homes to take proactive steps to help residents participate in elections,” according to an analysis by the Long Term Care Community Coalition, a nonprofit that advocates on behalf of patients in nursing homes and other facilities. A group of liberal senators argued that the new memo could serve to intimidate nursing-home workers who want to help residents of the facilities cast their votes.

Last month, the Election Integrity Network, a right-wing group headed by Cleta Mitchell, a key figure in the failed effort to overturn Mr. Trump’s 2020 loss, released a “tool kit” meant to help volunteers “confirm” that nursing home residents “are protected from leftist groups.”

During an appearance on Mr. Bannon’s “War Room” podcast, Ms. Mitchell argued that liberal groups “go into nursing homes, and they go into group homes, and they basically steal the votes of these most vulnerable people.”
Ms. Mitchell encouraged volunteers to guard against such actions, particularly in nursing homes located in “competitive House districts.”
Hacking into ‘a toaster’

Mr. Trump promulgated unfounded concerns about noncitizen voting after his 2016 election victory, when he claimed that millions of them illegally participated in the contest. At the time, the nonpartisan Brennan Center for Justice looked into the allegations and found them to be untrue. This year, Mr. Trump’s Justice Department sent letters to every state government threatening criminal prosecution if election officials counted ballots cast by noncitizens.

His allegations that mail voting was suspect began in the months before he lost his re-election bid in November 2020 — in the midst of the coronavirus pandemic, when state and local election officials had scrambled to expand their mail ballot programs to keep voters safe.

The president has continued that drumbeat this year — until this month, when, with his party facing low polling numbers in congressional races, he released a video urging Republicans to vote by mail anyway. Mr. Trump himself voted by mail in Florida primaries this year.

Mr. Trump also has a longstanding obsession with voting machines, and has claimed that they were somehow manipulated as part of a plot to steal the 2020 election from him. In a January 2026 interview with The New York Times, he said he regretted not ordering the National Guard to seize voting machines in swing states after his re-election loss.

Election security experts have found flaws in certain American voting machines; a 2022 report by the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, a part of Homeland Security, identified several vulnerabilities in machines manufactured by Dominion Voting Systems, which has since been acquired by the company Liberty Vote. Dominion sued multiple media outlets and Trump allies over their false claims about machine security, and reached settlements with all of them.

But the executive director of CISA at the time said there was no evidence that anyone had taken advantage of the vulnerabilities. And a number of election security experts agree that there is no evidence to show that machines have been exploited to manipulate recent elections.

“Voting machines, under federal law, can’t be networked, can’t be connected to the Internet,” said Representative Joseph D. Morelle, a Democrat from New York who works on election security issues as ranking member of the Committee on House Administration. “You could no more hack into a voting machine in America than you could hack into my toaster.”

Mr. Becker, the former Justice Department lawyer, noted that the courts, so far, have done much to block conspiracy-fueled efforts to change election procedures. Still, the disinformation had made the job of administering elections more difficult and sowed mistrust among voters.

In a recent interview, Phil McGrane, a Republican who serves as secretary of state in Idaho, said his office tries to push back against the mistrust with education campaigns and even one-on-one conversations with voters.
Mr. McGrane was also asked if he thought the Trump administration was acting irresponsibly in its embrace of conspiracies.
“I’m not going to comment on that,” he said.

nytimes.com/2026/10/17/us/politics/susan.headline: Susan Collins Says Rival’s ‘Oh, Shut Up’ Comment Reflects How He Treats Women

paragraphs.text: Senator Susan Collins, Republican of Maine, criticized her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, over a debate moment when he told her to “shut up,” saying the remark reflected how he treats women.

“I was struck by how reflexive the response, ‘Oh, shut up’ was,” Ms. Collins, the longest-serving Republican woman in Senate history, told Fox News on Friday, adding that “the fact that it seemed like such an automatic, quick reply was very telling.”

She said the exchange brought to mind what she described as the “reputation” that Mr. Jackson, a former State Senate president, had when he was a state lawmaker, “particularly when he’s dealing with women with whom he disagrees.”
“So in some ways, it didn’t surprise me,” said Ms. Collins, whose race could be critical in the battle for control of the Senate.
A spokeswoman for Mr. Jackson, Maggie Amjad, said in a statement that Ms. Collins had run a campaign “based on personal attacks” and was twisting the debate exchange.

On a debate stage Thursday night, Mr. Jackson, speaking in a low voice, told Ms. Collins to “shut up” after she said that a heckler disrupting the debate — by yelling about data centers — was a supporter of Mr. Jackson.
“This is obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” Ms. Collins said.
He replied: “Oh, shut up. I did not — I didn’t — I don’t even know that kid.”
Mr. Jackson has defended his response.

“She accused me of setting that up, which is completely untrue,” Mr. Jackson told WGME-TV in an interview published Friday. He added that he had sought to treat Ms. Collins with respect, but that she had “spent millions of dollars attacking” him in “a way that I don’t think is professional either.”
His spokeswoman, responding to Ms. Collins’s interview with Fox News, compared Mr. Jackson’s record with Ms. Collins’s on issues affecting women.

Ms. Amjad said in her statement that Mr. Jackson had responded in the debate to a false accusation from Ms. Collins, and that her “campaign’s attempt to turn that exchange into anything else is baseless.”

Ms. Amjad noted Mr. Jackson’s support for abortion rights and paid family and medical leave, and Ms. Collins’s vote to confirm a Supreme Court justice, Brett M. Kavanaugh, who later helped overturn a federal right to abortion.
During the race, Ms. Collins’s campaign has accused Mr. Jackson of bullying women when he was a state lawmaker.

Mr. Jackson was known to have a temper during his time in the State Legislature. In 2021, during an argument with Heather Sanborn, a state lawmaker, he threw a water bottle across a room. He has said that he regrets the episode, but that he will not apologize for “being passionate,” and that he fights hard for issues he believes in.

nytimes.com/2026/10/17/magazine/bono-and.headline: 50 Years In, What’s the Point of U2? Bono and the Edge Have Answers.

paragraphs.text: U2, as I’m sure you’re well aware, is one of the biggest bands of all time. The Irish quartet has released iconic albums like “The Joshua Tree” (1987), “Achtung Baby” (1991) and “All That You Can’t Leave Behind” (2000); staged some of the highest-grossing and most innovative tours ever; and won 22 Grammys, among myriad other achievements. Still, there are other rock artists on that level. Not many, but a few. Where U2 may truly be unparalleled is that all that success was earned by the same four guys.

The four members of the band — Bono on lead vocals, the Edge on guitar, Larry Mullen Jr. on drums and Adam Clayton on bass — still occupy the same positions they did when they first played together in suburban Dublin in September 1976 — 50 years ago this fall. (And from what I understand, they all still like one another, too.) Especially in the tempestuous world of rock ’n’ roll, that longevity and stability is to be celebrated.

Which is exactly what the band has done. On Sept. 25, U2 celebrated its golden anniversary with performances in front of giddy students at Mount Temple Comprehensive School in Dublin, where the members first met, and then, as a surprise, from a balcony of a former rock club in front of an instant crowd of thousands in the city’s center. Next month, on Nov. 13, U2 will release “Carnaval De Luz,” the band’s first full-length album of new material since 2017. (It follows two EPs, “Days of Ash” and “Easter Lily,” both released this year.)

On the day after those commemorative events, I spoke with Bono and the Edge, the band’s two principal songwriters, about their long working relationship, friendship, and what U2 still means — both to them and to the world.

I think of U2 as wanting to be the best and biggest band in the world. But it probably shouldn’t be the case that the best and biggest rock ’n’ roll band in the world is a band that’s been around for 50 years, comprising guys in their 60s.
Bono: That’s very, very hurtful, David.
The Edge: But fair.
So what do you think the purpose of U2 is right now? What should U2 be trying to be?

The Edge: We genuinely think that we might just write the best song we’ve ever written next week, or do the best show we’ve ever done next tour. When we talk about the best, we’re not thinking about rock ’n’ roll. We’re thinking about our favorite bands and what, if I’m in the audience at a show, would I want to see and hear. So it’s where rock ’n’ roll collides with activism, where rock ’n’ roll collides with ideas from fine arts. And I suppose a transcendent aspect as well. We’ve never thought it was necessary to hold back our own spiritual quests and questionings from our work. They are all expressed. And when we hit a song that has a transcendent quality, that’s the peak for me. I really think we’re in with a shout of the best songs we’ve ever written, the best tours we’ve done, still. That’s why I’m still in this band.

Bono: And therefore, the shout of the best songs anyone’s ever written. That’s where U2 gets really annoying. That grandiosity, which, by the way, is in all the artists that want to go there — the Beatles, Nirvana. I’m jealous when we’re left out of the pop charts. That’s a personality flaw, but deep down, it’s because I don’t want those ideas to be left out of the mainstream. My favorite artists stormed the mainstream. David Bowie, I think of his best work as being experimental and innovative, but even into his 40s, 50s, he could throw out a perfect pop song.
When you say there are ideas that you want to be in the mainstream, what are they?

Bono: The metaphysical thing, the gospel side of U2 — that was only allowed in rock ’n’ roll if you were Black. You can’t be white people talking about God, because generally white people who talk about God make our audience very nervous, you know? But not in the Black church in America. Coming to the United States, we’d just seen those televangelists, and we were like, Wow, these people are in deep trouble. Then you walk into a Black church and you hear the abandonment of the singing and that feeling — it’s fervor, but not freaky fervor. So being able to sing songs of faith and devotion and songs of doubt, to put the gospel with the blues, which is rock ’n’ roll. There’s nowhere you can’t go, including the pop charts. My constant argument is don’t cede the charts to just those pop mechanics. Hip-hop did it and got revolutionary ideas on the radio. But a lot of indie stuff just gave up. They weren’t even bothering.

You said that talking about God in your music can be a little uncomfortable for your audience, but I would argue that U2’s religious impulse is hugely important to your audience. It’s a big part of why people feel so connected to the band.

The Edge: I mean, yes, but we weren’t seeing it as a selling point. We were seeing it as the thing we have to speak about because it’s where we’re coming from. But people have said that we’re the band that people who don’t know that they believe in God like. It’s in the work in such a natural way. There’s no polemic there. It’s just our search, our inquiry. And it involves so much doubt. It has to, I think. Because if it’s not dogma, then it’s constantly in flux. I would say I’m agnostic about half of the week, and then the rest of the week I’ve got an incredibly strong faith. But it’s always changing, ready to be upgraded.
I want to ask about failure and success. Obviously, U2 had enormous successes. But there have been failures, too.
The Edge: A lot you wouldn’t even have seen or heard of.
So what does success or failure for the new album look like?
The Edge: I feel it’s already a success myself, because of the degree of time and effort and dedication to the work. I don’t really care that much what happens now because I know it’s really great.

Bono: I could say that, but I wouldn’t believe it. It’s a bit like you’re a comedian, you’ve got a routine, your punchline arrives, and if no one laughs, it’s not quite the same. Some of the songs, I would love to see even another artist take them somewhere. We were just talking about gospel music a minute ago. There is a song called “Glorify” on the album. We really ended up putting what’s like a demo on the album. It’s really minimal, the expression of the song. But that’s a screaming dance-floor hit. That’s how I imagine it. There’s a part of me that goes, [expletive], I want to do that version. I’m not sure we can. Somebody else should do that to help it cross over.

We’re speaking almost exactly 50 years ago to the day that you guys practiced for the first time in drummer Larry Mullen Jr.’s kitchen. Edge, in Bono’s memoir, “Surrender,” he writes that when you were teenagers, you and your brother, Dik, had a reputation as weirdos — pleasant weirdos but weirdos nonetheless. This was in reference to you and your brother blowing up your family’s garden shed?
The Edge: Quite likely.
Do you remember having any sense of Bono’s reputation before you all started playing together?

The Edge: First of all, that was an absolutely valid comment from Bono. Myself and my brother, there is some neurodivergence there of some sort. I’m not sure exactly what. A.D.H.D., autism, whatever. So socially speaking we were always a bit on the fringe. But, yeah, fascinated with explosives. I know way too much about how to blow things up than I ought to. But Bono’s reputation preceded him because one of my best friends growing up, Shane Fogarty, went to Mount Temple a year ahead of me, so I quizzed him about school, and he says, “It’s all right, you don’t have to wear uniforms, people are very nice, and there’s some fun heads there.” I said, “Like who?” He says: “This mad [expletive] head called Paul Hewson. He’s mental, but he’s good fun.” So even before I went, I’d heard about this character. I guess Bono’s always been that extrovert, exhibitionist performer, and he had that at age 13 already.

You guys have documented your career together in a bunch of different ways: in documentary films, in the “U2 by U2” book, in countless interviews. But are there ways in which your memories and understanding of how you came together has been superseded by the legend and the lore?

Bono: You’re suggesting we are not superheroes? [Laughs] I always saw us in some sort of mythological sense, if I’m honest. The names — think about it. We wished to escape suburbia and discover these other selves, and we gave those other selves names. The Ramones were key for us, and they are really well-drawn characters.
What you just said about coming up with the fictional names — this always killed me about the band. Bono! Edge! And then … Adam and Larry. Was there any discussion that they should have names too?

The Edge: We need to explain the whole name thing. We laughed a lot at that age. We would laugh at each other and ourselves and that was the deal. So the names were not necessarily designed for their heroic aspect. Bono’s very first name was in fact Steinrich Van Haitian Bang Bang Bang, and then I was Inchicore for a while before I became the Edge. Adam for a while was known as Mrs. Byrnes, and Larry for some reason was the Jam Jar. We were borrowing a lot from Monty Python.
Bono: It’s about inventing who you want to be rather than who you were given when you were born at a certain point, place and time.

Bono, when you and I spoke last, around the time of your book, you told me that U2 had been working on the album “Songs of Ascent,” but then thought you needed an album of “unreasonable” guitar music instead. Then I saw somewhere you, Edge, said that the band had been working on an album of “sci-fi Irish folk” with Brian Eno. And yet we’ve arrived at “Carnaval De Luz.” So in a practical way, can you describe when the concept for new music changes? Does Bono show up one day and say: “Guys, we’re scrapping sci-fi Irish folk. We’re doing ‘Carnaval’!”? How does that actually work?

The Edge: Really, the music tells you. As we were working on those projects, it was pure creative experimentation and exploration. There was no deadline, nothing booked or committed to. I had also spent the whole pandemic lockdown just working on music. So we had this beautiful opportunity to create with no agenda and just see where it took us. But what we had decided is that the album should be a countervailing mood to the times. The times are anxious, despondent. People are really a bit lost, and we were like, What is it that we can help with here? And we thought an album that’s a party, a celebration, a sort of bringing people together, a gathering around our common aspirations, would be the thing to do.

Bono: There’s a defiance to this, too. There’s a Dan Savage quote about when he was an AIDS activist in San Francisco in the middle of that crisis. He said: In the morning, we would bury our friends. In the afternoon, we’d go out to protest so we’d have less people to bury. Then, in the evenings, we would go out and dance, because the dance was what we were fighting for. I loved that so much. That is not surrendering to the melancholy. That’s the defiance. Sorry to do this as an Irish person, but again, if you go to the Black church during civil rights, they’re up. Sly and the Family Stone, no minor chords. It’s like, wow, “Dance to the Music.” That’s “Carnaval.” Defiant joy is the thing we were looking for.
Where’s the line between the defiance you’re describing and fiddling while Rome burns?
Bono: What do you think, Nero?

The Edge: Well, one is to be in denial, and one is to be fully aware, to stare darkness in the face and to still choose joy. That’s the difference. I think technology’s a big problem right now. Social media — people are in their heads too much. They’re in their part of the echo chamber of their own algorithm. What’s really important is the reset. We are so much more capable than we are led to believe, and by being isolated and by allowing the wave of negativity to go on unchallenged, people are feeling disempowered and dejected. They don’t understand that they can be part of something great. That’s what’s really positive about rock ’n’ roll shows and festivals. It gives people that sense of agency again.
Bono: Can I just say, rage is part of this. Rage is part of the right response. Anger is OK. To surrender to the melancholy is what we’re trying to avoid.

One could almost think of “Carnaval De Luz” as a protest album, but it’s a protest album without proper nouns. You’re not saying who you’re protesting against or naming anyone explicitly. And I’m thinking of this in the context of some of your peers at the top of the rock ’n’ roll pyramid. Bruce Springsteen was out on the road this year giving speeches railing against Trump and his administration and its policies. On the other side, I spoke to Mick Jagger earlier this year, and I asked him a question about the function of rock stars, and he basically said, Hey, I’m here to help you have a good time. Nobody wants to be lectured. And I wondered if making an album, like you did, of politically galvanizing, defiantly joyful protest music without actually mentioning politics, was your way of trying to walk a middle path there.

Bono: No. It’s picking the fight with the author of all of this mess. I found believing in God — or that God is love — unusually easy in my life. But the concept of evil was tricky for me. It wasn’t as easy to digest. So in the new song “If the World Is at War We Better Not Be,” the line goes:

I wanna speak to the spiritYou can feel it, but you can’t fear itBe ye kings or queens or emperors of despairWe’re not arguing the tossWe got some words for your bossWe’re speaking to who speaks through youTo the prince of the power of the airAll these shimmers and these glimmers, mirrors that must crack, all the neon fizzing flickers, we’re grateful for some of thatThe fiction of a nation, the stories we don’t tellWe need the light of illumination so you can go right back to hellIf the world is at war, we better not be.
That’s what this album’s about. We should be grateful that evil is out in the open. And on [the band’s February EP] “Days of Ash,” we name names. You know, I spoke to Renee Good’s family.
The woman killed by ICE in Minnesota.

Bono: We wrote a song about it a week later, and we had this line, “America will rise up against the people of the lie.” Edge had given me this book 30 years ago by M. Scott Peck called “People of the Lie.” It’s about the nature of evil, and a study of malignant narcissism. Anyway, I was explaining to the family, before we used the lyric, asking them for permission. They’re on Zoom, and when I get to the bit about “America will rise against the people of the lie,” the father said, “I have the book ‘People of the Lie’ right here.” I said, “The book Edge gave me 30 years ago?” He says: “Yeah, it’s right here. Just a month ago, I took it out to explain some of what’s going on to my son.” So with those songs in “Days of Ash,” we did go to names. But for “Carnaval De Luz,” we didn’t want to. There’s a line in the song “Midnight Sunshine” that goes: “Catastrophizing is the glamorizing of the world’s pain. If you don’t want to make a devil bigger, stop repeating his name.” Can I go on here for just a second?
You’ve never stopped before.

Bono: [Laughs] I know. I’m so sorry about that. But if you can separate a discussion about this administration from a discussion about the left and the right and conservatives and liberals, then I’m fine to go ahead with it. Because I think this is the most extraordinary moment. I mean, this is the greatest heist in the history of the world: stealing America. And it’s not a caper movie. It’s real, and it’s happening. I don’t want to put off good people who vote conservative, who vote Republican. Their party’s been hijacked, and it’s an aggressive takeover. I want to invite them back. I want them to return. People vote conservative for all kinds of reasons that are OK. So if we can talk about it without getting to the usual loggerheads — but this is a serious problem and I have serious personal dealings with this because of 25 years of work in development.
That development work has been decimated by DOGE and, by proxy, Elon Musk, and the Trump administration. Do you see evil in that?

Bono: For general clues on evil, look at the abuse of children. That’s always a clue. I don’t know how many fatalities will eventually be attributed to the DOGE cuts. There are many different estimates. If you go to, say, The Lancet, they suggest, I think, up to 2030, maybe five million children under 5. And let’s say they’re half wrong. What Christian household, what Catholic household, what Jewish household, anyone of faith, in fact anyone of conscience, would allow the hemorrhaging of human life that is going to happen as a result of these DOGE cuts? It’s unconscionable.

Well, here’s the test-of-faith question. I was listening just this morning to “Glorify,” and there’s a line that goes, “You spit in my eye, you’re a barefaced lie, and there’s nothing you can do to keep me from loving you.” It’s the idea of having love for your enemies. Do you have love for the people doing the things that you’re calling unconscionable?

Bono: Yeah, I love these people because I believe God loves them and Christianity calls us not only to love our neighbor but to love our enemies. But what’s going on with the man whose name shall not be mentioned is something way bigger than the man. It’s going on all over the world. This greatest heist in the history of the world? It’s the crown jewels. It’s freedom. It’s democracy. It’s like the [expletive] Enlightenment. Anyway, that’s it. Edge is just sitting here looking at me.
Edge, you have had the experience many times of being in situations like this and having Bono field questions of the kind that I’m asking. What is that like for you?

The Edge: I mean, look, we don’t mind getting deep and serious, but you want to keep some balance as well. That is why U2 pivoted so heavily after “Joshua Tree” and “Rattle and Hum” to “Achtung Baby,” because we realized we were being robbed of aspects of who we were. It just wasn’t reflected in the work and therefore in people’s understanding and perception of us. So the thing to remember about us is, yes, we can get very heavy and very deep, but actually we have a lot of fun, and when we’re together working, we laugh a lot and we fail a lot and we’re happy that we’re comfortable with failure. So, yeah, I share a lot of Bono’s views on these things and we feel a responsibility, I suppose, to address what we see going wrong with the world, but you can’t do it incessantly. So on our album we touch on it lightly, and then, as you say, we’re not mentioning names because we don’t want to get into finger wagging. What we want to do is draw attention to something that’s a kind of antidote, something that is better. And I think that’s the way people operate. You tell somebody they shouldn’t do something, it’s going to be a struggle. If you show somebody a better path, they’re going to go there.

So when you’re in the studio with Adam and Larry — you guys have known each other for 50 years — there have got to be things that make the rhythm section look at the front-line guys and go, “This drives me nuts!” What are they?

The Edge: Bands are weird things, let’s be honest. We are brothers in arms, for sure, but we don’t agree on everything by any means. We end up making decisions by consensus because we’ve learned over the years that if we’re arguing about something, there’s a problem. When everybody just goes, “That’s it!” we know we’re onto it. So we do argue, but generally speaking, it’s when something’s not quite right. And then it’s just a difference of opinion, like what road we take. So, yeah, I’m sure I’m very annoying at times.

Bono: I don’t think Edge is — and that’s annoying, by the way — because he’s a person of great reason. I would have the annoying gene the most. But it’s a thing about performers. The same portal that you open up to fit a whole stadium inside is maybe not a portal you can close enough in time to protect yourself from the outside world. You think about stadium-sized egos like myself, and you think about self-aggrandizement and much worse, but what happens is the opposite. It’s the collapse of the ego. Singing itself is a vulnerability if you’re any good.

I was reading the trades, as I do, and I saw an item not that long ago about you guys hiring a woman named Sulinna Ong as part of your management team. She had previously been at Spotify doing global curation. And Jeff Azoff, who manages Harry Styles, is one of your managers now. When U2 starts working with new management, presumably those people make an argument for what their value to you is. So what did they tell you that you didn’t already know about how U2 can find new listeners or move forward at this point in the band’s career?

Bono: You must have had surveillance on us, because just in the last couple of weeks we’ve been sitting around listening to people tell us to do things that we hadn’t thought of. Sulinna said it is almost impossible, the way people live now and listen now in their separate communities, to do something that everyone will be aware of. The amount of advertising you would have to spend, the amount of concerts you would play in every college town or around the world — people still might not know that you’ve put out a new album. So you should turn up in unexpected places. And they were suggesting some of them. Some of them were not things that we would have considered. And we were laughing, the four of us, and going, Are we still going to have to break into the charts? Nothing’s changed since we were kids. We were sitting around with Larry, who doesn’t normally like to do this kind of thing, and I was saying: “Are we ready to go out and meet people that may not know who we are? I’m used to it as an activist, but are we as a band?” I was surprised that all four of us were like, OK, give us another suggestion. Including Larry, who was like: “I’m listening. I’m suspicious, but I’m listening.” I thought that was good. For us, it’s still something we have to prove.
Maybe it feels gauche to get into the specifics, but are they suggesting licensing a song in a show you hadn’t thought of? Are they suggesting you play a pop-up at a Raising Cane’s?
The Edge: That’s a great idea! I’m going to write that down.
Bono: You’re going to get on very well at the corporation. You had some very good ideas during the interview. [Laughs]

The Edge: I think also this album, and where we’re going to take the tour, lends itself to some almost Dada-like opportunities to play around with the absurd, to do some crazy stuff no one was expecting. I’m looking forward to that. It’s hard to surprise yourselves as much as your audience, having done it so many times before.

I’ve always been curious about what your old manager Paul McGuinness said to you after the whole iTunes mess, where you put the then-new album [“Songs of Innocence” (2014)] on people’s iTunes without asking. Paul must have had something to say about that.

Bono: He said pretty much the same thing that Tim Cook said when I pitched him the idea, which is: You spent your whole life getting people to pay for music. Why would you want to give something away for free? I mean, we were experimenting. We wanted to see if we could get Apple or another company to pay for our music and then they distribute it. And look, it’s going to take some experimentation to fix the music [business]. It’s astonishing how little other musicians are paid and it’s frightening. But yeah, that was all on me.
Was it a reputational error for you?
Bono: I went too far on that one.
The Edge: We take risks. We have to. So you fail, you fall on your face at times. That’s part of the gig.
Edge, you alluded to playing live. Are there plans to go on tour next year?
The Edge: There are.
Your tours are always conceptual in some way. What is the new concept?
Bono: Well, the album title’s a clue.

The Edge: We can’t go too much into it because the plans are still forming, but we are interested in this intersection between shamanism and show business. All of the great showmen have, to some extent, to pull off a magic trick, which gets into a mysterious place. And it works both ways: The great politicians of this moment, who unfortunately in a lot of cases are supremely dangerous, are very shamanistic. They are dazzling people with an act. It’s the snake oil salesman aspect. And we’re living in a post-truth era because, unfortunately, there are so many opportunities to put fake narratives out there, and that’s being taken advantage of. Our buttons can easily be pushed, particularly when fear is the weapon that you’re taking advantage of. So we’re exploring these things in a good way and a bad way. The lyric of the song “Silencio” [from “Carnaval De Luz”] encapsulates those two extremes. The two types of silence. Contemplative, meditative, reflective silence is a beautiful thing. But the other kind of silence is when you are cowed and you’re afraid to speak because if you say the wrong thing, you will be punished, you might go to jail, you’ll be ostracized, and that’s super dangerous.

Bono: There’s a poem by Michael Leunig. [Pulls out his phone to read the poem] “There are only two feelings, love and fear. There are only two languages, love and fear. There are only two activities, love and fear. There are only two motives, two procedures, two frameworks, two results, love and fear. Love and fear.” There’s a lot of love at our shows, and it’s not an “up with people,” “let’s all give each other a hug” type of love. I think there’s a level of depth at a U2 show where people who genuinely don’t normally agree with each other’s politics feel safe. I’m very proud of that. If they’re in America, we want people to feel really good about their choice to probably pay too much to see us. But we are going to challenge them.
Presumably you have some say in the ticket prices.

Bono: Well, the whole problem with the live business is, very little. But what we do in our band is we take the best seats in the house and make sure that they’re often the most affordable. We also have no problem separating rich people from their money.

Let me wrap up with a holistic question. Even just in the course of this conversation, it’s obvious that U2 thinks about the story that we’re all living in and what the band can offer to that story. But you’ve been around for 50 years. This doesn’t go on forever. So where is U2 in its own story right now, and do you have some sense of how you want that story to end?
The Edge: We’re still creatively extremely inspired and active, and there are lots of songs that have yet to be released, yet to be finished. So I can’t see that ending anytime soon.
Bono: Edge, I think he might be interested in your speech to the band the other day about if you had to find another band.

The Edge: That’s the other thing about why I’m still in U2. Occasionally early on I would think, This is too difficult, I should really get out of this band, and I would start the inner dialogue. [Talking to himself] “So, what do you want to do with your life?” And I would say, “Well, I’m a creative person, and music is kind of my main thing, so I’d stay in music.” “OK, do you want to sing?” And I’m like: “I really don’t want to be the singer. I’m happy being a guitar player.” “So who’s the singer you most like to work with?” And I’d be like, “Well, clearly Bono.” So, OK, I’ll be doing a solo thing but Bono will be the singer. So then, “What’s the best rhythm section for you guys?” I’d be like, “That’s Adam and Larry, isn’t it?” OK, so it’s going to be a solo band with Bono on vocals, I’ll be the guitar player, and Adam and Larry will be the rhythm section. I basically would redesign U2. So yeah, there’s no doubt about it. This is where I belong.

Bono: More likely, I think, is that people tire of you and that we tire of going the distance to meet them, resulting in them tiring of you. I think if we keep playing live till we drop, there will always be people. But we have one problem in this regard, which is that we pledged to each other when we were 18, 17, 16, that we would never, ever walk onto a stage without it being everything. We haven’t betrayed that yet. We’ve had fistfights onstage, we’ve had them backstage, we’ve had madness, but we’ve never betrayed that.

The Edge: Yeah, it never was entertainment to us, ever. It was always something with a lot more importance and meaning. Some of the early shows we saw were the Clash on their first tour, the Buzzcocks, the Jam and Talking Heads. So when you’re around that kind of sense of urgency and the ideological aspect, it’s like you can’t take this stuff lightly. It’s way more than just entertainment.
Bono: It’s the thing they say about football: It’s not a matter of life and death. It’s something much more serious than that.
This interview has been edited and condensed. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.
