nytimes.com/2026/10/17/us/politics/penns.headline: How Pennsylvania Explains the Forces Shaping the Midterms

paragraphs.text: Rachel Wisniewski for The New York Times
To see the dynamics shaping the midterms, look no further than Pennsylvania.
Trump and Republicans dominated this quintessential swing state in 2024.
But this year, Pennsylvania offers clues for how House Democrats might run up the score — and how they might not.
No single state in America better captures the forces and fault lines shaping the coming midterm elections than Pennsylvania.

Just two years ago, Pennsylvania was at the epicenter of a nationwide Republican revival. President Trump swept its electoral votes. His party ousted an entrenched Democratic senator. And it was the only state where Republicans flipped two House seats.
Now the pendulum has swung. Mr. Trump’s support has crumbled. And Democrats are targeting four bellwether House districts in the state that together would give them the congressional majority.
What makes Pennsylvania so revealing is how emblematic those races are of the candidates, issues and demographic shifts that will determine outcomes across the country.

A Republican is clinging to power in sprawling suburbs that have otherwise turned blue. Democrats are trying to reclaim fast-growing Hispanic areas that swung to the right two years ago. White, working-class voters in aging industrial towns and rural areas have lost patience with the president’s promises.

“Pennsylvania runs the whole gamut of the midterms in four races,” said Jesse Ferguson, a national Democratic strategist involved in House elections. “If Democrats can win every kind of fight there, there is no district safe for Republicans in this moment.”

One race features the House’s most outspoken moderate Republican; another includes the former leader of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus. Stock trading and corruption is a recurring theme in advertising. Accusations of socialism are flying.
Yet for all the differences between these districts, there is a commonality to the G.O.P.’s troubles.
His name is Donald J. Trump.

The president’s approval rating had dwindled to 34 percent in the most recent Times/Inquirer/Siena poll of Pennsylvania voters. Three-quarters of voters disapprove of his handling of the cost of living.
Manpower and money are pouring into the state. More than $105 million in advertising on broadcast, cable and streaming is blanketing screens of all sizes in those four districts.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader, kicked off his 100-day sprint to the speakership in Pennsylvania over the summer. He returned last weekend for a rally in one district and made appearances in Black churches in another. A few days earlier, the man whose job he is trying to take, Speaker Mike Johnson, blitzed through the state’s battlegrounds in a single day on behalf of all four Republican incumbents.
Polls show that Democrats are heavily favored to flip the House. What the size of that majority, and its shape and direction, are likely to depend on are the results in places like Pennsylvania.
A flip in all four would signal a Democratic wave; a flip in none would represent an unexpected Republican revival.
Here’s a closer look at each of those races and what they tell us about what might happen on Nov. 3.
PA-1: Has a Republican survivor’s time run out?

With his dismal approval rating, Mr. Trump appears to be a drag for Republicans across Pennsylvania. But in no race does his unpopularity loom larger than in Pennsylvania’s First District, on the outskirts of Philadelphia.

The district voted against Mr. Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024. Yet each time Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a moderate Republican, managed to win anyway — the only member of Congress in his party to do so.

On paper, the suburban seat should be the easiest to flip of the four top battlegrounds. In reality, strategists in both parties say it is the toughest — because of Mr. Fitzpatrick’s unique staying power. He is a moderate Republican who counts the support of typically big Democratic organizations, including labor unions and some big environmental groups.

Mr. Fitzpatrick for years has been something of a white whale for national Democrats. But party officials believe the combination of Mr. Trump’s lowly standing and the popularity of the Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, has opened a door of opportunity. Mr. Shapiro had a 60 percent approval rating in the same Times/Inquirer/Siena poll.

Mr. Fitzpatrick’s Democratic challenger in 2026, Bob Harvie, told a crowd of Democratic activists earlier this month in Green Lane, a small borough in suburban Montgomery County, that he hopes to be swept into office with a Shapiro blowout.
“All of us who are running are going to be clutching both hands, white knuckles, onto those Josh Shapiro coattails,” Mr. Harvie said in a speech. “Because they’re going to take us somewhere.”

Mr. Shapiro has endorsed Mr. Harvie. He has appeared at events with him over two consecutive weekends. But he notably did not mention Mr. Fitzpatrick’s name in either, instead speaking narrowly about the implications of the race for congressional control.
“Not a coincidence,” Mr. Fitzpatrick said over coffee at a diner two days after the first event.

Mr. Fitzpatrick, who has not endorsed the Republican running for governor, called Mr. Shapiro a “friend.” He invited him to his wedding over the summer, though Mr. Shapiro did not attend. “He sent a lovely note,” Mr. Fitzpatrick said.
National Democrats recently started using images of Mr. Fitzpatrick, in black tie, toasting at his wedding in attack ads.
“I respect whatever Josh does, and I want him to do well,” Mr. Fitzpatrick said. “And he knows that.”
PA-7: Will Latino voters come back home to Democrats?

If Pennsylvania is a swing state, then Northampton, nestled in the Lehigh Valley along the New Jersey border, is one of its swingiest counties. Northampton has alternated between the two parties in every presidential election since 2012, voting with the winner each time: Obama, Trump, Biden, Trump.

Most recently, in 2024, Representative Ryan Mackenzie ousted a Democrat on the strength of a Republican resurgence in Allentown, which is majority Hispanic and the district’s biggest city. Some of its more diverse precincts swung 20 percentage points or more in that year’s presidential race. After he won, Mr. Mackenzie said he hired a Spanish-language outreach coordinator on “day one” for his congressional office.

Victor Martinez, the host of a popular Spanish-language radio show in the Lehigh Valley, had warned Democrats in 2024 about Mr. Trump’s rising appeal. This year, he said, local Republicans should brace for a Hispanic revolt.

“Here we are two years later and the sentiment is, ‘Wait a minute, it got worse!’” Mr. Martinez said of Latinos who gave Mr. Trump a chance on the economy. “Gas is more expensive! Groceries are even more expensive! Electricity is more expensive!”

Bob Brooks, his Democratic challenger and a union leader for firefighters, has his own Hispanic outreach effort. It is branded “Bombero Bob” — Spanish for firefighter — though he said the Latino community’s concerns are largely the same as those of the union members he represents.
“They have the same problems as everybody else,” he said. “They feel lied to.”
Today, the seat is generally seen as one of the most likely of the four to flip.

As Mr. Mackenzie took a seat inside the lodge of the Fraternal Order of Police in Bethlehem last week, he set out to make the case for why, as a freshman Republican he, might buck both parties’ history of midterm losses.

Just down the road, a billboard yoked Mr. Mackenzie to the president. But Mr. Mackenzie bragged about solving 10,000 constituent cases and securing federal funding for a firehouse in Alburtis and an upgraded emergency communications system in Carbon County. “It’s not just about the climate,” Mr. Mackenzie insisted. “It’s much more about individual candidates.”
Yet even some supporters fear the opposite.

“Unfortunately, I think people aren’t voting for the individuals,” said Lucy Lennon, 63, who owns a real estate company in Bethlehem, and came to a recent Mackenzie event. “They’re voting party. And there is some backlash on the Republican Party, for whatever reason.”
PA-8: Anger over stock trading in a working-class enclave

Just to the north, Pennsylvania’s Eighth District has become a national symbol of the Democratic Party’s steady decline in the Trump era among blue-collar workers. Centered around the city of Scranton, voters in the district knocked off a longtime Democratic incumbent in 2024 in favor of a Republican, Rob Bresnahan.
Mr. Bresnahan’s re-election campaign has been shaped by some of the same issues dominating races across America: congressional stock trading and grocery prices.
In 2025, Mr. Bresnahan emerged as one of the most prolific stock traders of that year’s congressional freshman class, after campaigning against the practice the year before.

In an interview, he said he explored putting his assets in a blind trust, but he concluded that it was unworkable. He said his financial advisers made trades independently. His individual stock trading has slowed, if not stopped entirely, since all the attention.
“The whole message that they’ve been running against me is over my stock trading,” Mr. Bresnahan said in an interview after a rally in a warehouse in Hazelton, denying he oversaw his own trades.

Accusations of insider trading among members of Congress have flooded races nationwide. In the Eighth District, Paige Cognetti, the mayor of Scranton and Mr. Bresnahan’s Democratic challenger, has made it a centerpiece.
She has also linked it to affordability, another major issue on voters’ minds.
“There is a clear line now between corruption and costs,” she said in an interview.
Democrats are trying to make this connection for voters all across the country.

Ms. Cognetti recorded a commercial recently in her husband’s grocery store, lashing prices and stock trading in the same spot. “Making that bread for themselves,” she said of Congress as she smushed a loaf of bread, “while the middle class gets squeezed out.”

Mr. Trump has carried the district all three times he has been on the ballot, so Ms. Cognetti is trying to run as a different kind of Democrat. She is leveraging past skirmishes with local Democrats and using the catchy tagline “Paige Against the Machine” from her mayoral run.
“There’s certainly frustration about the cost of groceries and the kitchen table issues,” Mr. Bresnahan acknowledged. He said his grandmother calls him almost daily to talk about rising prices.
“I’m asking for another chance to continue to move that ball,” he added.
Yet Mr. Trump still boasts a potent base in the region.

Dwayne McDavitt, a founder of Bikers for Trump Pennsylvania, came out to see Mr. Bresnahan at a rally with Mr. Johnson, the House speaker, at a warehouse in Hazleton. He said with disdain that the Democrats had only one message this year.
“What they’re running on,” he said, “is hating Trump.”
PA-10: A Trump ally under siege, even in a Republican district
Two years ago, Janelle Stelson, a former television newscaster, lost Pennsylvania’s 10th Congressional District to Representative Scott Perry, a Republican, by just over 1 percentage point.

In an interview, Ms. Stelson, a Democrat, described the central Pennsylvania region she hopes to represent as Republican, but she said Mr. Perry, the former chairman of the House Freedom Caucus, was too far right even for the 10th District.
“The most extreme of the extremes,” she said.
In her rematch, Ms. Stelson has run ads embracing parts of Mr. Trump’s agenda, such as cutting taxes on tips and overtime.

Republicans have tried to cast her as a “smooth talker” and hammered her as “too liberal for Pennsylvania,” comparing her to socialists and progressives in their ads: former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

Yet even in a district that Mr. Trump carried, Democratic groups have run ads urging Mr. Perry, a staunch Trump ally, to “stop voting with Trump” — a potential sign that politics are shifting even there.

“He has been a very willing acolyte for the president and we have seen the president’s poll numbers drop precipitously,” Ms. Stelson said. “You can’t stand up for somebody like that all the time and expect that you’re not going to be affected.”
Mr. Perry’s campaign did not make him available for an interview.

In recent days, the Trump administration further jolted the race. The Department of Homeland Security announced the arrest last week of a Nigerian man on charges of indecent exposure — and included in its announcement a scathing political attack on the Stelson campaign, alleging that he had worked for her.
“It’s unbelievable that Janelle Stelson would employ an illegal alien,” Charles Wall, deputy director of I.C.E., said in the news release.
The Stelson campaign said it wasn’t true. The man had neither worked for nor volunteered for the campaign or its vendors, the campaign said.

According to a police report, law enforcement found fliers for Ms. Stelson in the suspect’s vehicle. A watchdog group has since called for an investigation into whether the Department of Homeland Security had improperly engaged in partisan politics.
Meanwhile, on his recent swing through Bethlehem and Nazareth, Mr. Johnson noted that it was his seventh visit to that district — more than any other swing seat in America.
“The entire country is watching,” Mr. Johnson said, “what happens in about four districts of Pennsylvania.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/17/business/dealbook.headline: States Are Stepping Up as the New Antitrust Enforcers

paragraphs.text: Dealmakers have historically spent very little time thinking about state attorneys general. But during the second Trump administration, the threat of state interference has become a major part of every merger conversation.

As federal agencies take a laissez-faire approach to deals, states are ramping up their antitrust enforcement to compensate. They sued to try to stop Paramount Skydance from buying Warner Bros. Discovery for $110 billion and to prevent Nexstar Media Group’s $6.2 billion merger with Tegna. Another state coalition (unsuccessfully) tried to unwind Hewlett Packard Enterprise’s $14 billion purchase of Juniper Networks.

State attorneys general are also challenging nonmerger conduct. In April, a bipartisan state coalition won an antitrust lawsuit against Live Nation after the Justice Department separately settled with the company during the trial.
Trying to use politics to sail through the federal merger review process will backfire because other regulators are now involved, the antitrust chief at one large (red) state told DealBook.

The rapid increase in state antitrust lawsuits has frustrated business executives, who say merger approval by 50 states and two federal agencies isn’t efficient. Uncertainty over whether and when states will intervene is acting as an invisible tax on dealmaking and a drag on the U.S. economy, said Jon Orszag, who is a founding partner of Econic Partners, an economics consulting firm, and has advised on deals worth roughly $500 billion since early 2025.

Other corners of America’s antitrust community have applauded the uptick in state action. “Each episode of apparent manipulation by lobbyists is an opportunity for the states to stand tall and say we’re the last guardians of what is good about America’s antitrust system,” said William Kovacic, a former chair of the Federal Trade Commission.

But what could end up mattering most is something both sides agree on: States have relatively few resources to become powerful antitrust enforcers. The question on everyone’s mind is whether they can escalate enough to make a lasting difference, and on a large number of deals and cases.
The new hierarchy
Six years ago, states collectively employed 151 antitrust lawyers, according to a Yale survey. The federal agencies had all the muscle — around 1,000 antitrust and economics experts and staff.
That hierarchy has changed. States are still collaborating with federal agencies, but they have staffed up their own antitrust departments and are increasingly willing to go it alone.

The states’ role in antitrust predates federal laws: Iowa passed the world’s first antitrust statute in 1888, before the 1890 federal Sherman Antitrust Act. In recent years, the rise of Big Tech prompted a higher degree of activism, starting with states’ 1998 action alongside the Justice Department against Microsoft.

As big tech companies expanded and made acquisitions during the Obama administration, the F.T.C. and the Justice Department were slow to respond. In 2019, 50 states and territories led by Texas launched an action against Google, describing it as a necessary backstop against possible inaction by federal enforcers.

During President Trump’s first term, some F.T.C. commissioners, disappointed by the limits of what the agency could do to stop mergers in “kitchen table” sectors like hospitals, egged on the states to take independent actions. When Lina Khan took over as F.T.C. chair in 2021 and embarked on a no-holds-barred enforcement agenda aimed at reining in corporate power, the states were further inspired and emboldened.

The second Trump administration took the opposite approach, with leaders at the F.T.C. and the Justice Department quickly signaling they were open to remedies. By the time concerns about White House influence over the Justice Department started to grow and its antitrust chief, Gail Slater, was ousted, the states were staffed up and ready to go. With some notable exceptions, such as the coalition against Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, most of the states’ recent actions have been bipartisan.
Uncertain future

Phil Weiser, attorney general of Colorado, recently called for Congress to devote federal funds to states’ antitrust efforts, noting that the Justice Department spends $250 million a year on competition enforcement, several times the sum of all state antitrust budgets. Lacking capacity, the states have taken on only a handful of high-profile cases.

The states have more lawyers than in the past, but only a tiny group employ full-time economists to examine the effects that proposed transactions could have on competition. When they do, the economists are often recently qualified, lack a Ph.D. or lack a background in industrial organization economics, the basis for empirical analysis of market structures.

One strategy that states have used to overcome their limited bandwidth is to pool resources and work together. The National Association of Attorneys General, based in Washington, once used sizable litigation-support funds from large settlements with companies to make loans for new antitrust actions. Critics said money from such settlements should go to state treasuries, not to a private association, but NAAG still funds antitrust actions as well as training and coordination.

In 2021, 45 state attorneys general and NAAG wrote to Congress asking for funds to support state antitrust enforcement (without success). They are likely to seek federal funding again, as Colorado’s Weiser recommended in September. He also demanded new legal powers that would allow states to block anticompetitive mergers without rushing to obtain temporary restraining orders, a difficult and burdensome process for states and courts. More money and beefed-up legal rights would entrench the states as a permanent obstacle on the antitrust landscape.

It’s also possible that the states’ enthusiasm for antitrust fizzles. Supporters of the federal agencies say states may back away from aggressive action if attorneys general, who are politicians, overstretch and lose too many cases in federal court.

The suit against the Paramount-Warner merger, for example, is widely regarded as something of a defeat for the states because they settled for behavioral remedies after Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, publicly insisted that they would accept only structural divestitures.
But for now, the states’ ambition is still growing.

“Time and again, when the federal administration has stepped back from enforcing our antitrust laws,” Letitia James, attorney general of New York, told DealBook in an email, “state attorneys general have stepped up.”
IN CASE YOU MISSED IT

Kevin Warsh vowed to tame inflation. The Federal Reserve chairman’s comments at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund on Friday calmed investor fears that the central bank would raise borrowing costs this month. They followed a hot inflation reading released on Wednesday, with a 3.7 percent annual increase in consumer prices driven largely by higher energy costs.

The F.B.I. arrested an OpenAI employee accused of spying. The now former employee, Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi Arabian national, was charged with bugging a conference room at the company. The incident adds to concerns around security at other A.I. labs.

President Trump’s new press secretary was fired after less than a week. Katie Zacharia had a rough start at her first press briefing on Tuesday, and faced questions about whether she misrepresented herself as a lawyer despite failing a bar exam.

Anthropic prepared for its I.P.O. Several investors who attended presentations held this week by the A.I. giant reportedly lowered their expectations for what could be the largest-ever public offering, citing an apparent slowdown in the company’s annual revenue, Reuters reported. On Wednesday, Anthropic executives told a room full of investors that its revenue for the third quarter had jumped about 45 percent from the prior quarter to $16.8 billion.

More big deals: Netflix laid off about 6 percent of its work force amid slowing growth. JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo reported revenue short of analyst expectations. U.S. mortgage rates remained at three-year highs, while home sales plunged to a near-12-year low.
When (and when not) to use A.I.

It has been two years since Ethan Mollick, an associate professor at the Wharton School, published “Co-Intelligence,” his popular playbook for using artificial intelligence. In the fast-moving world of A.I., that means we’re now in a new era.

His new book, “Co-Existence,” is “about the era of the agent,” he told DealBook. Mollick and DealBook’s Sarah Kessler discussed how business leaders should think beyond the chatbot. The interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.
You write that management skills are essential to using A.I. well. Explain that.

Everyone used to say that A.I. is like an intern. Not anymore. You should think about A.I. as almost an external organization. If you are good at writing out what you want to have done, the way you want it done and when you want things checked in with you, you get good output from the A.I.

There’s a nice study out of Anthropic that suggests managers actually produce better code the first time using A.I. coding tools than coders do, because they specify the outputs they want rather than worrying too much about the details.
One of the most common tasks that managers say they automate with A.I. is writing performance reviews. You argue that’s not a great use of A.I. Why?
There are systems where the value comes from having a human involved. And as soon as you cross a line where they’re being automated, the entire value of the system collapses.
Even if Claude more accurately gives you feedback on what you’re doing, I don’t need the objective feedback as much as I need, subjectively, what does my boss think I’m doing right or wrong?
Your list of potential outcomes for A.I. has changed a lot since 2024.
When I wrote the first book, there was a real possibility that A.I. could hit a wall of some sort. I don’t think that’s possible anymore.
I think that people are still too much thinking about a world where A.I. is static and we can make assumptions based on the models of today.

If I had one message, as somebody who talks to lots of businesspeople and C-level executives, it’s that the biggest mistake you could make is assume that this is as good as it gets and make plans based on that.
Is there anything else you wish business leaders were thinking about more?
Their role in shaping how this technology is used as augmentation or automation. A lot of what I read is that A.I. is something happening to us, and so what do we do in response?

Rather than acknowledging that there’s an easy path, the path of automation, which I think will lead to trouble in a lot of ways. And then there is a harder path, which is how do we reinvent the organization around these systems that include both humans and A.I.?
Executives seem pretty dismissive of the argument that they can choose augmentation instead of automation, or that doing so can be practical.

Let’s say you were one of those companies that automated all of your marketing writing with Claude, because it was a very good writer back in January when no one was using these systems. Now anyone who has been on the internet can sniff out Claude writing, and it makes them vaguely nauseous.
Congratulations, you automated away a competitive advantage. And maybe there was a way to integrate human writers with A.I. in a way that makes everything better.
The way you get rid of your moat is you make your product just like everybody else’s and you make a company just like everyone else’s.

That doesn’t mean that some jobs don’t get automated, but I think that there has to be a more careful balance, or you’re going to end up running your company based on someone else’s mediocre models — because you went with a vibe.

nytimes.com/2026/10/17/opinion/trump-pho.headline: Trump’s Bubble Is About to Burst

paragraphs.text: Sometimes a candid photograph captures a moment in a presidency, and the essence of the officeholder, so tellingly that you get a penetrating portrait of an era.
It happened when L.B.J. yanked up his beagle by the ears for photographers and demonstrated his domineering leadership style.

It happened when a photographer captured W. being told, while reading to children in a Florida classroom, that a second plane had hit the World Trade Center. His look of shock raised questions about whether, after his decades of winging it, a parlous rendezvous with destiny might be too much for him to handle.

It happened in 2009 when every living president gathered in the Oval Office and Jimmy Carter so obviously kept his distance from Presidents Obama, Clinton and both Bushes that his sense of superiority was made clear.
It happened when Obama was photographed bending over in the Oval to let a Black child touch his hair, to see if it was the same texture as his own, capturing the historic nature of his election.

It happened again when Doug Mills, The Times’s dazzling White House photographer, took a picture on Tuesday of President Trump on Marine One with his blond aides/acolytes Katie Zacharia, his wobbly new press secretary, and Natalie Harp, his special assistant for floofing.
Mills took the shot from far away with a long lens, but it bristles with intimacy.
The president is leaning in to talk to the two Ivanka knockoffs, who look like sorority-sister clones, four eyes glued on the man they adore, two fervent smiles glazed with pink lip gloss.
It is a snapshot of Trump’s hunger for adulation that has dragged us to this fraught moment in America.
He desperately craves being the center of attention, and seeing blind devotion mirrored back at him as that devotion wanes with an increasingly disgusted, exhausted public.

Trump was on a trip, part of a self-affirming odyssey to red states, which seemed to be designed not only to boost his unappetizing slate of candidates but also to let him bask in applause from the last fanatical members of his dwindling fan base.

In Mills’s photo, Marines are at attention beside the curved open doors of the helicopter, giving the impression that we are peering inside a bubble — at the very moment that Trump’s White House bubble is getting smaller and more ingrown and fractious than ever. Here he is in a cozy huddle with his most essential type of staff member: obedient helpmeets who help construct and perpetuate his absurd alternative reality and paranoid worldview.

Zacharia, the inept propagandist, and Harp, the so-called Human Printer, who trails — and sometimes sprints — behind the president with a portable printer, giving hard copies of soft coverage to Trump, offering him validation for his delusions and lies.
Zacharia reposted Mills’s photo with the caption, “Best President in U.S. History!!!” But it really should have been the classic Henry Kissinger line: “Power is the ultimate aphrodisiac.”
Wags on X had their own captions, imagining Harp thinking homicidal thoughts about Zacharia.

But actually, the two women — scorned by colleagues eager to anonymously trash talk them — were cloistered on the edge of the playground, clinging to each other and to their orange prophet who told them to hang in there.
But it didn’t last, and by Friday, he was easing Zacharia out. “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,” Trump told her, as he later recounted to reporters. Soon after, she got the boot.

They were trying to fight back against their in-house critics. Harp showed Trump the Politico Playbook story on Thursday reporting that the president is shopping around for a new chief of staff. It also named the advisers who have cashed in. The right to cash in, in Trump’s eyes, is for him and his family only.

“Trump has bristled at recent reports showing several longtime advisers are profiting from foreign consulting business,” Playbook said, noting that Susie Wiles’s daughter Katie is working for a firm representing Republika Srpska, a pro-Russian Bosnian Serb territory.
The Daily Beast headline about the Wiles report blared, “Natalie Harp Knifes Ice Maiden and Sparks Trump ‘Freakout.’”
Tellingly and perhaps prophetically, Susie Wiles is in Mills’s picture, but mostly cut out of the frame. You can see her legs in red pants and the Louis Vuitton bag on her lap.
We can’t see the expression on Wiles’s face, but we know that she is no fan of the two gushing young women in the picture.

Alarmed by Harp’s fixation on the president, and her emotionally raw letters to him in 2023, Wiles attempted — in vain — to curb her access. Trump’s decision to appoint Zacharia to a critical job where she was doomed to flounder and likely end up in an “S.N.L.” cold open blindsided Wiles, according to news reports.

Even Trump seemed taken aback by the press gaggle after Zacharia’s debut news conference debacle and when The Times’s Shawn McCreesh, before the president and his aides took off for Alaska, asked Zacharia where she had passed the bar.

“When I moved to China,” she said, as Trump — who described her as an attorney when he announced her appointment — snapped his head around. The story unspooled that she hadn’t passed the bar anywhere.
But by the time they got to Alaska eight hours later, she was beaming at her boss and doing damage control.
(She told a far-right Pizzagate conspiracist in an interview that she wanted to be played on “S.N.L.” by “a Scarlett Johansson-type character.”)
Zacharia tried to fight back on “Hannity,” no doubt assuming she would be in friendly territory.

But she wasn’t. Sean Hannity asked her why she had put up 15 media posts identifying herself as an attorney. She lamely protested that they were “retweets of a title that had been given.” (Mistakes were made.)
Hannity pressed on: “Why didn’t you just say ‘I never practiced law’?” and asked about her first news conference, “Why only three questions in 14 minutes?”
Zacharia looked unnerved, as though she had been sandbagged by her foes in the White House.
As his hold on the country seems to be slipping through his pudgy fingers, Trump needs the unqualified love from his blond Praetorian Guard.

Not only do Democrats seem headed for success in the midterms, fueled by a swell of Americans who see Trump as a crook, enriching himself while costs rise for everyone else, but the president’s inner circle is going up in flames. Aides are turning on one another and sinking in a cauldron of corruption and boneheaded policies.

This week has been a cascade of embarrassing stories: Kimberly Guilfoyle getting iced as ambassador to Greece after a donor revealed that just before her Senate confirmation hearing, she tried to shake him down to pay her $100,000 American Express bill; the Trump loyalist Ric Grenell, who was the head of the ill-fated Kennedy Center, accused by the Trump loyalist Alina Habba Mildon and her new billionaire husband of misallocating a $5.6 million donation marked for the center; and our ally Volodymyr Zelensky saying he felt betrayed by Trump’s sordid deal with Vladimir Putin over diesel oil and the restricted access to Elon Musk’s Starshield amid Russian bombardment. Trump even had to cancel the nitwit plan of his frat boy Pentagon chief to livestream an execution.
Instead of running the country and dealing with the world he has set on fire, the president is focused on settling petty squabbles and a web of corruption in his incompetent — and dangerous — court.
Doug Mills has proved once again that a picture is worth 1,000 words, or in my case, 1,283.

I resisted the urge to sneak a peek at the questionnaire of the man sitting beside me at jury duty a few weeks ago. He’d been totally unknown to me a half-hour before, but now, through the accident of being summoned to serve this civic duty on the same day, he was part of my world, an object of curiosity, my neighbor for the day. Who was this 30ish man in a plaid flannel who didn’t crack a smile when the hammy lawyer released a fellow juror with the quip, “Always the bridesmaid, never the bride”? Who were any of these people who, as I had, took the day off work and stepped out of the currents of their lives to enter this fluorescent-lit parallel universe of judgment and justice?

Jury duty presents an acute instance of the makeshift community: strangers who come together for a short period, and in that time become their own little society with its own customs and laws, its own characters and gossip. These accidental communities happen all around us, all the time: the people sitting around you on the beach, fellow passengers on a flight, other fans who started queuing for concert tickets before dawn. Unlike when, say, staying in the same bed-and-breakfast or sharing a cubicle at work, socializing is not expected; but just by being present, you’re part of the play.

How quickly people go from invisible to mattering! At jury duty, the woman who works at a nonprofit and grew up in Kansas has such thoughtful answers to the lawyers’ queries: She is the most beloved of all my new neighbors. We share a smile when we’re released for lunch, the pop-up community equivalent of best friendship. And that man in the cap watching a movie on his phone: He’s breaking the no-devices rule, and we all revile him.

By afternoon, we have familiarized ourselves with routes from the metal detector to the assembly room, assembly room to bathroom: These are our neighborhood’s streets. We all know the same sleepy security guard, the no-nonsense courthouse staff; they live here too. Our outside lives become dim — do we really have jobs and spouses and full-fledged personalities? Our friends have no idea about these people to whom we’ve uttered not a word but have somehow become our confederates, no inkling of all the infrastructure we’ve erected.

Then, as quickly as this society materialized, it evaporates. Those of us who have not been empaneled are abruptly dismissed at 4:30 p.m. There is no duty keeping us here, no actual ties to unravel, so we spill out the doors and stagger back to our actual friends and neighbors. We will probably not remember one another, and isn’t there a tiny bit of grief in that? How strange to periodically take up residency in these disposable towns, to participate in their bureaucracies so intensely and then never revisit them. We return home to our established relationships, the people we’ve lived beside for years, those who know us and whom we know. How wonderful to be recognized, depended upon, to contribute to the ongoing project of building a community we hope will last.

Surprising things you should refrigerate

Of course, your milk and poultry need to be kept cool. But the chilly darkness of your fridge can also help many common household objects last much longer. Cold temperatures can prevent an open bottle of super glue from turning rock solid or slow the aging process of unused photo film. Same goes for expensive skin care products, like vitamin C serums. Use teeth-whitening strips? The cold helps delay the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide and other active ingredients. Just make sure any nonfood items are clearly labeled, out of sight or out of reach from anyone who might not understand that they are not safe to ingest. — Maki Yazawa

nytimes.com/2026/10/17/science/sothebys-.headline: For a Mere $2 Million, You Could Own Three Books That Unlocked the Universe

paragraphs.text: The primates known as humans, after ages of unawareness, managed to unveil the hidden dynamics of the universe in little more than a century.

It happened between 1543 and 1687, when Nicolaus Copernicus, Galileo Galilei and Isaac Newton overturned Roman Catholic dogma and replaced it with a startling portrait of the universe. Their individual toils illuminated the mysteries of the solar system and then expanded to those of the wider cosmos.

The masterworks of these pioneers, as well as hundreds of other rare science books, are now on display at Sotheby’s New York before they go up for auction on Oct. 20. The ensemble consists of landmark works and first editions that are, according to Sotheby’s, coming onto the book market after decades in private collections.

“It’s a re-emergence,” said Richard Austin, Sotheby’s global head of books and manuscripts. No gloves are needed, he added, if visitors wash their hands carefully before handling the books. “You can look at these things online,” he said. “But it’s a very different experience when you hold them in your hands and say, ‘This is a book that changed our understanding of the universe.’”

The exhibition, “Reason and Revolution,” highlights books that detail scientific turning points. The opus of Copernicus has the highest opening bid estimate — up to $1 million. Overall, Sotheby’s expects proceeds of up to $7 million.

Scholars have criticized the disappearance of rare, historically significant science texts into private collections. But Nick Wilding, a historian of science at Georgia State University, said that, in the long run, the rare books tend to “gravitate to public institutions rather than private collections.” One reason, he said, is that institutions tend to have longer lives than private buyers.

Church doctrine was the backdrop to the radical ideas of Copernicus, Galileo and Newton. Roman Catholic officialdom long held that humanity and the Earth sat at the center of the universe as the stars, planets and sun wheeled overhead. The heavens were said to be perfect, in stark contrast to the imperfections found on Earth. Then came the scientific revolution.
‘On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres,’ by Nicolaus Copernicus
Copernicus’s “De revolutionibus orbium coelestium” revolutionized astronomy and initiated the birth of modern science.
A triumph of intellectual history, this book laid out evidence showing that Earth and the other planets revolve around the sun.
The 400-page tome was technically bold, packed with math, drawings and tables.

Published in 1543, Copernicus’ manuscript contradicted the Catholic Church, and in time, the church decided to show its displeasure. In 1600, it had Giordano Bruno, an advocate of the heliocentric theory, burned at the stake. Today in Rome, a statue of Bruno overlooks the Campo dei Fiori, where the philosopher was burned alive for heresy, its shadowed face looking defiantly in the direction of the Vatican.

The book’s early pages feature Copernicus’s famous diagram of the solar system. It shows the sun at the center and the paths of the known planets arranged in increasingly larger orbits. The text, after discussing the orbiters, declares in Latin: In medio uero omnium residet Sol, “But the Sun resides at the center of everything.”

His planetary tabulations let astronomers, navigators and calendar makers use his heliocentric model to compute and predict with new accuracy the longitudes and latitudes of the planets, the sun and the moon for any given date. In time, his breakthrough played a role in the reform of the Gregorian calendar, which much of the world now uses.
‘Starry Messenger,’ by Galileo Galilei
Galileo’s “Sidereus Nuncius” was written in the thrall of discovery.
Galileo turned the newly invented telescope on the heavens, bringing into view lunar features and bright points of light once invisible to the human eye.
Overnight, he became the founder of modern observational astronomy.
Galileo made a run of findings that reinforced the Copernican worldview and reimagined what lay beyond.

The book was a steppingstone to his great work, “Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems,” published in 1632. His new endeavor strongly backed Copernicus, whose book the Catholic Church had put on its prohibited list. Galileo, too, felt the lash. In 1633, the Roman Inquisition put the Italian astronomer on trial. The spectacle of the elderly thinker being forced, under threat of torture, to recant his celestial views came to symbolize the church’s hostility to open inquiry.

Early in “Starry Messenger” (“Sidereus Nuncius”), Galileo lays out a diagram of a telescope “for the sake of easier understanding,” as he put it. The observer’s eye is at E and the shape of the tube is outlined by A, B, C and D, with the tube’s far end holding the curved lens. Lines extending outward suggest how incoming rays of light would become concentrated at the focal point of the eyepiece.

With detailed sketches, the book showed what Galileo saw when he turned his telescope on the moon: a surface torn by irregular mountains, suggesting brute upheavals. His observation ran counter to the church’s doctrine of celestial perfection.

The savant’s greatest discovery took up the greatest part of his book: that Jupiter was accompanied by four moons — a figure modern observers have expanded to 115. A Sotheby’s write-up notes that Galileo described the exact moment — Jan. 11, 1610 — when he increased his moon count from three to four. Once again, his finding undermined the church. The astute observer had demonstrated that not everything in the heavens circled Earth.

The most cosmic of Galileo’s discoveries was that the nighttime sky held at least 10 times as many stars as those visible to the naked eye. His diagram of the Pleiades cluster showed a field of 35 stars but just six (drawn larger) as naked-eye objects. So, too, he suggested that the bright band of the Milky Way and similar nebulous parts of the dark sky hinted at the existence of “innumerable stars grouped together” — setting the stage for the modern concept of galaxies.
‘The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy,’ by Isaac Newton
Newton’s “Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica” eventually became known simply as “the Principles.”
His forerunners had described the workings of the heavens. Newton explained them.
Here, Newton diagrams the path of the great comet of 1680, whose long tail arced across the night sky.

The ghostly streaks of comets had long been seen as portents of calamity. Kings trembled. Now, in Newton’s hands, they became just another part of nature’s great whirling machine, their arrival controlled by gravity rather than the malevolent gods.

Page after page of the book features knotty diagrams that explain the invisible forces at work on the moon, the sun, the planets and Earth — notably its oceans and tides. Newton showed why they rise and fall with great predictability. The book also took on pendulum rates, orbital anomalies, the precession of the equinoxes, the drag of fluids, the speed of sound and the spiraling marvels known as vortices.

Despite its reputation for unreadability — fostered by its hundreds of equations, diagrams and obscure references — Newton’s 1687 book became a sensation in his lifetime. His discovery of gravity unlocked the universe, and his magnum opus laid out a method of inquiry that became the gold standard.

Newton did not laud Copernicus and Galileo. That wasn’t his style, nor was it needed. As a top scientist, he and his book paid them the highest of tributes by adopting and extending their worldviews and findings, especially those of Galileo, who investigated not just the heavens but also terrestrial forces. Once, in a letter to Robert Hooke, a fellow scholar, Newton did express his gratitude: “If I have seen further, it is by standing on the shoulders of Giants.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/17/us/elections/hegs.headline: Hegseth Singled Out in Democrats’ Campaign Attacks for War and High Prices

paragraphs.text: A Democrat in a hotly contested House district in Colorado ridiculed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s workout routine in a social media post promoting his congressional campaign.

Another Democratic candidate in California invoked his name as she excoriated her Republican opponent for his support for the war with Iran — which she blames for higher prices Americans are paying at the pump.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat in line to be speaker should his party win control of Congress, has said repeatedly that one of their first orders of business will be to impeach Mr. Hegseth.

In the final weeks of a midterm congressional battle in which voters’ opposition to the war with Iran has become a major issue, Democrats are increasingly making Mr. Hegseth a main character in their campaign messaging.

It is an effort to turn one of President Trump’s most recognizable cabinet officials — and one who has been an unapologetic and visible cheerleader for a war that polls show is deeply unpopular — into a liability for Republicans’ fighting to keep their seats.

In a recent video he posted online, Manny Rutinel, the Democrat and former state legislator who is challenging Representative Gabe Evans of Colorado in one of the most competitive races in the country, featured unflattering footage of Mr. Hegseth working out with troops.

“This man is letting Trump raise your gas prices,” reads the type stamped on the video of a sweaty Mr. Hegseth seeming to struggle as he lifts weights alongside military personnel. “I’m going to put a stop to it,” it reads, as the video cuts to Mr. Rutinel doing pull-ups and lifting much bigger weights at the gym.

“Pete Hegseth is helping Trump start an unplanned forever war while Americans struggle here at home,” Mr. Rutinel wrote in a post circulating the video, which does not show Mr. Evans. “I’m running for Congress to stop them.”

More recently in San Diego, Marni von Wilpert, a city councilwoman running for an open House seat against Jim Desmond, a Trump-endorsed Republican, used an appearance by Mr. Hegseth to call for an independent investigation into conditions aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, the aircraft carrier that recently returned after a deployment of nearly 11 months amid reports of deteriorating morale and suicide attempts.

Mr. Hegseth had sailed back to port with the ship and praised the sailors for their performance in combat, presenting the carrier strike group with a Presidential Unit Citation as he pushed back against criticism of the deployment. But Ms. von Wilpert took the defense secretary to task, accusing her opponent of supporting a war that had exacted a heavy toll on military families.
“Secretary Hegseth owes their families answers about the deplorable conditions on board, not a photo op,” Ms. von Wilpert said.

The focus on Mr. Hegseth, the former Fox News host whose bravado, bellicose statements and dismissiveness toward members of Congress has generated an uncommon level of hostility even among members of his own party on Capitol Hill comes as Democrats work to force Republicans to pay a political price for the war.

It is an attempt to employ a strategy that both parties have long used to gain a political advantage in elections: turning prominent and divisive figures who are not on the ballot into a liability for candidates who are.
Cabinet officials are seldom the focus, but there is historical precedent for a defense secretary becoming a symbol of an unpopular war during a midterm election.

In 2006, Democrats in Congress singled out Donald Rumsfeld as they made President George W. Bush’s handling of the war in Iraq the main line of campaign attacks on Republicans. Mr. Bush repeatedly defended him, even declaring shortly before the midterm elections that he intended to keep him in office.

The day after voters handed Democrats control of Congress in what Mr. Bush called “a thumping” for Republicans, the president announced that Mr. Rumsfeld was stepping down, saying the Pentagon needed new leadership. The decision had been made before the election, though the White House had kept it private.

Mr. Trump has stood by Mr. Hegseth through repeated controversies. There is no public indication that he intends to replace him, though his decision this week to overrule the secretary’s plan to livestream a military execution by firing squad raised fresh questions about Mr. Hegseth’s standing.
Republicans argue that Democrats who attack Mr. Hegseth are misjudging what motivates voters.
“Going after Secretary Hegseth — a decorated combat veteran — won’t move the needle outside of D.C.,” said Natalie Baldassarre, a spokeswoman for the Republican National Committee.
And White House officials said Mr. Hegseth is one of the administration’s most sought-after cabinet secretaries for official appearances with Republican lawmakers in their districts.

“Secretary Hegseth is doing an incredible job leading the Pentagon, while Democrats have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people, just baseless targeting and obstruction,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, said.
Mr. Hegseth has sought out the political spotlight in ways few of his predecessors ever did.

He campaigned in May for Ed Gallrein, the Trump-backed Republican who went on to oust Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, an outspoken opponent of the war, in a primary. And he appeared in August at the Iowa State Fair with Representative Zach Nunn, a Republican who is facing one of the most competitive re-election races in the nation.

Those appearances drew criticism from some veterans who said he violated the longstanding tradition of defense secretaries’ avoiding partisan campaigning to preserve the military’s political neutrality.

“That line of the military as an institution — you know, that military loyalty is to the Constitution, not to a political party — and that line getting blurred, I think, is concerning,” Jessica Finucan, a retired Air Force veteran and director of policy for Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America, said.
Mr. Hegseth’s defenders have emphasized that his campaign appearances were undertaken in his personal capacity.
The targeting of Mr. Hegseth has been particularly pronounced among Democratic candidates with military backgrounds seeking office in districts with deep ties to the armed forces.

Leela Gray, a retired Army brigadier general challenging Representative Anna Paulina Luna in Florida, has called Mr. Hegseth an “unqualified frat boy.” Cait Conley, an Army combat veteran challenging Representative Mike Lawler in a competitive New York district, has called him a “disgrace.” And JoAnna Mendoza, a retired Marine running against Representative Juan Ciscomani in Arizona, has criticized his treatment of women in the military.

In South Carolina, Nancy Lacore, a retired three-star Navy admiral whom Mr. Hegseth removed as chief of the Navy Reserve last year without publicly explaining why, has made his leadership of the Pentagon an issue in her congressional campaign.
Eileen Laubacher, a Democrat challenging Representative Lauren Boebert in Colorado, has also invoked the conditions aboard the Lincoln in criticizing Mr. Hegseth.

There is evidence to suggest Mr. Hegseth presents a tempting target. A Quinnipiac University poll last month found that just 32 percent of registered voters approved of his performance as defense secretary, while 57 percent disapproved. Among independents, 65 percent disapproved, and 56 percent of voters expressed little or no confidence in his military leadership.

Still, focus-group testing conducted by campaign consultants has not found that Mr. Hegseth evokes strong reactions among voters, according to people familiar with the research. That may help explain why the attacks have largely remained on social media and the campaign trail, rather than becoming the focus of paid television ads.

At the same time, Democrats have shown considerably less hesitation about discussing Mr. Hegseth’s removal from office than they have about the prospect of impeaching Mr. Trump. Mr. Jeffries has raised the idea several times, though removing Mr. Hegseth would require both a majority of the House and a two-thirds supermajority in the Senate.
On the campaign trail, Mr. Hegseth’s presence has posed a dilemma for some Republicans struggling to keep their jobs amid voter backlash over the war.

The defense secretary had initially been scheduled to appear with Mr. Nunn in March at a “Top Gun”-themed fund-raiser called “Top Nunn,” a nod to the congressman’s time serving as an Air Force intelligence officer. But the joint appearance was scrapped days after the first deaths from the war were announced. Two of the dead were service members from Iowa.
Mr. Hegseth made the trip in August instead, and he praised Mr. Nunn as a loyal member of Congress.

“When we need an ally to call who understands why it’s important to fund our military in the way we need to fund it, but also do so in a fiscally responsible way, we call Congressman Zach Nunn,” Mr. Hegseth said.
Weeks later, Mr. Nunn returned to Capitol Hill, where he broke with the administration on the war with Iran.

After repeatedly opposing efforts to restrict Mr. Trump’s war powers, he joined Democrats and a handful of Republicans in voting to direct the president to end hostilities with Iran unless Congress authorized them.
“Having deployed multiple times and flown over 700 combat hours in the Middle East, I will not support another open-ended war,” Mr. Nunn said.

nytimes.com/2026/10/17/opinion/ukraine-r.headline: Why I Canceled Russian Culture for Myself

paragraphs.text: I was born and raised in Ukraine, but I grew up on Russian culture.

As a teenager, I was obsessed with Dostoyevsky’s novels and memorized the lyrical poetry of Alexander Blok. I discussed the mysticism of Bulgakov with friends and devoured Chekhov’s short stories like sweets.

That was then. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukrainians have toppled statues to Pushkin, Russia’s national poet, and others. They have changed the names of many streets. In 2023, residents of Kyiv voted to change the city’s Pushkin Park to Bahrianyi Park, after the Ukrainian writer Ivan Bahrianyi. The cancellation of Russian culture in Ukraine is well underway.
I understand the discomfort some people feel about that. I do not share that discomfort. It reflects a reality that I have come to see differently, too.
Let me explain.

For the first half of my life, I saw Ukrainian literature as secondary and inferior to Russian literature. At school, I don’t remember anybody ever saying this directly. Instead, it was communicated through what we read and what we overlooked.

Then the Iron Curtain fell, and in 1991 Ukraine gained independence. By the time I started college in the late ’90s, the curriculum included writers who had been marginalized or excluded in Soviet times.
I started reading the writers of the Executed Renaissance — Ukrainian literary artists who were killed in Stalin’s purges. I read the novels of Bahrianyi and the poetry of Lina Kostenko.

In the prose of Serhiy Zhadan, I found precision that reminded me of Chekhov, and for a while I thought of him as the “Ukrainian Chekhov.” Then I caught myself — why was I treating Ukrainian culture as something that needed validation through comparison?

One day, back at my parents’ house, I realized that some of the writers I’d only recently discovered, and many others, were there on the bookshelves. In fact, they had always been there. I’d just never reached for them.

The sense that Ukrainian culture was somehow lesser had not come from nowhere. That’s what a Russified education did. It did not forbid access to my own culture — it didn’t need to — it just quietly weakened my instinct to reach for it.

At some point after 2022, as a journalist reporting from towns devastated by the Russian occupation, I reread Blok. Only now some of the lines from his 1918 poem “The Scythians” — “Are we to blame then, if your ribs should crunch, Fragile between our massive, gentle paws?” — no longer seemed like metaphor.

For years I had written everything in Russian and translated it into Ukrainian. But I started to notice that I no longer needed that step — it had become more natural for me to just write in Ukrainian.
This war is a tragedy. One of Russia’s many errors is to have insisted so loudly and violently that Ukraine does not exist.
Ukraine exists. If it didn’t, Russia wouldn’t have to try so try to destroy it.
Vladyslav Holovin is a former deputy editor in chief of Forbes Ukraine. Anna Ivanenko is an artist and illustrator.

The Times is committed to publishing a diversity of letters to the editor. We’d like to hear what you think about this or any of our articles. Here are some tips. And here’s our email: letters@nytimes.com.
