nytimes.com/2026/10/15/movies/you-can-se.headline: ‘You Can See Everything’ Review: The Slippery Mind of Elizabeth Holmes

paragraphs.text: The nominal subject of the trippy “You Can See Everything” is Elizabeth Holmes, the celebrated entrepreneur turned celebrity jailbird. As a portrait, the movie is intimate and analytic, informative and incomplete. It’s also off-the-charts bonkers, which isn’t surprising given the participants. Directed by the comic Nathan Fielder and the filmmaker Lance Oppenheim, the movie is, among other things, a wily, disturbing, self-aware exploration of the relationship between documentarians and their subjects. It’s often funny, even if the questions that it raises about truth, reality and knowledge can make it feel like a tragedy — few movies speak as uncannily to the pathos and destabilizing confusions of the present moment.

At this point, it’s a tossup whether Holmes is better known for her pop-cultural profile or her real-world exploits or if Fielder, the creator of absurdist comedy TV shows like “Nathan for You,” is now the bigger draw. Her fame was relatively brief but sensational. In 2014, Forbes deemed Holmes, the founder of a blood-testing start-up named Theranos, the youngest self-made female billionaire. She claimed, among other things, that her technology would revolutionize health care, which proved untrue. By 2022, Holmes had been found guilty of four charges of fraud for deceiving investors, a turn of events that seemed to baffle even the presiding judge. “What was it that caused Ms. Holmes, regrettably, to make those decisions that she did,” Judge Edward J. Davila asked, before sentencing her to 11 years in prison.
You Can See Everything
Save to your watch list:

That question hovers over the movie, and is as much a head-scratcher as how Fielder and Oppenheim came to make it. At one point there’s an approving reference to Fielder being someone who looks “at things differently.” It’s a rich line for those familiar with his work; it’s obvious that Holmes and her life partner, Billy Evans, were not. It’s also obvious that they were out to shift public perceptions about her or, at least, the ostensible narrative, and that the filmmakers were aware of the role they were being solicited to play. It’s not for nothing that the documentary opens on a tight shot of Evans’s face. “Nobody knows who she is,” Evans says to someone on the phone, shortly before dropping the words “radical transparency.”

It’s instructive that Holmes isn’t the first person you see in the movie given how she appears in the movie. She was the most famous woman tech entrepreneur to emerge from Silicon Valley, which helped elevate her profile and added frisson of her fall. Her signature look was striking, including long hair that always seemed a smidge messy, as if she were just too busy innovating to comb it. She didn’t seem to blink, which emphasized the whites of her eyes and presumably held others rapt. It’s a neat movie actor trick for creating dominance, which might have been useful in tech-bro land. She blinks in “You Can See Everything” and her distinctive low-pitched voice also seems more natural; it’s about the only thing that does.

Shot over several years, the documentary opens in 2023, 34 days before Holmes entered prison. Throughout it, the filmmakers mix original and extant material, and embrace different documentary approaches (participatory, ethnographic and so on). For the most part, though, “You Can See Everything” — the title refers to a text Holmes sent Fielder — unfolds as a series of intense conversations with Fielder serving as the on-camera interlocutor. Many of these take place in Holmes and Evans’s beachfront place in Del Mar, Calif., where Fielder prods and pushes them in the dining room, on the sofa, wherever, sometimes with the couple’s two young children and her parents in attendance. A number of encounters are shot in such extreme, dermatologic close-up that you become intimately familiar with Fielder’s zits.

Every so often, other members of the small film crew show up on camera, too. These onscreen appearances are reminders of the inherently constructed aspect of the movie and, by extension, the documentary genre, and they dovetail with a movie’s preoccupation with questions of authenticity and artificiality. All the conversations in the movie take place, after all, in front of a small audience that is, in turn, recording these interactions for the far larger movie audience. Whether Holmes’s occasional blinks and tears in these chats are performative is open to question as are her grasp on language, truth, science and reality itself, all of which Fielder seizes on in a series of interactions that grow progressively weirder.

One of Fielder’s superpowers as a performer is his deadpan, which he generally manages to maintain no matter how outlandish the conceit. He’s put it to recurrently unsettling effect on shows in which he — or a version of himself — aggressively toys with the genre of reality television through his interactions with real people. In “Nathan for You,” he offers absurd advice to small-business owners, successfully persuading a frozen-yogurt store manager, for instance, to sell a lab-created fecal-flavored offering, a.k.a. “poo.” The more conceptually ambitious show, “The Rehearsal,” involves him helping people work through assorted personal issues with the use of hired actors and elaborate re-creations of real life.

Both shows are finally less interesting for what they say about their putative subjects than what they say about those of us who watch them and keep on watching in stitches, shock or horror. Fielder likes to test the limits of propriety and (canned) reality, and he’s having some laughs in the process. He’s also creating social psychological experiments that, in their effect, bring to mind Orson Welles’s 1938 broadcast of the H.G. Wells novel “The War of the Worlds,” about an alien invasion. Welles presented part of the drama as breaking news, which panicked listeners, made headlines and irked the Federal Communications Commission. Welles later said that he had underestimated “the extent of our American lunatic fringe.”

That fringe no longer seems marginal, if it ever was. That the world in “You Can See Everything” appears sane is partly because of the legitimacy conferred on Holmes by her fame and the hundreds of millions of dollars that went into Theranos. Serious people took her seriously, which can seem hard to believe given how slippery Holmes and Evans seem here. Indeed, the first image of Fielder in the movie suggests that he and Oppenheim have come to this project with a degree of incredulity. It’s a murky shot of Fielder peering through a window with what looks like comic skepticism. If it’s uncertain what Fielder is thinking at that moment, it is certain that he and Oppenheim have already begun to test your preconceptions.

One of the most gob-smackingly wild things about Holmes is how she was able to scam so many. That’s part of the story here, though the more interesting one concerns what we mean by truth in a world of profound epistemological uncertainty. Again and again, Fielder presses Holmes about her past and her present. He stares into her eyes, and she stares right back, as he interrogates her linguistic elisions and wonders about her grasp on a famous old comedy routine. He also watches her as she watches the 2022 TV drama series “The Dropout,” in which Amanda Seyfried plays Holmes. It’s a dizzying moment, all the more so given that we’re watching, too, swept up in a ricochet of gazes in the mirrored fun house we now live in.
You Can See EverythingRated R for language and male nudity. Running time: 2 hours 54 minutes. In theaters.

nytimes.com/2026/10/16/movies/nathan-fie.headline: What Critics Think About Nathan Fielder’s ‘Bonkers’ Elizabeth Holmes Movie

paragraphs.text: When the surprise premiere of “You Can See Everything” upended the Telluride Film Festival in September, gobsmacked attendees described the film as bonkers, to use the word our reviewer does. Now that it’s finally hitting theaters this weekend, we can finally see for ourselves what everyone is talking about.

In it, the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and her romantic partner, Billy Evans, have invited the comedian Nathan Fielder, who co-directs alongside Lance Oppenheim (“Primetime”), to film them in the 34 days before she is due to report to prison. She doesn’t understand why she has been convicted on charges of fraud for deceiving investors. Or does she?

The New York Times movie critic Alissa Wilkinson and comedy critic Jason Zinoman have their own thoughts, which they’re sharing in a conversation below. Let us know your take on the film in the comments section.
Spoiler alert! It’s hard to talk about this film without revealing key details. Be aware that this conversation as well as the comments section will contain spoilers.
JASON ZINOMAN Alissa, we’ve already talked about this movie, but in the spirit of Nathan Fielder, let’s consider that a rehearsal. Luckily, there’s so much to unpack in this brilliant mind-bender.

The premise is a face-off between two master manipulators, Fielder, perhaps best known for docu-comedies like “The Rehearsal,” and Elizabeth Holmes, but it unfolds as a seduction as much as a battle. We learn through his interrogation that her flirtation technique is to hold eye contact — and she does this with Fielder quite a lot. Her eyes are the stars of this show. They are so unblinking that every flip of the eyelid is dramatic. In an incredible shot in the car on her way to prison, they flutter.
Fielder clearly wants us to think that he was hypnotized, and then there’s the tension he has with her partner, Billy Evans, that carries the charge of a rival.

One of the things I love about the documentary is how it keeps dabbling in different genres, hitting notes of cringe comedy, spy thriller, horror. The vanishing blond protagonist and themes of voyeurism and doubling made me think of “Psycho,” and there’s even a shocking shower scene. But Fielder and his co-director Lance Oppenheim commit to romance, with a stunningly dreamy visual vocabulary. Documentarians often fall for their subjects, but it’s built into this story.
You are a longtime student of the Fielder method of reality-blurring. I am curious what you make of this? Did Fielder really fall for those long lingering stares? And does that even matter?

ALISSA WILKINSON I have gone back and forth on that very question. On the one hand, having seen a lot of Fielder’s work, I’d like to think I can tell when he is playing “Nathan Fielder” and when he has gotten walloped by reality. There are moments during “The Rehearsal” where it feels like the artifice he constructed has unexpectedly cracked him open, and by the end of this film, I thought that might be what happened.

On the other hand, a lot about that final sequence — a conversation in which he and a key interlocutor discuss whether Holmes is for real — feels staged. Did they create this ending for the film? Or …?
Readers, you probably have your own answers to this question. I’m comfortable not knowing; clearly the ambiguity was on purpose.

What’s more interesting to me is that this made me think about my relationship to what I just watched. It made me aware of my presumptions that what I see onscreen is “real” unless I’m told otherwise.

I keep saying that I think Fielder is best understood as a performance artist, by which I mean the sort who confronts you with something about the world or yourself that usually stays hidden. A lot of the time I see performance art in museum settings, but Fielder’s work comes to us through screens, in the form of movies and TV, because that is what his art is about: the ways we watch our entertainment today, especially reality TV and now, documentary.

Of course, this is far from the first documentary to do this sort of thing. Filmmakers have been doing this in nonfiction for a century. I think of Luis Buñuel, Shirley Clarke, Orson Welles, Sarah Polley, Robert Greene — I could go on. Yet it’s also clear to me that Fielder is bringing some kind of secret sauce to the mix. What do you think makes this movie so watchable, and so buzzy?

ZINOMAN As complex as Fielder’s work can be, the secret sauce, to me, is something simple: a radical commitment to surprise. Last time we saw him, in “The Rehearsal,” the man flew a damn plane. That’s quite a coup de théâtre. This documentary repurposes many elements we have seen from him before — re-enactments, boundary-blurring investigations of truth and fiction — but in the past, he was playing off ordinary people; now he is focusing on another star, a notorious tech entrepreneur. We’ve seen so many portraits of these people in features and documentaries recently, as you have written. But none so intimate and mysterious.

What’s riveting is that Holmes comes off as either impossibly naïve or spectacularly manipulative, without much room for anything in between. While she seems to win over Fielder (or the version of him in the movie), the filmmaking also points you in a direction to question her. It highlights extreme, implausible comments. At one point, she says she has never told a lie. I have never seen Fielder so flummoxed. “Liz, what?” he blurts out. His whole career is premised on investigating the ways we all perform, so seeing him confronted with this statement is hilarious.

Then there’s her fairy-tale story of meeting her partner, Billy Evans, a character out of reality television (he even says “the council has spoken,” a paraphrase of the “Survivor” catchphrase). Evans says he is aiming for “radical transparency” but spends much of the first half of the movie evading or interrupting Fielder. One of the surprises of this movie is how much it focuses on Evans. What do you make of him and why do you think he plays such a large role?

WILKINSON I thought a lot about him in terms of certain documentaries about “villains” — the kind Errol Morris makes — where you start out feeling, well, this guy seems kind of normal, and by the end he’s become terrifying just through what he’s said. Evans is obviously in this film so much to tug at one strand in the mystery of Elizabeth Holmes: Is she an innocent victim of a controlling man (as she implies onscreen in reference to her ex-fiancé and ex-business partner, Sunny Balwani, who was sentenced to nearly 13 years in prison for defrauding investors and patients), or is she using that as an escape hatch for the responsibility she bears as well?

I thought I knew the answer going into this film; now I’m not so sure. She does seem like a person who could be easily manipulated by someone like Evans. The choice to include the scene where the couple is making scrambled eggs (when Evans corrects Holmes) suggests that the directors want us to feel uncertain. On the other hand, isn’t that just what she wants us to believe?

Jason, this movie has tied me in knots, and though I know that it will infuriate some people, I find that to be delicious. I suppose that makes me like Fielder, in some ways: He has suggested that he made this film because he wanted to explore the pleasure of being deceived, as we are when we go to a magic show. I think that might mean he’s succeeded.

ZINOMAN Evans could be manipulating her, but there is also the possibility that she is manipulating him. And Fielder. The delirious fun of the movie is how it sends you down conspiratorial rabbit holes. I do think Billy Evans plays one other role. As Fielder shifts his sights to him, I couldn’t help but see some projection in the accusation that Evans is manipulating or using Holmes for his own ends. Isn’t Fielder doing the same thing? He’s made this buzzed-about movie, a career breakthrough already earning Oscar chatter, in part by inviting us to look at a variety of angles on Holmes. I see what you mean about the fun of being tied in knots.

thehill.com/homenews/senate/6155906-schu.headline: Schumer: ‘Trump just gave Putin the best birthday gift he’ll get this year’
thehill.com/homenews/senate/6155906-schu.author: Sarah Davis

paragraphs.text: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) accused President Trump on Saturday of giving Russian President Vladimir Putin “the best birthday gift” after he waived new sanctions on Russia days before they were set to take effect.

“By giving the Russian economy life support Trump’s deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier,” Schumer wrote in a post on the social platform X. “There’s nothing America First about Trump caving in to Putin and exempting Russia from US sanctions.”

A sweeping legislative package Trump signed into law last month would have imposed tariffs up to 100 percent on the top five purchasers of Russian fuel. The president’s Friday night executive order puts those sanctions on hold.

The move follows Trump’s decision last week to lift sanctions on Russian diesel products, allowing the country to “immediately” export 300,000 tons to the U.S. and the greater world economy amid global fuel shortages. The deal drew swift bipartisan pushback.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said these relief actions will further endanger his citizens, as Ukraine continues to fight back in a yearslong war against Russia.
On Saturday, the Ukrainian leader warned the “sanctions relief will continue” in a social media post.
Zelensky mourned the loss of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who the Russian sanctions package was named after and who pushed for more U.S. support to Ukraine during the war effort.
“It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest,” Zelensky wrote. “I want to thank both Democrats and Republicans who supported his bill. That was a major victory: this truly bipartisan support.

“And now, the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me,” he continued. “And it definitely helps only the Russians. It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people. This certainly does not stop the war.”

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), the top Democrat on Congress’s Joint Economic Committee, expressed his disapproval with the president’s new executive order in a statement released by his office late Friday evening.
“Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression,” Beyer said.

“Trump has proven he will twist this law and abuse the powers it conferred on him, and while he has let the tariff powers lie for the moment, the law as written also empowers Trump to weaponize new trade authorities against our allies and trading partners,” the Democrat continued. “Congress must fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure it truly supports Ukraine.”

Several Republican lawmakers also joined in on criticizing this relief, with retiring Texas Sen. John Cornyn posting on social media that “Lindsey would be appalled,” in reference to his late Republican colleague from South Carolina.
Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), a frequent critic of the Trump administration, called the relief “beyond irresponsible” in a statement shared on social media.

“It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Tillis said. “If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin.”

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/17/french.headline: Revealed: French police used UK-funded 4x4 vehicles to charge student protesters
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/17/french.author: Diane Taylor

paragraphs.text: French police have used 4x4 vehicles paid for by British taxpayers to charge at student protesters during the school protests that have swept the country.

The French government has confirmed that an investigation has been launched into why the cars, funded by the UK government specifically to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel, were used during a protest involving school students in Dunkirk.

School protests have been taking place across France for a third week with an estimated 160,000 people involved, with protesters raising concerns about crumbling schools and teacher shortages. Demonstrators have criticised policing tactics after teargas was fired at protesters in two areas.

The incident involving the UK-funded 4x4, a land cruiser known as Masstech VEZI (Vehicule d’Eclairage de Zone d’Intervention), was reported by French media outlet BFM TV on 10 October. The report included footage of the VEZI driving at speed, reversing backwards then driving forwards again with a bin caught under the vehicle’s front wheel and dragged along. Students can be heard screaming and scattering from the path of the vehicle.

According to reports, a 14-year-old girl was injured by the vehicle and was taken to hospital, sustaining a haematoma. She was later discharged from hospital. She is now recovering, but she told reporters that what happened to her was “unacceptable”.

The VEZI was earmarked for UK-funded operations on French beaches to stop asylum seekers boarding dinghies, part of an Anglo-French border agreement signed in January 2018 and known as the Sandhurst treaty.

This treaty specifies cooperation between France and the UK in combating irregular immigration and secures UK financial support for French efforts through the “Sandhurst funds”. These funds enable France’s National Gendarmerie (police service) to acquire additional resources such as all-terrain vehicles suited to dunes and beaches, including the VEZIs, which are reinforced with grilles.

According to a recent French parliamentary cross-party inquiry into Anglo-French border agreements known as Le Touquet, nine of these specialised VEZI vehicles have been bought under the terms of the Sandhurst treaty. The inquiry report states that to be eligible for Sandhurst funding the equipment must contribute directly to combatting illegal migration in the UK.

A spokesperson from the office of Laurent Nuñez, France’s minister of the interior, when asked why a vehicle funded by the UK and specifically earmarked for border control was used to counter a schools protest, said: “We can confirm the opening of an investigation into this.”
Sources close to the investigation said: “I don’t think the British are aware that their money is being used to beat French kids.”
Another expressed concern about the expanding militarisation of French policing to support authoritarian policies.

A spokesperson for Utopia 56, a French association that provides support to asylum seekers in northern France, said: “In Dunkirk, the 4x4 that ploughed into high school students during the protests is a vehicle funded by the British Sandhurst fund – money earmarked for combating Channel crossings. The practice of using 4x4s to chase people in the student protest is the same one used on the beaches.

“Disproportionate force is employed to silence, intimidate, and deter. The repressive tactics being tested at the border to prevent crossings should serve as a warning to everyone. These are surveillance, control and repression methods that will be replicated in other contexts. The incident involving the vehicle in the student protest is proof of this.”
The UK Home Office declined to comment.

engadget.com/2289602/anbernics-rg-dds-is.headline: Anbernic's RG DDS Is Almost Double The Price Of The Original Nintendo 3DS
engadget.com/2289602/anbernics-rg-dds-is.author: Jackson Chen

paragraphs.text: In creating a premium dual-screen handheld that's largely a callback to the Nintendo 3DS, Anbernic has made something that far surpasses the original in both price and power. Straying away from its reputation of churning out budget handhelds, Anbernic set its new RG DDS' price at $299.99, offering only a temporary preorder discount to $284.99.

To justify the cost, the RG DDS runs on a Snapdragon G2 Gen 2 that can emulate more than just 3DS titles. While we already knew the processor when Anbernic first teased its next clamshell device, the handheld maker fleshed out the rest of the specs, detailing two options between one with 8GB memory and 128GB of storage and an upgraded option with 12GB memory and 256GB of storage. However, both devices have a microSD card slot that can support up to 2TB of extra storage.

Anbernic said the RG DDS will use Android 16, allowing customers to take advantage of the many emulator apps out there. To round out the handheld, Anbernic included Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.4 compatibility, 1080p display output, a six-axis gyroscope sensor and a 3.5mm audio jack. As expected, there will be no glasses-free 3D graphics, as seen in the original 3DS, but the higher resolution displays might make up for it. As for the curious AI button that Anbernic revealed as part of the RG DDS' design, the company said it will offer game guides and strategies, real-time translation during gameplay and "more fun AI features."

Anbernic said the RG DDS will ship "gradually starting December 10, 2026." Confirming the colors teased in the video last week, the latest clamshell handheld will come in Glacier White, Basalt Black and Phantom Blue.

bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/c6rryq.headline: Emi Martinez injury mars first Chelsea clean sheet in nine months
bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/c6rryq.author: Nizaar Kinsella

paragraphs.text: Goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez was taken to hospital for "precautionary tests" after suffering what boss Xabi Alonso said was a concussion during Chelsea's win at Everton on Saturday.
Martinez had earlier played his part in the Blues securing a first Premier League clean sheet in nine months, a run stretching back 23 matches.
But the incident overshadowed an important 2-0 victory for Alonso's side at Hill Dickinson Stadium, secured by two goals from Pedro Neto.
Martinez collided with Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite in the 68th minute while attempting to claim a cross from Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall's free-kick.
There was an eight-minute stoppage before the Argentina international was replaced by Mike Penders, who made his Premier League debut for Chelsea, and saw out the remainder of the match.
Asked about the incident after the match, Alonso said: "It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.
"What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.
"We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait."

There are now doubts over whether Martinez will be fit for Chelsea's next three matches - they face Tottenham and Manchester United in the Premier League, with a Carabao Cup tie at Liverpool in between.
'We need to show we can win in this way'
Chelsea recorded their first Premier League clean sheet for nine months, since a 2-0 win against Brentford in January.

Although Alonso said he was "not obsessed" with keeping a clean sheet, his side, who had conceded a league-high 13 goals before kick-off, were keen to address that record after a much-improved 5-1 win over Bournemouth following the international break.

There had also been discussion about Chelsea being a "soft" team, particularly away from home in the north of England, having lost 19 of their previous 41 matches north of Luton over the past four years.

Last season, Chelsea lost 3-0 at Everton during Liam Rosenior's five-match winless run, a sequence that ultimately cost him his job. The Blues had also won just one of their past nine matches at the Toffees.
This time, however, Everton managed just six shots, their fewest in a Premier League game since recording five against Arsenal last December.
Chelsea also conceded only one clear-cut opportunity and allowed their lowest expected goals against (xG) figure against top-flight opposition this season at 0.45.
They started with a back three of Josh Acheampong, Maxence Lacroix and Levi Colwill, while goalscorer Neto and Jorrel Hato, who provided the assist, operated as wing-backs.
The midfield pairing of Moises Caicedo, returning from international duty, and new signing Jordan Henderson also brought much-needed solidity and experience.
It was £117m club-record signing Morgan Rogers, however, who set the tone for a combative display, squaring up to Everton defender James Tarkowski during an eventful first half.
"We needed to show that we can win in this way," Alonso added. "We looked solid, we played solidly, we were strong and we stayed in control.
"In the first half there were difficult periods with throw-ins, corners and pressure from Everton. You have to overcome those moments.
"In the Premier League it is very hard to have complete control in an away game, but you cannot lose your shape or your conviction."
Who is Martinez replacement Penders?

With difficult matches to come, there will be questions over whether Penders, who became Chelsea's youngest goalkeeper to play in the Premier League at the age of 21, is ready for the demanding run of fixtures ahead.
That concern would be heightened if tests confirm Martinez suffered a concussion, with Premier League protocols typically requiring a minimum 14-day return-to-play process.

Chelsea signed Penders from Genk for £17m in 2024 before loaning him back to the Belgian club. He then spent last season on loan at sister club Strasbourg, where he impressed in both the Conference League and Ligue 1.
Genk have developed a reputation for producing elite goalkeepers, and Penders is frequently compared to Thibaut Courtois by those who know him best.
Like the Real Madrid goalkeeper, Penders stands at 6ft 7in and has recently served as his understudy in the Belgium national team set-up.

He has worked with the same legendary youth goalkeeping coaches, Guy Martens and Gilbert Roex, who also helped develop Koen Casteels, Maarten Vandevoordt, now at RB Leipzig, Lucca Brughmans, who will join Liverpool next summer from Genk, and Nordin Jackers of Club Brugge.

They specialise in developing goalkeepers who are good with their feet, including Penders, who recorded the highest average position while playing out from the back under Rosenior at the Ligue 1 club early last season.
Roex, who has known Penders since his academy days, believes he is capable of matching Courtois' level of success at Chelsea, Atletico Madrid and Real Madrid.
He said: "We have produced a lot of great goalkeepers, but Mike is the one with the potential to reach the same level as Thibaut. His sense of calm is gold in goalkeeping."

cbsnews.com/news/trump-katie-zacharia-wh.headline: Katie Zacharia out as White House press secretary after first week on the job
cbsnews.com/news/trump-katie-zacharia-wh.author: Jennifer Jacobs, Kristin Brown, Stefan Becket, Kathryn Watson

engadget.com/2284034/samsung-galaxy-feat.headline: This Samsung Galaxy Feature Can Protect You From Untrustworthy Apps
engadget.com/2284034/samsung-galaxy-feat.author: Gabriela Vătu

paragraphs.text: Samsung's Auto Blocker keeps threats at bay, but it can also get in your way.

If you own a Samsung Galaxy phone running One UI 6.0 or later, you may have a built-in security feature called Auto Blocker working in the background without even realizing it. Enabled by default on devices that ship with One UI 6.1.1 or later, it filters out apps, USB commands and messages that could put your device at risk without you even having to lift a finger. For most people, that's a super useful layer of protection in a world where threats are extremely common and can come from apps, a public charging cable or images you get in a text.

But Auto Blocker isn't without its complications, especially for users who like to sideload apps, work with developer tools or install software from outside the Google Play Store or the Samsung Galaxy Store. Epic Games even filed a lawsuit against Samsung a couple of years ago, arguing that this very feature made downloading third-party apps unnecessarily difficult.

Understanding what Auto Blocker actually does and what it doesn't can help you make a smarter decision about whether to keep it on, turn it off or somewhere in between. Let's see what this feature does, how you can enable or disable it and what's the best thing to do.
What is Samsung Auto Blocker and what does it do?

Auto Blocker is a built-in security feature available on Galaxy devices using One UI 6 or higher. Its main job is to stop app installation from outside the Google Play Store or Samsung's Galaxy Store, efficiently closing off one of the most common ways malware ends up on a phone. It also takes things a step further and blocks malicious commands sent through a USB cable, which matters if you've ever charged your phone using a public cable. Beyond that, Auto Blocker filters images suspected of containing malicious code in messaging apps like Samsung Messages, Google Messages, Messenger, WhatsApp or Telegram.

For users who want even stronger protections, Samsung offers another mode called "Maximum restrictions," which adds extra safeguards, such as blocking device admin apps and work profiles, disabling 2G network connections, preventing auto-reconnection to unsecured Wi-Fi and stripping location data from shared photos. It's definitely a more aggressive setting, increasing security at the expense of convenience.
How to enable and disable Auto Blocker

Epic Games sued Google and Samsung back in 2024. The feature, they said, combined with existing Play Store and Galaxy Store flows, forced users to take over 20 steps just to download the Epic Games Store. The lawsuit was eventually dropped after Epic reached an agreement with Samsung, but the Auto Blocker stayed on.

If you need to sideload an app or run a developer tool, you can turn Auto Blocker off by going to Settings > Security and privacy > Auto Blocker and tapping the toggle. You'll need to authenticate before switching it off, which is a great feature that can protect you if someone gets their hands on your phone and tries to install some malware. The same path lets you turn it back on.

On phones running One UI 8.5 or later, you can also enable an option that automatically turns Auto Blocker back on 30 minutes after it's disabled. This lets you temporarily disable the protection to install an app without having to remember to reactivate it. You can find this extra toggle by tapping on the Auto Blocker feature in the menu.
Should you keep Auto Blocker enabled?

As you'd expect, Samsung recommends keeping Auto Blocker on, and for most users, that's sound advice. The feature is efficient in guarding against malicious apps, unauthorized USB access and tampered software updates; threats that are easy to overlook until something goes wrong.

The trade-offs are real, though, because Auto Blocker intentionally blocks APK installs from outside the Play Store and Galaxy Store, which affects anyone who relies on open-source apps or sideloaded tools. The most balanced approach is to leave Auto Blocker enabled by default and disable it only when you have a specific reason to install something from outside official app stores. Once you're done, you turn it back on, or, if you're running One UI 8.5 or later, you can have it automatically turn back on after 30 minutes.

If you're an advanced user who sideloads often, the auto re-enable option can feel like a nuisance. Just keep in mind that disabling Auto Blocker removes an additional layer of security. Other protections, including Google Play Protect, can still help guard against malicious apps, but it's important to verify the source of anything you install from outside official app stores. For people who want the opposite approach, Samsung's Maximum restrictions mode adds plenty of extra protections.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/17/protes.headline: Police clash with protesters as tens of thousands take to streets across France
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/17/protes.author: William Christou, Kim Willsher

paragraphs.text: Police have fired teargas and clashed with protesters supporting high school student grievances, as demonstrations across France were boosted by other groups angry over high prices and the fraying of a social welfare system.

Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across the country, and tensions erupted on the fringes of the nationwide demonstrations over absent teachers, decrepit school buildings and police violence.

In Marseille, protesters stormed the town hall, ramming the door with security barriers they removed from the street. They briefly managed to enter the municipal building, where a protester spray-painted an “A” for anarchy on a wall before the police removed them.

Around Place de la République in central Paris, a peaceful march turned violent, with police firing teargas at black-clad and masked rioters who threw fireworks and paving stones, attacked a bank and looted a sports shop. “We’re taking the Bastille!” one demonstrator yelled.

Others set wheelie bins on fire and threw firecrackers inside or pushed over glass recycling bins and picked up the bottles inside to use as missiles. A lorry was set on fire and flames spread to a nearby building.
Residents in surrounding streets were forced to close windows and doors as huge clouds of teargas rose to roof level.
French authorities detained dozens of protesters across the country, with more arrests expected.
Saturday’s mobilisation follows calls on social media to revive the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) movement, which emerged in 2018 against social injustice.

The protests began last month at schools ⁠in the poor northern suburbs of Paris, where ⁠anger over teacher absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
Saturday’s protests called for teachers and students, labourers, pensioners and farmers to join the protests and widen the movement.
French authorities said 140 protests involving 32,800 people had been recorded outside Paris by midday, blaming the unrest and violence on what they said was the “ultra-left”.
The CGT, one of France’s biggest labour unions, has also backed the protests, calling for “higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people’s needs”.
About 45% of French people are worried about the rising cost of living and inflation, according to a 2,000-person survey conducted in October.
Protesters ⁠in hi-vis vests blocked streets, an echo of the unrest that dogged President Emmanuel Macron’s previous term, and in Marseille rubbish bins were set alight.
Both the far left and far right in France sought to capitalise on the protest movement, with the left positioning itself on the side of the protesters and the right backing the police.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, marched in a demonstration on Tuesday and has expressed support for student protesters.

A large police presence was visible in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as ⁠the Avenue des Champs-Élysées and the Arc de Triomphe, which were excluded from the routes of the two official demonstrations.
About 100 people walked towards the police at the beginning protest yelling, “all cops are bastards!”.

“We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions,” said a 19-year-old protester in Paris who gave her name as Lola.
Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, leaving behind a polarised electorate and a badly fragmented political landscape.
On Friday, the president appealed for calm and respect for people and property as officials warned of possible violence.

“There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself, and I have always been vigilant and attentive that that right is fully respected,” he said. “But this right comes with the need to respect. Respect for people, respect for property, and therefore a commitment not to insult or destroy.”
Macron denounced as “unacceptable” the potential presence of people “solely to cause damage and create unrest”.
The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said hundreds of protest actions and more than 80 marches were expected nationwide, including spontaneous gatherings, street demonstrations and blockades.

Police banned some other proposed gatherings in central Paris. Many Métro stations were closed on Saturday at the police’s request, including those around the Champs-Élysées and near the presidential palace, parliament and government offices.

In recent weeks, there have been thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries, and schools set on fire as the new school year descended into nationwide student protests that are influencing the country’s presidential election campaign and drawing international attention.
The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence, while the French prime minister said that more than 900 police officers had been injured.

Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. Nuñez suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand, but said that they could be used on Saturday.
On Tuesday, the climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg joined students at a school in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.
Agencies contributed reporting

Things will get more difficult, at least in the short term, as forward Taylor Hall is week-to-week with an upper-body injury sustained in Tuesday night’s 4-2 victory over the Washington Capitals, head coach Rod Brind’Amour confirmed.

engadget.com/2284036/amazon-alexa-device.headline: What Does The Yellow Light On Your Alexa Device Mean And How Do You Clear It?
engadget.com/2284036/amazon-alexa-device.author: Alec Hively

paragraphs.text: Here’s what your Echo's yellow light is trying to tell you and what to do about it.

Your Amazon Echo's light ring is a valuable information hub. And while most users are familiar with the recognizable blue ring, many don't realize that the light ring can display nine different color notifications, some of which are intended to grab your attention. If you see a flashing yellow ring around your Echo device, don't panic: a yellow light emanating in slow bursts every few seconds means that Alexa has a message or notification it would like to share with you.

Introduced in 2017, this notification system transforms your Echo into a proactive assistant, capable of alerting you to everything from breaking news and calendar reminders to notifying you when Amazon has shipped your latest package. It is also useful for taking advantage of some of Alexa's more advanced features, such as Alexa for Shopping's price-drop alert tool. Ultimately, customizing your Alexa notification settings is the key to maximizing your Echo's functionalities.

If your device begins flashing its yellow light, you can easily clear the issue by asking Alexa a question regarding your notifications or messages. For example, try "What notifications do I have?" or "What messages do I have?" From there, Alexa will recite the list of relevant notifications, which you can respond to as you see fit. You can also move through your notifications using simple phrases (such as "next" or "repeat").
Managing your notification settings

You can edit notification settings via the Alexa app on your phone or tablet. Tap the More symbol, which looks like three horizontal lines, and select Settings (the gear icon). From there, navigate to Notifications. In this section, you can toggle the features, services and apps you would like to enable or disable notifications for.

One setting to customize is how Alexa interacts with reminders. If the flashing yellow light is for a reminder you have missed, you can clear the notification by asking Alexa, "What are my reminders?" Then, you can issue a series of helpful commands, including asking Alexa to turn off, dismiss, snooze or reschedule your reminder. To change reminder notification settings, navigate to the Notifications section of your Alexa app. From there, select Reminders on this Device and toggle your Notifications on or off.

Another useful notification center is your Alexa Skills hub. Alexa Skills are voice-activated applications that expand Alexa's capabilities. The apps span a range of functions, including Health & Fitness, Productivity, Smart Home features, Sports, Education and even Trivia games. To edit your Alexa Skills notifications, open the Alexa app, then navigate to More > Skills & Games. From there, select Your Skills > Settings > Manage Account Permissions, toggle Notifications on or off and select Save Permissions.

You may also receive a notification if your Alexa-connected smart camera or doorbell detects a person, a package or a similar camera event. To manage these alerts, return to your Alexa app and select Devices. From there, select your connected camera and tap Device Settings. Next, toggle Person or Package Detection Announcements to your desired setting. Now, when your Alexa+ answers the doorbell, you'll have a yellow notification ring waiting for you.
A guide to your Echo's light scheme

Your Echo uses a range of lights to indicate its status. You are likely familiar with the iconic cyan light, which tells you Alexa is listening and glimmers whenever Alexa has heard and is processing a request. The cyan ring will also shimmer whenever your device receives a software update. A teal-blue light, on the other hand, signals that Alexa is waiting for you to issue a command. If you see the two shades of blue spinning around the outer ring, your device is likely starting up or restarting after a completed software update.

A red ring shows a key functionality is turned off. Appearing when you press the microphone on/off button, for instance, it tells users that the device's microphone is disconnected. To get rid of the light, simply press your microphone button again. For an Echo with a camera, a red light bar indicates that the device will not share your video.

If you see a bright orange light spinning around the outside edge of your Echo, the device is either in setup mode or trying to connect to the internet. A pulsing green light, meanwhile, means that you have an incoming call. Once you answer the call, the green ring will begin to spin. The effect is also used for active Drop In intercom sessions. A brief purple flash means that your device is in Do Not Disturb mode. During setup, it indicates Wi-Fi issues. Lastly, a white light shows the volume level whenever you adjust it.

cnbc.com/2026/10/17/south-korea-semicond.headline: Semiconductor market to remain solid ‘at least through next year,’ South Korea finance minister says
cnbc.com/2026/10/17/south-korea-semicond.author: Amelia Lucas, Lisa Kim

paragraphs.text: The semiconductor boom will last at least through 2027, South Korean finance minister Lee Hyoung-Il said on Saturday.

"For now, our view is that we can sustain this growth at least through next year," Lee told CNBC on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. "That's because the gap between demand and supply for semiconductors is still very wide, and supply is still being expanded."

His comments come after semiconductor stocks fell sharply this week, hurt by investor concerns about interest rate hikes and rising competition from Chinese companies. South Korean chip stocks like SK Hynix and Seoul Semiconductor were part of the sell-off, along with U.S. giants like Nvidia.

Chip stocks have fueled volatility in South Korea's stock market this year, Lee said. He attributed the market's wild swings to the semiconductor industry's larger share of the economy than in other countries. Despite the market swings, South Korea's economy is "solid," Lee said.

On Thursday, an opinion column in Maeil Business Newspaper, a prominent South Korean publication, urged the country's government to prepare for the coming slowdown in the artificial intelligence boom. The author said two experts expect a "flood of new supply" of semiconductors that will turn the memory market "into a red ocean" by 2029, according to a CNBC translation.

While South Korea's semiconductors may be driving volatility in its stock market, the industry has also fueled tax growth. Lee said the country expects to collect more taxes than initially projected this year.
South Korea will ultimately be in a stronger fiscal position because of the chip boom, he added.

sports.yahoo.com/articles/broncos-lb-jon.headline: Broncos LB Jonathon Cooper removed from Commissioner's Exempt List

paragraphs.text: The Denver Broncos are getting back linebacker Jonathan Cooper for their Week 7 game against the Arizona Cardinals after it was announced that Cooper was removed from the Commissioner’s Exempt List.

Jonathon Cooper is coming off the commissioner exempt list today, and he is expected to be eligible to play in Denver’s Week 7 game vs. Arizona, sources tell me and @JFowlerESPN. pic.twitter.com/bGYJ5NNPmz— Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 16, 2026

Prior to this year, Cooper had not missed a game for the Broncos since 2022, after being drafted by Denver in the seventh round in 2021. Over the past two years, he had 18.5 sacks and 36 quarterback hits. Cooper also played on special teams, especially in his first two years in the NFL.

Even without one of their starting linebackers, Denver’s defense has been one of the best pass defenses in the NFL. In each of the past two games, they have generated three turnovers and are 4-2 after defeating the Seattle Seahawks on Thursday.

However, the Broncos have struggled defensively against the run. Cooper should help with that, as he was regarded as a solid run stopper for Denver last season. Especially with the Broncos facing the reigning Super Bowl MVP, running back Kenneth Walker III, in two weeks, they need Cooper back in the lineup.
This article originally appeared on Touchdown Wire: Broncos LB Jonathon Cooper removed from Commissioner's Exempt List
